====================================================================================================

‘I believed the hype’: the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:00:27 UTC
13:00:27 KST

When Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees, many white South Africans who believed that they were victims of racism in their country thought that their prayers had been answered.
However, in the past few months, dozens of applicants to the refugee programme have been rejected, with many left dismayed and confused as to why they would be left to face what Trump has falsely claimed is a “white genocide” in South Africa.
After Trump’s February 2025 executive order announcing the resettlement programme, which was expanded to include members of a “racial minority”, the first group of 68 white South Africans arrived in the US that May. The US also shut down the refugee programme for anyone else fleeing war and persecution.
Since then, more than 13,000 have moved to the US, according to state department figures. Arrivals are also accelerating, with more than 2,600 admitted in August.
Afrikaners, descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime repressed the black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.
Since the end of apartheid more than 30 years ago, affirmative action policies have helped to create a black elite and middle class. But about 38% of black South Africans are unemployed, compared with 9% of white South Africans, according to official data.
Meanwhile, the “black economic empowerment” policies, along with high crime rates that affect everyone, have fostered a feeling among some white South Africans that they are now the victims of racial discrimination.
The racist far right has also long highlighted brutal murders of white South African farmers, claiming them as evidence of white people being targeted. Official crime data does not show farmers or white people experiencing crime at higher rates. That has not stopped Trump amplifying these claims, in the face of the South African government’s furious rebuttals.
On 30 June, Facebook and WhatsApp groups for prospective and successful refugee applicants began to light up with news that people had begun to receive rejection letters.
“We are writing to inform you that, following review, USCIS [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] found your application to be ineligible for continued processing for resettlement to the United States at this time. This cannot be appealed,” the letters said, according to multiple rejections seen by the Guardian.
It is unclear how many have been found ineligible. USCIS did not provide data on the total number of refugee applications and rejections. One WhatsApp group set up to support rejects, called Hope beyond the Letter, had 311 members as of 10 September, according to one of the administrators, who noted that the membership fluctuated.
While the ineligibility letters did not give reasons for rejection, some applicants were given more information after making Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. The WhatsApp group administrator, a 64-year-old freelance TV professional, who did not want his identity disclosed, found that his case was initially “recommended for approval”. However, the recommendation was reversed because his ex-girlfriend, whom he had applied with, had a marijuana conviction.
“I cried like a baby,” he said, of receiving the rejection letter on 30 June, having finished the screening process in November. “It was something I actually believed was attainable. I believed the hype.”
Pieter and Liesl (not their real names) were told they were “conditionally approved” as refugees Last November. Both are Afrikaners who had a grandparent killed on a farm and were managing a farm when they applied to become refugees.
Pieter said he was convicted of trespassing in 2014, for which he said he paid a fine and did not go to court. He was granted multiple temporary visas to work on farms in the US between 2011 and 2024.
The couple’s youngest daughter was born in the US and is a US citizen. In the response to their FoI request, they noticed that USCIS had recorded her nationality as South African and incorrectly said that she would be left behind if they moved to the US as refugees.
They had already sold their house, car and many of their possessions when they received a rejection letter on 24 July. “We have to start all over again,” Pieter said.
Another applicant blamed not being able to speak in his native Afrikaans for what he claimed were misunderstandings that led to him and his wife being rejected. The reasons given in response to their FoI request were “crime involving moral turpitude” and “commission of acts of torture or extra judicial killing”.
The 67-year-old had admitted to shooting at least one black person when working as a security guard in 1995, but said it was in self-defence while responding to the mass break-in of an alcohol shop. “I was thoroughly investigated by the authorities,” he said. “I was not charged, because I did not break the law.”
In an emailed response that did not address specific cases, the USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said: “The Department of Homeland Security is committed to resettling Afrikaner refugees who are being persecuted by the South African government.
“[USCIS] reviews each refugee application on a case-by-case basis … [and] notifies aliens found ineligible for continued processing through the US Refugee Admissions Program, including those found ineligible for public safety concerns or criminal histories. This cannot be appealed. This administration will always prioritize the safety and welfare of the American people.”

====================================================================================================

I know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorship | Carolin Würfel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:00:27 UTC
13:00:27 KST

The fear that a fascist, far-right movement would rise to power again in Germany has been with me since my youth. On 6 September, the far-right, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) won a landslide in Saxony-Anhalt, becoming the biggest party in the state parliament, with a shocking 44% of the vote, on a record turnout. If it finds a way to power it will be the first far-right party to govern a German state since the Nazi era.
The night before the vote, I sent a message to a friend, who, like myself, has an East German background. Was she as worried, scared even, about the vote as I was, I asked. I’d fallen into a loop for days, scrolling videos, reels, reports, interviews done on the ground. And I knew these AfD voters. They could have been relatives, friends of my parents, old teachers, former schoolmates. Why were they saying such incoherent stuff?
I did not grow up in Saxony-Anhalt, but in Saxony – a sibling eastern German state, not entirely the same but similar in many core aspects. When I went to high school in Leipzig in the late 1990s and early 2000s, the presence of rightwing extremists was part of my coming-of-age experience. Every Friday night, you felt the fear that neo-Nazis would be waiting outside the clubs, the bars, the tram stops, fists clenched or baseball bats in hand. Every 1 May was a flashpoint when neo-Nazis were allowed to march through the city-centre. And still, Saxony’s first prime minister after reunification, Kurt Biedenkopf – a West German Christian Democratic Union (CDU) politician and a close ally of Helmut Kohl – promised, stoically, throughout his 12 years in office: “Saxony is immune to rightwing extremism.”
By 2004, a year before I graduated, the far-right National Democratic party (NPD) had entered the Saxon state parliament for the first time, with 9.2% of the vote. In 2005, I left Saxony and moved to Berlin. One reason was the unbearable, dangerous presence of neo-Nazis and rightwing extremists. Many peers did the same, because it was clear that the blooming landscapes that Kohl, the German chancellor in charge of reunification, had confidently promised in 1990 weren’t going to materialise.
Instead, rightwing extremism has grown steadily in eastern Germany ever since. Only the names have changed – from NPD, to Pegida (the anti-migrant protest movement launched in 2014), to AfD. I am terrified, if not surprised. Because fascist structures, left unchecked, will always keep going.
But this result is also a function of the deeply troubled relationship between the former East and West Germany.
A couple of weeks ago, Magnus Brechtken, deputy director of the Institut für Zeitgeschichte in Munich – Germany’s leading institute for contemporary history – gave an interview to the FAZ newspaper. It went viral. The headline: “Many west Germans have had enough now.”
The interview was framed as a reminder to angry east Germans – meaning, specifically, those tempted to vote AfD out of spite towards the west – of some historical facts. Brechtken argued that the differences east Germans have been complaining about for 36 years are, by now, emotional rather than rational – the product, he suggested, of a lack of honest self-examination. He went further: the German west, he said, has spent the past 75 years proving it understands democracy and knows how to handle extremism, that it is better equipped to counter radical movements and prevent parties like the AfD from rising in the first place – while east Germans, he implied, have always had an inherited longing for authoritarian solutions.
You couldn’t help but wonder how much of it was history, and how much was personal opinion. But I do think Brechtken was right about one thing. This supposed east German anger, the AfD’s popularity, the result in Saxony-Anhalt and – in all likelihood – the party’s performance in two upcoming state elections on 20 September should be used as a reminder of some actual historical facts, and of follow-up questions Brechtken apparently decided not to ask.
The AfD was founded in west Germany. A large share of its leadership was born and raised in western states such as Rheinland-Pfalz and Nordrhein-Westfalen. The question shouldn’t only be what draws the east of Germany towards the AfD. It’s just as much: what draws a certain kind of west German towards building a party like this one, pushing it, and choosing the east as the place to make it grow?
I believe the west German states – which officially claimed to have carried out denazification after 1945, and prided themselves on the culture of remembrance, or “coming to terms” with the Nazi past – need to look, just as urgently as the east German states, at why this fascination with fascism keeps recurring. And why, by now, are there no working structures against the rise of right-extremist movements, parties and agendas – but somehow still a system that lets them flourish?
It’s also worth asking whether a party like the AfD went east only because east Germans are more susceptible – or because the visible inequalities there are excellent material to organise around.
In 1989, a lot of east Germans had hoped for something between socialism and capitalism. Reunification wasn’t necessarily the preferred option. What followed felt, to many, badly mishandled – too fast, laws and decisions imposed rather than negotiated. And then there was the Treuhand – the agency put in charge of privatising the former GDR’s entire state-owned economy. In the process of reunification, 94% of East German companies were taken over by West German or international investors. Six per cent stayed with the people of East Germany. Six per cent. Approximately two million jobs were eliminated in the east.
In the autumn and winter of 1990-91, people took to the streets again – not against their own government’s repression this time, but against the perceived occupier: West Germany. They demanded new elections, a renegotiation of the agreements that had left millions empty-handed and jobless, as unemployment in the east skyrocketed. Detlev Karsten Rohwedder, head of the Treuhand and the key figure in overhauling the former East Germany, was asked in an interview back then by a TV host: “If it doesn’t get better, aren’t you afraid there might be another revolution in East Germany?”
In those years, the former East Germany was treated like a child that had to follow the laws and orders of its wiser western counterpart – a parent. Now, that child is all grown. But it remembers the experience – and quite possibly holds on to it too tightly. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s man in Saxony-Anhalt, was born the same year as reunification.
One of his main promises is to take back control. Maybe you could say that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt went beyond a question of control and was driven by the desire for a sort of revenge. The east, finally, daring to say to the overpowering west: enough. Or as Siegmund at his first victory press conference said, the result showed that the people of Saxony-Anhalt wouldn’t be “patronised” any longer. With this he was tapping into something almost visceral. The remark also clarified for me something about the motives of the countless potential AfD voters I had listened to over the past weeks and months. Most of them don’t actually read or know what’s in the AfD’s programme. And they don’t seem to care. What won people over was simpler: I hear you. I see you. Yes, you have every right to be unhappy.
Throughout the campaign, Siegmund travelled the entire state and threw parties: free sausages, free beer, dancing, music and maybe for some, it felt like the return of community. Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.
What many have not realised yet is that the AfD won’t improve life in east Germany. But that was never the point. It gave people attention in exchange for a vote.
And for now, that was what counted most.
Because the AfD is bigger than east versus west. It was built by west Germans, carried by east Germans, and now it strives for power across the country. Its programme runs on ideas Germany once needed a war and total defeat to bury: racism, the belief in superiority and a hierarchy of who really belongs, contempt for who doesn’t, a hunger for enemies dressed up as pride. That’s not a regional problem. It’s a national one, and it should frighten every single German citizen.
A vote for the AfD is a vote for that same set of beliefs. Whatever anger, disappointment, or legitimate demand to finally be seen or heard got bundled in alongside it.
In April 1932, the Nazi party became the strongest party in the state election in the region that now makes up Saxony-Anhalt, with 40.7% of the vote, and formed, with coalition partners, the first Nazi-led state government in Germany. Whatever happens next, it will be hard to say we didn’t know.
- 
  Carolin Würfel is a writer, screenwriter and journalist

Bank of England urged to slow or halt bond-selling to slash UK borrowing costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:00:26 UTC
13:00:26 KST

Economists have urged the chancellor, John Healey, to press the Bank of England to slow down its bond-selling programme that has already cost the exchequer billions of pounds.
The Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) meets this week to not only decide the level of interest rates but also whether they should freeze or slow the sale of government bonds, known as gilts, bought as part of the rescue operation after the 2008 banking crash.
That process was known as “quantitative easing” (QE), and over the past four years the Bank has been reversing it through “quantitative tightening” (QT) – selling the debt back to the market – to help reduce inflationary pressures.
However, the bonds are now worth less, so selling them crystallises losses to the exchequer while increasing the supplies to the market – suppressing demand and pushing up the interest rate, or yield, charged on the debt.
The cost of government borrowing is already at multi-decade highs owing to the turmoil on financial markets as the Middle East conflict drives up the oil price. On Monday the yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt passed 5.4%, its highest level since July 2007, while the 30-year rose to 5.93%, its highest level since March 1998.
In August the Bank estimated its QT stance could result in total losses to the exchequer of £120bn if interest rates remain on the path expected by financial markets.
Its governor, Andrew Bailey, has defended the policy, telling parliament’s Treasury committee earlier this year that it was not in the MPC’s remit to limit costs to the government in the short-term.
Bank officials have signalled that bond sales will continue, though at a slower rate than expected earlier this year.
On Tuesday it was reported that officials at Threadneedle Street have already drawn up plans with the Treasury and the Debt Management Office, which issues bonds on behalf of the government, to overhaul its money-printing programme. According to the Telegraph, the Bank will stop selling 20- and 30-year gilts bought under QT.
It comes amid growing criticism of the sales, with critics accusing the Bank from ignoring the escalating bill they are creating for Healey before his first budget next month.
Louise Haigh, the Cabinet Office chief who managed Andy Burnham’s campaign to be an MP, has previously pledged to stop Bailey from “pursuing policies that actively damage the government’s balance sheet”.
It is understood that Healey has rejected such calls from inside the cabinet to take a hard line with the Bank when he issues its new remit, preferring to accept assurances that it will be mindful of heaping extra losses on the Treasury.
Charlie Bean, a former deputy governor of the Bank of England, said: “I do not think it is politically sustainable for the MPC to be able to take such decisions without the involvement of the [Treasury] or else somehow reduce the magnitude of spillovers [to the Treasury].”
John Llewellyn, a partner at the consultancy Independent Economics and a former chief economist of the OECD, said the idea that there was a firewall between the Treasury and the central bank was a “fiction” and Bailey should expect to negotiate with the chancellor to minimise costs.
Since active sales of QE bonds began in late 2022, the Bank has overseen one of the fastest reductions in central bank bond holdings among advanced economies, cutting the portfolio from a peak of £875bn to under £490bn.
A year ago it cut its annual target for sales from £100bn to £70bn and is expected to lower that again this week to £50bn. The US Federal Reserve stopped actively selling its portfolio of bonds last year.
Christopher Mahon, a senior fund manager at Columbia Threadneedle Investments, and a visiting fellow at the Open University Business School, said rising costs showed the Bank “should scrap active sales outright”.
He said the Bank’s methods had proved to be twice as expensive as the European Central Bank’s and four times as expensive as the US Federal Reserve programme, mainly due to the type of bonds it bought, which have collapsed in value since 2008.
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the Treasury’s independent forecaster, has estimated the Bank’s bond sales will add about £47bn to government debt by 2031, assuming active gilt sales of £32bn a year.
The Treasury and the Bank of England declined to comment.

Digital ID comes of age as pubs and bars get go-ahead for biometric scan tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:00:26 UTC
13:00:26 KST

Younger drinkers in England and Wales will be able to prove their age with a digital ID starting this week as new laws give pubs, off-licences, nightclubs and restaurants the right to use biometric scanning technology to check customers are over 18.
Customers will be able to download software that scans their faces into their own phone to generate a QR code proving their age based on a stored proof of age. Other tech under consideration as part of the government push to digitise age verification for alcohol sales include a device which scans the veins in a drinker’s finger to verify their age. That system has not yet been approved for use.
The use of digital ID for alcohol comes despite Andy Burnham axing plans for a national digital ID this summer amid a wave of concern about the implications for civil liberties.
In this case, the digital ID will be provided by private companies and will not be mandatory. Plastic driving licences and passports will still work, meaning it may not spell the end for fake IDs. It could later be extended to purchases of vapes and tobacco.
Stephanie Peacock, the digital government minister, said: “This groundbreaking change in the law will mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information such as your name or address just to prove your age – allowing everyone to feel safer on a night out.”
The government believes the new system will reduce the effectiveness of fraudulent ID and the risk of sensitive data being exposed when customers are required to show bar staff passports or driving licences which display names and home addresses.
Different companies are supplying the apps – including Yoti and Luciditi. The customer will typically only have about 30 seconds between scanning their face on their phone and validating the credential with the retailer to avoid underage drinkers borrowing older friends’ phones.
In some cases the systems can cost retailers money to operate and Allen Simpson, chief executive of UK Hospitality, said it would work “to ensure the rollout of the scheme, with multiple supplier options available, is cost-efficient and not burdensome for the hospitality sector”.
Yoti estimates about a quarter of 18- to 25-year-olds in the UK have already downloaded its digital ID app or one called EasyID it provides with the Post Office, with about 8.5 million people in the UK using them overall.
With different alcohol vendors likely to accept different apps, a patchy start to the system is expected, similar to the rollout of contactless payment, which took nearly 20 years to reach ubiquity after its introduction in 2007.

Ebola outbreak in DRC has peaked, say authorities, as infection rates slow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
04:00:26 UTC
13:00:26 KST

Authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have announced that the Ebola outbreak ravaging parts of the country has reached its peak.
For the first time since the epidemic was declared in May, the numbers of people becoming infected is slowing down, according to officials.
Stressing that strict adherence to preventive measures needed to be kept in place, Samuel Roger Kamba, the Congolese health minister, said there was a decline in transmission of the Bundibugyo variant of Ebola.
“We are fighting a very dangerous virus that is killing many of our people. Today, we can say that the outbreak is under control,” he said. “At one point, we were recording about 120 cases per day; today, we’re seeing about 80 per day. So the number of new cases is decreasing every day.
“It has been more than 22 days since 10 of the 62 health zones have reported new cases. And so we can now definitively remove six health zones from the list because they have gone more than 42 days without new cases, and we can remove four health zones that have gone more than 21 days without a new case,” Kamba said.
Last week, the Sud-Ubangi region, on the DRC’s borders with Congo-Brazzaville and Central African Republic, became the sixth province to report the disease.
The Bundibugyo virus outbreak was declared by Congolese authorities on 15 May and is concentrated primarily in Ituri province, where ongoing conflict has created challenging conditions for those responding to the disease. It is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in the DRC since the highly contagious disease was first identified and named in 1976.
No effective treatment for the Bundibugyo variant has been found so far but there are clinical trials in the region. The DRC received more than 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine last month, which is the only approved treatment for the more common Zaire Ebola virus.
According to the latest data from the Congolese health ministry, the number of confirmed cases stood at more than 7,200, including more than 3,475 deaths, as of 14 September.
While welcoming the progress made, Iracan Gratien de Saint-Nicolas, an MP for Bunia, warned against what he called “triumphalism” and stressed that efforts must intensify to show people that the disease was under control.
Gratien Iracan called for lessons to be learned from failures in epidemiological surveillance that contributed to the rapid spread of the disease.
The MP also expressed some scepticism over the government announcement. “Claims that an epidemic is under control must be supported by objective indicators. If the indicators show that the epidemic is indeed under control, let’s make them public. Transparency in the data will strengthen public confidence,” he said.
He warned that some indicators that showed an epidemic was under control seemed to have been omitted by the DRC authorities, such as a sustained decline in new cases (over seven to 21 days), a decrease in deaths, a reduction in areas with active transmission, the majority of new cases originating from contacts already identified, and a high rate of contact tracing, as well as dignified and safe burials.
Early last month, Jean Kaseya, the director general of the African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, visited Bunia – capital of Ituri and a centre of the current Ebola outbreak – and said then that there was no way of knowing when the peak might be reached but that containment and contact tracing were still not effective enough.
Kaseya said: “A large portion of the mortality – 60 to 70% of deaths – comes from the community. The list of contacts we have just keeps growing. Epidemiologists say we’ve reached the peak when all cases come from the list of contacts.”
In Rwampara, a town in Ituri, people are exhausted from the past few months of living with the dread of the disease. Léa Munyere, 36, a mother of four, said she was relieved that the health authorities had announced that Ebola was under control. Two of her close friends had died and she was still struggling to come to terms with the loss, she said.
“We hope the disease will soon be declared over. It has robbed us of the people we cherish so much since it was first reported,” she said. “We just want to get back to our normal lives.”

"Applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections," it said.

S. Korea's money supply rises for 9th month in July
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:57:37 CST
12:57:37 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's money supply rose for a ninth straight month due to a strong shift toward time deposits, caused by aggressive monetary tightening, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The seasonally-adjusted M2, called broad money, grew 0.3 percent from a month earlier to 4,225.6 trillion won (3.13 trillion U.S. dollars) in July, keeping an upward trend since November 2025, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
Following a 25-basis-point increase in July, the BOK raised its benchmark interest rate by another quarter percentage point to 3.00 percent in August, prompting depositors to lock their funds into short-term fixed-income products.
Time deposits with a maturity of less than two years soared by 27.3 trillion won in July after gaining 7.1 trillion won in the previous month.
Capital inflows into money trusts under 2 years nearly doubled from 6.3 trillion won in June to 11.4 trillion won in July.
Affected by the monetary tightening, the M1, called narrow money, reduced 2.2 percent in July on a monthly basis.
The M1 refers to currency in circulation, demand deposits and transferable savings deposits equivalent to cash. The M2 adds money market funds, time deposits and financial products that mature in less than two years.
The liquidity of financial institutions, called Lf, declined 0.4 percent in the cited month, while the liquidity aggregate, the broadest measure of money supply, dwindled 0.5 percent.
The Lf includes financial products with a maturity of over two years and liquidity at insurers and brokerages along with M2. The liquidity aggregate adds state and corporate bonds to the Lf. ■

China's retail sales of goods, services up 2.5 pct in first eight months
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:57:14 CST
12:57:14 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's total retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of the country's consumption strength, increased by 2.5 percent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, official data showed Tuesday.
Retail sales of services rose 4.9 percent year on year during the January-August period, outpacing the 1-percent growth in goods sales, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.
Among service categories, retail sales of communication and information services, tourism consulting and rental services, and cultural, sports and leisure services posted relatively rapid growth.
In the first eight months, retail sales of consumer goods, including sales of goods and catering revenue, totaled 32.76 trillion yuan (about 4.84 trillion U.S. dollars), up 1.1 percent year on year, the data showed.
Online retail sales of goods and services reached 13.48 trillion yuan, up 4.6 percent. Of the total, online goods sales rose 4.3 percent to 8.42 trillion yuan, while online service sales increased 5.1 percent to 5.06 trillion yuan.
In August alone, retail sales of consumer goods stood at 3.98 trillion yuan, up 0.4 percent year on year. ■

====================================================================================================

Youngest Snowtown murderer to walk free from jail after 26-year sentence as parole upheld
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
03:57:14 UTC
12:57:14 KST

The youngest person jailed over the notorious Snowtown killings will walk free after serving a 26-year sentence behind bars.
A decision to release James Vlassakis by South Australia’s Parole Board was upheld by the Parole Administrative Review Commissioner on Tuesday.
Vlassakis pleaded guilty to four of the 11 murders between 1992 and 1999.
He was 18 when he became involved in the killings in 1998 and was sentenced to life with a minimum term of 26 years, which expired last August.
He also acted as a key prosecution witness against John Bunting and Robert Wagner, who were found guilty of 11 and 10 murders respectively.
The bodies of eight of their victims were found dismembered in barrels filled with hydrochloric acid inside a disused bank vault in Snowtown, north of Adelaide, in May 1999.
Most were murdered in the outer suburbs of Adelaide, more than 100km away – and just one was killed in Snowtown.
Investigators initially thought the men’s motive was simply to take the welfare payments of their victims, but a more complicated picture gradually emerged.
The court heard Bunting was the ringleader, and that he hated various groups including homosexuals, drug addicts and paedophiles. The murders were “often ritualistic and humiliating” and targeted people connected to the men.
In considering the review in May, the commissioner had revoked the 25-year-old suppression order that banned publication of Vlassakis’ image and description.
Last December Vlassakis – who is now in his mid-40s – had his parole approval overturned after the state government successfully fought a decision to grant his freedom, with a retired judge describing his crimes as “gross” and “disgustingly unusual”.
The Parole Board chief, Frances Nelson, had previously said Vlassakis did not represent a risk to the community and would be sent to the Adelaide pre-release centre for up to 12 months to undergo a resocialisation process.
Accomplice Mark Ray Haydon, 66, who was convicted for helping to cover up the crimes, was released on parole in May 2024 to live in the community under strict supervision.
There were 12 victims in the case, but a murder charge over one of the deaths was dropped due to a lack of evidence. Eight of the 11 killed were found in those barrels.
The murders received additional notoriety across the globe with the release of 2011 feature film Snowtown, which was marketed at the time as “Australia’s most infamous crime story”.
The South Australian attorney general and deputy premier, Kyam Maher, said the case was “traumatic” for the people involved.
“The people that were held by the court most responsible have been given a non-life sentence without the possibility of parole,” he said.
“There are others who have been released or applied for parole, James Vlassakis, who gave evidence against his co-accused, applied for parole, and it was granted by the Parole Board.”
Maher said the Parole Board would soon meet to consider appropriate conditions for release, which could include electronic monitoring, no drugs or alcohol and location limits.
“It is a very difficult thing for those who are still around to remember what happened so well,” he said.
“The gravity and the effect this has had in South Australia, the need for community safety, were always the primary concerns of the state government.
“I will ask for advice if there are further steps but it has already been considered by two different parole review commissioned and the supreme court.”

Declining US democracy emboldens global authoritarians: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
03:55:00 UTC
12:55:00 KST

Declining US democracy emboldens global authoritarians: Report
STOCKHOLM – The fall of US democracy indicators to their lowest level in half a century is inspiring hardline leaders around the world, a leading global intergovernmental political institute said on Sept 15.
“Major indicators of US democracy from press freedom to judicial independence hit their lowest levels in 50 years, and this is reverberating worldwide,” the Stockholm-based International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (IDEA) said in a report.
“Washington’s retreat from the rules-based international order has weakened confidence in multilateralism and emboldened authoritarian leaders and populists,” added the report.
About 57 per cent of the countries studied by International IDEA had seen a fall in at least one indicator of their democratic health between 2020 and 2025. The areas assessed included judicial independence, credible elections, freedom of speech and access to justice.
“Of course, patient zero of this global epidemic is the current president of the United States,” International IDEA secretary-general Kevin Casas-Zamora, a former vice-president of Costa Rica, told AFP, referring to US President Donald Trump.
“I think what happened in the US in 2020 has really had a global impact in terms of legitimising this kind of attack on the credibility of the electoral process,” he said of Trump’s refusal to acknowledge his election defeat to Democrat Joe Biden. Trump returned to office after a 2024 election.
The trend accelerated with the attack on the US Congress building on Jan 6, 2021, by Trump supporters, Casas-Zamora added.
This encouraged riots in Brasilia on Jan 8, 2023, when thousands of followers of conservative former leader Jair Bolsonaro looted Brazil’s Parliament demanding a military intervention against leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a week after he took office.
The IDEA chief said that “arguments that were used to gut and eventually close down USAID (the US foreign aid agency) were used in Serbia by the government to clamp down on civil society organisations”.
International IDEA was set up by 14 founding states in 1995 to help with elections and monitor democracies. There are currently more than 30 member states. The US had been an observer member but left in 2026. AFP

NMC seeks report on allegations medical college made ₹3.75 lakh hostel payment mandatory for MBBS internship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
03:46:54 UTC
12:46:54 KST

NEW DELHI: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has sought a detailed report on allegations that a private medical college in Bihar made payment of a ₹3.75 lakh hostel fee mandatory for MBBS graduates to start their compulsory internship, with a July complaint alleging that interns feared they would be denied internship if they did not pay.The NMC has forwarded the complaint to the Bihar Directorate of Medical Education and sought a detailed report within 15 days. It has also asked the college to furnish its report on the allegations.
The case involves R.D.J.M. Medical College & Hospital in Muzaffarpur, Bihar, where 2021-batch MBBS graduates allegedly faced restrictions on joining their Compulsory Rotatory Medical Internship (CRMI) unless they paid the hostel fee and stayed on campus.The issue was formally brought before the NMC on July 24 by the United Doctors Front (UDF), which represented the affected interns. The complaint alleged that students who had cleared their Final MBBS examination were being prevented from commencing internship and that some had already paid the hostel fee fearing they would otherwise be denied internship.Documents enclosed with the complaint include a July 18 college order stating that no student would be permitted to join MBBS internship unless the prescribed hostel fee was paid in full.
The order further stated that, after verification of hostel-fee records, only one student was then eligible to join the internship, while other students would be permitted to join only after clearing their hostel dues.The UDF argued that the NMC's requirements provide for accommodation for students and interns but do not authorise a college to make hostel residence compulsory or withhold internship for non-payment of hostel fees.
Dr. Lakshya Mittal of the UDF said, “medical students and interns cannot be treated as a source of forced revenue. If a student has fulfilled all academic requirements and is eligible to commence compulsory internship, imposing hostel residence and extracting lakhs of rupees as a precondition is a serious matter that requires regulatory scrutiny. We welcome the NMC’s intervention and expect the Bihar authorities to conduct a time-bound and transparent inquiry.”

Chinese factory output shows resilience to rise 5.3pc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
03:43:45 UTC
12:43:45 KST

China's value-added industrial output increased by 5.3 percent year on year in the first eight months of 2026.
Retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of the country's consumption strength, increased by 2.5 percent, fixed-asset investment dropped 7.2 percent and the surveyed urban unemployment rate averaged an unchanged 5.2 percent.
For the month of August, output grew 5.2 percent from a year earlier, quickening from a 4.5 percent increase in July and beating expectations for a 4.8 percent rise, data released by the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Tuesday.
Retail sales rose 0.4 percent, slowing from a 0.6 percent gain in July and below an expected 0.8 percent rise.
The figures underline the continuing mismatch between resilient production and exports on one hand, and fragile household consumption and investment on the other, and raised the stakes for more stimulus measures to address the weaknesses in the economy.
Extreme weather likely remained a drag on activity. 
Four typhoons made landfall in China during August, disrupting operations in the east-coast manufacturing and logistics belt.
Beijing has responded with faster government bond issuance and expanded loan interest subsidies for small private firms and consumers, while the central bank has pledged  additional policy support without signalling explicit cuts to policy rates or banks' reserve-requirement ratio.
The bureau says residents' ability and willingness to spend should be enhanced and the supply of high-quality goods and services should be improved.
It expects the economy to maintain steady growth even as it faces structural pressures.
"September could represent an important policy window to revive business confidence ahead of October's Golden Week holidays," analysts at ANZ said. (Xinhua/Reuters)

Scholars expect China to raise Taiwan at Trump-Xi summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
03:29:51 UTC
12:29:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Scholars said China is likely to talk about Taiwan at an expected Trump-Xi summit on Sept. 24, though there may be little room for detailed talks on the Taiwan Strait, CNA reported Monday.
Speaking at a forum on US-China competition, Central Police University Professor Wang Chih-sheng (王智盛) said Beijing would almost certainly bring up Taiwan. He said Washington may offer only a limited response, with both sides restating their existing positions.
Wang said the summit is expected to follow a tight schedule, leaving little time for detailed discussion of security issues. He said these could include US arms sales, presidential transits through the US, and broader Indo-Pacific security.
He said a greater concern is Beijing's effort to use high-level US-China exchanges to influence public opinion in Taiwan. Such messaging, Wang said, could deepen doubts about Washington's commitment and promote the idea that Taipei might be abandoned in a future agreement.
Wu Se-chih (吳瑟致), assistant professor at Tamkang University, said Washington and Beijing could reach limited short-term agreements on less sensitive economic matters. These could cover tariffs, agricultural and energy purchases, and fentanyl-related issues, per Economic Daily News.
Such agreements would not mean the two sides have resolved their bigger strategic differences, Wu said. Washington increasingly treats semiconductors, AI, advanced manufacturing, rare earths, critical minerals, military security, and the Taiwan Strait as national security concerns rather than ordinary bargaining issues.
Taipei City University Assistant Professor Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗) said US President Donald Trump should not be seen as representing the entire US policymaking system. Decisions on arms sales, security cooperation, technology controls, and Indo-Pacific policy also involve administration officials, national security agencies, and Congress, per Newtalk.
Hung said Beijing's demands should not be taken as evidence that Washington will make concessions. China can make requests, he said, but whether the US agrees to discuss them or changes its policy is a separate matter.
He said the public should follow the summit closely without assuming Taiwan will become a bargaining chip between Washington and Beijing. Instead, attention should focus on what the US does afterward, including any changes to arms sales, security cooperation, military deployments in the Indo-Pacific, and coordination with allies.

Their prior hospitality experience and familiarity with the local work environment and workplace culture should shorten training and adjustment periods, the ministry said. The workers will take on duties including housekeeping, reservations, and guest services, with some also bringing Mandarin or English skills that could benefit the tourism industry over the long term.
The program links foreign worker recruitment with higher wages for entry-level domestic workers, according to the ministry. Hotels can hire one foreign worker for each full-time Taiwanese rank-and-file worker who receives a monthly raise of at least NT$2,000 (US$62.92).
The program requires employers to pay foreign workers at least NT$32,000 per month. The ministry said the system aims to help businesses fill staffing gaps while ensuring domestic workers also share in the benefits of industry growth.
For more information on the program, visit the “Foreign Skilled Workers” section of the Foreign National Labor Rights Portal.

Taiwan's Aspeed secures ASE chip packaging capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
03:29:08 UTC
12:29:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Chip designer Aspeed Technology Inc. has signed a two-year capacity procurement agreement with Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc., reflecting limited availability of advanced semiconductor packaging and testing services, Anue reported Monday.
The agreement will run from Jan. 1, 2027, through Dec. 31, 2028. Industry sources said chip design companies generally do not sign long-term agreements with packaging and testing providers unless supply is particularly tight and future capacity is difficult to secure.
Aspeed’s latest move suggests that capacity constraints could persist through 2028. The company holds a 70%-80% share of the global server baseboard management controller (BMC) market, according to Pocket Securities.
BMCs operate independently of a server’s CPU and operating system, allowing administrators to remotely power servers on or off, monitor temperatures, and update firmware. With the expansion of cloud computing and large-scale data centers, these chips have become standard components in modern servers, according to Sinotrade.
ASE Technology Holding Co., the parent company of ASE, is pursuing 15 new construction and expansion projects this year. However, the additional capacity has not been sufficient to fulfill all customer orders, according to CTEE.
The capacity constraints come as demand for AI infrastructure continues to grow. Packaging and testing requirements are also expected to increase as AI chips enter higher-volume production and major cloud service providers begin mass-producing customized chips from next year.
AI chips are also becoming larger and more complex, requiring more packaging and testing steps and longer processing times. As a result, each chip requires more processing time and production capacity.
Aspeed Chair Chris Lin (林鴻明) previously said supply chain bottlenecks affected the company’s operations in the first half of this year, causing growth to fall short of initial expectations. Revenue totaled NT$7 billion in the first six months, up 62.77% from the same period a year earlier, according to UDN Money.
Lin expects revenue growth to strengthen in the second half as the supply situation improves. He said customer feedback indicates that strong orders will continue through 2028.

Air Force Will Hit Long-Elusive Goal to Train 1,500 New Pilots in a Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
03:26:42 UTC
12:26:42 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force is on track to reach its annual goal of graduating 1,500 new pilots that had proved elusive to this point, one year after the service launched a sweeping overhaul of its undergraduate pilot training program, Air Education and Training Command said Sept. 14.
Reaching the milestone under the new Future of Undergraduate Pilot Training, or FUPT, program, will help “support the Air Force’s broader effort to address a pilot shortage,” a release from AETC stated.
“Reaching 1,500 pilots is a milestone, but it is not the finish line,” Quinn said in the announcement, released during AFA’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference “FUPT was built to overcome long-standing constraints including instructor shortages and aircraft availability to deliver the aviators our combatant commanders require.”
AETC announced in spring 2025 it was moving to a hybrid private/military instruction model designed to reduce overall course time, a move aimed at ending the years of struggles to reach its benchmark of 1,500 trained pilots per year and “to produce elite aviators through a training system that is more deliberate, data-driven, and aligned with the demands of operational units,” Maj. Gen. Travolis A. Simmons, 19th Air Force commander, said in the announcement.
AETC’s new pilot training model offloads much of the basic, initial instruction to a commercial, university-based program, while retaining military-specific elements at Air Force training bases.
“Moving foundational flight training to civilian partners allows us to reserve military aircraft, instructor capacity, and flying hours for the advanced, military-specific training only the Air Force can provide,” Quinn said.
The new construct gives flight students 120 flying hours over 139 days at one of four flying universities, in a course now called Initial Pilot Training, or IPT. Upon completion, students receive their private pilot licenses—with instrument and multi-engine ratings—under FAA Part 141 standards. They then transfer to one of USAF’s four Undergraduate Pilot Training, or UPT, bases—Columbus Air Force Base, Miss.; Laughlin Air Force Base, Texas; Sheppard Air Force Base, Texas; and Vance Air Force Base, Okla.
“Achieving 1,500 validates that we can scale future undergraduate pilot training and we now continue the focus on refining the training to ensure the quality of our graduates matches the scale,” Quinn said. “Our instructor pilots, maintainers, and support teams adapted this enterprise to meet the need ensuring a steady flow of skilled aviators for our combatant commands.”
The Air Force pilot shortage stood at roughly 2,470 pilots at the end of fiscal 2025, a shortfall officials have attributed over the years to issues across the service, including pilot production, retention, and absorption.
Earlier this year, on May 20, Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach gave a hint that the benchmark was within reach, telling lawmakers on the House Armed Services Committee that AETC was “meeting our goals for creating 1,500 pilots per year.”
“We did that this year, and we see no issues with doing that into the future,” Wilsbach said during the hearing. “The challenge will be absorbing all those into line cockpits.”
At the time, the class of student pilots at Vance Air Force Base had just started their training. Their graduation will be what gets AETC to its goal of 1,500 new pilots in fiscal 2026, an AETC spokesperson said.
Wilsbach also stressed to lawmakers that the service needs the roughly $10 billion its requesting in the fiscal 2027 budget for a plus-up for pilot flying hours. The Air Force is asking for $7.4 billion to fund Active-Duty flying hours, which would be a 22 percent increase from the $6.1 billion budgeted in fiscal 2026. Another $1.6 billion would cover Air National Guard hours, and $867 million would go to Air Force Reserve hours, for a total of $9.9 billion. That funding would pay for the fuel, spare parts, and consumable supplies pilots and maintenance crews need to safely and reliably fly aircraft.
“This 2027 budget gets us about $10 billion for flying; the pilots want to fly, they don’t want to sit on the ground and do admin,” Wilsbach said, adding that the service will offer pilots the ability to stay at duty locations for longer periods of time versus moving every two or three years.
The hope is that these efforts will “help us with pilot retention and that will, in turn, help with the pilot shortage,” Wilsbach said.

US Supreme Court rejects Trump mail ballot restrictions ahead of midterms

US Supreme Court rejects Trump mail ballot restrictions ahead of midterms
US Supreme Court rejects Trump’s bid to tighten mail-in voting rules ahead of critical midterm elections.
The US Supreme Court has rejected President Donald Trump’s bid to allow the US Postal Service to enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots.
On Monday, the conservative-majority court refused to lift an order by US District Judge Indira Talwani that blocked the measure, dealing a blow to Trump’s efforts to restrict voting by mail before the November midterm elections.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Two dozen Democrat-led states sue Trump over mail-in ballot limits
- list 2 of 4Trump calls Virginia election ‘rigged’ after redistricting referendum
- list 3 of 4US judge rejects immediate block on Trump’s mail-in voting executive order
- list 4 of 4Supreme Court strikes down US campaign spending limits in landmark ruling
The postal agency adopted the rule after Trump signed an executive order in March seeking to tighten rules around mail-in voting. Under this measure, states were required to send the Postal Service a list of recipients and use ballot mail envelopes previously approved by the agency.
The Postal Service was allowed to deny ballots if they failed to comply with the new standards or were not associated with registered voters on the lists.
Talwani imposed an injunction blocking the rule, saying that it likely violated the US Constitution and would be impossible to apply given the nearing midterms.
Shortly after, the Trump administration issued an emergency request to the Supreme Court urging it to allow an “important federal policy to protect the mails from being used to commit voter fraud”.
In late August, the Supreme Court had temporarily allowed Trump to move ahead with his executive order on procedural grounds, but did not rule on the legality of the plan.
In the latest decision, the court said in an unsigned order that the administration was “unlikely to succeed on the merits” of its challenge. Justice Samuel Alito and Justice Clarence Thomas dissented, with Alito writing that some plaintiffs lacked standing while the rest were pursuing a claim the court had recently called a “Hail Mary pass”.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was appointed by Trump, voted with the majority against the administration, though he indicated he could support the policy at a later stage.
Critics warn the restrictions could disrupt the delivery of thousands of ballots and disenfranchise groups who rely on mail-in voting. In some states, primarily Democratic-leaning, voters cast ballots largely by mail. Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin have already begun sending ballots ahead of the midterm elections.
Trump has long cast doubt on the security of mail-in voting, repeating debunked claims of widespread election fraud, despite voting by mail himself, including during the 2024 election.

US military says Iran war has led to munitions shortfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
03:12:00 UTC
12:12:00 KST

US military says Iran war has led to munitions shortfall
- The US Defence Department reports a $33.4 billion cost for Operation Epic Fury, with $22.3 billion spent on munitions, causing strategic ammunition shortages and industrial bottlenecks.
- Significant losses include four F-15s destroyed, one F-35 damaged, seven tankers damaged, and up to 30 drones lost during the Iran conflict.
- President Trump claims unlimited ammo production despite reported shortages, while Iranian strikes damaged hundreds of US base structures across the Middle East, with repair costs uncertain.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The United States is facing a shortfall in ammunition as a result of its war against Iran, the Defence Department’s inspector-general confirmed on Sept 14, contrasting with President Donald Trump’s assertions of full stocks.
In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector said that between Feb 28 and June 30, Operation Epic Fury (OEF) had an estimated cost of US$33.4 billion (S$42.5 billion), including US$22.3 billion spent on expended munitions.
“The munitions expenditure on OEF has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” the report said.
OEF is the US name for its joint campaign with Israel to “destroy Iran’s ability to project military power,” according to US Central Command (CENTCOM).
To deal with shortfalls and delays, the Pentagon is “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions,” the report said.
Though it noted that expanding production capacities requires “significant lead time.”
The shortfall is likely to cause concern among governments like Ukraine and Taiwan, who rely on weapons purchases from the United States to fight or deter much larger, hostile neighbours.
Ukraine urgently needs more interceptor missiles for US-made Patriot air defence systems in its war against Russia, while Taiwan depends on arms agreements with Washington to ward off China, which claims the self-ruled island as its own.
Trump has repeatedly brushed off concerns of depleted weapons stores during the six months of war in the Middle East, saying recently the US has “virtually unlimited” ammunition.
On Sept 14, Trump posted to his Truth Social platform, saying again that the US is producing “more exquisite and elite weapons than at any time in our history”.
CNN previously reported that shortages of long-range guided missiles and air defence interceptors had affected Trump’s strategy in the conflict with Iran, with the US military having “nearly exhausted 80 per cent” of its stock of THAAD interceptors.
During the first 24 hours of war against Iran, the United States struck more than 1,000 targets, CENTCOM has said, and has not returned to such large-scale attacks in recent months.
The report identified losses to the American fleet, including four F-15s destroyed, one F-35 damaged, seven KC-135 tanker aircraft damaged and up to 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones destroyed.
It also confirmed that the US Navy’s main logistics hub in the region, located in Bahrain, had been targeted by Iran with drone and ballistic missile strikes.
Hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan have been damaged or destroyed by Iranian strikes during the conflict.
The report does not include those costs in its estimates, saying it is not yet clear if all the bases will be rebuilt, or who will foot the bill.
As of June 30, seven US service members had been killed in action and seven killed in non-hostile events during OEF combat operations, the report said.
An additional 417 service members were wounded in action, it added.
The US and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb 28.
For decades, Western powers have accused the Islamic republic of seeking nuclear weapons, a claim that Tehran categorically denies. AFP

TORONTO – Hundreds of activists rallied in downtown Toronto on Sept 14, demonstrating against Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s investment summit that seeks to attract interest in more than 160 mining, energy, technology and infrastructure projects.
Protest organisers said they opposed projects that would expand fossil fuel infrastructure, increase military production and transfer greater control of public assets to private investors.
The demonstration drew labour, migrant rights, environmental and social justice groups.
Carney’s approval rating remains above 60 per cent according to the latest Angus Reid poll, as Canadians back his efforts to stand up to US President Donald Trump’s tariffs on the country’s exports.
But Carney has angered the more progressive wing of his Liberal Party by rolling back many of his predecessor Justin Trudeau’s climate policies to restore friendlier relations with resource-extracting industries and prioritise economic growth.
Hailey Asquin, a spokesperson for Common Horizon, a group representing young workers, said protest participants were concerned that projects highlighted at the summit included fossil fuels, artificial intelligence and military-related industries.
“We’re young workers and we want good jobs, and we want to be part of building a country that we can be proud of,” Asquin said.
“We don’t want to see fossil fuels that are going to destroy our climate. We don’t want to see military weapons that are going to fill our world with violence. And we don’t want AI that is going to directly threaten workers’ jobs.”
The summit aims to match around 100 global investors with Canadian chief executives, companies and local officials to facilitate investments or partnerships.
Carney has been looking to diversify Canada’s economic ties beyond the US, its largest trading partner, by pursuing closer commercial relationships with investors and governments in the Middle East, Asia and Europe.
On Sept 14, Bell Canada said it was expanding a data centre project in Saskatchewan, while the finance ministry said it would prioritise advance income tax ruling requests for investments of C$1 billion (S$914 million) or more to help investors get a decision before they commit capital.
Carney has also pledged to increase defence spending.
Syed Hussan, executive director of the Migrant Workers Alliance for Change, said protesters opposed what they described as government support for private investors through subsidies and tax incentives. REUTERS

Feature: Indonesia's trail running boom takes runners from roads to mountains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:04:06 CST
12:04:06 KST

A runner competes at the Bandung Ultra 100 in Bandung, West Java Province, Indonesia, Aug. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Veri Sanovri)
by Hayati Nupus, Veri Sanovri
JAKARTA, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Trail running in Indonesia is expanding beyond highways to dirt tracks, forests, and mountains as runners look for new challenges and an environment apart from the rhythms of city life.
Because each path offers unique physical obstacles and scenery, Fitri Utami finds that trail running offers an experience that road running does not.
"I'm more comfortable on the trails. We can enjoy the scenery and even greet and converse with other runners because we are not overly concerned about pace," she told Xinhua on Monday.
The 45-year-old Jakarta-based worker began jogging in 2018 after prioritizing strength training. Later, she tried trail running since she loved trekking, mountain climbing, and camping.
Since competing in her first trail race in 2023, she has raced in Yogyakarta, Bali, Bromo, and the Dieng Mountains. She most recently finished a 100-kilometer race in Bandung.
The 2024 Coast to Coast Nite Trail Ultra in Yogyakarta, when she ran 80 km from 4 p.m. to 10 a.m. and completed barely five minutes ahead of schedule, was one of her favorite experiences.
She passed through a beach, gardens, a cemetery road, then back to the beach before encountering thick, slick mud after it had rained.
Because the terrain varies from rocks and roots to slick ground, water, and sand, as well as because runners must deal with heat, rain, wind, and cold weather, Fitri said that trail running is more physically taxing than road running.
According to the Indonesia Marathon website, hundreds of trail running competitions have been staged in Indonesia in recent years as the trend continues to spread, with at least 51 planned for 2026.
Indonesia offers a wide range of terrain that is drawing more and more local and international runners, with distances ranging from 15 kilometers to ultra-trail races and routes spanning mountains, forests, valleys, rivers, plantations, and coastal areas.
Trail competitions currently pass through Mount Rinjani in West Nusa Tenggara and the Merbabu and Lawu mountains in Central Java, in addition to Bromo, Dieng, Bali, Bandung, and Yogyakarta.
"I enjoy how the terrain is always shifting. In contrast to road running, which typically takes place on flat ground with views dominated by asphalt and buildings, we can run on dirt, rocks, and sand, through forests, and up mountains, so it never seems repetitive," said Hazet, 43.
Hazet, who previously loved mountain climbing, began running after the COVID-19 pandemic closed gyms. In 2023, he participated in his first trail race.
One of his most memorable experiences was competing in the Bromo Tengger Semeru 100 Ultra in the mountainous region of Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java, where he spent two nights on the trail and only got ten to fifteen minutes of deep sleep to replenish his energy. He typically trains in the hilly regions of Sentul and Mount Gede, both in West Java.
Purwaji Santoso, 38, started trail running in 2025 after taking up road running, badminton, and climbing. The tough terrain has become a means for him to decompress from work-related stress.
"My body and mind feel different, fresher after finishing a trail race," Purwaji said, adding that trail running helps him explore his physical potential and alleviate stress.
"To know how far our bodies can go, we need to experience fatigue and push that limit beyond," he continued.
Purwaji also recalled his grandmother's counsel to engage in activities that uplift the mind, as, according to him, a contented mind improves life and the body. ■
Runners compete at the Bandung Ultra 100 in Bandung, West Java Province, Indonesia, Aug. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Veri Sanovri)

Economic Watch: British analysts expect scale-up of China-Britain services trade, investment
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
11:03:58 CST
12:03:58 KST

LONDON, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Speaking highly of the rapid growth of China's services trade, British analysts are eyeing huge opportunities to expand services trade and investment between China and Britain.
The 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS), which concluded on Sunday, attracted a heavier presence of multinational companies compared to last year, with 473 of them being either Fortune Global 500 firms or industry leaders.
High-profile events like the CIFTIS play a key role in promoting key services export opportunities for Britain-based services firms, the City of London Corporation (CLC) told Xinhua.
The fair clearly reinforces China's continued commitment to a consumption- and services-driven growth model, openness to international investment, and further reform and opening of its services sector, according to the CLC.
The country's trade in services maintained steady growth in the first seven months of 2026. It totalled nearly 4.45 trillion yuan (about 663.3 billion U.S. dollars) during the period, up 8.3 percent year on year, China's official data showed.
"China's services trade expansion creates a new engine for growth and represents its next stage of internationalization," said John McLean, chairman of the China UK Business Development Centre.
A recent report from British consultancy Brand Finance showed China ranks second globally with 21 brands in the world's 100 most valuable trade in services brands, with a combined worth of 876.8 billion dollars.
Alex Haigh, managing director of Brand Finance Asia Pacific, said that by leveraging the synergies of digital platforms, communications networks and large financial institutions, Chinese trade in services brands are rising rapidly, reflecting a new trend of extending "Made in China" to "China services" and "China brands."
The growth of China's trade in services "offers fresh trade opportunities," McLean said. "I believe trade in services represents one of the strongest opportunities for the next phase of the China-UK economic relationship."
Britain has advantages in fields like financial and professional services, life sciences and creative industries, while China leads in fields such as digitization, advanced manufacturing and rapid commercialization of technology, he noted.
The two sides could create the greatest opportunity by combining their complementary strengths, he added.
Britain's financial expertise and China's large, expanding capital market offer huge complementarity, which will create significant scope to expand cross-border investments in areas including legal and accounting services, asset management and insurance, according to the CLC.
Hailing China's capabilities in technological innovation, including electric vehicles and green technology, the CLC noted that the ability to develop and implement green solutions at scale brings further opportunities to finance their global deployment to address the climate challenge.
China offers scale, a strong business ecosystem -- including supply chains, innovative companies, advanced technology and research -- and most importantly, the ability to drive change, or in other words, China speed, McLean said, noting these represent a strong platform for significant growth. ■

VIENNA, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- China officially donated a lunar sample collected by the Chang'e-6 mission to the UN at a handover ceremony on Monday at the United Nations in Vienna, marking the first time that a lunar sample from the far side of the moon has been presented to the organization.
The ceremony was jointly held by the China National Space Administration (CNSA), the Permanent Mission of China to the United Nations and Other International Organizations in Vienna, and the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA). More than 400 guests, including heads of international organizations in Vienna and permanent representatives of various countries, attended the ceremony.
CNSA Administrator Shan Zhongde, the United Nations Office at Vienna Director-General Monica Juma, UNOOSA Director Aarti Holla-Maini, and China's Permanent Representative to the UN and Other International Organizations in Vienna Li Song jointly unveiled the lunar sample, which will be permanently displayed at the UN headquarters in Vienna.
Exploring the vast universe is a shared dream and an enduring pursuit of humanity, Shan said in his remarks, noting that Chinese President Xi Jinping has pointed out that the Chang'e lunar missions belong to both China and all people in the world.
China's handover of the lunar sample collected by Chang'e-6 to the United Nations is a concrete action to put into practice the four major global initiatives proposed by Xi, fully implement the new development philosophy featuring innovative, coordinated, green, open and shared growth, uphold true multilateralism, safeguard the authority and role of the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space as the main platform for global space governance, and advance the implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, Shan said.
China is ready to share the fruits of space development with countries around the world, share opportunities and create prosperity together, so that advances in space science and technology can better benefit people of all countries, he said.
China will work with all countries to advance the peaceful exploration of outer space and better contribute to building a community with a shared future for humanity, Shan added.
Juma said the Vienna multilateral platform has a unique character that brings together science and diplomacy.
The permanent display of the lunar sample at the United Nations in Vienna is of great significance, she said, adding that the sample represents humanity's scientific and technological creativity and determination to explore the universe, while demonstrating China's support for the United Nations in addressing common challenges.
Holla-Maini said China's handover of the lunar sample and sharing of scientific research data are a perfect illustration that outer space is a common domain of all humanity.
She expressed hope that the lunar sample would continue to tell the story in Vienna of humanity's exploration of the moon and contribute to advancing global governance of outer space.
During the event, Li said the event demonstrated China's commitment to working with all parties to firmly uphold the role of the United Nations, improve global governance of outer space and ensure that the benefits of space exploration and development reach all humanity. ■

Plague was killing entire families thousands of years before the Black Death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
02:54:45 UTC
11:54:45 KST

Plague was killing entire families thousands of years before the Black Death
- Date:
- September 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of Copenhagen
- Summary:
- Ancient DNA reveals that plague was already killing hunter-gatherers in Siberia 5,500 years ago, long before cities and flea-driven epidemics. The prehistoric strains may have been especially dangerous because they carried a genetic factor capable of provoking severe immune reactions.
- Share:
Plague is often linked to rats, packed medieval cities, and the devastating epidemics that tore through Europe during and after the Middle Ages.
But new research published in Nature suggests the disease was already a deadly threat 5,500 years ago. At that time, it was killing people in small, mobile hunter-gatherer groups - long before farming and urban life created the crowded conditions usually associated with major plague outbreaks.
Ancient DNA Reveals Early Plague
An international research team studied ancient DNA recovered from human remains at four hunter-gatherer burial sites in the Lake Baikal region of East Siberia. By sequencing genetic material preserved in teeth, the scientists were able to reconstruct ancient bacterial genomes and identify previously unknown early forms of plague.
"Whether the earliest forms of plague were mild or virulent has been a matter of debate, but our findings demonstrate that these ancient strains were already highly lethal," says senior author Eske Willerslev, Professor at the University of Copenhagen and the University of Cambridge.
To understand what happened within these prehistoric communities, the researchers combined genetic evidence with archaeology and radiocarbon dating.
"Based on the plague DNA, the genetic relationships between the victims, the archaeological analysis and the radiocarbon dating, we've built a really clear, complete picture of what happened during these outbreaks," says lead author Ruairidh Macleod, who carried out the work while a PhD student at the University of Cambridge - and is now Research Fellow at the University of Oxford.
The team found DNA from Yersinia pestis - the bacterium that causes plague - in 18 of the 46 people tested. That means nearly 40 percent of the individuals carried evidence of plague, a detection rate even higher than that reported at some medieval plague burial sites.
Early Plague May Have Been Far Deadlier Than Expected
Earlier research had shown that ancient strains of Yersinia pestis were missing some of the genetic features that eventually allowed bubonic plague to spread efficiently through fleas and rodent hosts. Because of that, scientists had often assumed that the earliest versions of the bacterium probably could not trigger severe outbreaks.
The new findings challenge that view.
At the two largest cemeteries, researchers found an unusually large number of children and young teenagers among those who had died. Archaeologists had struggled for decades to explain why so many young people were buried there over such a short period.
"The unusually high number of children and the short timespan was a real puzzle that we've been trying to solve since the 1990s. Finding out that plague was the cause is extraordinary, but it makes so much sense," says archaeologist Andrzej Weber of the University of Alberta, Principal Investigator of the Baikal Archaeology Project.
Radiocarbon dating indicates that many of the deaths happened close together in time. In some cases, siblings appear to have died together, while other graves contain parents and children who may also have died during the same outbreak.
A Possible Clue to the Plague's Lethality
The ancient plague strains also contained a distinctive superantigen - a toxin-producing genetic factor not seen in historic plague strains. Superantigens can cause the immune system to react with unusual intensity, potentially leading to severe inflammation and making an infection much more dangerous.
"This finding changes our understanding of the earliest plague outbreaks: Even before the bacterium evolved efficient flea-borne transmission, these ancient strains appear to have carried a potent combination of virulence factors that could make infection highly lethal," says senior author Martin Sikora, Associate Professor at the University of Copenhagen.
Taken together, the evidence suggests that some of the earliest known plague outbreaks may already have been as deadly as later historical epidemics, particularly for children. That appears to have been possible even before the bacterium developed the efficient flea-based transmission associated with later bubonic plague.
Did Plague Spread From Marmots to Humans?
The findings also add support to the theory that plague may have first emerged in Central or North-East Asia before spreading more widely across Eurasia through populations of wild rodents.
Archaeological evidence indicates that the hunter-gatherers living around Lake Baikal had close contact with marmots - large burrowing rodents that still carry plague today. Researchers therefore suspect that some of these prehistoric outbreaks may have begun when the disease passed directly from infected marmots into humans.
If so, plague was already capable of causing deadly outbreaks in small human communities thousands of years before the rise of cities, crowded settlements, and the flea-driven epidemics that would later make the disease infamous.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Copenhagen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Ruairidh Macleod, Frederik V. Seersholm, Bianca De Sanctis, Angela Lieverse, Adrian Timpson, Rick Schulting, Jesper T. Stenderup, Charleen Gaunitz, Lasse Vinner, Olga Ivanovna Goriunova, Vladimir Ivanovich Bazaliiskii, Sergei V. Vasilyev, Erin Jessup, Yucheng Wang, Christopher Bronk Ramsey, Mark G. Thomas, Russell Corbett-Detig, Astrid K. N. Iversen, Andrzej W. Weber, Martin Sikora, Eske Willerslev. Lethal plague outbreaks in Lake Baikal hunter-gatherers 5,500 years ago. Taichung selected for state-level drone laboratory

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taichung said on Monday that it has been selected to host a future state-level drone technology testing laboratory.
The Cabinet has designated Taichung as the site of its national drone testing laboratory. Legislator Yang Chiung-ying (楊瓊瓔) invited government agencies, local officials, and drone firms like Thunder Tiger to inspect the location, per a press release.
Taichung City Economic Development Director-General Chang Feng-yuan (張峯源) said Taichung alone has about 50 drone firms capable of research and development, production, and testing. He added that the site will test medium- to large-sized drones and electronic warfare capabilities.
Chang said that the industry is all about speed, as time to verification affects orders and time to market. He added that the site will begin by accommodating tests for drones below 25 kg. Chang noted that 200 meters of runway and buffer zones will be built for fixed-wing aircraft.
Standards Bureau Director-General Chen I-ling (陳怡鈴) approved the site in early September. Initial development will cost about NT$30 million (US$944,000), require 1,197 square meters of land, and take three years to build. The facility will have an electromagnetic chamber for single units or swarms of 25-kilo drones. Planning and design are expected to be completed by 2027, with construction to begin in 2028 and completion by 2029.
The bureau said the decision was made because some local drone firms still have to conduct tests elsewhere, which not only adds to transportation and testing expenses but also delays rollout. It said it will continue to secure more land to prepare for future expansions.
Thunder Tiger said that drone technology is constantly evolving and competent authorities should gather industry feedback to ensure that regulations are updated. Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation and 17 other firms also attended the inspection.
