Trump administration suffers double legal setback over immigration rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
02:31:18 UTC
11:31:18 KST

Trump administration suffers double legal setback over immigration policy
Courts and Democratic-led states mount legal challenges against Trump administration visa and green card limits.
US President Donald Trump’s administration has suffered two setbacks to its immigration agenda as a federal judge halted proposed visa caps and dozens of Democratic-led states launched legal challenges against broader residency restrictions.
A US federal judge on Monday blocked the administration from imposing fixed time limits on how long foreign students and journalists can remain in the country without applying for extensions. At the same time, a broad coalition of states filed suit to stop a separate federal regulation that would allow immigration authorities to deny green cards to immigrants who make lawful use of public benefits.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US deports nearly 2,300 Mexicans to Guatemala over Mexico’s objections
- list 2 of 4Trump administration seeks to formalise H-1B fee of more than $100,000
- list 3 of 4US plans to revoke business, tourism visas of 200,000 asylum seekers
- list 4 of 4US immigration agents arrested more than 49,500 people in July
Court halts visa caps
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regulation was scheduled to take effect on Tuesday before US District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV in Boston granted an injunction requested by a coalition of trade unions and higher education advocacy groups.
Under Trump’s proposed limitation, F visas for international students and J visas that allow cultural exchange programmes in the US would be capped at four years. I visas for journalists, which currently can last for years, would be limited to 240 days.
Saylor, who was appointed by Republican President George W. Bush, called the DHS’s rationale citing national security and the need to prevent fraud in the visa programme “exceptionally weak”.
He noted that the existing system has allowed tens of millions of scholars to contribute to groundbreaking research and substantial economic expansion, warning that the damage to higher education and the wider US economy would be “catastrophic”.
The measures would affect roughly 1.6 million international students holding F visas and about 500,000 exchange visitors on J visas.
States challenge public charge rule
Two lawsuits were filed in a Manhattan federal court on Monday to derail a DHS regulation scheduled to take effect on Friday. The measure seeks to broaden the criteria by which immigration officers can deem applicants inadmissible as a “public charge”, a legal standard historically applied to individuals likely to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence.
New York, California and Illinois are leading a coalition of 22 states and the District of Columbia seeking to block the policy, joined by a parallel suit from six cities and counties.
Under the Biden administration, immigration officers could consider cash aid when evaluating green card applicants, but were barred from penalising the use of non-cash support such as food assistance and Medicaid. The Trump administration is now seeking to revive first-term policies that treat non-cash assistance as a disqualifying factor, while also extending scrutiny to benefits received by an applicant’s family members.
A DHS spokesperson defended the regulation, describing the plaintiffs as “left-wing leaders” who were “terrified they will lose federal funds because hundreds of thousands of illegals and noncitizens might remove themselves from American welfare programs”.
In a statement, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the rule “seeks to push immigrant families away from the programs that have kept people fed and healthy for decades”.
The lawsuits argue that the administration overstepped its legal authority by bypassing Congress, which holds the sole power to set the criteria for permanent residency.
By penalising applicants who lawfully use non-cash assistance like food stamps and Medicaid, the plaintiffs contend the administration established an unlawful restriction that contradicts federal statutes.

Under the virtual mobile operator, the "Simka 60" plan will also be available to users as part of the bundled "Fiber+Simka" service, the company said.
U Mobile's website states that all existing 3Mob-brand subscribers will continue receiving mobile service on the current terms of their chosen tariff plans, with no changes.
At the same time, U Mobile said that following the launch of tariff plans under the newly created mobile brand, the next step will be to stop connecting new subscribers to 3Mob-brand tariff plans.
"We are sincerely grateful to every subscriber who has chosen the 3Mob brand over the years, and we're glad to continue providing you with quality mobile service at this new stage in our company's development," said Oleh Boiko, director of Trimob LLC, the provider of mobile services under the U Mobile brand, as quoted in the release.
U Mobile is a trademark for mobile services provided by Trimob LLC, whose sole founder is Ukrtelecom, which has been part of the SCM group since 2013.
As reported, Ukrtelecom announced the launch of the U Mobile virtual mobile operator on social media in late August, providing a link to the operator's official website.
According to the National Commission for State Regulation of Electronic Communications, Radio Frequency Spectrum and Provision of Postal Services (NCEC), Trimob, the mobile operator founded by Ukrtelecom, had 60,700 mobile subscribers in the first quarter of 2026.
Ukrtelecom provided mobile services from 2007-2011 under the Utel brand, and later continued operations through Trimob.
Trimob received Ukraine's first 3G license back in 2005. Its network was based on UMTS/HSDPA technology in the 2100 MHz band. In 2019, the company returned nearly all of its national 3G frequencies to the regulator and focused on providing services only in Kyiv. From 2020, Trimob held a license for the 1940-1945/2130-2135 MHz bands, which were used to provide 3G services within Kyiv.
In May 2025, the NCEC transferred the last radio frequency resources remaining with Ukrtelecom's subsidiary to Vodafone Ukraine.
Ukrtelecom increased total revenue by 12.6% year-on-year in January-June 2026, to UAH 2.78 billion, while EBITDA grew 50% to more than UAH 810 million.
As of today, the company has more than 95,000 km of fiber-optic network and continues a large-scale infrastructure modernization across the country.
In August, Ukrtelecom and Kyivstar, another Ukrainian mobile operator, also began cooperating under an Open Access model, which will involve using part of both operators' networks and will initially launch in Odesa, Vinnytsia and Kirovohrad regions.

The moment this Knights finals rookie will hold onto forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
02:24:43 UTC
11:24:43 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Why Jermaine McEwen will never forget Newcastle's finals win over Souths
Last Friday's semifinal win over South Sydney was one of the great nights in Newcastle's recent history, and nobody enjoyed it more than Jermaine McEwen.
In his first finals match, the 21-year-old had the game of his young life, inspiring the 20-10 upset victory that has the whole Hunter dreaming big ahead of Sunday's sudden-death clash with the Warriors.
McEwen scored the first double of his NRL career and ran for 187 metres, the best mark of his 37 first-grade matches, and set the tone for the Knights' right-edge defence with a physical brutality that would make a mafia kingpin proud.
On a night of many highlights, McEwen's personal favourite was his second try that helped Newcastle kick clear in the second half, as he backed up winger Dom Young to score right in front of the Knights faithful.
McEwen crawled the last few metres before slamming the ball down so hard it's a wonder they could dig it out of the turf.
"The only reason I slammed it was because my parents and my family were right in front of me. I just looked at them, and I was like, 'hell yeah,'" said McEwen.
"That was the best moment I have ever had in my footy career. That moment right there, that's something I will hold forever. So I am just super grateful and so happy."
McEwen's first try of the evening helped get things started as he again trailed Young after the Englishman claimed a bomb inside the first five minutes.
It brought Newcastle into the match and gave the team the start they needed en route to their first away finals win since 2013 and just their third since their last premiership 25 years ago.
Repeating the dose in Auckland is a tall order, but even before the win over Souths, McEwen and his teammates did not lack for belief.
"The Knights have given me everything, and I believe in the coach, Justin (Holbrook). He's allowed me to be the greatest version of myself on that field," said McEwen.
"But when I put the ball down and looked up and saw all the fans, I was (thinking) how happy I am to be a Knight. I'm just so grateful.
"We just wanted to go out there and play with energy and lift each other up."
McEwen spent much of the week thinking about how the Knights would shut down South Sydney's left edge, which is just about the most dangerous attacking weapon in the NRL.
Between them, Alex Johnston, Latrell Mitchell, Tallis Duncan and Cody Walker scored 63 tries in 2026, two more than Newcastle managed as an entire club last season.
But McEwen, Sandon Smith and Dane Gagai rose to the occasion magnificently, locking onto the superstars and refusing to let go, moving and defending as one.
Souths did end up scoring down the left through Jye Grey, but only after McEwen had left the field late on.
"When you have challenges, you get more prepared for it. You think about it more. When you're at home or training, you get flashbacks of what you have to do," said McEwen.
"When I have Cody Walker and their left edge — they do it the best in the whole comp. Cody Walker, he is just so good at that stuff.
"Us in D, we had a big job to do, and we just went out there and did it."
The journey through this year to Sunday's knockout final has not always been smooth for McEwen.
He was suspended for one match in June after being charged with low-range drink driving, an incident for which he apologised unreservedly and left him "deeply ashamed".
At the time, McEwen said he let his community down, and he's been trying to make amends ever since.
"Bro, at the end of the day we're all human and just because I play footy doesn't mean I'm special," said McEwen.
"In those circumstances, with the rollercoaster (of this year), that has taught me a lot in life.
"I feel like people can either shy away from it or own up to it. I wanted to show up for the fans and show them what I could do, and repay them in that way."
"Because I know how much the town speaks to this club and the hold this club has on the town. I wanted to repay them with good footy."
A sellout crowd is expected at Eden Park on Sunday, and a win would send Newcastle to just its second preliminary final in the last 25 years.
They'll again be underdogs against a Warriors side that beat them just three weeks ago, and the match marks the biggest game of McEwen's career, as it is for several of his teammates.
But the same was true last Friday, and by leaning on the experience of men like Gagai and prop Tyson Frizell, McEwen was inspired to make a difference, and all he wants is to do it all over again.
"These are experienced boys who have been in the game for a lot of years, and when you have them talk to you, it makes you more comfortable," said McEwen.
"You're not nervous. You're going out there to do a good job."

DOJ says millions in Iran oil proceeds laundered on Binance
- The US Justice Department seeks forfeiture of US$61 million laundered through Binance from Iranian black-market oil sales used to finance military and terrorist activities.
- Two Chinese entities, Blessed Trust Limited and Hexa Whale Trading Limited, allegedly used Binance and the US financial system to funnel over US$1.5 billion to Iran.
- Binance denies wrongdoing, cooperates with law enforcement, and has off-boarded the implicated entities; the case highlights ongoing scrutiny of Binance's compliance with anti-money laundering laws.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US Justice Department is seeking forfeiture of US$61 million (S$77.6 million) it says was generated from Iranian black-market oil sales and laundered through the cryptocurrency exchange Binance.
In a civil forfeiture claim filed on Sept 14, federal prosecutors in Manhattan alleged that Iran used cryptocurrency to launder more than US$1.5 billion in illicit oil money.
According to US prosecutors, two Chinese entities used trading accounts on Binance as part of a scheme to funnel the oil proceeds to Iran, its agents and proxies, where the funds were used to finance military and terrorist activities.
The two entities, Blessed Trust and Hexa Whale Trading, presented themselves as a wealth management firm and commodities broker, respectively, prosecutors said.
They allegedly also used the US financial system to send and receive tens of millions of dollars as part of the scheme.
Blessed Trust did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and contact information for Hexa Whale could not immediately be found.
Manhattan Deputy US Attorney Sean Buckley said in a statement: “Today we are seizing and seeking to forfeit more than US$61 million of the government of Iran’s money, which otherwise would have promoted hostile military action and terrorist attacks against the US and our allies.”
Prosecutors did not accuse Binance of wrongdoing.
The firm said it did not permit any transactions with people who were sanctioned.
“We will continue to cooperate with law enforcement on this matter, and where sanctions or illicit-finance risk is identified, we will always investigate, restrict or freeze accounts where appropriate, offboard users, and report to relevant authorities,” Binance said in a statement.
The forfeiture claim is the latest legal manoeuvre by US prosecutors involving Iran in recent months as fighting between the countries continues.
The US alleged on Sept 14 that accounts holding the illicit oil proceeds were used to transfer crypto to an Iranian crypto exchange and money transmitters that are fronts for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Iran’s UN Mission did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In February, the New York Times and Wall Street Journal reported on an internal Binance investigation finding more than US$1 billion had moved through the platform to Iranian entities with links to terrorist groups.
Following the reports, Binance said in blog posts that it cooperated with law enforcement officials and that its compliance programme was robust.
Binance has said it offboarded Hexa Whale and Blessed Trust before the reports earlier in 2026.
The cryptocurrency exchange’s controls were under intense legal scrutiny in 2023 when the Justice Department charged the company and its co-founder over flouting anti-money laundering rules.
In that case, prosecutors said terrorist groups, people living in sanctioned countries and cybercriminals used the platform to move hundreds of millions of dollars.
Binance paid a US$4.3 billion fine to resolve the probe and co-founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to violating banking laws.
He spent four months in prison.
US President Donald Trump granted Zhao a pardon in 2025. BLOOMBERG

pink inflatable canopy brings soft shade to new york’s streetscape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
02:10:32 UTC
11:10:32 KST

The Bower’s clustered inflatable forms form shaded public space
Brooklyn-based architect and artist Elsa Ponce’s The Bower considers shade as an essential form of urban care. Commissioned by the NYC DOT Art Program for Summer Streets 2026, the temporaryinstallation creates a shaded public space where visitors can rest, draw, and gather beneath a canopy of clustered inflatable forms. The project responds to increasingly hot New Yorksummers and the uneven availability of shade across the city. In neighborhoods such as Sunset Park, East Williamsburg, and Red Hook, where tree canopy can be scarce, parasols and other forms of sun protection have become part of everyday life. Shade is free, but access to it is not evenly distributed, affecting older adults, children, outdoor workers, and even pets. The Bower at Foley Square during NYC Summer Streets | all images by Carlos Galek Sefchovich
Soft inflatable forms contrast with New York’s hard surfaces
The idea is also connected to the Mexican expression vete por la sombrita, roughly translated as ‘walk in the shade’. Familiar from Ponce’s upbringing in Mexico, the phrase extends beyond practical advice for avoiding the sun, functioning as a small gesture of affection and protection. This understanding of shade as care forms a central idea behind The Bower. The installation by architect and artist Elsa Ponce takes its name from leafy shelters found across cultures, where they have provided protection, respite, and places for social connection. Its geometry draws from the dappled shadows cast by trees, using a composition of mass and void to produce changing patterns of light and shade throughout the day.
Set against New York’s hard surfaces and rectilinear streetscape, The Bower introduces a deliberately soft architectural form. Clusters of inflatable elements hover above the pavement, filtering sunlight and creating a temporary landscape of shadow beneath them. The color palette references the jacaranda, a tree associated with Ponce’s memories of growing up in Mexico, with tones shifting from pale lilac to pastel pink as the sunlight changes. The temporary nature of Summer Streets also informed the construction. Designed to be installed and removed within a single day, The Bower had to remain lightweight and transportable while allowing a small crew to assemble it without specialized tools. For several hours, the structure converts a section of pavement into a temporary public room, providing a place to linger and interact within the street.
The Bower creates a temporary canopy of shade during NYC Summer Streets
Moving shadows become part of the soft lilac and pink canopy
The shaded area also functions as a participatory surface. Bags of colorful chalk allow visitors to contribute to a collective mural, with some tracing the shadows cast by the inflatable canopy as they move across the pavement, while others draw freely, experiment with color, or sit on stools and observe the work developing around them. The changing position of the sun becomes part of the installation. As shadows migrate across the pavement, new drawings follow their movement and individual marks accumulate into a record of the visitors passing through the space. Cyclists and outdoor workers also use the canopy as a place to pause and seek relief from the summer heat.
Presented across three Saturdays at Park Avenue and Foley Square, The Bower operates simultaneously as a public artwork, participatory space, and piece of climate-responsive infrastructure. Its temporary canopy demonstrates how shade can shape patterns of movement, occupation, and interaction in the city, while raising the question of whether access to shade should be considered an essential part of urban infrastructure rather than simply an amenity.

If AI Has Read the Internet, Why Do I Need to Explain Everything?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
02:10:15 UTC
11:10:15 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
The objectives passed the vibe check. Unfortunately, vibes are not instructional design.
Around the time AI tools first became publicly usable, we were working with a client on developing a course for IT Support Technicians.
I was testing the bounds of AI, so I dumped my thoughts into Claude and asked it to help me draft some learning objectives.
At first glance, they looked pretty good.
The client followed Bloom’s taxonomy, and each objective started with a verb. The objectives had varying levels mixed in, and they were all polished. They all said the things that learning objectives are supposed to say.
But the more I looked at them, the more I realized they were weak.
They were hard to assess. They were too generic. They were hard to create content for. In general, they sounded like they belonged in a broad course on technology, not a course specific to IT support technicians.
This was one of the first times where I realized that while AI might ‘know everything’, the problem was actually that it knew too much in general, and not enough about this specific course.
AI knew IT fundamentals. It did not know this course.
Every large language model is trained on training data.
The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI defines training data as the collection of examples—such as text, images, audio, or other information—used to teach machine learning models how to perform specific tasks.1
Context is different
Context is what the model needs from you so it can answer this question, for this audience, inside this set of constraints, toward this outcome.
Training data helps the model produce something that sounds generally right.
Context helps it produce something that is actually useful.
That is where a lot of AI frustration starts.
A model can know a lot about IT fundamentals. It can know what a learning objective usually looks like. It can know Bloom’s taxonomy. It can know the general shape of a course.
But unless it knows the learner, the job role, the actual performance expectations, the source material, the standards, the constraints, and what “good” means in this specific situation, it will often give you the most statistically normal version of the answer.
And sometimes the most statistically normal answer is a beautifully formatted pile of gobbledygook.
Frasier accidentally explains AI output
I saw a scene in Frasier recently that made me think of this.
Bebe introduces Frasier to a man named Professor Pete (played by Doug Carfrae), whom she aggressively pitches as a “human encyclopedia”. The exchange goes as follows: [1, 2]
Bebe: Frasier, this is Professor Pete, the human encyclopedia. Ask him anything, he can’t be stopped.
Frasier: Oh, all right. Explain Freud’s theory of the superego.
Pete: (Mechanical, as if reading a textbook entry) Sigmund Freud, noted psychiatrist, was born in Vienna. (He abruptly stops)
Frasier: (Confused) That’s not what I asked. [2]
Which is the energy of so many AI interactions.
You ask what feels like a specific question. The tool gives you something vaguely related, weirdly confident, and technically adjacent. It isn’t completely wrong, but it definitely isn’t what you needed.
More words do not always mean more relevance
A lot of people hear “context” and think they need to write a longer prompt.
Sometimes, yes. More detail helps. But context is not just prompt length; it’s all about relevance.
For learning work, you might include context such as:
- 
your goal
- 
who the learner is
- 
what job they are doing
- 
what they need to be able to do after they finish the course
- 
what constraints you have on design
- 
how their work will be assessed
That context can live inside a prompt. It can also live in a project file, a source document, a style guide, a rubric, a SME transcript, a job task analysis, or a set of design standards.
Why this matters for instructional design
Generic AI output creates a fake sense of progress. You might get something that looks done, similar to my learning objectives for the IT support course. Everyone gets a tiny dopamine hit because there are words on the page. Look at us go.
But then you, or another reviewer, will end up spending a load of time figuring out why it feels so wrong.
At that point, AI did not save time.
It moved the hard decisions to review, where they are more expensive, more annoying, and usually happen after someone thought the work was done.
That is why context matters so much.
If your organizational context is scattered, stale, inconsistent, or stuck in people’s heads, AI will reflect that problem back to you.
The issue is bigger than prompting.
It is source material. Standards. Decision history. Review loops. Knowledge management. Workflow.
AI cannot use context your team cannot find.
And if the context is missing from the system, it will be missing from the output.
[1] https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-definitions/what-is-training-data
[2] https://www.kacl780.net/frasier/transcripts/season_4/episode_17/rozs_turn.html

Obama calls for AI safety measures, rebuking Trump approach

Obama calls for AI safety measures, rebuking Trump approach
WASHINGTON – Former US president Barack Obama voiced support for federal laws and regulations governing artificial intelligence safety, saying that the technology could unleash “potential catastrophe” if not properly managed.
In a statement on Sept 14, Obama said that AI policy “should be at the centre of our public debate” and Washington policymakers must “get proactive” in crafting proposals “that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids, and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread”.
The former president criticised the hands-off approach to AI regulation championed by US President Donald Trump, though he did not mention his successor by name, saying that “voluntary standards made by a handful of tech companies won’t be enough”.
A June executive order signed by Trump established an optional framework for AI developers to give the government advanced access to frontier models to review potential security risks.
“Given what we know about technology, we can’t stuff AI back in a box. But we can collectively determine how it’s developed and how it’s used, rather than sitting back and letting AI and its fallout happen to us,” Obama said.
The rare public statement from Obama amounts to his most in-depth comments yet about AI, which has come to dominate the national conversation as leading industry executives and lawmakers call for slowing the development of cutting-edge models.
Without a clear leader in the party, many Democrats still look to Obama for advice and guidance on policy and political strategy. By injecting himself into the debate, Obama is positioning his party as a champion of greater AI safety measures as it heads into the November midterm elections and the start of the 2028 presidential contest.
Such a stance would place Democratic candidates in direct contrast with Trump, who has become increasingly strident in his resistance to AI regulation. On Sept 14, he released a torrent of social media posts dismissing existential fears about AI as a “hoax” and calling efforts to rein in development a gift to China.
The New York Times reported on Sept 13 that Obama urged party leaders during a recent private fund raiser to quickly form a plan to prioritise the issue in the coming years and said 2028 presidential candidates ought to have a “clear plan” to respond to safety and economic concerns spurred by AI. Why Hong Kong’s economic future still hinges on national security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
01:30:05 UTC
10:30:05 KST

Why Hong Kong’s economic future still hinges on national security
Whether under British rule or modern superpower competition, Hong Kong’s value as a strategic gateway makes it a vital security asset
In any conversation about Hong Kong’s future, one question often emerges: when will the city pivot away from national security and back to economic development?
To most, Hong Kong is fundamentally a commercial hub. After the turmoil of 2019, most reasonable people agreed that restoring public order was imperative. Today, the orchestrators of that unrest and the radicals are largely imprisoned or have fled. While occasional flare-ups and various forms of “soft resistance” persist, society at large appears to have reclaimed its traditional pragmatism. Few doubt that national security laws are here to stay, yet many wonder whether it’s time to turn the page and refocus on economic growth.
As a journalist, I work in one of the most affected industries and this question is constantly on my mind. I have come to a conclusion that may sound counterintuitive, if not sacrilegious, coming from a media professional: national security will always remain a top policy priority for Hong Kong. It is not a handicap undermining our commercial interests; rather, our economic future depends entirely on our ability to manage these concerns to the nation’s satisfaction. Any sober examination of the facts, framed by current geopolitical realities, makes this conclusion inescapable.
Hong Kong’s strategic position has always been dictated by national security considerations. When Great Britain took the territory by force from China in 1842, it was not seeking natural resources, but a protected gateway to a vast Chinese market and a naval stronghold for the Royal Navy. Admiral John Fisher, architect of Britain’s global maritime strategy, notably served at the naval headquarters here. The British colonised Hong Kong specifically to serve the security needs of the British Empire.

S. Korea's August import prices fall for 3rd month on strong currency
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:23:51 CST
10:23:51 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Prices for imported goods to South Korea fell for a third consecutive month, driven by the strong domestic currency that canceled out soaring crude oil prices, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The import price index retreated 2.4 percent in August from a month earlier, extending a downward trajectory from a 4.2 percent drop in June and a 1.0 percent decline in July, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The average South Korean won versus U.S. dollar exchange rate dived 6.1 percent over the month to 1,406.30 won in August.
The price of Dubai crude, South Korea's benchmark, averaged 88.75 U.S. dollars per barrel in August, up 15.6 percent compared to the previous month.
Prices for imported raw materials, including mining products, rose 1.5 percent in August on a monthly basis, keeping an upward momentum for two months in a row.
Import prices for intermediate goods tumbled 4.0 percent, while those for capital and consumer goods went down 4.2 percent and 4.4 percent each.
The export price index dropped 3.7 percent in August from a month earlier, marking the steepest monthly decline in 44 months since December 2022.
The export prices remained highly volatile throughout 2026, showing a brief rebound of 0.9 percent in July before succumbing to currency factors in August. ■

S. Korea's August export volume keeps double-digit growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
09:23:46 CST
10:23:46 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's August export volume kept double-digit growth, driven by an unyielding global demand for semiconductors and computer storage devices, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The export volume index surged 25.9 percent in August from a year earlier, accelerating from the 20.1 percent spike in the previous month, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The index continued to go up for 10 straight months since November 2025.
In terms of volume, exports for computers, electronic and optical devices soared 30.5 percent on the back of surging demand for memory chips and solid state drives (SSDs) used for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Backed by soaring chip prices, the export value index jumped 75.8 percent in August compared to the same month last year.
The import volume index gained 12.0 percent year-on-year in August, maintaining a steady momentum after a 14.7 percent expansion in July, while the import value index spiked 23.1 percent.
The higher inbound shipment was led by semiconductors, computers and semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The net terms-of-trade index for goods, or a ratio of export prices to import prices, was up 27.1 percent in August on a yearly basis due to a faster increase in export prices than import prices.
It marked the steepest gain since the central bank began compiling the data in 1988. ■

Panama Canal to cut maritime traffic again due to El Nino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
01:14:00 UTC
10:14:00 KST

Panama Canal to cut maritime traffic again due to El Nino
PANAMA CITY – The Panama Canal is planning further reductions to maritime traffic through the waterway after already slashing numbers due to the El Nino weather pattern, the canal’s administrator said on Sept 14.
Panama has declared a nationwide emergency over El Nino, a phenomenon developing over the Pacific Ocean that is affecting worldwide weather patterns and pushing up global temperatures.
These conditions have provoked a severe drought in Central America, which poses huge problems for the interoceanic Panama Canal.
Five per cent of global trade passes through the waterway, which cannot function without the water it uses to power its locks that lift and lower ships at the start and end of their crossing.
Canal authorities cut daily transits from 36 to 32 on Sept 4 to preserve water and will slash them further to “an average of 29.5 transits” a day from October, according to a draft budget submitted to Panama’s Parliament.
The approved budget “ensures that the canal continues to operate safely, continuously, efficiently and profitably”, said Minister for Canal Affairs Jose Ramon Icaza.
The El Nino in 2026 is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago.
In 2023, the phenomenon forced a reduction in daily transits through the canal from 38 to 22.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has pushed up traffic through the channel given the standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas. AFP

Trump nominates Lee Greenwood's wife to serve as ambassador to Barbados

Trump nominates Lee Greenwood's wife to serve as ambassador to Barbados
President Trump on Monday nominated Kimberly Greenwood, the wife of "God Bless the USA" singer Lee Greenwood, to serve as ambassador to Barbados and several other Caribbean countries.
Kimberly Greenwood's nomination was sent to the Senate along with dozens of other nominations for judgeships, ambassadorships and administration officials.
She was tasked to serve as ambassador to Barbados and, "without additional compensation," as the U.S.' top envoy to Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica, Grenada and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. It's common for a single person to serve simultaneously as ambassador to Barbados and several nearby Eastern Caribbean island nations, most of which are small and do not have their own separate U.S. diplomatic posts.
Kimberly Greenwood thanked Mr. Trump in an Instagram post that included a photo of her with Lee Greenwood and the president, calling it "one of the greatest honors of my lifetime."
"If confirmed by the United States Senate, I will work every day to earn that confidence, to listen and learn, to build genuine relationships, and to make sure the people of every nation I am privileged to serve know how deeply America values their friendship," she wrote.
Lee Greenwood congratulated his wife for the nomination, writing on X: "I know Kim will serve with humility, dignity and a sincere desire to strengthen the friendships between the United States and the people of these seven Caribbean nations."
Lee Greenwood has been closely associated with Mr. Trump for much of the president's political career. Mr. Trump has long used Lee Greenwood's "God Bless the USA" as his rally walk-up song, and in recent years, the country singer has performed the patriotic anthem live at certain Trump events. The president also worked with the artist to sell a line of Bibles.
In an interview with Sean Hannity over the summer, Kimberly Greenwood said her professional relationship with the president predates her husband's. A former Miss Tennessee, she worked with Mr. Trump for years in his capacity as the former owner of the Miss Universe pageant.
Kimberly Greenwood has directed the Miss Tennessee, Miss Mississippi and Miss Georgia competitions, according to a biography on the Miss Georgia website.
"Kim has always approached every responsibility with a servant's heart and a deep commitment to excellence," Lee Greenwood wrote on X. "Kim worked with President Trump for 18 years through the Miss Universe Organization while directing multiple state pageants, and I am deeply grateful for the confidence he has once again placed in her through this nomination."
Mr. Trump is far from the first president to pick political allies to serve as diplomats in some cases, but a Washington Post review last month found the Trump administration has filled a larger-than-usual share of its ambassadorial posts with political supporters rather than career Foreign Service officers. Many posts remain unfilled.
The president has nominated Trump-backed former Senate candidates Herschel Walker of Georgia and Kari Lake of Arizona to serve as ambassadors to the Bahamas and Jamaica, respectively. Charles Kushner, the father of Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, serves as ambassador to France and Monaco. And Kimberly Guilfoyle, a pro-Trump former Fox News host who previously dated the president's eldest son, was chosen as ambassador to Greece.

Trump cancels one of the main climate restrictions for power plants in the United States
Kyiv • UNN
The EPA repealed Biden-era rules requiring power plants to cut 90% of their emissions by 2032. The authorities expect savings of $300 billion.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced the repeal of greenhouse gas emissions limits for coal- and gas-fired power plants introduced under the administration of Joe Biden. NBC News reports, writes UNN.
Details
The rule in question is from 2024 and provided for the gradual tightening of requirements for power plants. In particular, by 2032 they were supposed to capture and store at least 90% of the carbon emissions produced.
The EPA also proposed repealing other greenhouse gas regulations. The agency claims that the Clean Air Act does not grant it the authority to regulate such emissions in the context of climate change.
Trump administration calculates $300 billion in savings
The EPA said that repealing the requirements would allow the energy industry to save more than $300 billion and help increase energy production in the United States.
The Trump administration has taken action to protect American energy and make sure you can afford to keep the lights on
The decision was part of a broader review of the climate policies of previous administrations. In February, the EPA had already repealed greenhouse gas emissions standards for vehicles and the legal rationale underlying the agency's relevant regulatory authority.
Environmental organizations said they would challenge the Trump administration's new decisions in court. If the repeal of the rules withstands legal challenges, it could also significantly limit the ability of future U.S. administrations to reintroduce requirements to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants.

Etihad says Mid-East rivalry shields passengers from higher fares
DUBAI – The fierce competition between Middle East airlines means the rising costs of jet fuel will not be passed on to customers just yet, Etihad Airways’ chief executive said.
Fuel prices will have to stay higher for a longer period of time before carriers consider raising ticket prices, Antonoaldo Neves said in an interview.
Oil soared after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran and remained above US$100 a barrel on Sept 14 as Washington and Tehran wrestle for control over the Strait of Hormuz.
“In the Middle East, because of competition, it’s much harder to pass on prices,” Neves said at the Arabian Travel Market conference in Dubai. “It’s the most competitive market in the world in terms of aviation.”
Analysts expect airfares to remain elevated for longer, putting pressure on carriers’ margins and their bonds.
The war forced Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad to temporarily cut back operations and rework their international networks because of suppressed demand and closed airspace.
Etihad, the national carrier of the United Arab Emirates, is hedged at about 60 per cent until year end.
However, the reluctance to raise prices applies only to passenger service. Etihad also has a big cargo business and Neves said higher prices are passed on “automatically” to those customers.
The Abu Dhabi-based carrier said regional conflict is only one of many geopolitical issues affecting its operations.
The Trump administration is tightening eligibility and raising fees for visas, including the H-1B visas central to information technology staffing and technology industries. At the same time, the US and Canada are slapping tariffs on each other’s products and industries.
“We see more impact in July and August because the student visas in the US and Canada have changed than because of the conflict, so we need to take a wider perspective,” Neves said. BLOOMBERG

U.S. judge blocks new stay limits for foreign students, journalists
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
08:32:02 CST
09:32:02 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- A U.S. federal judge on Monday blocked a Trump administration rule that would impose fixed limits on how long foreign students, exchange visitors and representatives of foreign media may stay in the United States.
Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV of the District of Massachusetts granted the plaintiffs' request to postpone the rule's effective date under Section 705 of the Administrative Procedure Act. The rule was scheduled to take effect on Tuesday.
The new rule, published by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security in July, would have replaced the "duration of status" system currently applied to F-class academic students, J-class exchange visitors and I-class representatives of foreign information media with fixed periods of admission.
Under the rule, F and J nonimmigrants would generally be admitted for the duration of their academic or exchange programs, subject to a maximum of four years, followed by a 30-day departure period. Those needing additional time to complete their studies, training or exchange programs would need to apply to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for an extension.
I-class foreign media representatives would be admitted for the period necessary to complete their activities or assignments, for no more than 240 days at a time, with extensions available.
Several organizations, including NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the American Federation of Teachers, the United Auto Workers Local 2322, The NewsGuild-CWA and others, filed a lawsuit on Aug. 18 seeking to block the rule. ■

====================================================================================================

F-35 Readiness Surged in Epic Fury; Now Pentagon and Lockheed Eye Broader Gains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
00:30:31 UTC
09:30:31 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—For years, sustainment challenges and spare parts shortages have hindered the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter’s readiness. But the Air Force’s experience flying F-35s heavily in operations against Iran have showed what the jet can be capable of, if maintainers get all the supplies and support they need.
Brig. Gen. Brian Laidlaw, director of operations for Air Combat Command, said during a Sept. 14 panel discussion at AFA’s Air Space & Cyber conference that the F-35 “absolutely proved itself” during Operation Epic Fury—and keeping a steady flow of spare parts was critical.
“When properly resourced, we showed without a doubt how well this airplane can perform in combat,” Laidlaw said. “When we send our aircraft into harm’s way and they go downrange, they enjoy a higher priority for spare parts and all the things that the logistics trail can get to them. What we saw is how remarkably well the F-35 airplane withstood and maintained really high mission capable rates over a long period of time in the toughest of combat situations.”
The challenge now facing the Air Force, F-35 prime contractor Lockheed Martin, and other parts of the Joint Strike Fighter enterprise: how to keep that level of readiness up, even for aircraft not on the front lines of combat?
A Government Accountability Office report released this June made clear the F-35’s readiness woes are still an issue—just one in four U.S. jets were considered “fully mission capable,” or ready to carry out all their missions at any given time, in fiscal 2025. The Air Force’s full mission capability rate was highest of all U.S. services at 28.5 percent, while the Navy and Marine Corps’ F-35s ranged between 15.3 to 22 percent.
The GAO report cited multiple problems, including spare parts shortages and the military’s decision years ago to prioritize buying more F-35s early in the program’s life cycle instead of investing in critical depot and repair capability. That choice led to a historic underinvestment in sustainment, GAO officials said, that has resulted in a sustainment system that can’t fully support the F-35 fleet.
Yet recent development have shown the Air Force’s larger sustainment enterprise kicking into high gear. In his keynote address Sept. 14, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink continued to harp on the importance of readiness, a frequent theme in his tenure, and said targeted campaigns such as the North Star Readiness Campaign for bombers is helping improve aircraft availability.
During Operation Epic Fury, Meink said, sustainment centers surged procurement of parts by nearly 120 percent to keep aircraft flying. Contractors have also spent billions of their own dollars to stock up on parts military aircraft need, he said.
“The result: our fleet health is showing meaningful progress,” Meink said. “And with Congress’ support, we’ll follow that up with record-high spare parts investment in the next year, and years to come.”
For the F-35 in particular, Dina Halvorsen, vice president of F-35 global sustainment at Lockheed Martin, pointed to several steps the company and the U.S. military have taken to turn around the fighter’s lagging availability in a briefing with reporters at the conference.
In early 2024, Halvorsen said, Lockheed and the F-35 Joint Program Office teamed up to create a “joint model” that spelled out what kind of parts, and how many, would be needed to make F-35s 80 percent mission capable—able to carry out at least one mission—and 65 percent full mission capable.
“It had become very clear that jointly, we [Lockheed and the military] had underinvested in sustainment for the number of jets that we had and flight hours that we wanted to fly,” Halvorsen said.
The team spent about 18 months working on that model, she said, and when it was ready in late summer 2025,, Lockheed made its first $1 billion investment in spare parts.
“We knew what parts were needed, and we didn’t want to wait another year, which is the cycle it would take to get through a congressional budget and get that funding aligned,” Halvorsen said.
Buying that first tranche of spare parts cut out nine or 10 months of lead time, Halvorsen said—and started to position the F-35 for the intense pace of operations that 2026 would bring. Flight hours on all F-35s worldwide are up 25 percent year over year, Halvorsen said, which she said is “putting even more stress on the system.”
But that major infusion of cash didn’t solve everything.
“With all the work we did to buy those initial parts, we realized there were some capacity gaps within the supply chain,” Halvorsen said. “So I could go buy parts, but I wasn’t going to get them in time.”
So Lockheed invested another $1 billion to try to fill that shortfall, Halvorsen said, and figure out what critical components it needed to invest in. That led to a second tranche of spare parts purchases, she said.
In July, the F-35 Joint Program Office awarded Lockheed a record $1.6 billion contract for critical spare parts, which Halvorsen said “liquidated” some of the first tranche of parts Lockheed had bought.
Halvorsen also said Lockheed plans to do more advanced procurement of spare parts to be ready for 2027 and further shrink supply times. That kind of buy-ahead is needed to fully engage the vast array of subcontractors that make F-35 parts, she said—and shows why multiyear purchase agreements for both production and sustainment are so important for the fighter.
“We’re going to keep the supply chain engaged, because to build the capacity, you have to have the demand,” Halvorsen said. “So if you don’t put your total demand into the supply chain, they will never build to the capacity that you need. … We think it’ll drive down overall cost, because if you buy year-to-year, you’re certainly paying for that sort of thing.”

Geneva talks put Rwanda-DRC peace deal to the test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
00:26:06 UTC
09:26:06 KST

Geneva talks put Rwanda-DRC peace deal to the test
The talks come amid continued fighting and disputes over the implementation of key security commitments.
Officials from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda are due to reconvene in Geneva on September 16 and 17 for talks on the implementation of the 2025 Washington Accords.
The two-day meeting of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (JSCM) will bring together representatives of the two countries, with mediators from the United States, Qatar, Togo and the African Union Commission. The mechanism was established to monitor and coordinate the implementation of security commitments between the two countries.
The meeting comes as fighting continues in the eastern DRC and key commitments under the peace process remain unresolved.
The peace agreement between the DRC and Rwanda was signed in Washington, DC on June 27, 2025. The Washington Accords for Peace and Prosperity, signed on December 4, reaffirmed the parties’ commitment to implementing that agreement.
Among the key security commitments are the DRC’s obligation to neutralise the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and Rwanda’s disengagement of forces and lifting of defensive measures.
What is at stake?
The September talks will focus on whether the two sides can make further progress on those commitments.
The agreement is part of a wider diplomatic effort to end decades of conflict in the eastern DRC, a region bordering Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi that has been plagued by armed groups and repeated fighting.
The conflict has repeatedly drawn neighbouring countries into the eastern DRC. Rwanda has long said armed groups operating from DRC territory pose a threat to its security, while the Congolese government has accused Kigali of supporting armed groups seeking to seize territory and influence in the east.
“The Washington Accords reaffirm the parties’ commitment to implement the Peace Agreement between the DRC and Rwanda, agreed to in Washington, June 2025, and achieve the vision of the Regional Economic Integration Framework, to create a bold roadmap for peace, security, and unprecedented economic growth,” a US Department of State spokesperson said.
But fighting has continued.
A September forecast by Security Council Report said clashes between the Congolese Armed Forces (FARDC) and the M23 armed group had continued in North and South Kivu, two provinces in the eastern DRC. It also said two central obligations under the Washington process, the neutralisation of the FDLR and Rwanda’s lifting of defensive measures, had yet to be declared complete.
Rwanda has repeatedly accused the DRC of supporting, arming and working alongside the FDLR.
The FDLR has its roots in forces and militias that fled Rwanda after the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. Some of its members were linked to the former Rwandan army and the Interahamwe militia. The group has remained active in the eastern DRC and has long been a central security concern for Rwanda.
Kinshasa, meanwhile, has accused Rwanda of supporting M23, allegations Kigali denies.
M23 first emerged as a major armed movement in 2012. After withdrawing from territory it controlled, it resurfaced in 2022 and launched a new offensive in the eastern DRC.
The group made major territorial gains in 2025, including the capture of Goma, the capital of North Kivu province, and Bukavu, the capital of neighbouring South Kivu.
Although M23 is not a party to the Washington agreement, it remains central to efforts to end the wider conflict.
The US-backed process requires Rwanda and the DRC to support a separate Qatar-led dialogue between Kinshasa and M23. That process produced the Doha Framework for Peace, signed by the Congolese government and the Congo River Alliance (AFC/M23) in Doha on November 15, 2025.
Where things stand
The September meeting follows the sixth JSCM meeting, held in Geneva on August 12 and 13.
At that meeting, the DRC and Rwanda agreed to advance two initiatives aimed at strengthening monitoring and verification of the Washington Accords on the ground. They asked the US to consider the initiatives and provide feedback at the next JSCM meeting.
The DRC also presented its Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration (DDR) plan for the FDLR and responded to questions from JSCM members.
The parties also agreed to hold a trilateral planning conference in October that will culminate in a revised operations order guiding their coordinated efforts.
The FDLR dispute
The neutralisation of the FDLR is expected to remain one of the most difficult issues.
On July 28, the Congolese government said a faction of the FDLR had accepted and signed a protocol covering disarmament, demobilisation and cantonment. Kinshasa presented the move as progress towards meeting its obligations under the Washington agreement.
Rwanda rejected the move, arguing that the Washington agreement requires the FDLR to be neutralised rather than negotiated with. Kigali has also accused Kinshasa of continuing to support the group.
The disagreement matters because progress on the FDLR is tied to Rwanda’s own commitments under the Washington process.
Rwanda has maintained that its security measures along the border with the DRC are necessary to protect the country from armed groups operating in the eastern DRC. Under the Washington agreement, Rwanda is expected to disengage its forces and lift those defensive measures as part of the wider security arrangements.
For the September meeting, the FDLR issue will remain a central point of contention as the two countries try to resolve the commitments that remain at the heart of their dispute.

The Supreme Court Just Blocked Trump’s Efforts to Control Mail-In Voting for the Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
00:23:42 UTC
09:23:42 KST

The Supreme Court has rejected the Trump administration’s bid to impose severe restrictions on mail-in voting just weeks ahead of the midterms.
The court, which was divided 7-2, with conservative justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissenting, upheld a lower court’s injunction blocking the United States Postal Service from implementing new rules around who can receive a mail-in ballot ahead of November’s vote.
Under this new rule, states would have had to submit lists of eligible voters to the Postal Service, which would then confirm that ballots were sent only to people on that list. The USPS does not typically hold such a role.
“The Government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court’s preliminary injunction,” Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote in a concurring opinion with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson.
Kavanaugh did add, however, that “there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority. But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious … because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”
Voting by mail has also already begun in some states ahead of November’s elections, making the implementation of this plan even more difficult for Americans across the country to vote.
This is a major loss for President Donald Trump, who has long railed against mail-in voting, claiming without evidence that it led to election fraud, and the latest legal defeat the president and his administration have faced in a multipronged approach to undermine trust in US elections.
The White House and the USPS did not respond to a request for comment about the ruling.
“Today, Donald Trump lost another battle in his unconstitutional war to choose his own voters, and the American people are winners,” Cisco Aguilar, Nevada’s secretary of state, wrote in an emailed statement. “This ruling affirms what our Constitution has always held: Elections belong to the American people, not a desperate man in Washington. Democratic secretaries of state applaud the court on upholding this fundamental principle, and we stand ready to fight any attempt to cause chaos, fear, and intimidation in our elections.”
The mail-in voting battle has occurred since the spring, when the president signed an executive order in March titled “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections.” The order demanded that all states send the Postal Service a list of voters who would receive mail-in ballots. In turn, the USPS could refuse to deliver ballots to voters not on the lists or ballots that didn’t comply with new rules around barcodes and envelopes.
The majority of the provisions of the executive order were quickly blocked by federal courts before the Trump administration appealed the rulings to the Supreme Court in July. Last month, the conservative court ruled along ideological lines to allow the new rules to proceed, writing that the states that sought to block the rules didn’t have standing because the rules hadn’t been implemented yet.
In the wake of the ruling, a USPS whistleblower claimed that the online portal for the new rules had been hastily thrown together without the necessary care and attention needed for such a critical piece of software.
“The whistleblower’s allegations make clear that USPS lacks the technical or operational capability needed to effectively implement the [executive order’s] provisions in a way that safeguards every citizen’s right to vote in the upcoming midterm elections,” Senator Richard Blumenthal, who disclosed the whistleblower's warning, wrote in a letter to the postmaster general. “Despite this, the Trump administration appears intent on USPS moving forward with its flawed plans, no matter the chaos they may create.”

What is celebrated on September 15 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
03:15:55 EEST
09:15:55 KST

What is celebrated on September 15 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On September 15, the United Nations International Day of Democracy, World Lymphoma Awareness Day, and the national holidays of five Central American countries are observed. The faithful honor Nicetas the Goth.
On September 15, the world observes the UN-sponsored International Day of Democracy, Battle of Britain Day, and the Independence Days of five Central American countries, while according to the church calendar under the new style, Saint Great Martyr Nicetas the Goth is commemorated, UNN writes.
International Day of Democracy
An official international UN observance established by the General Assembly in 2007 at the initiative of the Inter-Parliamentary Union. The date marks the 20th anniversary of the adoption of the Universal Declaration on Democracy in September 1997. The day is intended to draw attention to the importance of respecting human rights, the rule of law, freedom of speech, holding free elections, and actively engaging citizens in state processes, emphasizing that democracy is not only a goal but also an ongoing process of building a just society.
World Lymphoma Awareness Day
A global medical and educational initiative established in 2004 by the international organization Lymphoma Coalition. The event aims to raise public awareness of malignant tumors of the lymphatic system, draw attention to the first symptoms of the disease, and promote timely detection and patients' access to modern immunotherapy and chemotherapy methods.
Software Freedom Day
A global unofficial celebration of the IT community dedicated to promoting free and open-source software (FOSS) and users' digital rights. Launched in 2004, it brings together programmers and developers to exchange experience in creating free operating systems, open algorithms, and tools that ensure transparency, privacy, and independence from monopolistic technology corporations.
Independence Day of the Central American Countries (Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, El Salvador)
A joint principal national holiday of five Central American states commemorating the signing, on September 15, 1821, in Guatemala City, of the Act of Independence of Central America from the Spanish Empire. The holiday is traditionally marked by the "Torch of Freedom" relay, which passes through all five countries, school parades, national dances, and ceremonial raising of national flags.
Battle of Britain Day in the United Kingdom
A military commemoration established in honor of the decisive air battle of September 15, 1940, during World War II, when the Royal Air Force (RAF) successfully repelled the largest daytime raid by the German Luftwaffe on London. The defeat of the German air force forced Adolf Hitler to postpone and later completely cancel Operation "Sea Lion," the planned invasion of the British Isles.
Engineers' Day in India
An official professional holiday established in 1968 in honor of the birthday of Sir Mokshagundam Visvesvaraya (1861–1962), an outstanding Indian civil engineer, statesman, and creator of the country's foundational hydraulic structures, dams, and irrigation systems. The holiday recognizes the significant contribution of engineering sciences to the modernization of infrastructure and the state's economic development.
Feast Day of Saint Great Martyr Nicetas the Goth
Under the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saint Great Martyr Nicetas the Goth—a Christian soldier of the fourth century who preached the Gospel among the Goths on the banks of the Danube and was burned to death on the orders of the pagan ruler Athanaric after brutal torture. The Post-feast of the Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Giving Cross of the Lord also continues on this day, as believers glorify the Cross as a symbol of salvation.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate the holy martyr Mamant, as well as his parents, Theodotus and Rufina, who suffered martyrdom in the 3rd century for refusing to offer sacrifices to pagan gods. In addition, this day commemorates the Venerable John the Faster, Patriarch of Constantinople (6th century), and the Venerable Anthony and Theodosius of the Caves — the founders of the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra and the progenitors of Ukrainian monasticism.

In loss for Trump, Supreme Court won’t let US Postal Service restrict mail ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
00:10:00 UTC
09:10:00 KST

In loss for Trump, Supreme Court won’t let US Postal Service restrict mail ballots
- The US Supreme Court blocked the Postal Service from enforcing a new rule restricting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to Trump's efforts to limit mail voting before the midterm elections.
- The contested rule required states to provide voter lists and use USPS-approved envelopes with barcodes, but courts found it likely unconstitutional and disruptive to voting.
- Voting rights groups and Democratic-led states praised the decision, emphasising election laws belong to states and Congress, not the president or USPS, protecting voters' constitutional rights.
AI generated
The US Supreme Court declined on Sept 14 to let the United States Postal Service (USPS) enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump’s effort to restrict voting by mail ahead of November’s midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
The justices denied the Department of Justice’s request to lift a ruling by Boston-based US District Judge Indira Talwani that blocked the USPS from enforcing the measure while legal challenges by states and voting rights groups proceed.
The agency adopted the measure after Trump issued a March executive order aimed at tightening rules governing mail voting.
“The government is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the District Court’s preliminary injunction,” the court said in its brief, one-paragraph order.
Justice Samuel Alito, joined by fellow conservative Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented from the Sept 14 decision, writing that the Trump administration “is likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal”.
Trump’s fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms. Restricting mail-in ballots would stand to benefit Republicans given that Democratic voters disproportionately use mail-in ballots, according to various surveys.
Under the rule, states must provide lists of mail ballot recipients to the USPS and use agency-approved outbound and return ballot mail envelopes outfitted with unique barcodes. 
The USPS could then refuse to send out ballots that do not comply with the new standards or are associated with voters who do not appear on the lists.
Critics have said the plan could disrupt the delivery of thousands of legitimate ballots as the Nov 3 vote approaches and cause chaos given imminent plans by many states to send out mail ballots to eligible voters.
Talwani imposed an injunction on Sept 4 blocking the rule, finding that it likely violated the US Constitution, under which states administer elections.
Talwani also said it would be impossible for the states to comply given the rapidly approaching midterms.
Another federal judge, Washington-based US District Judge Carl Nichols, also blocked the rule on Sept 13.
‘Testing the limits’
Sophia Lin Lakin, voting rights project director at the American Civil Liberties Union, which helped to represent some of the challengers to the USPS rule, welcomed the Sept 14 decision.
“This administration keeps testing the limits of its power, as if the rules governing our elections are merely suggestions to ignore when they don’t suit the President’s agenda,” she said.
“But the Constitution gives states and Congress the power to set the rules for federal elections – not the president, and not the Postal Service,” she added.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose state led one of the lawsuits against the rule, said: “Today is a good day for democracy, the rule of law and the American people looking to exercise their constitutional right to vote.
“Trump’s attacks on democracy these last 20 months have been nothing short of un-American.”
Trump signed his executive order targeting mail-in ballots after years of casting doubt on their security, though he often votes by mail himself. 
Trump has made false claims of widespread fraud in US elections, including his 2020 loss to former Democratic president Joe Biden.
The administration in a Sept 6 emergency request urged the Supreme Court to allow it to implement an “important federal policy to protect the mails from being used to commit voter fraud”.
Conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh, in a concurring statement on Sept 14, said there is a “fair prospect” that the rule falls within the USPS’ authority.
He said, however, that state and local election officials “do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule” before the 2026 elections.
In his dissent, Alito likened some of the challengers’ claims to a “Hail Mary pass” that is “unlikely to be successfully completed”, using a football analogy.
“The Postal Service has broad authority to regulate the mail,” Alito added.
States challenged the rule
A coalition of states, most of them Democratic-governed, and Washington DC, as well as a number of voting rights groups, challenged the new USPS rule.
The Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals refused on Sept 10 to put Talwani’s order on hold. 
The 1st Circuit said that the rule “will likely result in the disenfranchisement of millions of voters across the country while providing minimal – if any – gains in combating voter fraud”.
The battle over mail ballots is one in a series of efforts by the administration to boost federal involvement in voting ahead of the midterms. 
On Aug 24, the Supreme Court lifted an earlier injunction imposed by Talwani in June blocking Trump’s executive order, including the USPS rule before it had been finalised. REUTERS

CMSAF to Airmen: Use AI or ‘End Up in Everyone’s Rearview Mirror’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
00:06:57 UTC
09:06:57 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Today’s Airmen are going to have to embrace artificial intelligence the same way Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David R. Wolfe learned to love desktop computers and email in the 1990s, the senior enlisted Airman said Sept. 14 during AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Wolfe has taken a strong stance on the advantages AI will offer the the Air Force and Airmen of all ranks at a time when much of society remains skeptical over how much control to give the rapidly advancing technology.
“We must overcome this fear if we’re going to fully realize the power of AI,” Wolfe said. “If you choose not to use AI, you are going to end up in everyone’s rearview mirror. … Artificial intelligence will not replace the judgment, discipline, or ingenuity of Airmen, but it can help us see farther down the track, anticipate problems sooner, and make better decisions at the speed the future will demand.”
Wolfe added that the creation of AI isn’t much different from the creation of personal computers and email, innovations he had to learn to adapt to more than 30 years ago.
“When I was given my first email address, honestly, I was skeptical,” Wolfe said, describing how he questioned, “where does this go when I hit send? How do I know who got to the right person? How do I know this is safe?”
“The questions felt pretty reasonable at the time,” he added. “I also thought my leadership was crazy when they told me every desk would soon have a computer on it, but I was wrong. Technology kept moving. We had to learn it, understand it, and figure out how to use it responsibly.”
Shortly after becoming CMSAF late last year, Wolfe stood up an AI Action Team that initially started with 40 members.
“Today we sit at over 200; we brought Airmen together from across the Air Force and asked them to take real problems they understood and see where AI could help,” Wolfe said, adding that the team is “completely rank agnostic” and that the most influential members are often junior Airmen.
Wolfe previously said in May that the service is developing a new training program to ensure every Airman is educated on how to use AI in their everyday job, just weeks after the Air Force released its artificial intelligence strategy.
Noting that he understands the general skepticism around AI, Wolfe said his goal is to reduce the fear many Airmen have of using AI, primarily broken down between two camps: those who worry that AI makes mistakes, and those that fear AI will replace them.
To the former, Wolfe said, “my response is ‘Well, sometimes, so are you.’”
To the latter, Wolfe said, “we’re in an age where that kind of learning is going to be taking place, and the machines are going to be able to make the decisions sometimes at a higher success rate than we will.”
But he stressed that “these capabilities are going to be additive at this point.”
Eventually, Wolfe said, AI may automate enough tasks that leaders can repurpose manpower “to do something else that only humans can do,’’ adding “Why wouldn’t we do that?”
“We’re going to have to make decisions like that sometime in the future,” he said. “But I think it’ll be it’ll be additive as we go on. Think of AI as an increase to the manpower in your units, folks.”
Wolfe encouraged Airmen to let AI allow them “to imagine solutions that were previously unavailable because of human limitations.”
“Technology will keep moving, just like it did when computers and email started showing up on our desks,” Wolfe said. “Our choice is whether we learn fast enough to move with it.”

Houthis strike Saudi targets anew as talks over Strait of Hormuz stall
RIYADH, Sept 15 - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis launched a new wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia and were digging into positions on the western coast of Yemen along the Red Sea, Yemeni officials said, as urgent deliberations took place in Riyadh over how to respond to their lightning advance.
Meanwhile, Gulf Arab states postponed planned talks with Iran, raising concerns the Middle East conflict could spread further and threaten global oil supplies.
The Houthis on Monday said they fired dozens of missiles and drones at a military airbase in Khamis Mushait in southern Saudi Arabia, targeting aircraft hangars, radar systems, runways and ammunition depots in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen.
Saudi authorities issued emergency alerts there and in three other southern cities. Thirteen civilians were wounded in the Houthi attacks, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.
The Houthi advances in recent days, including the taking of Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea, have put further pressure on Saudi oil exports after an aerial attack on Thursday knocked Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline offline. Riyadh blamed the pipeline attack on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
Saudi Arabia built the 1,200-kilometer (745-mile) pipeline across its territory from the Gulf to the Red Sea in the 1980s to bypass the Strait of Hormuz when it came under threat from the Iran-Iraq war at that time.
Traders said a prolonged shutdown of the Saudi pipeline could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply while the strait is largely blockaded. Riyadh has not said when operations might resume.
Responding to the Houthi offensive, the Saudi and Yemeni air forces have stepped up aerial bombardment of Houthi targets, including around the historic Red Sea port of Mocha, but the Houthis have maintained effective control over almost the entire western coast of the country along the Red Sea, the officials with Yemen's internationally recognised government said.
“The Houthis are being put under heavy pressure. They in turn are putting more and more pressure on the Saudis, increasing their campaign of missile and drone attacks,” one of the Yemeni officials said.
Crude oil prices rose more than 4% on Monday before settling about 1% higher.
AMERICANS HESITANT TO STEP IN
The renewed Yemen conflict poses another challenge for U.S. President Donald Trump.
Three sources have told Reuters that Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention beyond intelligence support. Trump said over the weekend he had spoken with the Saudi crown prince and that the Houthis had also contacted Washington urging it to stay out of the conflict.
Saudi state media reported that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met U.S. regional commander Admiral Brad Cooper in Jeddah on Monday.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015, but the conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in recent years. Fighting reignited this month, with the Houthis pushing back forces aligned with the internationally recognised government.
HOPES FOR DIPLOMACY FADE
Oman had been due to host a meeting on Monday with Iran and Gulf states to discuss negotiations aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried 20% of the world's oil exports. But Oman announced that the meeting had been postponed. Iran said the postponement was at the request of Saudi Arabia.
Trump on Monday repeated his frequent claim that Iran was eager to make a deal quickly, but Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called the president's message a distraction, saying on X, "No talks until Iran's conditions are met."
Underscoring the volatility of shipping through the region, conflicting reports circulated about how and when an oil tanker was damaged.
Without giving a date, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said the Panamanian-flagged oil tanker El Gaia was hit by sea mines as it passed through a prohibited zone south of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Fars news agency reported on Monday.
But the U.S. military's Central Command immediately said the report was false and the tanker was "struck by an Iranian missile last month and rendered inoperable."
The United Nations' International Maritime Organization reported El Gaia was damaged on Saturday, but did not say how, and that two seafarers were missing.
Reuters could not immediately contact the ship's owners in Dubai to verify any of the accounts.
The world's most important oil shipping lane has been mostly shut down since the war began on February 28 as Iran has threatened vessels that transit the waterway without its authority.
"The IRGC Navy firmly declares that the Strait of Hormuz is closed and still under our smart control," the Revolutionary Guards said in the statement. REUTERS
