One Nation MP open to slashing family visas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
19:00:58 UTC
04:00:58 KST

One Nation MP flags 'potential' slashing of visas for partners, children of Australian citizens
In short:
One Nation MP David Farley says his party is open to cutting visas for family members of Australian citizens.
On Monday, One Nation unveiled its policy to reduce Australia's temporary migration intake by 750,000 people over three years, including a ban on families of temporary skilled workers and international students.
What's next?
Mr Farley said One Nation had commissioned "extensive" economic modelling of its migration plan and would reveal more of the party's immigration strategy.
One Nation MP David Farley has left the door open to "potentially" cutting visas for family members of Australian citizens, as the party prepares to reveal more details of its immigration plan within coming weeks.
Mr Farley said whether the party considered preventing citizens from bringing family members to Australia to live would be dependent on the availability of services, including housing.
"It's a hypothetical question, but can we grow our health system, our education system and other infrastructure we need to make sure the existing population that's here … are not under pressure?" he told the ABC.
On Monday One Nation revealed its plan to reduce Australia's temporary migration intake by 750,000 places over three years, partly by barring the families of temporary skilled migrants and international students from entering the country.
Mr Farley, who previously stated One Nation's migration policy would be "not too different" to Labor's, rejected suggestions that cutting family visas would deter the skilled migrants needed to plug critical workforce shortages from coming to Australia in the first place.
"It is 2026. People have the ability now to work remotely … the reaches of the world are all 12 or 14 hours on a flight, and ultimately in an employment contract of skilled labour, everything is negotiable," he said.
The minor party did not detail what its permanent migration intake would be, but Mr Farley said its immigration plan would be rolled out "completely" within the next fortnight.
Caps on family visa intake 'illegal'
Former deputy secretary of the Immigration Department Abul Rizvi said it would be illegal to cap family visas issued for Australian citizens.
Despite that, Labor's current intake of permanent family visas is limited to 52,460 per year.
"Under section 87 of the migration act, the government doesn't have the legal power to cap visas for the partners and dependent children of Australian citizens and permanent residents," Mr Rizvi said.
"Regardless, successive governments have administratively — and illegally — limited the number of such visas issued."
Mr Rizvi said, as a result, the backlog of partner visa applications was now about 120,000 and growing.
"None of the parties have indicated what they will do about this illegal behaviour," he said.
The government has been contacted for comment.
One Nation to reveal 'complete' migration policy
Meanwhile, One Nation is also facing calls to reveal the economic impact of its proposal to send Australia into "net negative migration" for three years.
Labor frontbencher Murray Watt said the plan would destroy regional economies and likely send Australian into recession, while Shadow Immigration Minister Jonno Duniam demanded to see the party's costings.
Mr Farley said One Nation had commissioned "extensive" economic modelling of its migration plan.
"We've done the modelling and we will roll our strategy out on immigration completely over the next fortnight," he said.
Weeks after Immigration Minister Tony Burke was forced to shelve a speech in which he was expected to unveil sweeping changes to Labor's migration settings, pressure is mounting on the government to unveil its policy to the Australian public.
"I think they're going to be two years too late, but it's critical," Mr Rizvi said.
"Part of the reason for One Nation's strength is because the government has failed to explain its policies, and the merit of those policies, to the Australian public."
Senator Duniam said the Coalition would release its policy, with full costings, within weeks.

====================================================================================================

The RBA says Aussies are 'furious' about inflation. Many are angrier with the bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:52:39 UTC
03:52:39 KST

analysis
There are three main reasons inflation is rising. Higher rates won't fix them
Bloodletting is an ancient therapy, dating back at least three millennia, and traditionally used to "cure" a range of ills.
Whether through leeches or lancets, practitioners drew blood from the patient to rebalance their humours in hopes of a cure.
But the outcomes were no laughing matter for many unfortunates.
Perhaps most famously, the USA's first president, George Washington, had more than one-and-a-half litres of blood removed in an attempted cure for epiglottitis that likely caused, or at least hastened, his death in 1799.
Fortunately for us, the practice fell out of favour as medical science progressed in the 19th century, and is now restricted to a few specific diseases where it has been shown to help.
Unfortunately, the economic equivalent of bloodletting remains the treatment in vogue whenever inflation is the symptom, whatever the underlying cause of the disease.
That panacea is higher interest rates. Draw money out of the economy by jacking up the cost of debt and the patient will recover … if the treatment doesn't kill them.
Rate rises don't fix supply problems
Last week, the Reserve Bank's deputy governor Andrew Hauser told 7.30 that Australia's economy has "one big problem and that's inflation".
Loading...
Echoing words from his boss at her last press conference, Hauser told Sarah Ferguson that:
"Inflation has been above target for a long period of time and, at some point, we will have to say that is long enough."
And, if we get to that point, what's the solution?
"We will raise interest rates further than otherwise we would need to do so," the central banker responded.
"We're not at that point yet, but some of these upside risks to inflation are certainly on our mind."
Loading...
So what exactly are these "upside risks" that could mean inflation is higher and more stubborn than the RBA's existing forecasts? Hauser listed three.
"One is the Middle East and the ongoing crisis there, one is a really unexpected global boom driven by AI, and one is the weakness of the supply potential of the Australian economy," he said.
Will higher Australian interest rates influence any of those things? No.
The US and Iran will not stop attacking each other because Australian mortgages have become more expensive.
The money behind the AI boom is mainly coming from US multinationals, so higher local rates are likely to make little difference to investment in that sector.
Loading...
And higher rates are more likely to weigh on the supply capacity of the Australian economy rather than grow it, as they send some businesses broke (handing their surviving rivals more pricing power) and discourage firms from borrowing to increase capacity and productivity.
As CBA's chief economist Luke Yeaman explained on The Business last week:
"The economy is slowing, but not fast enough for their liking, and an extra rate hike now could help drive that growth down lower and bring it more in line with the supply capacity of the economy."
Hence the analogy with bloodletting. Rising rates mainly lower inflation by destroying demand, hopefully more quickly than they reduce supply.
Loading...
Are Australian home owners paying for the AI boom?
A lot of column inches have already been devoted to the role that the Middle East conflict and Australia's productivity crisis have played in our lingering inflation problem.
However, it is telling that the RBA has elevated the AI boom alongside those issues.
Hours before Andrew Hauser appeared on 7.30, the Reserve Bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter spoke at an AFR property summit.
She said the bank was hearing anecdotes about workers being sucked in, at inflated wages, to build new data centres, adding to cost pressure across the construction sector.
"They want these centres built really rapidly, as fast as possible in some cases, and it's definitely adding to demand," she said.
"You can see business investment has picked up really strongly over the last sort of nine months or so, nine to 12 months, double-digit growth, and a decent chunk of that is data centres."
Research from the Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA), released last week, shows business investment spending is at 12.6 per cent of GDP, its highest level in more than a decade, since the mining boom wound down.
CEDA economist Julie Toth said the boom was driven almost entirely by the information, media and telecoms sector as businesses ramped up investment in data centres, cloud computing and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Investment in this sector almost doubled over the past year.
Comparisons to the mining boom are apt.
Just as investment in that sector, concentrated in WA and Queensland, contributed to interest rates rising around the country and created a two-speed economy earlier this century, the AI boom will inflict pain across other sectors.
With most economists seeing the economy running above capacity, as evidenced by inflation, all the demand added by data centre construction must be offset by the RBA raising rates to smash activity in other areas.
As with the mining boom, much of the benefit from the AI boom will likely be captured by overseas shareholders of the multinational companies driving it, while the costs will be borne domestically through higher interest rates and slower growth in other sectors.
Is the public 'furious' with inflation or angrier with the RBA?
That brings us back to interest rates and the RBA's tricky decision about whether to hike in two weeks.
Markets are pricing in at least a 75 per cent chance the cash rate will rise to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent on September 29.
They are pricing in a virtual certainty of two rate hikes by February, with a 50/50 chance of a third by mid-next year.
A cash rate of 4.85 per cent would be the highest since rates were slashed over late 2008 in response to the global financial crisis.
Andrew Hauser said getting on top of inflation was not only the bank's primary mission, but the community's expectation.
"People are furious about inflation," he said on 7.30.
"It's the most profound message that we get. Everywhere I go, I hear cost, cost, cost, inflation, inflation, inflation. And that's our responsibility. We have to put that right."
The RBA's own community survey shows he's right, with two-thirds of people putting it as one of their top three economic concerns.
But the same survey turned up another finding that has the Reserve Bank worried. They see the RBA as part of the inflation problem, not as the solution.
"Only 25 per cent of respondents assessed correctly that higher interest rates would ultimately lead to lower inflation, while more than half indicated that higher interest rates would lead to higher inflation," the report lamented.
And statements like this from the Reserve Bank governor are unlikely to help those public perceptions.
"People who have mortgages, at least, they see increases in interest rates as an increase in the cost of living, but it's not really," she said in response to my question at a business economists lunch in July.
"So interest rates are the response to high inflation; they're not causing high inflation."
While mortgage repayments may have been deliberately excised from the Consumer Price Index at the RBA's request in the late 1990s, they are a very real cost of living for anyone with a mortgage.
It's no wonder then that a constant refrain in interactions with our audience when we're covering interest rates is, "Surely there are less painful and more effective ways to lower inflation?"
And there potentially are. I wrote about some of these ideas back in May.
But while governments continue outsourcing inflation management to unelected technocrats at central banks who only have access to one treatment, the economic bloodletting is likely to continue.

JR sends giant wave across vatican apostolic library facade with ‘diluvium’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:46:41 UTC
03:46:41 KST

A giant black-and-white wave by JR now stretches across the sixteenth-century facade of the Vatican Apostolic Library. DILUVIUM runs roughly 70 meters across the wall facing the Cortile del Belvedere, catching the water at the instant before it seems ready to crash into the architecture.
Unveiled on September 14th, 2026, the site-specific installation opens AQVA, the first exhibition in the library’s five-year Catastrophe and Wonder cycle, and draws its image from Gustave Doré’s 1866 illustration of the biblical flood.
The idea began with a very practical fear. ‘The library at the Vatican came to see me because, for them, water represents their biggest fear,‘ JR explains. ‘It’s the fact that one day water comes and takes away all the memory … all the trace of a civilization that they’ve been preserving.‘
Set against a building devoted to keeping centuries of knowledge intact, the wave makes that vulnerability immediately visible from across the courtyard.
JR quickly pulls the image of the wave beyond the walls of the Vatican Apostolic Library. ‘This wave talks about way more than that,’ the artist says. He connects it to climate change and extreme heat, then to political polarization and ‘the wave of AI itself.‘ The metaphor keeps widening, but the image stays simple: an enormous body of water bearing down on a place built around preservation.
Doré’s flood gives the work an older visual language, with the drama of a nineteenth-century biblical engraving enlarged to architectural scale. Across the pale Renaissance facade, JR turns a familiar historical image into something that feels unusually current. The threat shifts depending on how you read it. Water can erase an archive in a matter of hours, or technology can absorb the same archive at a scale that would have seemed impossible only a few years ago.
AQVA takes that tension as its starting point. Water can destroy paper, but it also plays a role in the making and restoration of books. JR contributes the site-specific work, DILUVIUM, while the wider exhibition looks at the element through the Vatican Library’s collections and contemporary interventions.
Pope Leo XIV inaugurated the exhibition during his first visit to the Vatican Apostolic Library as pontiff. The public opening follows on September 25th, with AQVA running through May 14th, 2027. Outside, JR’s wave remains the bluntest image in the project, as centuries of stored knowledge sitting behind a facade suddenly looks as if it could disappear beneath water.
from zucchini ballet flats to shoes covered in flowers and dandelion seed heads, the artist turns fleeting plant materials into playful studies of footwear.

Australia needs AI 'early warning system', cyber security chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:44:43 UTC
03:44:43 KST

Australia needs an AI 'early warning system', top cybersecurity chief warns
In short:
Abigail Bradshaw has called for Australian organisations to use AI to defend themselves and share warnings with each other about emerging threats.
Global tech executives last week warned the race to develop AI could outstrip humanity's ability to control it.
What's next?
The federal assistant science minister says Australia should help shape any global slowdown effort.
Australia needs an artificial intelligence "early warning system" to help defend against the dangers of the increasingly powerful technology, according to the nation's cyber intelligence chief.
Australian Signals Directorate director-general Abigail Bradshaw also urged Australian organisations to embrace AI for its defensive capabilities, saying it was one of the crucial tools that the nation needed to protect itself.
It comes as Australian politicians and AI company executives respond to a growing international chorus of warnings the race to develop AI could outstrip humanity's ability to control it.
Speaking at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute's (ASPI) Sydney Dialogue AI Masterclass on Monday, Ms Bradshaw said intelligence and security agencies needed to work with AI companies to identify early risks.
"What we are missing at the moment, which we have in a cyber context but we don't yet have it formalised in an AI context, is an early warning system,"
Ms Bradshaw said bringing together reports of individual incidents would help identify wider patterns, adding that these risks extended beyond cybersecurity to areas such as biotechnology.
The public servant, who is tasked with Australia's cyber offensive capabilities, balanced the warning with a more optimistic assessment about AI capabilities helping those tasked with defence.
Loading...
She pointed to existing cyber partnerships between government and industry, and international arrangements for quickly sharing technical information.
Australian government agencies had been granted access to major AI companies' cutting-edge models that were limited from wide release.
She confirmed that this included Anthropic's Mythos, which was temporarily restricted after the US government placed it under an export control, and OpenAI's cyber versions of their models.
Ms Bradshaw said her agency used this access to help Australian organisations fortify their systems and identify potential vulnerabilities.
"What would have taken cybersecurity experts in ASD weeks and weeks of work has been done in hours," she said.
Ms Bradshaw urged organisations to maintain basic security measures while using AI to defend their networks.
Defenders needed capabilities on par with those available to cybercriminals and state-backed attackers, she said.
In a separate panel on Monday, Australia's AI Safety Institute general manager Kate Conroy urged companies and agencies to let their teams, or their staff, experiment with advanced AI.
"If you don't already have it your teams are probably already doing it in their free time,"
Calls for global AI slowdown
In July, more than a thousand employees of leading AI companies signed onto an open letter that called for the US government to step in to help pave the way for an AI development slowdown.
Loading...
In the past week the high-profile resignation of Anthropic staffer Jacob Coxon and an essay published by the company's chief executive reignited a global conversation over a global slowdown effort.
Australia's assistant science minister, Andrew Charlton, told the ASPI conference that Australia should help shape the response.
"I am not in favour of leaving it to the companies and I'm not in favour of leaving it to the superpowers,"
Mr Charlton said governments should assume AI would keep becoming more capable, given companies' financial incentives, and despite executives discussing slowing down.
OpenAI vice-president of global policy Ann O'Leary told the event the company was working with governments and AI safety bodies, such as Australia's AI Safety Institute, as well as providing models for review before release.
But, she said, the absence of wider laws slowing development meant OpenAI and other companies were employing their own voluntary co-ordination efforts to "pace" progress.
Ms O'Leary said OpenAI was eager to train its AI models in Australia, saying it was in talks with the federal government about copyright.
"We are deep in conversation with the Australian government about these questions," she said.
"You have caught our attention."

Canada Seeks 'Unique Alliance' With E.U. Amid U.S. Trade War. Here's What It Could Look Like
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:32:01 UTC
03:32:01 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is seeking a “unique alliance” with the European Union as he aims to strengthen international ties amid a deepening trade war with the U.S.
“What we are looking, and will begin discussions for, [is] a unique alliance with the European Union,” Carney told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday. “We share the same values, we have the same priorities, and we have very complementary strengths.”
Canada’s European pivot has been months in the making, following growing tensions between Carney’s government and the Trump Administration. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect last week, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. after negotiations collapsed last month. Carney has encouraged Canadians to take back economic power at the kitchen table, and many have embraced a boycott of U.S. products. Trump has also repeatedly threatened Canada’s sovereignty, speaking openly of his desire to annex the country and make it the “51st state.”
The U.S. accounted for 72.5% of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025, according to the country's annual trade report, making it Canada’s largest trading partner. But Carney is keen to build an international support network that isn’t reliant on the U.S.
At the E.U.-Canada summit in June 2025, Canada established a new Security and Defense Partnership with the bloc. “Our partnership is grounded in the core values we share: democracy, human rights, the rule of law, and open, rules-based markets," read a joint statement marking the occasion.
In January, Carney notably met with China’s President Xi Jinping to forge what he referred to as a “new strategic partnership” to end Canada's economic reliance on the American market. Carney agreed to cut his country’s 100% tariff on Chinese electric cars in return for lower tariffs on Canadian farm products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
Continuing with these efforts, Carney on Monday brought together executives and senior leaders from global investment firms to encourage them to invest in the country at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto.
He’s heading for a three-day trip to Europe on Tuesday, where he’ll meet with various European leaders including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. He’s also set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday, in what could symbolize the mark of a new era between Canada and Europe.
Here’s a look at the alliance options on the table between Canada and the bloc, and what that could mean for U.S.-Canada relations.
Is Canada trying to join the E.U.?
Canada is not looking to join the E.U. as a member, Carney clarified amid questions over what a firmer relationship between his country and the 27-member bloc might look like.
“We’re not looking to become a member,” Carney said, emphasizing he’s instead keen to form an alliance. “We’re stronger together, and this is at a time where the world’s more dangerous and divided, and friends need to stick together in these times.”
Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union explicitly states that any “European State” can apply for membership, making Canada ineligible.
However, a report in the Wall Street Journal, quoting officials from both sides, said Carney is keen for Canada to become an “associate member” of the E.U.
When approached for comment, the European Commission directed TIME to remarks made during a Monday press briefing in Brussels.
“Canada is a strategically important partner for the European Union, and indeed a close friend,” the European Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill told reporters. “We deeply value this co-operation. You will recall that at our E.U.-Canada summit last year, we set a very high level of ambition for cooperation across the board, this year our ambition is even higher.”
When asked directly what discussions had taken place between Canadian and European officials, or what this “unique alliance” could look like, Gill declined to answer.
TIME has reached out to the Canadian Prime Minister’s office for comment.
Frank Schimmelfennig, a professor of European politics at ETH Zurich, predicts that Canada may wish to pursue deeper cooperation through additional trade agreements, or take inspiration from countries that have close relationships with the bloc without being E.U. members.
“Canada is already one of the most integrated non-European countries. It has the densest network of institutional relationships with the E.U.,” he tells TIME, referencing the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), a major free-trade deal between the E.U. and Canada, signed in 2016, and Horizon Europe, an initiative on collaborative research launched by the European Union in 2021 and joined by Canada in 2024.
“Canada could have more of the same, which means additional sectoral agreements for sectors that haven't been covered yet,” he says. “That would basically be a lateral extension of the current relationship. Anything more, would mean access to the internal market which would require an arrangement like the EEA.”
The European Economic Area (EEA) includes countries such as Iceland and Norway, which are not members of the E.U., and provides for the free movement of goods, services, and people within the E.U.’s member states, while enabling cooperation across multiple industries.
“The EEA countries have access to the E.U. internal market in return for adopting the relevant E.U. regulations and directives, so that would be a much denser legal integration than what Canada has now,” says Schimmelfennig.
Burgeoning E.U. relationship comes amid deepening U.S.-Canada trade rift
At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney declared a "rupture" in the international rules-based order. He said "great powers" were using tariffs and financial systems as instruments of coercion. He did not directly name Trump or the U.S.
The speech came at a moment of acute transatlantic tension over Trump’s push to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland and his short-lived threats to tariff European allies until Denmark relented.
Patrick Leblond, an associate professor at the University of Ottawa, says Carney’s movements now are in response to the world “seeing a United States that is becoming more protectionist, nationalist, and willing to use its leverage points to gain concessions, including on very close allies like Canada and Europeans.”
“For Canada, [the consensus is] we need to do more with partners who share our values based on liberal democracy, open markets, rule of law, international agreements, and the first port of call for Carney is the European Union,” Leblond tells TIME.
These trade efforts, he continues, may allow Carney to “build momentum, and hopefully bring other countries” into a broader coalition of what the Canadian leader has often called “middle powers."
In July, Carney, in a joint op-ed with Finland’s President Alexander Stubb, urged the “middle powers of the world” to “unite.”
Championing middle power countries that possess significant economic power and diplomatic influence, but lack market or military power, the leaders implored: “In a rapidly changing world, we have the grit and the sisu to chart the path ahead—and we know that so have many others whom we invite to join us on this quest.”
Leblod explains that “ultimately trust has been eroded” with the U.S. and Canada must re-think its place in the wider global economy in the long-term.
“The first time we thought Trump was a blimp, but he's not, and we're looking at what's happening in terms of democracy and political polarization, and a lot of Canadians think we can't rely on the U.S.,” he says.
According to a poll by Nanos Research, conducted between Aug. 30 and Sept. 2, 74% of Canadians disagreed that “the U.S. is a trustworthy ally of Canada.” An earlier poll by Angus Reid Institute, conducted between July 10-14, found that 42% of respondents said they think the Canadian government should approach the U.S. as an enemy/potential threat.
The E.U. has also clashed with Trump over tariffs, his Greenland annexation threats, and the wider split between the U.S. President and several European leaders.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in February warned of “a deep rift” between Europe and the United States, arguing that the latter “will not be powerful enough to go it alone.” But relations have since soured further amid the fallout of the Iran war, particularly between Merz and Trump.
Meanwhile, Canada has also embraced Europe in the cultural space. It was announced earlier this year that Canada will join the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027, becoming the first new participant since Australia in 2015.
Carney to address European Parliament
Carney’s highly-anticipated speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg this week stems from an invitation extended by European Parliament president Roberta Metsola.
Leblond predicts Carney will use the speech “to reiterate a lot of the things he mentioned at Davos,” but with a strong, intentional focus on the E.U.
“I would expect that he will use that address to call on the E.U. to work with Canada to push this idea of co-operation beyond the North Atlantic and include partners and allies in the Indo-Pacific,” he says.
The Canadian leader is also expected to be a guest at the State of the European Union debate, where European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is due to deliver a speech outlining the Commission's work and plans for the future.
Von der Leyen called E.U.–Canada ties “one of the closest partnerships in the world” when she celebrated 50 years of E.U. diplomatic presence in Canada in May. She declared the two sides were “closer than ever” as they confronted wars, an energy crisis and “new fractures in old alliances.”
Schimmelfennig says Canada inching closer to the E.U. is a strong display of “how both partners are affected by the deteriorating transatlantic relationship” with the U.S. “They feel that they need to move together because the world is getting more dangerous, and more difficult for both [parties],” he says.

Argentina's Milei plans bill to toughen sanctions against firms operating in Falklands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:31:42 UTC
03:31:42 KST

Argentina's Milei plans bill to toughen sanctions against firms operating in Falklands
BUENOS AIRES, Sept 14 - Argentine President Javier Milei is preparing legislation this week to toughen sanctions against companies operating in the Falkland Islands, a move analysts say raises uncertainty over whether he may escalate tensions with Britain by targeting other sectors of the disputed islands' economy.
The proposed bill will build on sanctions proceedings that Argentina's government says it has opened against at least 60 companies and individuals linked to offshore oil exploration around the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and claims as its own even though Britain controls them. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982 and fought a 10-week war over them before surrendering to Britain.
Congress is set to receive Milei's 2027 budget proposal by Tuesday. It is expected to boost defense spending to address a sharper focus on sovereignty issues.
This month, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested Washington could reconsider its traditionally neutral position on the Falklands dispute. Since then, Argentina has accelerated efforts to target companies involved in oil drilling activities around the islands.
Milei's proposed legislation includes tougher penalties for unauthorized operations around the islands, congressional aide Marcelo Seghini told Reuters. He said it would extend sanctions to affiliates and cover other activities affecting Argentina's natural resources.
It follows a criminal complaint filed last week against companies linked to the Sea Lion offshore project in the Falklands.
Argentina's government has not responded to Reuters requests for comment or provided a list of companies facing sanctions proceedings, though names have been reported by local media.
Analysts said they were uncertain about the scope of Milei's proposed "national sovereignty defense" bill but called his sanctions an aggressive effort to translate Argentina's sovereignty claims into legal and commercial pressure.
"It was not a project developed over time or meticulously prepared," said Marcelo Elizondo, Argentina's representative to the International Chamber of Commerce. Trump's comments, he said, "created a climate that the government sought to exploit quickly."
Companies and investors are weighing whether sanctions could ultimately affect firms with operations in Argentina, including those involved in the country's vast Vaca Muerta shale oil formation.
The government has already faced pushback over the reported sanctions. Dutch geodata specialist Fugro published a statement saying it had been incorrectly identified by local media as collaborating with the Sea Lion project, adding that its activities in the area were limited to work on a sub-sea telecommunications cable.
BROAD SANCTIONS
Experts said the measures could complicate development of the Sea Lion project by creating a chilling effect around companies working with project owners Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration.
Both companies have said the oilfield project holds valid licenses from the Falkland Islands government and have indicated they do not expect Milei's actions to derail development.
A government document reviewed by Reuters included a range of shareholders and financial intermediaries among companies marked for possible sanctions. They included Vanguard, First Eagle, Canaccord, Aberdeen-owned Interactive Investor and Hargreaves Lansdown.
Oil majors SLB, Baker Hughes and Halliburton have said in recent days they would not participate in activities on the islands.
“Without major service companies, one would have to turn to mid-sized firms with less established technical capabilities—companies that might be more expensive or slower to mobilize,” Juan Jose Carbajales, a former undersecretary of hydrocarbons in the former center-left government of President Alberto Fernández.
Seghini, the congressional aide, told Reuters the Milei government was considering expanding sanctions to the fishing industry in the expected legislation, potentially targeting a sector that underpins much of the Falkland Islands economy.
"The more you widen the supply chain, the more risk you run that these sanctions will be costly to you," said Federico Merke, a political scientist at the University of San Andres in Buenos Aires.
OPPOSITION PRESSURE
The sovereignty package will be a legislative test for Milei, whose libertarian coalition lacks majorities in Congress and has struggled to secure support for some economic reforms.
Center and left-wing opponents have long accused libertarian Milei of not doing enough to defend Argentina's claim on the Malvinas, and they now say he is acting for political reasons ahead of a likely 2027 reelection bid.
"He is clearly using the Malvinas for political opportunism," said Aldo Leiva, an opposition lawmaker. "If he wanted to defend the sovereignty of the Malvinas in these two years of government, he had the tools to do it."
Marcelo Garcia, a Buenos Aires analyst at the consultancy Horizon Engage, said Milei’s legislation makes investors uneasy because it may help the opposition force him to escalate measures against the United Kingdom.
“There was already concern about the elections next year, what if there’s a populist backlash in Argentina?” said Garcia.
Francisco Cafiero, a former secretary for international relations at the defense ministry, said the episode reflected a broader lack of strategic clarity.
"Here, we navigate amidst uncertainty and improvisation," he said. REUTERS

Air Force Leaders Eye Point Defense Acquisition Czar, Say It’s No Longer a ‘Side Hustle’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:23:59 UTC
03:23:59 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Air Force officials are exploring the idea of creating a new acquisition office to oversee the point defense mission, in the service’s latest move to intensify its focus on defending airbases from drone and missile attacks, Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink said Sept. 14, during AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Since late 2023, the Air Force has been racing to get ahead of rapidly growing drone threat after unidentified drones hovered unchecked over Langley Air Force Base, Va., catching base commanders off guard. Since then, the service has been on a steady march to bolster airbase defense against drones and other new missile threats with everything from new doctrine on the “Point Defense of Air Bases” to plans for creating a point defense career field to ensure personnel are trained and equipped to defend bases from aerial attack.
Meink and Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach both devoted significant portions of their keynote addresses at the conference to point defense—reflecting the growing focus and urgency from senior leadership to tackle the issue.
“We can no longer treat point defense as a side hustle,” Wilsbach declared. “We must make it a core function of air and space power.”
On the personnel side, the new point defense career field will be operational in two years, Wilsbach said. Already, the Air Force has selected its first two career field managers—Wilsbach recognized one of them during his keynote.
On the acquisition side, the Air Force is now considering standing up a new portfolio acquisition executive, or PAE, to focus on “the kit side” of point defense “to further increase security for our Airmen and Guardians,” Meink said.
“How do you make sure that they have the kit they need to do the job?” Meink said, adding that the explosion of counter-drone innovations from industry “is a rapidly changing environment.”
PAEs are a new construct, introduced during recent Pentagon acquisition reforms to replace program executive offices. The idea is to combine several programs within a single mission area and give PAEs authority to move funds between programs and adjust requirements based on evolving needs. The Department of the Air Force currently has 26 PAEs—17 in the Air Force, nine in the Space Force.
“We are delegating almost every authority we legally have to our PAEs for most programs,” Meink said. “That now includes milestone decision authority, a big first on our acquisition community.”
Meink cautioned that the creation of a point defense PAE is “not going to be tomorrow.” But he sounded confident that it is a matter of when, not if, the new organization is created: “We’re already walking down the road, and eventually we’ll evolve into PAE for it.”
The need, he added, is clear.
“There definitely has to be continually increasing focus on making sure we can defend our Airmen and Guardians wherever they are in the world,” Meink said.
Wilsbach teased one acquisition program that may one day fall under the future point defense PAE, saying the Air Force will create a “point defense weapon system,” an umbrella effort that will bring together kinetic and nonkinetic counter-drone capabilities. He offered no further details about the new program.

three centuries-old japanese craft traditions converge in loudspeaker collection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:10:39 UTC
03:10:39 KST

Animism Objects brings japan’s craft traditions into audio design
Tokyo-based VOID Inc. launches Animism Objects, a loudspeaker label that brings traditional Japanese materials and artisanal techniques into contemporary audio objects. The project is set to be presented during London Design Festival 2026. Animism Objects draws from San’in, a region where Japan’s creation myths have been passed down for more than a millennium. In this landscape, nature is understood not simply as a resource, but as part of everyday life, memory, and ritual. The region is also associated with materials and techniques developed over centuries, including Washi, made by hand from natural plant fibres; Aizome, the traditional Japanese practice of indigo dyeing; and Yakisugi, a woodworking technique that chars the surface of cedar boards to increase durability and fire resistance. These processes bring distinct material qualities to the speakers while retaining visible traces of their making. The surfaces reflect variations in the natural materials and the work of the craftspeople who produce them, connecting the finished objects to accumulated knowledge, care, and ritual practice. Each technique gives the speaker a different tactile and visual character.
Traditional craft and technology converge in three speakers
The first Animism Objects collection comprises three editions: Washi, Aizome, and Yakisugi, with each limited to 10 sets. The three finishes establish different relationships between the speaker’s contemporary form and the traditional processes used to construct its surface. The project takes its conceptual starting point from Animism, understood here as an approach in which people, nature, and objects exist in relationship with one another. For the London exhibition, this idea is considered through the combination of traditional Japanese craftsmanship, technology, and contemporary design. By incorporating established materials and techniques into audio products, Animism Objects examines how inherited knowledge can continue to operate within contemporary design. The project positions craftsmanship not only as a form of preservation, but as a material and cultural practice that can inform new objects and their relationship to everyday life.

EU Fails to Renew Russia Sanctions as Slovakia Seeks to Protect Russian Oligarchs
European Union ambassadors meeting in Brussels failed on September 14 to renew one of the bloc's core Russia sanctions schemes, leaving the measure a single day from expiry.
Five EU diplomats told POLITICO about the deadlock, and three noted that ambassadors would reconvene later that same day for further discussion.

Unanimous agreement was required on Monday because the regime—which governs asset freezes on roughly 3,000 individuals and companies— expires Tuesday, according to POLITICO.
Slovakia has demanded that the bloc strike two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from the sanctions list, the diplomats told POLITICO. France has reportedly sought to broker a compromise by proposing that only Usmanov be delisted.
France reportedly attempted to reach a compromise by suggesting that only Usmanov be delisted.
Most other capitals were unwilling to consider removing anyone while Russia fires record numbers of missiles at Ukrainian civilian targets, the report noted.

Are gender differences really power differences? Large-scale analysis finds strong behavioral parallels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:00:57 UTC
03:00:57 KST

New research suggests that many psychological and behavioral differences between men and women might actually stem from differences in social power. The findings indicate that holding a high-power role produces behavioral effects strikingly similar to traits often associated with men, while low-power roles produce effects resembling traits often associated with women. This research was published in PNAS Nexus.
The origins of behavioral differences between men and women remain a topic of intense debate in the social sciences. Evolutionary theorists tend to trace these differences back to natural selection and biology. In this view, men and women developed distinct psychological attributes to adapt to different reproductive and survival roles in early human history.
Sociocultural theorists approach the issue differently, emphasizing how societal roles and social power shape behavior. They argue that hierarchical structures and unequal resource allocation reinforce gendered behaviors beyond any biological roots. A 2019 review indicated that human brains and hormonal systems are not strictly divided into two distinct categories, which supports the idea that many gender differences are shaped by culture rather than rigid biology.
At the center of this debate is the concept of social power, defined as the actual or perceived control over valuable resources. Across many areas of society, men tend to hold more power than women, occupying more leadership roles and controlling more financial assets. Because power differences are so frequently tied to gender, some researchers suspect that power dynamics might be the true source of many presumed gender differences.
Adam D. Galinsky of Columbia University and his colleagues set out to systematically test this idea. They wanted to see if the behaviors resulting from experimental manipulations of power would match up with known differences between men and women. By comparing these two separate areas of research, the team aimed to determine if power imbalances could provide a useful explanation for gender differences.
To conduct the analysis, the researchers first collected data from experiments that randomly assigned people to high-power or low-power roles. They performed a statistical check on 270 of these experiments to ensure the existing literature on power was reliable. From there, they identified 59 distinct psychological and behavioral outcomes that are genuinely affected by having or lacking power.
Next, the research team gathered 102 outcomes from meta-analyses of sex and gender differences. Meta-analyses are large-scale statistical reviews that combine data from many individual studies to find overall trends. The researchers then grouped the findings from both the power experiments and the gender meta-analyses into four broad categories for comparison.
These four categories included agency, communion, self-evaluation, and cognitive processes. Agency involves striving for independence, assertiveness, and control over one’s environment. Communion relates to social connection, empathy, and cooperating with others. Self-evaluation involves how people view their own abilities, and cognitive processes include attention, problem-solving, and spatial reasoning.
The comparison yielded a massive overlap. The researchers found that about 71 percent of the recorded gender differences were entirely consistent with the effects of power differences. In contrast, only about 8 percent of the gender differences showed the opposite pattern.
Sonya Xinyue Xiao, a developmental psychologist who directs the IBAY Lab and was not involved in the study, told PsyPost that her confidence in the results is “pretty high.”
“The method they used is very rigorous in testing their hypotheses that focus on whether power effects are aligned with sex/gender differences when there is a significant power effect,” she said.
Specifically, high-power individuals and men both tend to display higher agency, including traits like dominance and a willingness to take risks. They also both show more positive self-evaluations and display similar cognitive processing styles. On the other hand, low-power individuals and women both tend to display higher communion, exhibiting more interpersonal sensitivity and social cooperation.
To check if this alignment was unique to power, the researchers ran a similar comparison using the personality trait of extraversion. Extraversion is known to correlate with having power and influence, so the team wanted to see if it would also perfectly mirror gender differences. The results showed that it did not.
While extraverts and high-power individuals share some traits, they diverge in the area of communion. Extraverts tend to be highly communal and social, whereas high-power individuals and men tend to score lower on communion. This divergence provides evidence that social power has a specific and uniquely strong relationship with gender differences.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relies on comparing two separate bodies of literature, meaning the link between power and gender is observational in this context. The researchers did not conduct a new experiment to see if giving women high-power roles would immediately erase the observed gender gaps in these specific traits.
“The gender differences in many constructs are very small, but power differences may be large; it is important to keep in mind that the findings are pointing at similarity in directions rather than magnitudes,” Xiao noted. “As the authors mentioned in their discussions, their findings do not actually prove causal relations between social power and sex/gender differences.”
Additionally, grouping dozens of distinct psychological concepts into broad categories requires subjective judgment. Although the researchers used independent experts to classify the traits, personal biases or cultural perspectives could have subtly influenced how the categories were organized. The authors note that their results do not mean power explains all behavioral differences between men and women, but rather that it is likely a major contributing factor.
Future studies could directly test these ideas by assigning men and women to high- and low-power roles in the same experiment. This would help clarify exactly how power shapes behavior across different genders in real time.
“As a developmental psychologist, I am curious to see research examining how the potential causal relation between social power and gender difference changes over time — perhaps the role of social power increases as we age,” Xiao said. “Because gender is highly salient during childhood, whereas one’s gendered experiences of social power may come later.”
The study, “Are many sex/gender differences really power differences?,” was authored by Adam D. Galinsky, Aurora Turek, Grusha Agarwal, Eric M. Anicich, Derek D. Rucker, Hannah R. Bowles, Nira Liberman, Chloe Levin, and Joe C. Magee.

NEW DELHI: NCP (SP) leader Supriya Sule on Monday questioned the registration of a CBI FIR into the death of Disha Salian, saying she was surprised because the case had earlier been treated as closed by the same government.Salian, a former manager of late actor Sushant Singh Rajput, died after falling from the 12th floor of a building in Mumbai’s Malad area on June 8, 2020. The CBI registered an FIR on September 13 following a direction from the Bombay High Court for a fresh probe into the circumstances surrounding her death.“I was surprised to hear how this (registration of an FIR by CBI) happened because it is the same government that had closed the case. I do not understand what is happening,” Sule told reporters in Pune.She said she would speak to Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut to understand the latest developments.
What is in the CBI FIR?
According to CBI officials cited by news agency PTI, the FIR does not name any individual as an accused, in line with the Bombay High Court’s directions. It invokes IPC provisions relating to criminal conspiracy, gang rape, murder, disappearance of evidence and public servants allegedly framing incorrect records.
The FIR followed a September 2 order by the Bombay High Court on a petition filed by Salian’s father, Satish Salian. The CBI began recording statements after the court directed it to conduct a thorough investigation.The court had criticised the Mumbai Police investigation, noting “glaring discrepancies” and observing that the probe “raises more questions than answers”.It had also directed that nobody should be treated as an accused unless investigators found sufficient grounds for reasonable suspicion based on the material collected during the probe.
Advocate claims names are in FIR
Advocate Nilesh Ojha, who represents Satish Salian, claimed on Monday that the FIR contains the names of several individuals, including Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray, Rohan Roy, Rhea Chakraborty, Param Bir Singh, Dino Morea and Sooraj Pancholi, among others.
However, the CBI has not publicly confirmed the names claimed by the advocate, according to PTI.Ojha said the FIR was registered after the CBI conducted preliminary verification of Satish Salian’s complaint and recorded his statement. He said the case covers allegations of gang rape, murder and an alleged cover-up, invoking IPC Sections 376D, 302, 201, 217, 218 and 120B.Satish Salian had earlier approached the court alleging that his daughter was murdered.Speaking to news agency ANI on Friday, he said he had provided investigators with the names of people whom he wanted examined.“I stated the facts exactly as they were; I told them everything that happened to my daughter. I listed all the names: Aditya, Sooraj Pancholi, Dino Morea, and the bodyguards. They noted everything down,” he said.
Sule raises political conspiracy claim
Asked whether she saw a possible political conspiracy behind the development, Sule did not give a direct answer.“Anything is possible,” she said, while referring to what she called “ICE” — Income Tax, CBI and Enforcement Directorate — and alleging that central agencies had previously been used against political figures who later joined the ruling party.
AIMIM leader Waris Pathan, meanwhile, said the case should not be politicised and should be left to the courts.“There is no need to give the Disha Salian case a political colour. There is no need to politicise it,” Pathan said, adding that the matter was sub judice and that “it is best to let the court decide”.
Salian’s death had earlier been recorded as an Accidental Death Report. The Bombay High Court had raised concerns over the fact that no FIR was registered despite allegations by her family that she had been murdered.The court also noted that copies of the post-mortem report and ADR had not been provided to her family for years.Sushant Singh Rajput was found dead at his Bandra residence six days after Salian’s death.The CBI later submitted a closure report in Rajput’s case, concluding that he died by suicide; that report remains pending before the competent court.The Bombay High Court has directed the CBI to investigate the Salian case and has left it to the agency to determine whether a criminal case is made out based on the evidence collected.

India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14

India to supply Nepal electricity after floods wrecked hydropower projects
India to provide Nepal with 654 megawatts of electricity daily to meet urgent needs after devastating glacial floods.
India has approved the expedited export of electricity to neighbouring Nepal to help it overcome shortages caused by extensive damage to hydropower infrastructure from devastating floods last month.
In a statement on Monday, India’s Ministry of Power said up to 654 megawatts of electricity would be transmitted for 18 hours per day until December 31.
“The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal,” it said.
It added that in December it would also review the amount of power to be exported from January.
The flooding, triggered on August 26 by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border, killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal and Tibet.
At least 12 hydropower projects in Nepal were hit, with at least 900 power station workers among the more than 5,500 people still missing in the country.
Almost 100 percent of the country’s energy needs were met by hydropower before the floods hit. Since then, Nepal has been forced to import electricity after years of exporting surplus energy to India.
Thousands of displaced people are sheltering in aid centres, with little hope of returning home soon. The United Nations and its partners are appealing for nearly $50m to help survivors.
Nepali officials say at least $5bn is needed for initial rebuilding, adding that the disaster shows how climate change has hit poor countries that did little to cause it.
The Himalayas, where Nepal is nestled, are approaching a tipping point as glaciers melt faster than a decade ago, threatening water security as the region approaches “peak water” by mid-century, according to a study released this month.

In Gen Z Romance Shows Like Crew Girl, Sports Are the New Sex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:52:09 UTC
02:52:09 KST

In the Netflix teen drama Crew Girl, 16-year-old solo rowing champ Teagan Tao has her life uprooted when her hotel-magnate dad gets a tip that he’s about to be arrested for financial crimes and disappears. Suddenly, Teagan (Miku Martineau) and her flighty mom, Ella (Jessica Paré), are broke and moving across the country to the crumbling New England house where Ella grew up. The town is all clam shacks and marinas—and the prestigious Easton Prep, where Teagan matriculates thanks to an education trust that was somehow spared from the seizure of the Taos’ assets. The only problem, besides the rampant snobbery, is that Eaton has no girls’ crew team. Forced to coxswain for the boys, Teagan starts falling for two of her teammates: kind, working-class townie Cam Dillinger (Kyle Clark) and bratty airline scion Josh Regis (Sam Braun), who’s locked in a premature succession battle with his cousin Ryder (Connor Paton). Meanwhile, a gay rower, Baloo (Jude Wilson), is secretly hooking up with a guy on a rival team.
All of which is to say that Crew Girl, whose first season is now the no. 1 show on Netflix, plays like a greatest-hits compilation of teen romance tropes. First among the classics is a love triangle (see: Twilight, Riverdale, The Vampire Diaries, My So-Called Life). As is often the case, this one is enhanced by the quaintness of its small-town setting (Dawson’s Creek, One Tree Hill) and complicated by both wealth disparities (Gossip Girl, Pretty in Pink) and one character’s fish-out-of-water, new-kid-in-school status (The O.C., Beverly Hills, 90210). There’s also a youthful mom (you might remember Paré as Mad Men’s Megan) doing a painfully slow will-they-won’t-they dance with an old friend (Thomas Cadrot), à la Gilmore Girls’ Lorelai and Luke.
But what’s remarkable about Crew Girl—which is, despite an effervescent lead and a few fun storylines built around eccentric minor crew-boy characters, otherwise decidedly mid—is how comprehensively it showcases the conventions unique to the genre’s newest generation. TV has, in the last few years, capitalized on publishing’s pandemic-era romance boom, churning out love stories tailored to the young, female audience driving authors like Emily Henry and Ali Hazelwood up best-seller lists. Often, that means adapting popular YA or New Adult novels; Prime Video’s success with Jenny Han’s coming-of-age, beach-town love triangle The Summer I Turned Pretty paved the way for Netflix’s take on Ali Novak’s My Life with the Walter Boys as well as XO, Kitty, Han’s spinoff of her book-to-film franchise To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before. Queer romance, mainly of the gay male variety, from Netflix’s tender and chaste Heartstopper to the spicy Canadian phenomenon Heated Rivalry, which streams on HBO Max in the U.S., has also jumped from page to screen. (Crew Girl isn’t an adaptation, but a novelization released in tandem with the show suggests it’s meant to feel like one.) This year has seen a particular glut of new titles, from Netflix’s figure-skating drama Finding Her Edge to Prime’s Off Campus and Every Year After. The latter platform even scored a hit in August with an exceptional original teen romance, Sterling Point, proving the niche isn’t entirely dependent on preexisting IP.
These shows have all the love triangles and class struggles and outsider angst that have defined youthful romance tales since Jane Austen was writing them, capturing eternal adolescent fantasies (being desirable enough to have two people fighting over you) and fears (not measuring up to the rich kids) alike. Pretty appears to have sparked a mini-trend of siblings competing for the same crush, a trope that also pops up in Every Year After, Walter Boys, and Finding Her Edge. The fraught post-DEI-backlash politics of representation, especially for the most racially and ethnically diverse generation on record, are evident in the shows’ leads. Like Crew Girl’s Martineau, many are multiracial but play characters with vaguely defined backgrounds who live with either a single white parent or a white surrogate family. (New York magazine just spotlighted the "Wasian generation," a long list of up-and-coming white and Asian stars, citing Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams, Pretty’s Lola Tung, and XO, Kitty’s Anna Cathcart among other white and Asian stars.) Liberal and minority viewers get to see mixed-race families and romances, and a TV landscape that isn’t all white. The anti-”woke” crowd is spared identity politics, non-English dialogue, and often all other forms of cultural specificity. Savvy streamers avoid backlash from both sides.
What’s most striking about these series, though, are the novel ways in which they embrace physicality. With the steamy exceptions of Heated Rivalry and Off Campus (both geared toward a slightly older age range), the sexual content is pretty PG-13. Objectification is kept to a minimum, at least by characters we’re supposed to like. Yet bodies are conspicuously activated, in what feel like pointed responses to—and, for young viewers, escape hatches from—digital disembodiment.
Summer romances, and specifically those that bring together wealthy vacationers and the locals who work for them, aren’t new to fiction. It’s the prominence of nature in the recent crop of teen romances (and teen hits in other genres, like Netflix’s Outer Banks) that makes an impression. As it toggles between protagonist Percy’s (Sadie Soverall) life in her late 20s and a sequence of idyllic teenage lake-house summers glimpsed in flashbacks, Every Year After uses its setting to visualize two brothers’ rivalry for her affection. In one recurring image, Percy sits at the edge of her house’s dock, looking on as sensitive Sam (Matt Cornett) and arrogant Charlie (Michael Bradway) shove each other off a slippery wooden raft. Sterling Point brings a high-strung New York City girl (Ella Rubin) to an island in Canada’s Muskoka region, a paradise of lush, lakefront forests. Her rich-vs.-poor-boy love triangle plays out over lazy days spent boating, swimming, and sunbathing on rocky beaches. Cellphone service is conveniently spotty.
An abundance of sports romances make such physicality even more explicit. In Off Campus and Heated Rivalry, the boys who serve as eye candy for any viewer attracted to men are always slamming into each other on the ice and changing together in the locker room. In Finding Her Edge, a show about young Olympics hopefuls at a residential training center, an ice-dancing duo is bound to become a love affair (as long as the guy is into girls). Even the neurotic hero of Heartstopper (Joe Locke) finds first love on the rugby field. Crew Girl casts many thirsty gazes on the musclebound upper bodies of Teagan’s teammates. These stories aren’t just about the sweaty sensuality of athletes in motion, though. They’re about ambition and passion and the competitive spirit as romantic accelerants—about how the shared commitment to spend hours every day striving for excellence while one’s peers are screwing around online can bond people.
Why use athletics as a fig leaf for sex in the uncensored age of streaming, years after shows like Euphoria and Skins obliterated the notion that TV for teens should be wholesome? Maybe because modesty is in. Gen Z’s squeamishness about sex on screen has fueled successive waves of hand-wringing among their elders. The so-called sex recession plaguing this cohort in real life has been duly noted, with suggested explanations ranging from extreme onlineness in general to poor socialization during the COVID years of Zoom school and virtual prom in particular. The thing is, biologically speaking, teens are the same jumble of hormones in 2026 that they were during the Summer of Love. “Many of them are very horny,” Carter Sherman, the author of The Second Coming: Sex and the Next Generation's Fight Over Its Future, assured WIRED last year. “They would like to be having sex, and in fact they feel a lot of shame over the fact that they haven't had sex yet or that they’re not having sex enough.” As transitional objects to ease anxieties around physical intimacy, swimsuits and erg machines make a lot of sense.
The most salient takeaway from Crew Girl and its ilk might be buried in a less eye-catching finding of 2025’s Teens and Screens, the annual UCLA report on young people’s attitudes toward entertainment media that reliably stokes the “Gen Z hates sex scenes” panic. Relatability is the new watchword. Whereas millennials wallowed in wealth porn, took vicarious flight with superheroes, and sucked the life out of vampire content, today’s adolescents ranked “people with lives like mine” as the No. 1 element they’re looking for in TV shows and movies. Although they’re aspirational enough to feel escapist, with their summer houses and prep-school popularity contests, this season’s teen romances reflect that shift. For a generation raised in the sensory deprivation tank of the internet, whose fears of infinite digital liminality just gave us the horror movies Backrooms and It Ends, the fantasy is humbler than superpowers. It’s being grounded in physical space, a human body capable of sharing tactile experiences with other embodied people. Sex is one way to make those connections. Crew is another.

EXPLAINER - Historic Cardiff declaration: How Britain enters new era of self-determination talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:50:40 UTC
02:50:40 KST

- In joint declaration, leaders of Scottish National Party, Sinn Fein, and Plaid Cymru call on UK government to prepare for, plan, and facilitate constitutional change
- In response, Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he 'believes strongly in the union'
Monday's meeting in Wales’ capital Cardiff between the first ministers of three devolved UK nations marks the latest step in a long-running debate over the future of the union, with a joint declaration signed by nationalist party leaders stressing the right to determine their own future and also calling on the UK government to “prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change.”
Landmark self-determination declaration
The joint declaration signed in Cardiff by Rhun ap Iorwerth, first minister of Wales and leader of Plaid Cymru; John Swinney, first minister of Scotland and leader of the Scottish National Party (SNP); and Michelle O'Neill, first minister of Northern Ireland and vice-president of Sinn Fein, said the political landscape "is changing."
The Celtic Alliance leaders said they believe the "future of our nations belongs in the European Union," adding that, for the first time ever, there are first ministers in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland "who are all committed to independence from the UK."
The move came after US President Donald Trump said Sunday that integrating Ireland and Northern Ireland represents "one of the naturals of all time," suggesting historical partitions should be resolved.
On Saturday, visiting Ireland, he also said he would "love" to see a united Ireland.
The new declaration, however, is only the latest step in a long-running debate over the future of the union since 1997.
Good Friday Agreement and beginning of devolution era
The Good Friday Agreement, also known as the Belfast Agreement, was a landmark peace deal signed in 1998 to end decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland known as the Troubles.
It states that Northern Ireland's constitutional status can only change through a majority vote, known as the "principle of consent," an important point which has loudly been raised by Irish nationalist party Sinn Fein.
Scotland and Wales’ devolution processes began with public referendums in 1997 which led to the passing of the Scotland Act 1998 and the Government of Wales Act 1998, and the official opening of both the Scottish Parliament and the National Assembly for Wales (Senedd) in 1999.
Northern Ireland’s devolved institutions also began operating under the Good Friday Agreement framework the same year.
SNP victory and Scottish independence referendum
In 2007, the Scottish National Party (SNP) led by Alex Salmond managed to enter government with 45% of the vote, forming a minority government.
But in the 2011 elections, the SNP was able to win a landslide of 69 seats to form a majority government in Holyrood, the first majority government since the opening of the Scottish Parliament.
In 2013, the pro-independence SNP reached a deal with the UK on the Scottish Independence Referendum Act 2013 setting out an independence proposal requiring a simple majority to pass.
The referendum asking voters "Should Scotland be an independent country?" was held in Scotland on Sept. 18, 2014.
The “no” side won with just over 2 million (55.3%) votes against independence and some 1.62 million (44.7%) votes in favor with 84.6% turnout, the highest recorded for an election or referendum in the UK since the January 1910 general election.
Brexit, UK Supreme Court ruling
The idea of holding another independence referendum flared up in Scotland once again with the UK’s 2016 Brexit referendum. Although an overall majority in the UK voted in favor of leaving the EU, most people in Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to remain in the bloc.
In 2019, when Boris Johnson became British prime minister, he stressed that he would reject any request to hold a second vote on Scotland's future in the UK.
In 2021, the SNP, led by Nicola Sturgeon, won another election in Scotland, paving the way for a possible second independence referendum returning to the center of Scottish politics.
However in 2022, the UK Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the Scottish Parliament lacks the legislative competence to hold a second independence referendum without consent from the UK government
Changes in Wales, Northern Ireland leadership
After capturing the largest number of seats in the Northern Ireland Assembly for the first time in 2022, the Irish nationalist Sinn Fein Party won the 2024 elections and its leader Michelle O'Neill was appointed Northern Ireland's first-ever nationalist first minister.
In Wales this May, Plaid Cymru made history in the Welsh Senedd elections, ending 100 years of Labour control and making Rhun ap Iorwerth the first minister of Wales.
In the 2021 Senedd election, Plaid Cymru had committed to holding a referendum on Welsh independence by 2026 if the party won a majority in the Senedd.
Thus this May saw, for the first time in history, the three devolved governments of the UK—Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland—all led by pro-independence first ministers who have pledged to leave the UK.
In response to Monday’s declaration, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he “believes strongly in the union.”

5,000-year-old drainage network, workshop-houses unearthed in W. Türkiye
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
01:46:40 CST
02:46:40 KST

ISTANBUL, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists in Türkiye's western Izmir province have unearthed a 5,000-year-old stone drainage network and ancient "workshop-houses," shedding new light on prehistoric urban planning, authorities said Monday.
The findings were uncovered at Liman Tepe in Urla, a 5,300-year-old Bronze Age port city known for hosting both land settlements and Türkiye's first underwater harbor excavations, according to Vasif Sahoglu, head of the excavation team and director of Ankara University's Research Center for Maritime Archaeology.
The 5,000-year-old settlement dates back to the Early Bronze Age, a pivotal era when early Anatolian cultures established fortified coastal cities and extensive trade networks across the Aegean Sea.
Detailing the discoveries, Sahoglu noted that the stone channels were built between terraced levels to divert rainwater away from the settlement. He described the water management network as a rare engineering feature, with very few examples found in Western Anatolia and the broader Aegean region from that era.
The excavations also revealed "long houses" -- measuring over 25 meters in length and about 5 meters in width -- featuring large storage jars embedded into the floors at their entrances, likely used to hold water or grain.
Sahoglu described these buildings as "workshop-houses," as archaeological findings, including weaving weights and metallurgical remains, indicate they were used for both daily living and manufacturing.
The comprehensive research at Liman Tepe, which began in 1992, involves both terrestrial and maritime archaeology. Underwater excavations at the site began in 2000, with this year's work focusing on determining when the ancient harbor's stone breakwater was built and how long it was used.
During these underwater operations, marine teams also recovered organic materials such as olive pits and grape seeds, which Sahoglu noted provide crucial insights into the ancient settlement's maritime trade. ■
