"Trump is transactional. If we win Congress, he’ll have to deal with us on Ukraine": Rep. Vindman
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
20:44:00 EEST
02:44:00 KST

"Trump is very transactional. If we win Congress, he’ll have to deal with us on Ukraine": an interview with Rep. Vindman
"I understood everything you said in Ukrainian," Eugene Vindman said at the beginning of our conversation. Vindman is a Democratic congressman and one of Ukraine’s advocates in the US House of Representatives.
Vindman was born in Kyiv in 1975, but he didn’t live there for long – when he was four years old, his father emigrated to the United States with his children. Vindman grew up there, built a military career, and later moved into public service at the US National Security Council.
In 2019, his actions had a decisive impact on the course of US politics: reports by Eugene and his twin brother Alexander initiated a process that led to Donald Trump’s impeachment. The following year, after the proceedings concluded, Trump initiated their dismissal. In 2024, Eugene Vindman was elected to Congress as a Democratic Party candidate.
This is Congressman Vindman’s first big interview in Ukraine and about Ukraine. We spoke on the sidelines of the annual Yalta European Strategy meeting, organised by the Victor Pinchuk Foundation, which was attended by a large congressional delegation.
But we didn’t dwell on the past.
The main question now is whether the US House of Representatives will pass the Lindsey Graham Bill, which would create new sanctions mechanisms for putting pressure on Russia. We also discussed what would happen if the bill is not passed during this legislative week.
Finally, we talked about the expected shift in US policy, given that the Democrats are highly likely to take control of the majority in Congress.
"There are some unique issues to the Lindsey Graham bill, but I hope it will be passed"
We’re looking forward to a new plenary week. Do you expect anything important concerning Ukraine to be adopted?
I hope that the Russia sanctions package bill will hit the floor next week. It has not been noticed yet, but the package, now named in honour of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, is a serious sanctions package – probably the most serious sanctions package, if passed and implemented the way that Congress intends it, on Russia since the major phase of the war began.
How realistic is it to expect this bill to be passed by the House?
I think it's realistic. There are some complications with the law that are very separate from support for Ukraine. There's still overwhelming bipartisan – frankly, non-partisan – support for Ukraine among the American people.
I see it every day.
I mean, I drive around in my region in Virginia and people have the Ukrainian flag.
I see it in Congress – that there is bipartisan support in Congress. There are some unique issues to this bill that are complications.
What are they exactly?
A lot of them relate to tariffs and how the president has used tariffs during the first 20 months of his career. That has caused, you know, prices of goods in the United States to increase. And that has been contrary to the will of Congress.
But, you know, that's getting into the weeds. I think the key element here is that if we look at what the bill is designed to do, it’s to punish Russia, bring them to the negotiating table.
That's where I'm focused. That's why I'll be supporting the bill, and I will be advocating vigorously for it, and I know that there are a number of my colleagues that will. But first, we have to have the Republicans agree to bring it to the floor for a vote.
I simply cannot understand how we could have 86 senators voting for it – that’s not just a bipartisan majority, it’s almost unanimous – and yet there is still discussion about whether it can actually be passed. I find it hard to believe that those opposing it don’t understand that blocking it also harms Ukraine.
Look, the House and the Senate are two different chambers – and so that's a simple explanation of why something can pass in the Senate, but not necessarily in the House.
I think this was the best bill that the senators thought they can come up with.
There are some concerns about it in the House, but I think that you're still going to have a vigorous discussion. You're going to have people like myself that are advocating for the passage of this bill, because ultimately it is about supporting Ukraine to me.
Even if there are some flaws in the legislation…
A lot of the problems are based on lack of trust.
There's a lack of trust between Democrats, certainly, and the president. That's where this stems from.
Could you please explain what happens procedurally if the bill is not passed now? As I understand it, the House then goes into a pre-election recess, so does that mean the bill will not be passed this year at all?
What happens is: it has to pass the House, it has to pass the Senate, and it has to be signed by the president, or, as the president recently did, not signed or vetoed within 10 days. And then it becomes law.
The Senate passed it.
We have a very short window of time between now and election day to have a session of the House. It's possible that it could be on the floor of the House next week. But even if it's not, then it could still come up between the election and the end of Congress before the next Congress takes effect.
Politically speaking, do laws normally get passed after the House has been re-elected?
Yes. It's a lame duck session for Congress, but laws pass all the time.
"The President is very transactional. When we have power in Congress, he’ll negotiate with us"
Let’s talk about bipartisan support. Do you expect it to continue?
For Ukraine? 100%.
What makes you so confident?
There have been a number of votes, and there is one outlier that occurred because of the way a bill went to the floor of the House.
But in the previous votes, 75% of members of the House voted in favour of bills that supported Ukraine. There is one on a Ukraine-related matter recently that because of the way it procedurally went to the floor was slightly different, but I think there’s overwhelming support from Democrats and Republicans, and I hear that in conversations I have regularly.
Ultimately, the reason why I am certain that the bipartisan support will continue is because
Ukraine is on the right side of history. It's as simple as that.
The American people – even though we have our challenges in Congress right now on the political side – recognise that Ukraine is fighting for freedom. For the same values that our country was formed for.
And that is why I am certain that bipartisan support will continue, despite a sense of fatigue.
Let me be frank with you. Sometimes I don’t feel that the United States or the US administration is on the right side of history.
Well, look… I think that some of the policies of this administration are not consistent with our values, our historic values. It's true related to the way we treat immigrants and people that have lived in our country for extended periods of time.
It's true about how we treat our neighbours – like Canada, or Denmark.
But that is a temporary political situation that within 54 days could be very easily remedied. We got ourselves into a situation with an election, and we're going to get out of this situation with an election.
But what will actually change in practical terms? The president will be the same. The balance of power in Congress could change, but what would that actually mean? And in which chamber do you expect the majority to change?
Well, that's a good question, and obviously the president would remain in place.
I'll give you a couple of different answers to this.
For one side, if the Democrats had power, then we would have the gavels, which means that we would have the ability to call hearings, that we would have subpoena power, and ultimately the power of Congress is the power of the purse. It means we would be able to allocate the budget.
For one thing, I sit on the defence committee, and last year we allocated $400 million that still has not been released to Ukraine. We would put tremendous pressure on the administration to release those funds.
And if we win both the House and the Senate, obviously, that will be even more significant pressure.
And the one thing that I've seen personally from this administration is that the president is very transactional.
So when we have the power in Congress, he will negotiate with us.
I’m also a little… well, I wouldn’t say sceptical, but cautious. I’m afraid it could lead to a situation where no one is able to get anything done.
I think you're right to be cautious.
I'm an optimist by nature, and so this sense of being able to actually do things in the next Congress is part of what motivates me.
It's going to require tremendous work. And it's going to require negotiation and dialogue. It's going to require a smart policy. But everything that I've seen so far in my short 20 months as a politician indicates to me that there will be some areas where there's no movement and potentially a stalling of any activity, but there are going to be areas where we're going to be able to make progress.
Take the budget, for example. I worry that it could lead to one government shutdown after another. That’s one area where I don’t expect Trump to be particularly willing to compromise.
You know, that's speculation, about whether there are going to be shutdowns or not. Obviously nobody wants a shutdown. But again, everything that I've seen indicates to me that the president, when faced with a united front, will negotiate.
Do you expect both chambers to flip?
I think the prospects are much better for the House.
It's possible in the Senate. But in any case, I think that when there is a change in leadership in Congress, the prospects for more productive good work to help the American people and to help our international allies, including Ukraine, are improved.
I can tell you one thing for sure: that if the status quo remains, it is bad for Ukraine and it's bad for our allies.
What do you mean by the status quo?
That Republicans maintain power in the House and Senate. We've seen what that looks like over the course of the last 20 months.
"NATO is the greatest alliance in history. Re-dedication is very important"
What practical areas could see changes? We were used to a very different US policy before. Now Trump has introduced a new approach. Do you expect a return to the old policy, or are those days over?
There is not going to be an absolute return to the status quo.
And frankly, I think that even under the previous administration, which was Democratic, the support was not robust enough. I would have been much more assertive in support for Ukraine and for our European allies.
In Ukraine, we call it "по одній краплі" (one drop at a time).
Yeah, drop by drop, right? I think it will not necessarily return to the status quo before this administration, but a sort of re-dedication to our basic principles and support.
What do you mean exactly? Because, to be frank, I don’t expect Ukraine to receive the same level of financial assistance as before, or the same amount of weapons provided free of charge. Or am I being too sceptical? Do you think even that could be reversed?
Look, I gave you one concrete element, which is the $400 million that has been passed and is now law, but it has not been released yet.
I mean, obviously $400 million is only part of the need, but it's that plus whatever is appropriate going forward.
There's money that has been passed in previous legislation that has not been released as well.
Could that be renewed?
It is a pot of money, so that still exists as a bottom line.
What else could change? I believe US policy towards NATO could definitely be reversed, or am I wrong?
Well, certainly NATO is the greatest, most significant alliance in history. A sort of re-dedication to that alliance is going to be very important.
Including maintaining a presence in Europe. And that's a bipartisan issue.
I hear about it from my colleagues, including the Republican chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, who talked about making sure that our commitments in Europe remain stable, that they're based on the needs of the mission and based on the needs of the alliance rather than any political considerations.
What about international justice and accountability for Putin? Do you expect any changes in that area? Because now we see that this policy has been reversed under Trump.
Yes, and this is the project that I worked on before my time in Congress.
You know, international justice as it relates to war crimes is a long-term process. In 2023, when I was travelling extensively to Ukraine, the Germans had just finished an Auschwitz case – so 80+ years.
These cases take a long time.
The most important work that can be done right now is to fix the facts, to gather the evidence, and to make sure that when the time is appropriate, criminals can be held accountable.
I would like it to be a much shorter period of time.
And some of these people are under indictment or under an international arrest warrant, like the one that exists for Vladimir Putin now (it has not been enforced, but it does exist) – it's going to follow him for the rest of his life, unless there's a resolution.
And so it's important not only for the eventual prosecution, but also to hold the accountability over these people's heads for the rest of their lives.
"Make sure you continue to have faith in your own abilities"
Do you expect any broader changes in US policy?
It's hard to say. I think there will be an interest in pursuing accountability. But it may be something that would have to wait until the next administration.
What does Ukraine need to do? What can Ukrainians do to improve our relationship with the United States and keep it strong? What can we do better?
I think it’s the people-to-people connections.
We receive delegations all the time from Ukraine. It's visiting communities, it's visiting churches, it's having conversations that are absolutely critical.
There's a lot going on in the world. We have a war with Iran as well that is frankly taking a lot of people's attention – and resources for that matter.
But continuing to tell the story of the Ukrainian people who are fighting for freedom, fighting for our values. They are some of the best ambassadors – and also, President Zelenskyy is still very highly regarded in the United States.
He's a popular figure among ordinary people.
Should we change our domestic policies or policies on our relationship with the US?
If we think about what the narratives are that the Russians certainly attack Ukraine with, one of them is corruption.
So I think making sure that corruption is eliminated to the maximum extent possible.
Also, I think, cohesiveness – the government working together, recognising that this country is at war and so the less friction there is between the different elements of government, the better, to demonstrate stability. And probably maybe the most important thing is success on the battlefield, military success.
This may be the most difficult thing to do,
but we saw with Operation Spiderweb that that was a moment that shocked [the West].
It changed warfare, I believe.
It was a historic moment because it changed the way people thought about the nature of warfare going forward. And the Ukrainian people were capable of doing that once.
That level of audacity, resilience, innovation, and making sure that you continue to have faith in your own abilities, is critically important.
I think this is possible. As you mentioned anti-corruption efforts, perhaps a new US administration, especially if both chambers flip, would pay closer attention to what is happening in Ukraine in terms of fighting corruption. Would congressional control changing hands make a difference in that respect?
Anytime you have a corruption narrative that is taking hold, and then the American people and us as elected representatives don't have a feeling like our efforts and the money that we're applying is being used in the best way possible, the least corrupt way, that would be problematic.
I think this is an area for improvement.
There are plenty of mechanisms in the Ukrainian system, with NABU and the anti-corruption prosecutors, SAPO. These anti-corruption organs have to do their work – they have to be robustly guarded. Then that will be a good thing.

Carney pitches Canada to global investors amid US trade war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:42:33 UTC
02:42:33 KST

Mark Carney pitches Canada to global investors amid US trade war
Hundreds of investors overseeing nearly $120 trillion in assets will gather in Toronto for the Canada Investment Summit.
For decades, one of Canada’s biggest selling points to foreign investors was its access to the world’s largest economy next door.
Prime Minister Mark Carney is now trying to sell something bigger — to bet on Canada itself.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Canadian economy recovers sharply in Q2 but shadow of US tariffs in future
- list 2 of 4With the US and Canada locked in a trade war, fears of a recession lurk
- list 3 of 4The losers of the US-Canada trade war
- list 4 of 4Bombardier looks to hire 500 new workers in US, despite Trump threat
On Monday and Tuesday, hundreds of global investors will gather in Toronto for the Canada Investment Summit. The invitation-only meeting will bring some of the world’s largest pension and sovereign wealth funds and asset managers together with corporate executives, Canadian premiers and federal officials.
Carney, a former central banker with deep ties to the global investment world, wants them to put money into everything from mines and pipelines to ports, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing. It is part of a much bigger push to catalyse $1 trillion in investment in Canada over the next five years, with about $280bn in public investment and government incentives to help draw in private and institutional capital.
The summit comes just days after another escalation in Canada’s trade war with the United States which has been ongoing since President Donald Trump started his second term and unleashed a wave of tariffs across the world, including on Canada, one of its historically closest allies.
Relations have ruptured as Trump has repeatedly referred to Canada as the 51st state of the US and Carney as its “governor”. The threats are particularly damaging to Canada which, pre-tariff, sent nearly 80 percent of its exports to its southern neighbour.
After talks collapsed last month, Washington imposed levies of 50 percent on about US$20bn worth of Canadian goods, prompting Ottawa to impose retaliatory tariffs of 15 to 50 percent on a similar value of US imports.
While the two sides have been negotiating, Carney has also been travelling the world to shore up relations and re-start or beef up trade ties, efforts that are bearing some fruit in Toronto with the summit.
“Carney is trying to turn a period of external pressure and uncertainty caused by the Trump trade war into an affirmative agenda,” said Vina Nadjibulla, cofounder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a non-partisan policy think tank in Canada. “Build more at home, diversify Canada’s economic relationships abroad and attract the capital needed to do both.”
While the uncertainty of the trade war makes Canada a harder sell in some ways, it becomes a more compelling one at the same time.
“It cuts both ways,” Nadjibulla said. Investors may be wary of projects that depend heavily on the US market. But the turmoil also gives Carney a chance to sell Canada as “a relatively stable, rules-based jurisdiction” in an increasingly volatile world.
Carney has pulled in a large audience for that pitch. Getting roughly 300 major global investors focused on Canada for two days is unprecedented and a political win in itself, Nadjibulla said.
But getting them into the room is the easy part.
“The summit can open doors and create relationships,” she said. “Success will ultimately depend on how many of those conversations turn into serious investment, financing and projects that actually get built.”
What is Carney selling?
He is making the case that Canada has a lot for investors to bet on beyond its access to the US, from energy to critical minerals to skilled workers to connections to markets around the world. Through trade agreements with 51 countries, Canadian businesses have preferential access to 1.5 billion consumers around the world, the government said in a news statement ahead of the summit.
“We’re trusted, because we’re reliable and because we have what the world wants,” Carney said on Sunday. “That’s why the world is coming to our door.”
A leaked prospectus prepared for the summit lays out 167 potential investments across energy, mining, ports, transportation, technology and advanced manufacturing.
They range from satellite technology to some enormous infrastructure projects, including a proposed oil pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia’s coast.
But the list is heavily weighted towards resources and energy. Minerals and metals alone account for nearly 38 percent of the projects, as per Nadjibulla’s calculations. Add energy and power infrastructure and the share rises to almost 70 percent.
“The summit is fundamentally about financing the physical productive capacity of the Canadian economy,” she said, pointing to mines, processing, energy generation, export infrastructure, ports and manufacturing.
Not all of the projects, however, are ready for investment. Some of those on offer are fully permitted, while others are still at the concept or feasibility stage.
“Some are quite large and expensive and are unlikely to be ready for prime time,” said Rachel Ziemba, an adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, a policy nonprofit.
Canada also has to prove it can build
For investors, getting major projects to that point has long been a sticking point.
Ziemba pointed to lengthy regulatory reviews, particularly for projects that need both federal and provincial approval.
Nadjibulla similarly cited “long and uncertain approval processes” and questions about whether projects can move “from announcement to execution”.
“Investors will want to see a credible pipeline, faster and more predictable permitting, policy stability, clearer revenue models and better coordination across provincial and federal jurisdictions,” Nadjibulla said.
Carney is trying to convince them that things are changing. His government has created a Major Projects Office to speed up approvals for projects it considers to be in the national interest, alongside a “one project, one review” approach aimed at reducing federal-provincial overlap.
The summit is a chance to show investors how that will work, Ziemba said. “But this is still early days.”
What does all of this mean for Canadians?
Even if Carney gets more of these projects financed and built, a bigger debate remains over who ultimately stands to benefit. In an interview with Democracy Now, Avi Lewis, leader of Canada’s New Democratic Party, criticised the prime minister for “selling our airports and our ports and privatising more of our economy to the benefit of foreign investors”.
That debate will be playing out just outside the summit. Labour, Indigenous, housing and climate groups are planning a Monday rally under the banner “The Many vs. the Money,” arguing that Canada’s economic future should not be shaped primarily by corporate executives and global investors.
The trade war has been shifting Canada’s investment focus from manufacturing and other industries built around the North American market to ports, pipelines and logistics that can help Canadian resources reach new markets.
Ziemba also pointed to another potential trade-off – those sectors require a lot of capital without necessarily creating the same number of jobs. That “may limit the benefits to Canadians looking to replace the US-integrated sectors,” she said.
Even if there are any major announcements this week, they will only tell part of the story.
Ziemba said she will be watching how much investors actually commit, the timelines and “clarity on who pays”.
“The summit helps with the first problem, showing investors what is available,” Nadjibulla said. “But execution will determine long-term success and whether the capital actually arrives.”

Businessman close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr's wedding celebration

Source: the investigation by ProPublica
Details: According to ProPublica, Kremlev paid for the private island where the reception was held and the guests stayed. Renting the island costs about US$100,000 a day. He also paid around US$70,000 for the fireworks display through the company organising it, and his team helped organise the event.

A spokesperson for Trump Jr did not deny that Kremlev had paid the expenses and described him as a personal friend, stressing that there is no business relationship between them. Kremlev's press service also said that he has never discussed political issues with any of his American friends and acquaintances.
Kremlev has headed the IBA since 2020. The association was previously funded by Russian energy giant Gazprom. Ukraine has imposed sanctions on the businessman, citing, among other things, his ties to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin and the Russian security services.
Background: In September 2025, Trump Jr spoke at an IBA conference in Istanbul alongside Kremlev, where he criticised the participation of trans women in women's sport.

PARIS, September 14. /TASS/. Estonia is in talks with France about joining Paris’ initiative on so-called forward nuclear deterrence, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told AFP.

He also announced plans to expand the country’s nuclear arsenal, while Paris no longer plans to disclose the exact number of warheads.

How The Early Spring Ends—And Sets the Stage for More Chinese Dramas on Netflix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:36:01 UTC
02:36:01 KST

A happy ending for Shang Zhitao (Sun Qian) and Luan Nian (Jing Boran) on Netflix’s Chinese workplace romance The Early Spring was incredibly hard-won. At the start of the 24-episode series based on a web novel by Gu Niang Bie Ku, recent college graduate Zhitao is hired by Beijing advertising agency Lime—against bigwig Nian’s wishes. The initial power imbalance between ordinary office worker Zhitao and her boss Nian is significant, and there is a company policy against romantic entanglements between co-workers. Still, they quickly fall into bed together. Over the next six years, the two are on-again, off-again as a prideful, emotionally repressed Nian struggles to say nice things to Zhitao and Zhitao struggles to balance her love for Nian with her commitment to her career.
Why does Shang Zhitao leave Beijing?
For Zhitao, Beijing isn’t just a place—it is a symbol of her career ambitions, and the kind of life she aspires to. While The Early Spring’s central focus is romance, the C-drama also delves into other aspects of Zhitao’s character and journey. A major throughline of the show is Zhitao’s efforts to make Beijing a home, and to succeed not just at a company or in a bustling metropolis, but in one of the most prestigious companies in one of China’s most global cities. So, when Zhitao chooses to leave Beijing in Episode 21, “A Grand Retreat,” she isn’t just retreating from Nian, she is retreating from the lifestyle that Beijing demands for success.
It’s not just one event that informs Zhitao’s decision to leave Beijing. When she tells Nian that she wants to get married and he tells her he doesn’t really think about it, Zhitao begins to reconsider their relationship. Then, one of Zhitao’s best friends dies by suicide. Finally, she gets passed over for a promotion in favor of a less experienced, nepo-baby co-worker. When she seeks comfort from Nian, he offers none. It’s the final straw for Zhitao, who begins to feel like all the time and energy she has committed to their relationship might not have been worth it.
The Early Spring’s happy ending
Heading into the final installments of the drama, Zhitao has finally called it quits on her toxic dynamic with Nian, moving home to Harbin and starting her own advertising agency in the snowy, northeastern city where she grew up. A few years pass before a bereft Nian attempts to reconcile. Zhitao’s company has partnered with Lime for a local project, and Nian uses it as an excuse to see Zhitao again. Zhitao is understandably reluctant to let Nian back into her life, but Nian uses the excuse of their dog, a Samoyed named Luke, to spend time with his ex-girlfriend.
Over the following months, Nian elbows his way into Zhitao’s life and attempts to show her that he has changed. He apologizes for his past behavior, and mostly listens to her when she asks for space. Eventually, Zhitao’s love for Nian wins out and she lets him back into her heart and her life. Nian makes it clear to Zhitao’s parents that he intends to marry their daughter, and then proposes to Zhitao by decorating an art gallery with photos from their time together. He calls it Flora’s Museum of Time and Eternity, using the English name Zhitao used when she worked at Lime. Lian gifts Zhitao a necklace with the “L” key from the typewriter Zhitao knocked over in his office during their first in-person meeting. He invites Zhitao’s closest friends and family, and asks the woman he has loved for almost a decade to marry him. She says yes, finally believing that the two can have a relationship as equals. In the final scenes of the show, we see Zhitao and Nian splitting their time between Harbin and Beijing, happy together.
Will there be a second season of The Early Spring?
The Early Spring has done incredibly well on Youku and Netflix, where the C-drama has steadily been in the Global Top Ten list. East Asian dramas don’t tend to have second seasons, but The Early Spring could easily be extended with the adaptation of the second book in the web novel series. Titled Miss Talkative, the sequel novel follows the unlikely romance between Zhitao’s work bestie Lumi and her stoic, more traditional co-worker Will. A developing relationship between the two is hinted at in The Early Spring TV series, but the plot line is left unresolved.
Netflix’s increasing commitment to Chinese dramas
Though Netflix has become known as a home for Korean dramas, with the U.S. streamer investing billions of dollars into the East Asian country’s TV and film industries, the same has not been true for Chinese dramas.
China is not interested in giving any U.S. company too much power in its economy, which has kept the streamer from setting up shop in the country. In 2016, Netflix released a letter to shareholders alongside a quarterly earnings report stating: “The regulatory environment for foreign digital content services in China has become challenging. We now plan to license content to existing online service providers in China rather than operate our own service in China in the near term.” That same year, the Chinese government implemented a de facto ban on South Korean entertainment in China following the announcement that the U.S. would be installing an anti-missile system in South Korea. Netflix is still not legally available in China.
In the decade since, Netflix’s catalogue and business model have become increasingly international. As Netflix focuses on expansion into international markets, C-dramas have become an increasingly valuable asset. While C-dramas have a growing audience in the U.S., they are even more popular in countries like Pakistan, Bangladesh, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Vietnam. “Audiences in Asia have long loved this category, but we're making them accessible to an even bigger global viewership,” Maya Huang, Head of Chinese-Language Content at Netflix, tells TIME.
Netflix has been growing their Mainland China offerings since 2024. Recent hits have included historical fantasy romance Pursuit of Jade and costume drama Ashes to Crown, adding to the organic popularity of earlier series like The Untamed, a historical fantasy romance based on a BL web novel that blew up in popularity during the pandemic. As Netflix looks towards the future, C-dramas are part of their plan, with “a team dedicated to finding the most authentic and best-in-class Chinese language stories” including ones—like The Early Spring—that are simulcast with a Chinese streamer. “With Netflix's reach, dubs and subtitles, and our ability to release titles simultaneously worldwide, we're seeing audiences discover these stories in the U.S., South America, Europe and the Middle East,” says Huang. “We want to give these fans more of what they love—so there's plenty more to come from our Chinese language slate.”

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday thanked the people of Rajasthan after the BJP emerged as the largest party in the state’s municipal elections, winning more wards than the Congress and securing majorities in four of the 10 municipal corporations.In a post on X, PM Modi said the results reflected support for the BJP’s policies of development and good governance under the “double-engine government”.“Heartfelt thanks to the people of Rajasthan for delivering a resounding victory to the BJP in the municipal elections,” PM Modi wrote.“This is a testament to the triumph of truth over the jhooth ki goonj (echo of lies),” he added.

BJP ahead of Congress in urban polls

BJP crosses majority in Kota
In Kota Municipal Corporation, the BJP secured 55 of the 100 wards, while Congress won 40 and Independents three. In Bundi, the BJP initially emerged as the largest party with 29 wards, two short of a majority. Congress won 20 wards, while Independents secured 11.Later in the day, three Independent candidates, Prabhat Devi, Aatmaram Chopdar and Vishal Sharma, joined the BJP, taking the party to a majority and enabling it to form the board.The BJP had also captured the previous mid-term board after Congress council chairperson Madu Nuwal was suspended.Congress leaders had expected to retain control but faced criticism over ticket distribution. Former councillors Devraj Gochar, Ankit Buliwal and Jeeshan Ali, who were denied Congress tickets, won as Independents.
BJP calls results a mandate for governance
BJP president Nitin Nabin thanked Rajasthan voters for what he described as a “historic victory”, saying the results showed continued faith in Modi’s leadership.
BJP national spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi also cited the party’s performance in Kota, where Congress leader Rahul Gandhi had conducted the student-centric programme ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’.“In Kota, where Rahul Gandhi had gone and attempted to create ‘jhooth ki goonj’, the BJP appears to be winning spectacularly,” Trivedi said.He claimed the results demonstrated that the Congress had “more propaganda and less reality” in its claims.

Mezuzahs smashed at Wilfrid Laurier University campus during Rosh Hashanah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:31:29 UTC
02:31:29 KST

Jewish students returning to campus at Wilfrid Laurier University (Laurier) after the holidays discovered that mezuzahs hung on their residence doors had been smashed and torn down over the High Holy Days.
The incident drew swift condemnation from community organizations, with Hillel Ontario and StandWithUs Canada issuing a joint statement on social media on Monday declaring that they "are horrified that, over the holiday weekend, Jewish students at Wilfred Laurier University were targeted with antisemitic hatred in the place they call home on campus."
The joint statement emphasized that "this cannot be the welcome Jewish students receive when they come to university," adding that "students have a right to feel safe and secure in their residences and to express their Jewish identity openly and proudly without fear of being targeted."
The organizations noted that the timing amplified the gravity of the incident, stating that "this occurred over Rosh Hashanah, making it all the more disturbing," and that "at a time when Jewish students should have been marking the beginning of a new year with pride, renewal, and hope, they were targeted by despicable hate."
Addressing the institutional response, the groups stressed that "there can be no tolerance for antisemitism on campus," and noted that "Hillel has been in touch with university leadership to ensure this matter is dealt with decisively."
Jewish students 'will not be intimidated into hiding who they are'
The organizations asserted that "Jewish students are not going anywhere," and that "they will not be intimidated into hiding who they are or removing the symbols of their Jewish identity" because "they are proud, they belong at Laurier, and they deserve to be safe being openly Jewish on campus."
In a statement to the Jerusalem Post, Jay Solomon, CEO of Hillel Ontario, said, “We condemn this act of antisemitism in the strongest possible terms. It is not an isolated incident, but part of a broader pattern of escalating hostility toward Jewish students that we have seen across campuses in Ontario and Canada. We have been in touch with university leadership and expressed our alarm at this incident, which follows similar violations on other campuses since October 7. The administration has assured us the matter is under investigation.”
“This cannot continue. All institutions of higher learning have an obligation to keep Jews safe, and we urge all schools to enforce their policies and hold perpetrators to account swiftly and transparently,” Solomon said.
In a statement to the Post, Laurier said the university “is aware of an incident of vandalism that involved widespread damage along various residence hallways. We are treating this matter very seriously, and our Special Constable Service is leading the investigation.”
The university added, “The students have connected with university residence staff, and appropriate supports are in place and available to them. We take the safety of our students very seriously. We strongly condemn acts of antisemitism and have zero tolerance for hate speech, racism, threats, and harassment.”
The incident comes amidst a surge in hate incidents targeting the Jewish community throughout Canada in recent months, including on university campuses, mirroring findings from a federal report released in August by the Department of Canadian Heritage and produced by the Association for Canadian Studies and the Metropolis Institute.
Known as the Campus Antisemitism and Student Experience (CASE) report, the study documented that over 95 percent of surveyed Jewish students experienced or witnessed antisemitism on post-secondary campuses nationwide.

EU states to raise game as Arctic becomes strategic geopolitical frontier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:30:36 UTC
02:30:36 KST

EU states to raise game as Arctic becomes strategic geopolitical frontier
Europe racing Russia, China and US to seize security and economic opportunities.
European Union member states have agreed to increase investment in the Arctic amid a growing scramble for security advantages and vast natural resources.
Labelling the Arctic a “geopolitical hotspot”, a Monday meeting involving 12 countries called for the EU to “take on a more strategic and proactive role in the European Arctic”, meeting participants said in a joint statement.
The meeting, which featured the leaders of Finland, Denmark, Estonia, France, Greece, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania and Sweden, focused on the race for influence over the Arctic as receding ice opens opportunities in the northern region. The discussion identified Russia as the largest threat to the European Arctic, but also noted the ambitions of China and the United States.
“This region has become a geopolitical hotspot,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told a news conference.
Despite Germany not being an Arctic country, Merz said his presence at the summit testified to the importance of the region to overall European security and suggested years of relative neglect should end.
“Let me put it this way: High north – and low attention – is over,” he said.
Russia, Canada, Iceland, Norway and the United States are considered Arctic countries, in addition to EU members Finland, Sweden and Denmark.
All have become involved in increasing geopolitical competition over the region as the retreat of ice sheets – spurred by climate change – has exposed its security and economic opportunities.
Russia has beefed up its military presence in recent years, reopening and modernising bases abandoned since the Soviet Union collapsed.
“Russia poses the most significant and long-term threat to Arctic security and stability. In order to respond to the threat posed by Russia, the EU must treat the Arctic as a strategic frontier,” said Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo after the meeting.
The warming climate is opening up the Arctic for shipping, fishing, drilling and mining. China has made no secret of its interest in the territory, which is rich in natural resources.
The race has also stirred tension among NATO allies. Greenland, which is not part of the EU but overseen by Denmark, has become a bone of contention between the EU and the United States, with US President Trump claiming that Denmark cannot protect the Arctic island from Russia and China.
“I think everybody recognised that Greenland has been under a big pressure,” said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Last week, the European Union signed a declaration with Greenland, promising a stronger partnership and announcing a 200-million-euro ($232m) investment package to soothe anxiety caused by repeated threats from Trump to annex the self-governing territory.

Female athletes, including Olympic champions, have criticized a viral sports gambling advertisement starring US actor Sydney Sweeney, accusing the campaign of sexualizing women’s sports and reducing athletic imagery to a marketing device.
 
The criticism centers on the “Just Sports” campaign for US sports prediction-market company Novig, released Sept. 9. The advertisement shows Sweeney wearing little or no clothing while sports equipment is positioned across her body as she imitates activities including tennis, hockey, golf, basketball and American football.
 
Sweeney repeatedly says “sports” during the advertisement, which ends by inviting viewers to test their sporting knowledge on Novig’s platform.
 
The campaign quickly attracted tens of millions of views online, but athletes from several sports began responding with footage of themselves training and competing under variations of the message: “This is what a woman in sport looks like.”
 
Former US gymnast Gracie Kramer was among the first to respond, sharing competition footage on Instagram and contrasting it with Sweeney’s portrayal of sports.
 
Olympic swimmer Lani Pallister and sprinters Bree Masters and Amy Hunt later joined the online response, sharing images of their training, races and achievements. The Australian Institute of Sport also posted footage of women taking part in archery, gymnastics, boxing and softball, as well as sports scientists working behind the scenes.
 
Four-time Olympic swimming champion Ariarne Titmus described the campaign as “an absolute joke.”
 
“I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,” she wrote on US-based social media platform Instagram, arguing that it disrespected women who had devoted their lives to their sports.
 
Titmus said women’s sports represented teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence and unity, questioning why women’s bodies were still being sexualized to generate revenue.
 
Australian Olympic water polo medalist Tilly Kearns also posted a compilation of women competing in sports and said she “absolutely” hated the advertisement.
 
World champion boxer Skye Nicolson said the criticism was not directed at women embracing their appearance or femininity, but at the use of sexualized imagery to market a sports-related product.
 
“There’s a big difference between looking ‘sexy’ because you do sport compared to use sex to sell ‘sport’,” Nicolson wrote on Instagram.
 
She said the campaign made a “mockery” of women in sports and disregarded generations of athletes who had fought to be recognized for their performances.
 
Sweeney is not only the campaign's public face. Novig announced she had joined the company as a strategic partner and equity holder.
 
She also told Complex that she had been involved in creative discussions from the beginning, saying she did not want simply to attach her name to a company without having a role in the project.
 
Novig defended the concept as an attempt to emphasize that its prediction market focuses exclusively on sports.
 
“The campaign was about embracing a fun idea,” Sweeney said in the company’s announcement, describing its approach as one of “confidence, humor and a playful edge.”
Sweeney appeared to respond indirectly to the criticism Sunday by sharing previous ESPN Body Issue covers featuring nude or partially clothed female and male athletes.
 
She did not directly respond to the athletes’ criticism or explain whether the ESPN covers were intended as a defense of the campaign.

Air Force Plans Hundreds of Autonomous Fighter and ISR Drones by 2032
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:25:53 UTC
02:25:53 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force plans to field at least 500 semi-autonomous fighter drones known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft by 2032, and another 500 cheap reconnaissance and strike drones known as Massed Modular Aircraft that same year, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14.
In his keynote address to open AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Meink said the service would bolster its combat capability—which for decades has mostly come from crewed aircraft such as fighters and bombers—with lower-cost drones that operate with minimal direction from Airmen.
And that future is coming fast, Meink said.
“Because of the steps we are taking today, we will have a significantly different force by 2032,” Meink said. “By then, our special operators will have the ability to employ thousands of autonomous one-way attack systems, and we will have autonomous fighters like Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCAs.”
The first iteration of CCAs—General Atomics Aeronautical Systems’ FQ-42A and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A—are now rolling off the assembly line and will specialize in air-to-air missions. Future “increments” of CCA could focus on other missions, such as air-to-ground strikes, reconnaissance, or electronic warfare operations.
“We intend to have at least 500 of these in service by 2032,” Meink said, and by that time the drones will be performing many of the same missions crewed fighters perform today, he added.
Meink’s projection is the most ambitious target the Air Force has yet to announce for the CCA program. In 2024, his predecessor as Secretary, Frank Kendall, said the service would have 100 CCAs by 2029. Earlier this year, Meink said he expected to have 150 by the end of the decade.
The Air Force is also accelerating a program called Massed Modular Aircraft, which will field drones to take on some of the missions the MQ-9A Reaper performs today. The service in recent months has grown concerned over the pace of Reaper losses in operations against Iran—roughly 45 have been lost so far, or about a quarter of the Air Force’s fleet—and moved to speed up its plans to field MMAs.
Like CCAs, MMA drones will have autonomous capabilities, but they will be cheaper and less complex than CCAs. Air Force officials told reporters Sept. 3 that the air vehicle of an MMAs will cost roughly $10 million, without sensors or other systems included, while CCAs will cost twice as much, at $20 million per air vehicle.
Meink said the Air Force plans to field 100 MMA drones by 2029 and 500 by 2032—higher than previous estimates from Air Force officials.
In a roundtable with reporters later, Meink also said the the Air Force plans to have multiple types of MMA drones from different contractors in its fleet, similar to how its CCA program is working with multiple vendors.
Asked about the expanded plans for the MMA program, Meink pointed to the program’s relatively low cost and the importance of the MQ-9’s combined strike and recon mission.
“That [ISR and strike] mission is a very important mission,” Meink said. “We’re looking at how we do that with a mix of different platforms. … The ability to bring low-cost mass is a driver here, and we expect these to be significantly cheaper than even the MQ-9s or the CCA.”
When asked if the Air Force could buy more than 500 MMA drones, Meink said that will depend on how much money Congress provides in the budget, but added “I think it should probably be much higher than that.”
When the two autonomous drones—MMA and CCA—are in the field, Meink said, they will transform the way the Air Force fights wars.
The sixth-generation F-47 fighter and B-21 Raider stealth bomber are “phenomenal aircraft” that “will be able to do things no other aircraft has ever done before,” Meink said. But they won’t be able to deliver the “massive scale of combat power we need” on their own, he warned. That’s where lower-cost, uncrewed autonomous platforms like CCA and MMA come in.
“When we pair manned aircraft with lower-cost autonomous systems, we will be able to unlock combat power at scale,” Meink said.
Both CCAs and MMAs are being built around an open systems architecture approach that will make it easier to swap different sensors or other capabilities into the drones, using standardized interfaces. Emphasizing the modularity that comes with open systems architecture will accelerate procurement of the systems, Meink said, and increase competition from industry, which will ultimately lower prices, give the Air Force more choices, and improve the drones’ combat power.
Meink told reporters in the roundtable that CCAs will continually evolve, even within the same increment, but that it was too soon to predict what the fleet of 500 will look like by 2032.
“It depends on how the current ones perform, and what additional capabilities the users are saying they need,” Meink said. “Can we evolve that into the current iteration? Do we need a different iteration? We’re working our way through that right now.”
Meink also said the Air Force plans to have “tens of thousands” of the new low-cost Family of Affordable Mass Munition, or FAMM, weapons in its inventory by 2030, and that they are already being used today.
Meink also revealed a name change for General Atomics’ CCA, which the company had been calling Dark Merlin. The FQ-42 will now be called Vengeance, he said. Anduril’s FQ-44 will continue with the name Fury.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a text to Air & Space Forces Magazine that the company will cease using the Dark Merlin name now that the Air Force has chosen its own moniker.
“We love when our customers name their aircraft,” Brinkley said. “Vengeance pretty much sums up what the FQ-42 brings to the fight.”

Syria fuel price hikes test public patience with economic recovery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:25:13 UTC
02:25:13 KST

Syria fuel price hikes test public patience with economic recovery
Anger rises in Syrian cities as fuel price hikes burden struggling households amid an ongoing cost-of-living crisis.
The sight of protesters blocking roads and burning tyres on the streets of several Syrian cities and towns has highlighted popular anger over a government decision to increase fuel prices and a wider cost-of-living crisis.
The protests, which erupted on Sunday, come after months of complaints about soaring energy costs and criticisms that the lives of many Syrians have not improved since the fall of former Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Protests break out across Syria over fuel price increases
- list 2 of 3Will the Houthi attacks activate the Mecca Pact?
- list 3 of 3At least seven killed in fire at prison in northern Syria
The Syrian government has defended its efforts, arguing that it will take time to overcome decades of economic stagnation and international isolation.
The trigger for Sunday’s protests was a government announcement that diesel prices would rise by 40 percent, petrol by at least 25 percent and cooking gas around nine percent.
The government said the increases were temporary and caused by a spike in refined petroleum products following the US-Israeli war on Iran and renewed hostilities in Yemen. However, the Syrian parliament has summoned Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir for a hearing on rising fuel costs, a sign that officials were concerned by the public outcry.
Public anger
When anti-regime forces overthrew al-Assad’s government, much of the country erupted in celebration.
It came after more than a decade of war and the 50-year rule of the al-Assad family, which had led to international sanctions on the country.
Aside from expectations that freedoms would increase after the fall of the regime, which operated as a police state, many Syrians also hoped the country’s dire economic conditions would improve.
That has been a tough task for the new Syrian government, led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Since coming to power 21 months ago, the government has focussed on securing international legitimacy and lifting the complex network of sanctions placed on Syria.
On that front, it has largely been successful.
In August, Syria was removed from the US state sponsors of terrorism list, building on earlier decisions to lift sanctions by the US, the European Union and other world powers. This allowed for Syria to be reintegrated into the world economy and receive increased foreign investment.
There has been optimism in Syria, but while the government insists that the positive impact of the removal of sanctions and other government actions will take time, patience has run out for some.
“Fuel itself is not an isolated energy issue right now; it’s related to the cost of living crisis for every household and business in Syria,” Vittorio Maresca di Serracapriola, sanctions lead analyst at Karam Shaar Advisory, told Al Jazeera. “The anger right now reflects a deeper concern that the recovery stemming from the sanctions relief and Syria’s gradual reconnection with the global financial system is not yet translating into affordable [prices].”
“The protests show that Syrians increasingly hold their own government responsible for what they pay,” Nanar Hawach, a Syrian political analyst, told Al Jazeera. “Sanctions relief weakened the argument that hardship comes from outside and raised expectations at the same time. Much of the anger is also coming from areas that backed the change of government, making this the kind of discontent a government can answer only with results.”
Syria’s poverty rate is around 90 percent, according to the UN’s World Food Programme. The rise in fuel costs has a universal impact, affecting the price of transport but also food and other services.
“A 40 percent diesel hike is not just inconvenient; it is really a threat to [people’s] economic survival on a daily basis,” Maresca di Serracapriola said.
Syria remains highly dependent on energy imports. The country produces around 102,000 barrels of oil per day, compared with domestic needs of around 325,000 barrels per day, al-Bashir said. Syria refines some of its crude domestically but its refineries cannot produce enough petroleum products to meet demands, forcing it to import substantial quantities of diesel, petrol and other fuels.
The Syrian government said it was working on an overhaul of the Baniyas refinery – the country’s largest – in the hope that it will raise processing capacity at the facility from around 80,000 to 130,000 barrels per day.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Energy said prices would continue to be reviewed as global market conditions change. It also said it would work over the long term to expand refining and storage capacity.
Government action
Authorities will now look for ways to temper public anger.
Hawach suggested a “protected diesel price for public transport and farmers”, as well as the government announcing dates for when temporary price increases would end.
“[This] would likely cost the treasury less than the concessions it has tended to make after protesters block roads, and would give people a reason to wait rather than take to the streets,” he said.
The protests have come about as the Syrian government attempts to rebuild the country after a war that devastated much of the country and killed hundreds of thousands of people.
Sanctions removal has borne some fruit: the World Bank approved around $491m in grants to Syria to support infrastructure and economic development since last year.
Still, after a July visit, the International Monetary Fund recommended that the Syrian government collect more revenue and be more selective about what it spends money on “to create the fiscal space needed to create room for development spending and to enhance the social safety net to protect the most vulnerable segments of the population”.
So far, the government has benefited from a degree of patience among Syrians. But despite the progress made over the past year, that patience is beginning to wear thin – particularly among the country’s most vulnerable, who have yet to feel the benefits of economic growth.
“The question is whether this whole process of recovery will translate into credible relief for households, workers, small businesses and farmers facing the knock-on effects of inflation and higher energy prices,” Maresca di Serracapriola said.

Private schools become a costly choice for struggling parents in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:22:48 UTC
02:22:48 KST

Private schools become a costly choice for struggling parents in Gaza
Gaza families face difficult choices: send children to schools in tents with few resources to pay for private school.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip — In their tent in central Gaza, Khadija Abu Qados gets her 11-year-old daughter, Jouri, ready for another day at school amid the ongoing Israeli air raids and crippling financial crisis.
The family has been living in a camp for displaced Palestinians in Deir el-Balah since their neighbourhood, Sheikh Radwan, in northern Gaza, was destroyed in the Israeli offensive in Gaza City last September.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How Israel systematically dismantles Palestinian life in occupied West Bank
- list 2 of 3Burnham must establish an inquiry into Britain’s role in the Gaza genocide
- list 3 of 3‘Silent Cold War’: Why calls to slow AI have sparked new US–China frontier
Like their home, the classrooms for Jouri and her 14-year-old sister, Ritaj, at Elyaa’ School are also tents. There are few chairs or desks, so children usually sit on mattresses and carpets when they learn. There is no air conditioning or fans, so the heat makes it difficult for children to focus.
The children have already spent long periods out of school since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023. Online classes were a challenge due to difficulties in internet access during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Now, Jouri and two of her siblings attend a nearby school run by volunteer teachers near their camp, which charges 30 shekels ($8) a month. Even though it is far cheaper than private schools, the modest fee is difficult for the family to afford when food, water and other basic needs come first.
“If I could afford it, I would send them to private school,” 39-year-old Khadija told Al Jazeera.
Before the war, her daughters attended an UNRWA school in Gaza City, where her children performed well and were praised for their achievements.
Now, she watches them study in tents. The conditions may be difficult, but the teachers are helping her children catch up with missed school time.
“The teaching here is excellent [but] I feel sad for my children because they are studying in these difficult circumstances. There are no chairs and no proper seats. This is not an educational environment at all,” she said.
“Even the stationery is something I can barely afford because prices have become so high. A single notebook costs between four and six shekels.”
The family’s experiences reflect a wider education crisis in Gaza after nearly three years of war.
Around 700,000 children aged between four and 17 had missed formal, face-to-face schooling for almost three consecutive school years during Israel’s war on Gaza, UNICEF said in May.
Just two percent of all school buildings are undamaged and 93 percent of them require major repairs or complete reconstruction. About 420,000 children – three in five – had no access to face-to-face learning.
Israeli air raids are a constant threat, with at least 300 children killed since last October’s “ceasefire”. Last week, eight-year-old Wafaa Akila and her father were killed when their car was struck on the way back home from school in western Gaza.
With the formal education system in ruins, parents and teachers have stepped in, opening temporary learning spaces in tents and volunteer initiatives.
Noha Khadra, who spent 10 years as a teacher, opened the Elyaa’ School in January, operating under the supervision of the Ministry of Education.
Pupils learn in tents with a few desks and not enough chairs, while other essentials such as blackboards are in poor condition.
More than 1,100 students have enrolled in the ‘field school, but there are only 40 volunteer teachers and administrative staff.
Despite the obstacles, she said there is high demand for places in the school, but a lack of resources and staff has meant a gruelling initial nine months for the principal.
“At the beginning, there were no tables. The children were sitting on mattresses. Many students come to us without stationery… so we buy it for them ourselves as much as we can,” she told Al Jazeera.
“I am honestly upset about the classroom conditions. This project has drained my energy, and I cannot provide more than what I am already doing.”
The school provides children with a place away from the everyday pressures of displacement and also access to essentials for survival, such as water.
Private schools
The situation in private schools is better than the voluntary centres, but the high costs make them affordable only to a minority of parents in Gaza.
Zahra Saleh, 25, enrolled her six-year-old son, Ibrahim, in first grade and her five-year-old son, Karam, in kindergarten at the Abdul Aziz Private School in the west of Gaza City.
After finding most private schools too expensive, she finally found one she could afford. Zahra’s husband, like many men in Gaza, is unemployed, so paying the 400 shekels ($131) monthly school fees is difficult. But she did not want Ibrahim, who was beginning his first year of formal schooling, to lose any more education.
She also wanted her children to have a regular routine, with classes from 7am to noon. Learning subjects such as Arabic, English and Mathematics as they would have done before the war, was also her hope.
“I’m in a very difficult financial situation. I had to work at the school so I could reduce the cost of the fees for my children,” Zahra told Al Jazeera.
“I taught him at home as much as I could, but children don’t learn everything at home. In the end, we had to send him to a school. It’s just a normal school environment. That’s what I want.”
Families are also struggling with the growing costs of school supplies, with 12 notepads selling for six shekels ($1.96) before the war but now costing four shekels ($1.31) for just one.
Financial crisis
The schooling crisis comes at a time of acute financial hardship for almost every Palestinian in Gaza.
Abdul Aziz began as a field school in tents with volunteer teachers in 2024, before moving to its current rented building in Shujaiya, west of Gaza City, for the new school year starting this month.
Around 20 staff teach 300 students, aged between three and 15, a much lower student-to-teacher ratio than in non-private schools.
Gaza’s labour market is now “largely nonfunctional”, with more than 90 percent of working-age people without a job. The World Bank estimated in May that $71.5bn was needed for Gaza’s recovery and reconstruction.
The financial pressure facing families is part of a broader economic collapse in the Strip. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics said Gaza’s GDP contracted by 84 percent in 2025 compared with 2023, while unemployment reached 78 percent.
Doaa Qdeih, Abdul Aziz Private School’s director, is mindful of the financial difficulties families face, so has some leeway on payments with parents, including Zahra.
“I found a lot of flexibility. They welcomed me, supported me and understood my circumstances,” she said.
The school does not have one fixed fee for every student. Qdeih said she considers each family’s circumstances before deciding what it can pay.
“I don’t set a fixed amount. Before I set the amount, I look at the situation of the people — what they do for work and what the child’s circumstances are — and then we decide what they can afford,” she said.
“We have families who support each other. You find someone who can afford to pay 300 shekels ($80) contributing, while another family cannot pay anything. There is solidarity among us.”
Almost all this money from the fees goes towards rent and operating costs. Qdeih also used profits from another business she owns to furnish and repair the building the school now uses. But she does not see private schools as the solution to Gaza’s education crisis.
“I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: if the government or the ministry provides places for education, we are ready to volunteer,” she said.
“We don’t want anything in return. We just want to continue serving the children and give them the education they deserve.”

Ukrainian Drone Crew Hits Four Russian Grad Rocket Launchers in One Mission, One 45 Km Away

Ukrainian Drone Crew Hits Four Russian Grad Rocket Launchers in One Mission, One 45 Km Away
A Ukrainian drone crew destroyed two Russian BM-21 Grad multiple rocket launchers and damaged two more during a single deployment, with one of the strikes carried out after a 45-kilometer drone flight.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 42nd Separate Mechanized Brigade on September 14, the operation was conducted by a crew from the Perun Unmanned Systems Battalion. The crew commander, who uses the call sign “Zhulyk,” said the four Grad systems were the first targets of this type struck by the battalion.
“During this operation, our crew destroyed two Grads and hit two more. These were the first Grads in our battalion. We set every record we could: both for time spent on position and for range. We flew 45 kilometers and struck the target,” Zhulyk said.
The brigade did not disclose the exact location of the strikes or specify what type of drone was used.
The crew remained at its position for 60 days, conducting operations during both daytime and nighttime. Its personnel included an FPV pilot, an explosives specialist, a navigator, and other members responsible for supporting long-range drone missions.
Zhulyk said the crew operated continuously because each member had a separate role and there was no replacement team available.
“We have a 24/7 workload. We work at night, we work during the day. There is no rotation where one person flies while someone else sleeps—there is nothing like that. Everyone has their own job,” he said.
According to the brigade, reaching and leaving the position presented an additional challenge because Russian forces were also conducting aerial reconnaissance in search of Ukrainian drone teams. The crew reached the position in roughly half a day, while leaving it after the two-month deployment took nearly two days and required stops along the route.
The BM-21 Grad is a truck-mounted 122mm multiple launch rocket system originally developed by the Soviet Union and remains widely used by Russian forces for battlefield fire support.
Earlier, on September 11, Ukrainian forces destroyed a rare North Korean Type-75 multiple-launch rocket system deployed by Russia, according to Ukraine’s 40th Separate Artillery Brigade. The launcher, which carries 12 rocket tubes, was located and then struck directly by a Ukrainian drone.

EU envoys extend Russia sanctions by seven days to debate six-month renewal, EU presidency says
BRUSSELS, Sept 14 - European Union envoys have pushed back the expiry of EU Russia sanctions listings by seven days until September 22, a spokesperson for the EU's Irish presidency said on Monday, after failing to agree on a six-month renewal.
At issue is whether to de-list Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov. France has joined Slovakia in a call to remove him, citing national security concerns, EU diplomats said.
"France is one of the countries most committed to increasing pressure — by all means — on the Russian war machine, as well as to supporting Ukraine," a French diplomatic source said. "We face a specific national security issue and wish to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr. Usmanov."
France's foreign ministry spokesperson declined to comment.
The designations, which target nearly 3,000 companies and individuals with asset freezes and travel bans, had been due to expire on September 15.
"In order to allow additional time for member states to comprehensively examine proposals for the renewal, Coreper has agreed to prolong the regime by a period of 7 days, until midnight Tuesday 22 September," the spokesperson said, referring to the Comité des Représentants Permanents — the body of EU ambassadors that prepares work for the 27 heads of member states.
EU sanctions require unanimous approval from all 27 member states and must be renewed every six months.
Usmanov had a net worth of $18.8 billion as of early 2026, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, and is subject to EU and U.S. sanctions and a travel ban.
Usmanov, a metals and mining mogul, has launched multiple lawsuits in Europe with the ultimate goal of having the sanctions lifted. In some, his lawyers contested statements in the media that were used as grounds for the sanctions.
The billionaire also holds assets in telecoms, internet companies and media, and he owns Russian business daily Kommersant.
EU countries frequently debate Russia sanctions renewals until the last moment, in the past largely due to demands from Hungary's former leader, Viktor Orban, and Slovakia, which has better relations with Moscow than most other EU states.
In June, EU countries agreed for the first time to renew the bloc's sectoral sanctions, such as those on energy, for a year to reduce the opportunity for such debates. REUTERS
