The legal, ethical war which NAZA highlights and Israel is still barely showing up for - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:12:53 UTC
02:12:53 KST

Movies are always sensationalized and simplified. Anonymous accusations are always problematic. But no one should understate the legal and ethical harm that Israel and the IDF now face following the launch of the NAZA film, which frames the 2023-2025 war in Gaza as a genocide.
It is not the first video footage or detailed, specific accusations against Israel.
Those have been pouring in since nearly the start of the war.
And Breaking the Silence, 972 Magazine, The New York Times, and other media have occasionally gotten Israeli soldiers on the record making accusations against the IDF.
But here are 24 (presumed) Israeli soldiers on camera (even if anonymous) from a variety of different roles, especially relating to artificial intelligence (AI) and targeting, making genocide and war crimes accusations in a film made by two Israelis.
There are Israel-haters and anti-Semites who could care less about facts and are dead set on labeling Israel for genocide to try to tear it down and prevent the IDF from exercising self-defense.
Separately, there are naïve, well-meaning persons who are clueless about the scope of systematic human shields Hamas has used, from schools to UN facilities to mosques to hospitals.
These accusers in the NAZA film know all or many of these facts and are still making the accusations, and that is why they are so problematic for Israel legally and ethically.
Going after the IDF accusers legally will not solve any problems, because they are just adding credibility to already seriously researched allegations.
An April 2024 report by 972 Magazine and a December 2024 report by The New York Times brought some of the targeting and AI issues which NAZA seems to raise (even if without specifics) into clear contrast.
Past Israeli commission set a high threshold for proportionality
Simply stated: assuming Hamas systematically uses human shields and that the Israeli military was going to have to kill far more Gazans in this war than in prior ones in order to decisively beat Hamas militarily after the terror group’s October 7 slaughter of around 1,200 Israelis and its taking of 250 hostages: when does the ratio of terrorists to civilians in a particular attack, and as a matter of policy, violate even the most extreme interpretation of proportionality?
Can killing 100 civilians (as claimed by past media reports) or 500 civilians (as claimed by NAZA) be justified to kill even the most senior single terrorist? Can Israel say it is justified to kill 20 civilians "merely" to kill mid-level terrorists?
A prior Israeli judicial commission about 15 years ago found that an IDF assassination of Hamas military leader Saleh Shehada in 2002, which killed 13 civilians, including his wife and minor daughter, was not a war crime. Yet, the commission found the attack to be borderline, meaning some of the numbers critics have accused Israel of in this war, if true, would likely violate proportionality limits.
The 2024 New York Times report contended that the IDF assassination of senior Hamas terrorist, Jabalya Central Battalion Commander Ibrahim Biari in late October 2023, had a 100-to-1 ratio.
972 Magazine's 2024 report asserted that the December 2, 2023 bombing of Hamas Shejaia Battalion commander Wisam Farhat endorsed a 100-to-1 ratio.
According to reports – no Israeli government or IDF officials have yet been allowed to see the film – the NAZA film, without identifying a specific date or incident, sends the ratio up to the stratosphere of 500 to 1.
Here, the problem is less the film, which makes an amorphous allegation that cannot be checked, but the fact that the IDF never really responded to the seriously researched New York Times and 972 stories which came out with similar allegations nearly two years ago and more than two years ago.
The IDF needs to respond to the AI targeting accusations with much more transparency, both in general and to specific incidents that prior reports raised, which the NAZA films merely dramatized.
In fact, shockingly, the IDF did not put out its first report responding to specific war crimes allegation files until August 19 of this year – nearly three years after the start of the war.
Some of the problematic delay came from former IDF military advocate general Yifat Tomer Yerushalmi resigning in October 2025, leaving her predecessor, current IDF MAG Maj. Gen. Itay Offir to start picking up the pieces in November 2025.
But countries and militaries do not come down to single individuals.
The fact is that the Post has received repeated messages throughout the Israeli legal establishment that there was pressure from Israeli government officials to delay publications of many of the decisions.
Some of this pressure was due to the fear of government officials that portions of their constituency would hold them partially accountable for probing and prosecuting IDF soldiers, something which is very unpopular domestically.
Another source of pressure was the self-defeating concern that publicizing details of probing and prosecuting IDF officials would be used against soldiers by the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ). Meanwhile, as former deputy attorney-general for international affairs Roy Schondorf already pointed out in May 2024, the delay in publicizing details of the probes and prosecutions is exactly one of the mistakes Israel made, which allowed the ICC and ICJ to jump forward, wrongfully claiming that Israel was not probing or prosecuting anyone.
There have been other technical reasons for the delays: that the war kept continuing, leading to opening more news cases being opened; that there are over 3,000 review cases being checked and over 150 criminal probes being checked, which far exceeded the resources that the IDF legal division had to move forward promptly (the number of criminal cases is five times the number opened in 2014 and the number of review cases is six times more.)
But this issue became clear within a few months, such that had the government and IDF prioritized the issue, the resources issue probably could have been resolved by mid-2024.
In December 2024, the Post learned from off-record IDF sources that there are no set ratios and that the IDF viewed the NYT report's message at the time that these ratios are essentially part of a factory-style free-for-all blow-everyone-up strategy as inaccurate.
Rather, the Post understands that the IDF's view is that the NYT report confused various minimal parameters that may exist for setting what level of senior-ranked IDF officials are mandated to sign off on certain strikes with the end of the process of approving or not approving a strike.
For example, the IDF revealed in April 2024 that only an IDF brigadier-general-level officer had the authority to approve a strike on a Hamas fighter who was taking actions near a humanitarian food delivery caravan.
An unanswered question is whether the IDF lived up to these standards at the start of the war in October-November 2023. The Post learned in December 2024 that the IDF would acknowledge it had less time and fewer resources to evaluate each target during that period than in other periods.
However, the IDF would still contend that it properly checked its targets for civilian casualties, including with multiple tools.
This last point leads into the various reports which have also raised questions about the IDF’s target bank and AI warfare methods for incriminating some Gazans and for estimating how many civilians are nearby.
Hamas is responsible for using its people as human shields and so has probably committed tens of thousands of war crimes against its own people during this war.
But does this excuse the IDF from catching a repeat error in estimating civilians where – according to the reports – it was estimating civilians sometimes from cell phone use or from old records – without using drones or forces on the ground to double-check changes?
On November 16, 2023, the IDF allegedly killed dozens of members of the Malaka family, including a number of women and minors. According to the 2024 NYT report, the IDF’s estimate of civilian harm was around 16 based on cell phone use and former records. Yet cell phone use was out, and dozens more people had come to shelter in the same area because there were no other non-bombed areas to take shelter in. Unlike earlier wars, the report said the IDF did not invest in localized resources to check if its civilian estimates were correct.
If the IDF misestimated civilians by the dozens not only this time, but many times, at one point, does such an error carry a new level of responsibility, potentially even criminal?
Airwars, a London-based conflict monitor, documented 136 IDF strikes that it said each killed at least 15 people in October 2023 alone.
Presumably, a certain number of these people were Hamas terrorists, and the Airwars numbers may have other deficiencies, but until now, the IDF has only addressed five controversial cases with specific decisions and details, and only on August 19.
The Post has learned that the IDF's view is that overgeneralizations about its overreliance on AI and cell phone tracking to determine potential civilian harm are inaccurate. But even now the IDF has continued the mistake of refusing to publicize what its other tools have been for checking potential civilian casualties.
Previously, the Post has reported that drones are regularly used to follow the status of civilians in a target area and that there have been hundreds, if not thousands, of cases where the IDF called off an attack when the drones revealed that too many civilians were in an area about to be struck.
Maybe that has been the tool which has been used to check for civilians, maybe Palestinian collaborators or pro-Israeli gangs who were revealed in 2025, maybe Israeli special forces on the ground. But the impact that these charges are having on national security already far exceeds whatever tactical losses might come from revealing some of Israel's techniques for reducing civilian harm.
Viewers who applauded the NAZA film for 25 minutes at its opening probably won't take the time to review Israel's detailed rebuttal. Most probably presumed Israel committed genocide before the film started.
But many fair-minded Americans and Europeans still will, and Israel and the IDF need to go into overdrive putting out detailed responses to two- and three-year-old allegations before even those fence-sitters shut off any willingness to hear the other side of the story.
AI targeting is not only under new scrutiny in Israel, but worldwide.
And Israelis, after three years of militarily defeating and clobbering enemies on all fronts, should also be ready for an honest look at instances in which individual soldiers departed from the open fire rules. Even if most soldiers followed the rules, some will need to pay a legal price for their actions, both because that is the IDF's value and because such accountability may yet save the Jewish state as a whole.

Britain’s House of Commons has been the place where many outstanding speeches have been delivered.

Worse, he predicated Britain’s new policy decision on his being Jewish, saying, “I do so as a proud British Jew.”
He then continued, expressing “the deepest gratitude to the State of Israel for giving a home to my grandmother” after she lost her husband and 60 other family members at the hands of the Nazis.
Complacently and blindly, in declaring sanctions to force Israel to accept a political solution Israel has decided for itself that would endanger its very survival, a solution the Arab side has itself rejected for at least 90 years, he ignores the distinct probability that he is facilitating a version of Islamist Nazism in its goals to eliminate the Jewish state he once picked oranges in at a kibbutz.

Perhaps applying sanctions to persons, businesses, banks, and governing institutions that support anti-Jewish Arab terror? If not in Israel and the Palestinian Authority, then at least in the United Kingdom?
If Britain is struggling with anti-Jewish violence and refusing to deal with the underlying prop-ups of the shootings, stabbings, and the fire bombings, is it not hubris to presume the Arab wars against Israel are a problem England can solve with sanctions on Israel?
Recipe for disaster
Miliband's crutch of declaring himself a “good Jew” with a good Jewish family in Israel, while admitting he is an atheist with a non-Jewish wife, is an unworthy trick of seeking to lull Jews into trusting his policy.
Despite him being “proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” there is very much a contradiction between that and support for the state of Palestine, as he posited.
I, too, am a proud Jew, and I proudly suggest to Miliband and to Andy Burnham that it’s about time that supporters of an Arab Palestine realize that Jewish rights must be acknowledged, among them Jewish national identity and our historic national home, as the League of Nations decided in 1922 and as Lord Balfour wrote in 1917.

“Jewish settlement” in the land where Jews lived for millennia, since at least 1250 BCE, is a natural right, and the League of Nations recognized it as such.
Britain and its government have erred terribly. How long until the error is realized and corrected?

Phases of Objects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:12:00 UTC
02:12:00 KST

What happens to a clay statue after you squash it? Some say it ceases to exist, but the lump of clay—a distinct object that had been co-located with it—continues to exist. Others say that the statue ceases to exist and is replaced with a new object, a squashed lump of clay. Here’s a different answer. The statue, which is also a lump of clay, continues to exist and merely ceases to be a statue. Being a statue, the idea goes, is just a phase that the lump of clay passes through, just as being a teenager is a phase that a person passes through. This natural, “phasalist” treatment of the statue-clay puzzle has not received the attention it deserves. There are no representatives of phasalism in Rea’s landmark anthology Material Constitution, for instance, and the Stanford Encyclopedia entry on material constitution devotes only one sentence to it.
In Phases of Objects, Justin Mooney rectifies this neglect. He defends a general metaphysics of material objects that delivers the phasalist account of statues and lumps, while also rendering verdicts on a wide variety of other puzzling cases. For example, his view entails that a human being can become a corpse, that the Ship of Theseus can become a cabin in the woods, and much more besides. The book is full of careful, fine-grained engagement with metaphysical subtleties and thoughtful analyses of hard cases. And it’s a refreshing and invigorating return to the golden age of material-object metaphysics, before it was dominated by universalism vs. nihilism, metametaphysics, and grounding.
This is a terrific book, and we recommend it enthusiastically to anyone with an interest in persistence and coincidence puzzles. In what follows, we present Mooney’s view in greater detail (§1), examine some of its unappealing implications (§2), and discuss some alternative versions of phasalism that may be more palatable (§3).
1. Phasalism and Spatiotemporalism
Mooney’s primary innovation is filling out the basic phasalist picture with a carefully crafted spatiotemporal criterion of identity (43-50), applied across the board to any material object of any sort, people included. According to this criterion, a material object will persist just in case two conditions are met. First, there’s a continuity condition: the object must follow a spatiotemporal path that includes no excessive causal or spatiotemporal discontinuities. Second, there’s a closest-continuer condition: the object must follow a spatiotemporal path that exhibits greater continuity than any rival path. We’ll call his thesis that all material objects are subject to this sort of criterion spatiotemporalism.
Spatiotemporalism delivers the phasalist treatment across a wide range of cases. The statue merely ceases to be a statue when squashed, but continues to exist since the squashing exhibits the needed unrivaled spatiotemporal continuity. When a long piece of yarn is knitted into a sweater, unraveled, and then knitted into a scarf, there all along was just the one material object, which was a sweater and a piece of yarn, then was just a piece of yarn, and is now a scarf and a piece of yarn (87-89). A pumpkin can become a carriage (44). A terrier can become an amorphous mass of cells (70).
Spatiotemporalism is similarly liberal about part loss and replacement. In some cases, this liberalism has attractive consequences. Clay statues and, thus, the pieces of clay with which they are identical, can gain and lose parts without ceasing to exist (66-67). (Here we applaud Mooney for breaking with the bizarre dogma that lumps have all their parts essentially.) In other cases, the results are more surprising. For example, material objects can survive the replacement of all of their parts. And not just organisms and ships: a piece of lead can become a piece of gold (68). That’s the good news for alchemists. The bad news is that you need to already have the gold and the patience to swap it out one piece at a time. Spatiotemporalism also has the surprising consequence that, if we were to dismantle the Empire State Building by removing one small portion after another, we might finally arrive at a situation in which the Empire State Building is a small piece of steel that fits comfortably in a breast pocket (cf. 62-65).
So how do material objects cease to exist on Mooney’s view? Sometimes they cease to exist when they break into pieces. A windowpane ceases to exist when it’s shattered—unless one piece is over half the size of the original windowpane, in which case the windowpane survives as the largest shard (62). This is also how people normally cease to exist on his view: not when they die, but at some point in the process of cremation or decomposition (186-188). Though, depending on the order of events, your end might be later than you think, and, like the Empire State Building, you might wind up as a piece of bone that comfortably fits in a breast pocket.
Objects also cease to exist when, as a result of part loss, they would otherwise shrink down to a region already occupied by one of their parts. For instance, when a door composed of a board and a knob loses its knob, the door ceases to exist, not because it isn’t spatiotemporally continuous with the board, but because the post-knob-loss board is a closer continuer of something else, namely the pre-knob-loss board (104-106). (As Mooney sees it, part loss doesn’t always result in shrinking down to a region already occupied by a part, since he doesn’t believe in arbitrary undetached parts.)
2. Remnant Survival
To our minds, the hardest cases for spatiotemporalism involve what Mooney calls “remnant survival”, where an object is split into differently sized pieces, the smaller of which seems to have the better claim to being the original object. One such case that Mooney addresses involves a vining plant that covers an entire brick wall, and that is later snipped right at the base (69-71). The living plant, now just a couple of inches high, continues to grow. Intuitively, this very plant (pointing to the two-inch remnant) once covered the wall. But according to spatiotemporalism, the two-inch-high plant cannot be the plant that once covered the wall. No material object can survive that sort of abrupt spatial discontinuity. Mooney bites the bullet, and you might think that’s not so bad. But there are more troubling cases of remnant survival. We will mention two.
First, suppose the Statue of Liberty—a hollow, copper statue—is seamlessly filled with copper, one small bit at a time, until it is completely solid. Imagine that we were to remove the internal “core” all at once, apparently returning the Statue of Liberty to its initial state. Surprisingly, spatiotemporalism entails that the Statue of Liberty is the removed core in this case (97-98). The hollow statue that remains is a perfect duplicate of the statue we started with, made of exactly the same copper atoms, which were (we may suppose) never disturbed. Nevertheless, spatiotemporalism entails that it is not the Statue of Liberty. Indeed, despite the fact that there’s a piece of copper there that is made of exactly the same copper atoms as the original piece, arranged in exactly the same way, this piece is not identical to the original piece according to spatiotemporalism.
Second, and in our view most troublingly, are cases of remnant survival involving people. Take the real-life case of Jasmine Ramirez. At the age of 14, Jasmine’s tumor-ridden leg was removed after it had grown to 174 pounds, leaving behind a roughly 100-pound one-legged amputee. Mooney cannot say that Jasmine becomes the amputee, since no material object (on his view) can survive such an abrupt spatial discontinuity. Nor, for that matter, does Jasmine become the severed leg (since that’s what the pre-surgery leg becomes). Nor will Mooney identify Jasmine with a scattered object composed of the amputee and the severed leg, since Mooney thinks there are no such scattered objects (3-4). Rather, Mooney is forced to say that Jasmine simply ceases to exist when the leg is removed.
It gets worse. We just saw that the amputee can’t be Jasmine herself according to spatiotemporalism, so what was the amputee up to prior to the surgery? The spatiotemporalist is faced with various options, none of which is especially attractive. For example, one option is to say that the amputee was a second person co-located with Jasmine prior to the amputation. But, as Mooney acknowledges in connection with disembodied brains (192-196), this option runs directly into the familiar problem of “too many thinkers”. Mooney could instead embrace immaterialism about people, something he is understandably reluctant to do (162-163), and which would in any case not answer the question of what to say about the history of the one-legged organism. Another option is to say that the amputee came into existence at the time of the surgery. But it seems obvious that, if there’s a conscious person at all where the amputee is, that person is Jasmine, the person who once had two legs. In light of this, we suppose the spatiotemporalist might try simply denying that there’s a conscious person where the amputee is. This is in effect Mooney’s line on brains in vats, but it strikes us as intolerable when applied to our relieved amputee.
3. Other Phasalisms
Some metaphysicians may be inclined to dismiss the whole phasalist approach on account of the counterintuitive implications we’ve highlighted here. But you know what they say about throwing stones in glass houses. (We’re looking at you universalists, nihilists, mereological essentialists, plenitudinists, and all Lewisians.) What’s more, Mooney does attempt to ameliorate some of his troubles by developing a nonstandard account of what it means to be “the same F” (125-133). This account allows him to say that the tiny vining plant is the same plant as the (numerically distinct) massive plant that was once covering the wall (153), that the piece of lead is not the same piece of matter as the piece of gold that it becomes (cf. 139), and that the filled-in Statue of Liberty is the same statue as the (distinct) statue with the core removed (140). In any case, whether or not these efforts to render the view more palatable succeed, it really is a tidy picture that Mooney gives us: all material objects are ultimately the same sort of thing, all with the same persistence conditions, and within Mooney’s system it is always clear which object is which.
But even for those who, like us, are unconvinced, there is great value in the book. In the course of developing his own tidy and extreme (tidy because extreme!) metaphysics of material objects, Mooney touches on various decision points for the phasalist, and in doing so, effectively illuminates a whole family of underexplored phasalist approaches. We see his book as a helpful jumping-off point for a fruitful investigation of the different versions of phasalism.
Indeed, Mooney himself at times contemplates departing from spatiotemporalism in ways that could secure a more intuitive treatment of some of the cases we’ve mentioned. In connection with the vine case, he makes an intriguing suggestion that the spatiotemporal continuity condition could in principle be relaxed in cases where some other robust form of continuity is present (71). If biological and psychological continuity are permitted to trump spatiotemporal continuity in this way, the phasalist could say that Jasmine survives as the amputee, since the one-legged girl exhibits significant continuity of both sorts with Jasmine pre-amputation. The downside of such adjustments is that the view gets messier, and is unable to deliver clear verdicts about the full range of cases unless supplemented with guidelines for what trumps spatiotemporal continuity and under what conditions. But for those (like us) who doubt that a tidy metaphysics can capture the messiness of our world, this is a promising avenue to explore.
Another version of phasalism pairs it with a view on which there are two fundamentally different types of material objects, only one of which is subject to the spatiotemporal criterion. For instance, Carmichael (2015) develops a view on which there are, at bottom, two kinds of material objects. First, there are “lump-like objects”, which include stones, statues, sweaters, lumps, and pieces of yarn. Second, there are “event-based objects”, paradigmatically, organisms. By adopting the spatiotemporal criterion just for the former, and applying, e.g., a biological criterion to the latter, we can retain the phasalist treatment of statues and sweaters, while also securing the intuitively correct result in the various remnant survival cases (including Jasmine). This view would also, for better or worse, entail that living organisms do not persist as corpses.
Finally, it’s worth exploring what we might call a “pure immanence” view. As indicated above, persistence (on Mooney’s view) requires a sort of causal continuity: an object persists partly in virtue of the fact that there being something that’s a certain way at the later time is “immanently caused” by there being something that was (largely) that way at the immediately preceding time (44-46). Perhaps this causal constraint can stand on its own, without any spatial or temporal constraints. When multiple objects at some later time are immanently caused to have some range of properties by O having those properties at the earlier time, O survives as whichever object is immanently caused to have O’s properties to a greater (and sufficient) extent. This would, among other things, open the door to persistence across a temporal gap (see Zimmerman, 1999).
4. Concluding Remarks
Two thumbs up! An impressive debut from Mooney.

Feeling nervous? Work the system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Feeling nervous? Work the system
Take a deep breath — there are tons of ways to regulate your nervous system
When you’re stressed, you lose control. Your sympathetic nervous system takes over, triggering the release of stress hormones into the bloodstream, which increases heart rate, blood pressure and breathing pace. These changes happen involuntarily, whether you’re facing true danger or just an overflowing email inbox. But scientists are learning how to regain some control, guiding the nervous system out of fight-or-flight mode and into relaxation.
Some techniques for doing so are probably already second nature, like recentering yourself with slow, deep breaths. But there’s also mounting data to support a range of zany-sounding practices, including humming, tapping on the skin and cold-water immersion. “Consciously, you can’t tell your heart to slow down,” says neurologist Patricio Millar Vernetti of NYU Langone Health. “But by doing these interventions, you have a little bit more control.”
On social media, these practices are often described as ways to “regulate” the nervous system. They’re actually ways to call off the sympathetic nervous system and let the calming parasympathetic nervous system take over, leading to lower stress hormone levels, heart rate and blood pressure. Doing so successfully may yield significant health benefits, since an over- active stress response can, over time, contribute to hypertension, strain on the heart, excess inflammation and other issues.
Stimulating the vagus nerve, which runs from the brain stem to the abdomen, is one way to activate the parasympathetic nervous system. Breathing exercises can stimulate the nerve. A trendier approach, cold therapy, might too, research suggests. In a small study, scientists observed 25 people as they performed mental math. Twelve participants wore a facial cooling mask beforehand, meant to mimic submerging the face in cold water —a known way to stimulate the vagus nerve. Their levels of the stress hormone cortisol spiked lower and returned to baseline faster than those of people who hadn’t worn the mask, the team reported in 2022 in Scientific Reports.
Techniques like humming and tapping on the skin also seem to activate the parasympathetic nervous system. Slow breathing plus humming can increase heart rate variability, a measure of the fluctuating time between heartbeats, scientists reported last year in Physiology & Behavior. High heart rate variability is a marker of a well-regulated nervous system. It signals that “your body is doing less fighting itself on the inside” and is seamlessly switching between stress and relaxation, says physical therapist Karin Steere of the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma, Wash.
Tapping on specific spots on the skin, meanwhile, may generate electrochemical signals that travel from nerves to the brain, telling the parasympathetic nervous system that it’s time to take over, argued a 2025 research review. Existing data suggests tapping can lead to drops in stress hormone levels as well as declines in heart rate and blood pressure. The practice is also one element of Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing therapy, a treatment for conditions such as PTSD.
There are small, one-off pilot studies supporting nearly every viral nervous system regulation technique, says Darshan Mehta, medical director of the Benson-Henry Institute for Mind Body Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. That means it’s hard to identify one superior tactic. “It’s not important which practice [people adopt],” Mehta says. “It’s important that people do practice.”
Modern science isn’t the only support for these practices, Vernetti says. Chanting and humming, for instance, are part of some ancient spiritual practices. “This is one of those things that science has caught up with relatively recently,” he says, “but people have been doing for centuries.”

Will strategic Marib hold the key to Yemen's conflict?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:58:17 UTC
01:58:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Will the strategic province of Marib hold the key to Yemen's conflict?
Amid the renewed fighting between Yemen’s Houthi rebels and government forces and the Houthis’ capture of the whole of the country’s Red Sea coast, there is increasing speculation that the oil-rich province of Marib will be the next major theatre of conflict.
For many years, Marib has served as an impenetrable barrier against the expansion of the Houthi movement. It is one of the last strongholds of the internationally recognised government in northern Yemen and occupies a strategically important position 120 kilometres east of the capital Sana’a, which was captured by the Houthis in 2014.
Government forces in the area have so far adopted a defensive strategy, but amid the renewed fighting, it could become a base for them to seize the initiative and launch offensive operations.
This strategic shift has already been reflected on the ground in recent developments. Last week, government forces announced the launch of a wide-ranging military operation to take control of Houthi-held areas of the province.
These included an intensive assault by units of the Seventh Military Region, which broke through Houthi defences and recaptured strategic positions northwest of Marib city, alongside a successful flanking operation in the Mahzam Mas area.
In the south, government forces also took control of the Al-Akad Al-Ramli area and positions near Mount Al-Balaq amid fierce fighting that resulted in many deaths and the capture of Houthi prisoners as well as the seizure of military vehicles.
These operations coincided with the Yemeni armed forces repelling two major attacks launched by the Houthis against military positions in the south and west of the province. 
The fighting was described as the most severe since 2021 and has marked the beginning of a new phase on the battlefield, in which the government is on the attack.
The government currently maintains full control over the province’s heartland and all its strategic points.
The tipping point of the Yemeni conflict
Marib is seen as the tipping point of the balance of power in Yemen – a key area on which the entire structure of the internationally recognised government rests.
It covers 17,478 square kilometres, with terrain ranging from rugged mountainous areas to vast desert plains.
Its population before the war was around 348,000, but around two million internally displaced people have fled there, living in hundreds of camps and shelters.
This places enormous pressure on its infrastructure and public services.
As the last major stronghold of the government in northern Yemen, it has become a key administrative centre where state institutions and military and security forces are concentrated.
Its survival is seen as key to the continuation of the Yemeni national project. 
Militarily, Marib is a highly complex and vital geographical hub. It forms a strategic link between Al-Jawf, Sanaa, Al-Bayda, Shabwa and Hadramawt province, while also acting as a fortress that has repelled some of the Houthis’ fiercest attacks. 
The fronts surrounding it have therefore become the first line of defence for Yemen’s east and south.
Financial and military lifeline
Economically, Marib is the country’s most important financial lifeline. It contains the major oil and gas fields in Safer, as well as a key power station, which supplies large areas of the country with electricity. It also generates sovereign revenues that finance a significant portion of state expenditure and essential services.
The military control map in Marib is characterised by considerable geographical complexity, with front lines intersecting and defensive and offensive positions overlapping between government forces and tribes on one side and the Houthi movement on the other.
While the government controls most of the province, including Marib city and the strategically important Al-Wadi district, the Houthis are present in peripheral mountain and desert areas, including areas bordering Al-Jawf governorate to the north and Al-Bayda and Shabwa governorates to the south and west.
This military overlap makes Marib an open front, with every possibility still on the table. Government forces are attempting to secure their security perimeter by taking control of  high ground in frontline districts, thereby cutting off potential routes for Houthi missile launches and ground attacks on the province’s population centres.
The potential military and strategic objectives of a government offensive appear clearly defined.
Military and political objectives
One major objective is to recapture the remaining districts under Houthi control, as well as secure and clear the western and northwestern areas bordering Sanaa and Al-Jawf. 
These areas have served for years as major launching platforms for missile and drone attacks against residential neighbourhoods and critical infrastructure in Marib city.
Government forces are supported by a paramilitary organisation called the Popular Resistance, made up of residents of Houthi-controlled governorates who have been displaced to Marib. 
Government-allied tribal fighters also constitute an active force, possessing heavy weapons and extensive knowledge of the terrain. 
On the Houthi side, the movement relies on mobilising ideological and regional military formations belonging to what it calls the “Central Military Region.” These are stationed at strategic camps that the Houthis have seized and converted into advanced offensive platforms.
The most prominent include Mas Camp in northwestern Marib, as well as the Tamah and Khashm Al-Jafina camps.
The Houthis rely heavily on a war of attrition, using an arsenal of ballistic missiles and drones to attack government positions.
Government camps and fronts constitute the final defensive shields protecting the population centres, economy and energy facilities, while Houthi camps serve as major launch bases for threatening the front lines and attempting to penetrate the defensive perimeter around Marib city.
If the government does manage to make major advances in Marib, taking control of some or all of the Houthi positions in the province, this would represent a major turning point capable of redrawing the map of Yemen’s conflict and altering the balance of power.
Politically, it would likely push the Houthis toward serious engagement with peace negotiations while militarily opening routes towards the Yemeni capital Sanaa.
Most importantly, it would constitute clear confirmation of the internationally recognised government’s ability to determine the outcome of the conflict and restore confidence in the Yemeni national project.

2026-09-14
16:58:06 UTC
01:58:06 KST

DEHRADUN: Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Monday reviewed the functioning of the CM Helpline 1905 at the Secretariat and directed officials to ensure the swift, time-bound and satisfactory resolution of public grievances.The chief minister said that the CM Helpline is an important mechanism for addressing the problems of the common people. He stressed that grievance redressal should not be limited to formally closing complaints on the portal, but must ensure an actual resolution of the complainant's problem.Dhami directed district magistrates to review complaints department-wise in districts where a particular category of grievances is being received in large numbers and ensure their early resolution. He also called for an analysis of the reasons behind repeated complaints of the same nature and effective measures to address such issues permanently.The chief minister directed all district magistrates to conduct surprise inspections of tehsils. During these inspections, special attention should be paid to whether mutation-related cases are being disposed of within the prescribed timelines. He said complaints related to land fraud should be addressed on priority. The chief minister stressed that people should not be made to make unnecessary visits to government offices for revenue-related matters and that prescribed services must be delivered within the stipulated timeDhami directed officials to accord top priority to ensuring the availability of clean drinking water.
He said complaints related to drinking water should be acted upon immediately. He directed the concerned officials to conduct an audit of water pipelines and sewer lines within 15 days and submit a report. Timely resolution of disruptions in water supply, leakages and other related issues should be ensured.The chief minister directed officials to pay special attention to grievances pending for more than 30 days. Secretaries, heads of departments and district magistrates should regularly review pending complaints at their respective levels. Accountability should be fixed for officials in cases where complaints are not resolved within the prescribed timeframe.He further directed that long-pending complaints be resolved on the highest priority. During the meeting, a department-wise status of complaints pending for more than 180 days was also presented. Dhami said such old cases should be regularly monitored at the departmental level and the reasons for their pendency should also be reviewed.The chief minister instructed officials not to close complaints unnecessarily under "Special Close" or "Force Close" categories. He said the satisfaction of complainants must be given due importance in grievance redressal. Before closing any complaint, officials must ensure that all necessary action has been taken at the appropriate level to resolve the issue.Dhami said the feedback mechanism for complaints received through the CM Helpline should be further strengthened. The quality of grievance redressal should be assessed on the basis of feedback received from complainants. The portal has provisions for obtaining public feedback and monitoring the action being taken by various departments and nodal officers.The chief minister said officials and personnel performing well in grievance redressal should be encouraged, while accountability should be fixed for those found guilty of unnecessary delays or negligence. He said the fundamental objective of the CM Helpline is to establish effective communication between the government and the public and ensure real, time-bound and satisfactory resolution of citizens' problems.During the review, the chief minister also spoke to several complainants over the phone to ascertain the actual status of their grievances and their redressal.Dhami spoke to Sanjay Kumar Rawat regarding a complaint that had been closed inappropriately. Rawat informed him that medical reimbursement bills related to the treatment of his late father had not been paid. The chief minister directed the concerned officials to take immediate necessary action and ensure payment of the pending medical reimbursement. He said people should not be unnecessarily harassed in such sensitive cases and warned that accountability would be fixed if similar complaints arise in the future.The chief minister also spoke to Baby Kotnala, a resident of Pauri Garhwal, regarding her issue related to destitute women's pension. She informed him that despite registering a complaint a long time ago, the issue had not been resolved. Dhami directed the District Magistrate, Pauri Garhwal, to take immediate appropriate action and ensure resolution of the matter.
Dhami also spoke to Haridwar resident Geeta, who informed him that a water tank had been constructed near her house around three months ago, but water supply from the tank had not yet commenced. Israel eyes Yemen role as US holds back from Saudi-Houthi war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:57:51 UTC
01:57:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel eyes Yemen role as US holds back from Saudi-Houthi war
Israel has signalled that it is prepared to play a greater military role against Yemen's Houthis, although Saudi Arabia is unlikely to embrace Israeli assistance despite Washington's reluctance to intervene directly.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has offered assistance to countries in the Arabian Peninsula as part of a wider campaign against the Houthis, according to Israeli media reports citing US sources.
The offer comes as Saudi Arabia seeks greater military support against the group while Washington has stopped short of direct intervention, instead offering intelligence-sharing and targeting assistance.
It follows major Houthi advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast, including the capture of Perim, or Mayyun, the strategically important island sitting in the Bab al-Mandab Strait between Yemen and Djibouti. Pro-Saudi Yemeni government forces on the Red Sea are said to have "collapsed" in the face of Houthi offensives.
Dr Andreas Krieg, a Middle East security expert at King's College London, told The New Arab that US reluctance did create an opening for Israel "in a narrow military sense", but warned against interpreting this as the beginning of a new Saudi-Israeli security alignment.
"Riyadh does not want to move from dependence on Washington to dependence on an Israeli security architecture," Krieg said.
"The Saudis increasingly regard Israel itself as one of the actors generating regional instability. They may see tactical convergence against Iran or the Houthis, but that is very different from trusting Israel with the defence of the Kingdom."
Israel has a direct interest in preventing the Houthis from consolidating their position around Bab al-Mandab.
The strait, just under 30 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean and is one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints.
For Israel, it is also the maritime gateway connecting the southern port of Eilat with the Indian Ocean.
Houthi attacks on commercial shipping following the outbreak of Israel's war on Gaza had already severely disrupted Red Sea traffic, while Israel has repeatedly struck Yemen in response to Houthi missile and drone attacks.
Krieg said Israel could potentially offer sophisticated intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic warfare, cyber and targeting capabilities, as well as its experience attacking Houthi missile, drone and command infrastructure.
But the fundamental Saudi problem, he said, was not a shortage of military firepower.
"The Saudi problem is therefore not primarily a lack of aircraft or bombs. It is political and strategic," Krieg said.
"Air strikes can destroy launchers, warehouses and command centres, but they cannot permanently remove the Houthis from Bab al-Mandab or govern territory in Yemen. Saudi Arabia discovered this painfully during its previous intervention."
Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis beginning in 2015, but years of airstrikes and fighting failed to defeat the Houthis, who consolidated control over much of northern Yemen while developing increasingly sophisticated missile and drone capabilities.
Renewed Houthi advances now confront Riyadh with a difficult strategic problem as insecurity affects both of the principal maritime routes connecting Gulf energy exports with international markets.
Iran threatens shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while Houthi control around Bab al-Mandab puts additional pressure on the Red Sea route. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, designed to bypass Hormuz by carrying oil to the Red Sea coast, has also demonstrated its vulnerability after coming under drone attack.
Yet direct Israeli involvement could potentially worsen Saudi Arabia's predicament.
Krieg said overt Israeli assistance could bolster the Houthi claim that Riyadh was fighting as part of an Israeli-American coalition, while increasing the domestic and regional political costs for Saudi Arabia.
It could also make Saudi infrastructure appear an increasingly legitimate target to Iran and its regional allies.
Some indirect cooperation remains conceivable, particularly intelligence passed through American channels, Krieg said, while Saudi and Israeli forces could separately operate against the same threat.
But he cautioned that parallel operations "should not automatically be interpreted as an alliance or even close coordination".
Instead, Riyadh appears to be seeking a more diversified security architecture as doubts grow about Washington's willingness to bear the costs of defending its Gulf partners.
Krieg pointed to Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, alongside European maritime partners and greater Gulf and Arab-Islamic security cooperation, as more likely components of Saudi Arabia's attempt to reduce its dependence on Washington.
"The lesson Riyadh appears to be drawing is not that Israel should replace the United States," he said.
"The lesson is that Saudi Arabia needs a much more diversified security system in which it has greater agency."
Israel's willingness to intervene against the Houthis therefore exposes a convergence of Israeli and Saudi interests, particularly around Red Sea security, without necessarily bringing the two countries strategically closer.
"Replacing American dependency with Israeli dependency would not represent strategic autonomy," Krieg said.
"From the Saudi perspective, it would simply exchange one vulnerability for another, and potentially for a much more politically dangerous one."

After the SDF: What comes next for Syria's Kurds?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:54:45 UTC
01:54:45 KST

Breadcrumb
After the SDF: What comes next for Syria's Kurds?
Damascus, Syria - The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) were dissolved by their commander-in-chief, Mazloum Abdi, on 25 August, bringing an end to Rojava, a 14-year-old experiment in autonomous self-administration in northeast Syria.
Abdi is to take up a new role as a special adviser to President Ahmed al-Sharaa, whilst the senior leadership will occupy various positions within the government.
Sipan Hamo, the former head of the YPG - the primary fighting force of the SDF - had already taken up a position as Deputy Defence Minister for the Eastern Region. Ilham Ahmed, the head of the SDF’s civilian administration, is reported to have been offered a position in parliament.
The dissolution comes seven months after a surprise government offensive in January against the SDF, which saw the armed group lose large swathes of its northeastern territory and be forced into an integration agreement.
Since then, the integration has been advancing on the ground, with this latest development being “largely symbolic” according to Alexander McKeever, a researcher and author of the This Week in Northern Syria newsletter.
“Although the SDF is technically dissolved, on the ground its military and civilian structures continue to operate,” he explained to The New Arab.
“They work in parallel to the government structures that are increasingly visible as integration continues.”
The future for female Kurdish fighters
As part of the dissolution, Mazloum Abdi announced that the SDF’s military had been entirely integrated into the Ministry of Defence.
However, there was one major oversight. Seated next to Abdi during his meeting with al-Sharaa was Nowruz Ahmed, the commander of the YPJ - the SDF’s all-female fighting force.
The YPJ were prohibited from joining the Ministry of Defence because the “government simply has a perspective that women don’t belong in the military,” says McKeever.
Following the announcement, the YPJ released a statement about a meeting with the Ministry of Interior saying, “it was emphasised that the YPJ could be integrated, as a distinct organised force, into the Ministry of Interior”.
There had been previous reports that the YPJ had been offered a role as a counter-terror unit within the Ministry of Defence, but this was denied by Ruksan Mohammed, the YPJ spokesperson, a week before the announcement.
She acknowledged that previously they had been offered to integrate into the Interior Ministry as administrative staff, which they rejected outright.
“It should not have reached a point where the dissolution was announced before a solution to the YPJ issue was found,” Muaz Al-Abdullah, a Middle East Research Manager at ACLED, a conflict tracking organisation, told The New Arab.
“It reflects the balance of power between the two sides, where Damascus is largely able to dictate terms in negotiations.”
However, this strategy presents a danger, he adds, “it will ultimately give a group of trained fighters the reasoning to go against the government either as a group or as lone wolves”.
What role for the Kurdish language?
Another bone of contention surrounds the future role of the Kurdish language within the northeast’s education system.
Many Kurds fear a return to the situation under the Assad regime, before the ‘Rojava Revolution’ in 2012, in which “the state did not recognise Kurdish identity as a legitimate part of Syrian identity. Kurdish language instruction and Kurdish cultural expression were banned,” explains McKeever.
As a result, al-Sharaa has sought to assuage Kurdish fears. In January, following the offensive against the SDF, he announced the recognition of Kurdish as a ‘national language’.
However, McKeever notes that this does not make Kurdish an ‘official’ language of Syria. Syria doesn’t currently have a full constitution, with the law either operating on old Assad-era mandates or 2025’s constitutional declaration.
“Full recognition of Kurdish as an official language may come with the drafting of the constitution but, for now, we cannot know,” he says.
As part of the integration agreement between the SDF and the government, Damascus has stipulated a one-year transition period in which Kurdish language classes are offered for three hours per week, alongside one hour for an elective class on a number of topics like women's history, sociology, or philosophy.
The system for the years after has yet to be decided upon. However, for the last 14 years, Kurdish has been the medium of education and so the disagreement between the SDF and Damascus “comes down to whether there will be a fully translated curriculum”.
Effect on the Turkish peace process
The dissolution of the SDF would have been considerably harder to achieve without the parallel peace process between Turkey and the PKK.
In October 2024, Ankara announced that it was commencing negotiations with the PKK, a Kurdish armed group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the government.
In May 2025, following a call by its leader Abdullah Ocalan, the PKK announced that it would destroy its weapons and dissolve.
Turkey considered the SDF as the Syrian branch of the PKK, and so “Turkey is the biggest winner in this whole situation,” Al-Abdullah tells The New Arab.
“The whole Kurdish situation is shifting regionally with Kurdish non-state actors increasingly having to engage with their relative states,” he adds.
“The dissolution of the SDF will only add onus on the PKK to reach a settlement with the Turks.”
However, it is regarding language rights that Turkey’s Kurds might have the most to gain from the SDF integration agreement.
“Turkey completely banned the Kurdish language, and has struggled with the Kurdish file for decades, partly as a result,” Henri Barkey, an Adjunct Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, told The New Arab.
“Whilst the deal that was signed in Syria is bad on language rights, it is far better than what Turkish Kurds have, and so they might look to Syria as a model for their own aims in negotiations.”
Managing Kurdish fears
The Syrian government is seeking to simultaneously entrench its control over the northeast whilst allaying Kurdish fears and distrust of the government.
According to analysts, many Kurds are sceptical of the government's Islamist roots, and its history of violence against minority groups, including a series of massacres targeting Alawite and Druze minorities.
For Barkey, “Sharaa can’t afford to alienate the Kurds as they have over a decade of experience organising and fighting”.
Equally, many in the local Arab communities distrust the SDF and its leadership, due to the perception that, despite the SDF’s official support for ethnic pluralism, it developed a system that centralised power in the hands of Kurdish communities at the expense of local Arabs.
The “greatest challenge” lies in knitting together a social fabric between “communities that have often lived separately for the last decade, with displaced Kurds now returning to areas with large Arab populations and displaced Arabs doing the same in reverse,” says Mckeever.
In August, a convoy of displaced Kurds, who were returning to Ras Al-Ain, were attacked by local Arabs, which triggered a day of riots by Kurds against the government in Hasakah and Qamishli.
A day later, an attack by unknown elements on a security point manned by former SDF fighters who had been recently integrated into the Ministry of Defence killed three and injured several.
“This is the same pattern that you see across Syria along these social fault lines, where you have old grievances and a lack of security,” Mckeever adds.
Whereas for ACLED’s Al-Abdullah, the primary risk is that integration “will remain political, and that Kurds won't actually be brought into the national community and so will continue to identify as Kurdish more so than Syrian”.
The government has offered senior SDF leadership positions, likely so they can play the role of “intermediary between the state and the Kurdish communities within which they still have a lot of support”.
What next?
Whilst integration is far from finished, the dissolution of the SDF has “expedited certain things on the ground,” explains Mckeever.
The government’s internal security forces, previously only deployed within the grounds of a few government compounds, have reportedly deployed to a number of Arab neighbourhoods in Hasakah city.
Equally, certain SDF internal security units have begun the integration process and will likely begin patrols under the Syrian flag.
For al-Sharaa, with integration and the Kurdish file moving from a major political issue to one more technical and bureaucratic, he can likely turn his attention to the last holdout beyond the control of the state - Suweida.
The dissolution of the SDF represents the death knell for a vision for Syria, advocated by Israel and the Druze militias in Suweida, of fragmentation.
“With the government empowered domestically and backed internationally by the US and Turkey, it will be looking towards resolving the Suweida situation,” Al-Abdullah says.
“Israel is using Suweida as a card, and will likely abandon it when its interests require,” says Al-Abdullah.
“The Syrian government now needs to be working on winning back the people of Suweida, who felt so betrayed by the government's actions against them.”
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues
Follow him on X: @CP__Ward

How Israel systematically dismantles Palestinian life in occupied West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:53:11 UTC
01:53:11 KST

How Israel systematically dismantles Palestinian life in occupied West Bank
Israeli rights group B’Tselem argues that settlement expansion, displacement and restrictions are not isolated abuses, but a decades-old, coordinated system.
Bethlehem, occupied West Bank – On any given week, Palestinians across the occupied West Bank can experience dozens of what appear to be isolated acts of Israeli violence and suppression.
In early September, Israeli forces killed two teenagers during a military raid in al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah. Days later in Masafer Yatta, Israeli forces demolished every home in Khirbet al-Tabban, leaving about 70 people, including 30 children, without shelter. In Qusra, south of Nablus, settlers have kept three families under siege inside their homes for more than a month, cutting off their water and power.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Israeli demolitions threaten schools and homes in Masafer Yatta
- list 2 of 3Animated map shows spread of illegal Israeli settlements across Palestine
- list 3 of 3Israel working to eliminate Palestinian presence from West Bank, NGO warns
In a new report published on Monday, Israeli rights group B’Tselem argued these are not separate incidents. Together, they work towards a single end: Making Palestinian life on the land unsustainable and replacing it with permanent Israeli control. The reality in the West Bank, the group said, is “neither a temporary crisis nor a collection of random human rights violations”.
Instead, it is “an accelerated and explicit phase in an ongoing project of elimination that operates within the Israeli apartheid regime and is driven by a settler-colonial logic of dispossession, displacement, and the establishment of Jewish-Israeli sovereignty”, the publication – called The Elimination Project – added.
‘The Elimination Project’
Drawing on nearly 2,000 Palestinian testimonies, the report said that seemingly separate Israeli violations are part of what it called “a comprehensive mechanism of elimination”.
By “elimination”, B’Tselem referred to the systematic dismantling of Palestinian society, eroding its institutions, economy, freedom of movement and social life.
The report placed this within what it called the “basic logic of settler colonialism”: Establishing “permanent settler sovereignty over a territory already inhabited by an Indigenous people” by “pushing them out, dispossessing them and dismantling their collective existence”.
It identifies five interconnected fronts through which that process operates: Violence and intimidation, movement restrictions, economic strangulation, social and political destruction, and ethnic cleansing and territorial takeover.
B’Tselem traced that logic to the 2017 “Decisive Plan” authored by Bezalel Smotrich, now Israel’s finance minister. The plan, the group said, gave Palestinians three choices: Accept Jewish supremacy while giving up their national claims, leave, or face violent suppression.
None of this is new, the report argued; the mechanism has run for decades. What has changed is that it has grown far more severe and open, escalating since the current far-right government took office in late 2022 and sharply after the start of the genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The reality on the ground
For roughly 3.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, that system is felt in the steady narrowing of daily life: Roads they cannot use, land they cannot reach, and fewer places where they can safely live, work and move.
By December 2025, Israel had at least 925 physical obstacles set up across the West Bank, the most the United Nations has recorded in two decades.
Yusef Kashur, a driver and father of six from Dura, south of Hebron, told B’Tselem that the growing network of gates and checkpoints had turned his work into a “torment”, forcing him onto long, dangerous backroads and to turn down fares he once relied on.
“These drives are exhausting, take a very long time, and the fuel costs so much that I don’t make enough to cover our household needs,” he said.
The restrictions feed a wider collapse. Under an occupation that controls its borders, trade and revenue, the West Bank economy has little room of its own, and it has buckled: Unemployment at the end of last year had roughly doubled to 27.5 percent compared to October 2023, driven in part by the freezing of work permits for about 115,000 Palestinians.
The squeeze is deliberate, the report argued: A family that cannot earn is easier to uproot, and when Palestinians fall back on their own land, the pressure follows them there.
After losing his job inside Israel, Jamil Abu Rayan turned to his grapevines near Halhul, only to find settlers had established an illegal outpost at his main plot. Soldiers also barred him from another plot, calling it “[Israeli] state land”.
He told B’Tselem he lost about 60 percent of his 2025 grape harvest and that he can no longer properly work his land.
Recounting a late January attack in the South Hebron Hills, where entire communities face forcible displacement, Isma’il Khalayleh told the rights group earlier this year that a settler pressed a rifle to his forehead and gave him a deadline: “I’m giving you 24 hours to leave this place.”
Agricultural and grazing outposts have “violently taken control” of nearly 20 percent of the West Bank, according to Israeli settlement-watchdog group Peace Now. More than 1,600 settler attacks were recorded by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) last year.
The same pressure extends to where Palestinians can build; Israeli authorities make it “virtually impossible for Palestinians to obtain building permits”, according to OCHA, leaving many families who build without them under constant threat of Israeli demolition.
As Palestinian communities are cleared, more illegal Israeli settlements expand. The current government has approved a record 104 new settlements since 2022.
The suppression also extends to the institutions that hold Palestinian society together, with B’Tselem documenting a series of raids and closure orders faced by charities, trade unions and universities.
Ahmad Dweikat told the rights group that in May 2026, soldiers ransacked a Nablus association he co-founded to help women, children and families, confiscating computers and cash, including money set aside for orphans.
Running beneath all of it is the military’s lethal force. B’Tselem counted about 1,087 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the West Bank since October 2023, roughly a quarter of them children.
Among them was Jamil Hanani, a 17-year-old boy from Beit Furik who was shot during an army raid on the town. “It’s as if they go out hunting, only they’re hunting human beings,” his father, ‘Atef Hanani, told B’Tselem.
The system behind the violence
For years, foreign governments have urged Israel to show restraint. That framing misses the point, B’Tselem argued: The violence, closures and demolitions are not failures of the system, but the system working as intended.
Sanctioning an individual settler, reopening a road or freezing a single settlement plan would “leave intact the structure that produces violence, dispossession, and oppression”, it said.
Seen this way, the question is not whether each individual act is an isolated violation, but what they produce together: A steadily shrinking space for Palestinians to live, work, build and remain on their land.
And the West Bank, the report argued, cannot be read apart from Gaza. The two are “different manifestations of the same regime project, directed against Palestinians’ ability to exist as a people”.

Netanyahu says Gaza documentary 'NAZA' is 'shocking incitement'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:51:41 UTC
01:51:41 KST

Netanyahu says Gaza documentary NAZA is ‘shocking incitement’
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sept 14 that a new documentary film which alleges that mass civilian deaths were routinely built into targeting decisions in Gaza was part of a wave of global incitement against Jews.
NAZA, directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival on Sept 12 and received a 25-minute standing ovation when it was screened on Sept 10.
The film takes its title from an Israeli military term for expected “collateral casualties” and is built around anonymous interviews with intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the war.
“It’s shocking. We are fighting global anti-Semitic incitement and when it comes from within us it is intolerable,” Netanyahu said in a video posted on Telegram. “And now two Israeli directors portraying the IDF (Israel Defense Forces) as war criminals receive applause at the Venice festival.”
Netanyahu’s comments followed a statement from the Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir, who said the film constituted an attack on the state of Israel.
“Based on what has been published thus far, this is not a film offering criticism of the IDF, nor is it an attempt to establish the truth. It is based on blood libels, deliberate distortions of reality, and grave, false accusations against IDF soldiers and commanders,” Zamir said.
The military said that Zamir has instructed the Military Advocate-General, whose legal powers are confined within the military, “to examine and advance possible legal measures concerning the film and those involved in it”.
The film-makers could not immediately be reached for comment.
“We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist and this is why it is especially important for us that Israelis watch this film, it is our country that is doing these crimes,” Abraham said in his acceptance speech on Sept 12.
Gaza health authorities say more than 73,000 Palestinians, most of them civilians, have been killed in Israel’s military campaign that has left much of Gaza in ruins.
The war was triggered by Hamas’ Oct 7, 2023, attack on Israel which killed 1,200 people, most of them civilians.
Israel says it has gone to great lengths to avoid civilian casualties as it battles Hamas militants who embed in sites such as hospitals, schools and shelters.
Hamas denies using Gaza’s civilians as human shields. REUTERS

How Syria's fuel protests could challenge Sharaa's government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:51:17 UTC
01:51:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Fuel protests sweep through Syria, posing growing challenge for Damascus
Protests have erupted across Syria, particularly in the north and northeast, after the government’s decision to raise fuel prices for a second time in nine days – putting further strain on an already war-battered society, especially farmers.
Diesel rose by 40% to 175 Syrian pounds ($1.32) a litre, while petrol increased by 28% to 195 pounds ($1.47) a litre, according to the state-run news agency SANA. The country’s Energy Ministry described the hike as a "temporary measure" imposed by rising costs of securing fuel on global markets amid the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz crisis.
The ministry said Syria is currently being affected by higher global costs for securing petrol, diesel and fuel oil, while the shutdown of the Baniyas refinery for maintenance has increased the need to source petroleum products from abroad during the maintenance period.
It said the price adjustment "aims to ensure the continued flow of petroleum products and their availability in the local market, amid higher supply costs and the need to secure requirements while the refinery is shut down."
Syria produces around 100,000 barrels of oil per day, while domestic demand is estimated at around 300,000 barrels per day.
Heavy impact in Syria’s agricultural heartland
As soon as the government announced the new prices, protests broke out in several Syrian provinces, with demonstrators blocking major roads and intercepting oil tankers heading towards the Homs refinery.
The latest protests also come amid a broader rise in demonstrations over economic conditions. According to ACLED data cited by Syrian analyst Muaz al-Abdullah, 45% of protests recorded in Syria during the first week of September were driven by economic demands.
But the protests have been particularly prominent in northeast Syria, where demonstrations in Hasakah and Deir Ezzor have taken on a more confrontational character.
Abdullah said protests had become "more violent", with demonstrators burning tyres and erecting barricades to block major roads, including the M5 highway linking northern and southern Syria.
"Barricades were being used to cut off roads, and this is something that we didn't used to see a lot in Syria," Abdullah told The New Arab, noting that demonstrations since the fall of former dictator Bashar al-Assad’s regime in December 2024 had mostly been peaceful.
The protests are also significant because they come after a second fuel price increase in just nine days. The first hike was announced on 4 September, followed by another on 13 September.
Abdullah said the protests should be viewed as part of a broader accumulation of economic and social grievances rather than simply a reaction to the latest fuel prices.
"Of course these protests might turn into a challenge for the government, they are super significant. This is a result of accumulating crises and worsening socioeconomic conditions in Syria," he said.
Fuel prices affect virtually every aspect of daily life, from transport and food production to heating and basic services.
The impact is likely to be felt even more heavily in northeast Syria, which includes Hasakah, Deir Ezzor and Raqqa – areas that form the country’s agricultural heartland and produce much of its wheat.
"The northeast of Syria, specifically Hasaka and Deir Ezzor, these regions produce oil in Syria, but now they’re unable to receive basic services and carry out day-to-day affairs because of the fuel price hike," Abdullah said.
The region is also approaching a crucial agricultural period, with farmers expected to begin cultivation in late September and early October.
"Irrigating and cultivating lands and transport can’t happen without fuel," Abdullah said, adding that Hasakeh, Deir and Raqqa produce Syria’s main agricultural product, wheat.
An already fragile state
The fuel hike comes after existing tensions between farmers and the government in the northeast, where protests had already taken place over the price set by Damascus for purchasing wheat and delays in payments.
The timing is particularly sensitive because northeast Syria is undergoing a major political transition as the authorities in Damascus seek to integrate the region and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces into the Syrian state.
The Kurdish-led SDF and Damascus forces fought deadly clashes for weeks earlier this year, with government forces overrunning areas formerly under SDF control. A deal to integrate the SDF into the government is now underway.
"It’s not in the government’s interest, with the transition happening in Kurdish-majority areas, to increase fuel prices," Abdullah said.
He said accumulating economic grievances and deteriorating conditions could delay the integration of northeast Syria into the wider state and social fabric of the country.
The danger for Damascus is that economic frustration could become tied to the region’s broader political transition, reinforcing perceptions among some residents that their situation has worsened as the northeast comes under greater control of the central government.
Such sentiment could prove particularly damaging as Damascus seeks to reunite a country that remains deeply divided after more than 13 years of civil war.
A growing challenge for Damascus
But the unrest is not confined to the northeast.
Protests have also been reported in Hama, Aleppo and Idlib, with agriculture again emerging as a common factor.
"There is one primary thing in common for all these regions – agriculture," Abdullah said.
The protests are among the most significant anti-government demonstrations since Assad’s fall, according to Robin Yassin-Kassab, an author and political commentator.
"There’s been a lot of protests in Syria since the liberation, most of them over economic conditions, price rises, so on, but these are by far the most significant," Yassin-Kassab told The New Arab.
He said the protests were particularly worrying for the government because they were occurring in areas where support for the new authorities might otherwise be expected to be strong. In some demonstrations, protesters chanted: "the people want the fall of Jolani," President Ahmed al-Sharaa's nom de guerre, while others called on the energy minister to resign.
"They could absolutely develop into a broader challenge to the government," Yassin-Kassab said.
While the immediate trigger is the fuel price increase, it is also exposing much deeper frustrations with living conditions across the country.
"It’s both – it’s definitely about fuel prices," he said, pointing to the impact of the war in Iran and the resulting global rise in fuel costs. "But of course in Syria there’s a huge amount of rebuilding to do," he added.
Patience wearing thin
The conflict, which began in March 2011 after Assad’s forces violently cracked down on protesters, left much of the country in ruins. Millions of Syrians remain without adequate housing or employment, while large parts of the country continue to lack reliable electricity, running water and basic civilian infrastructure.
For more than a year, many Syrians have given the new government the benefit of the doubt, Yassin-Kassab said, partly because of their relief at the end of Assad’s rule and partly because they recognise the scale of the task facing the new authorities.
But that patience may not last.
"As we approach two years after the liberation, people’s patience will run out," he said.
Yassin-Kassab said the current protests reflected a population facing a "huge cost of living crisis" while still waiting for the civilian infrastructure needed to rebuild their lives.
For the government, the problem is deepened by its limited resources. Damascus has little income and enormous demands on its finances, particularly as it attempts to rebuild the country and provide basic services after years of war.
Abdullah said the government should explain the decision more clearly and consider measures such as subsidies or other assistance to help struggling households absorb the increased costs.
"The problem isn’t the fuel hike itself, it’s that the government didn’t study this before issuing the price hike. There was no clear study or strategy," he said.
President Sharaa may therefore face pressure to reverse or reduce the increase, at least temporarily, in an attempt to defuse tensions.
But the consequences of the price rise will extend beyond the immediate protests. Abdullah said the problem was beginning to threaten the country’s social peace.
Higher fuel costs are already affecting transport, with taxi drivers increasing fares and disputes emerging with passengers over the new prices. As winter approaches, the cost of heating is also likely to become another source of pressure, with many Syrians relying on mazut to heat their homes.
Yassin-Kassab said the protests showed that the government’s economic difficulties could develop into a much broader political problem, particularly as Syrians become less willing to tolerate worsening living conditions while waiting for the country’s basic infrastructure to be rebuilt.
For a government still trying to stabilise a country emerging from more than a decade of war, the protests offer a warning that economic grievances can quickly become political.
As Yassin-Kassab put it, the economic situation has the potential to "break the [post-Assad] transition."
