New York Seizes a Dozen Celebrity Deepfake Websites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:50:00 UTC
01:50:00 KST

For the best part of a decade, abusive deepfake “pornography” websites have published thousands of nonconsensual videos depicting women, including high-profile celebrities, politicians, and public figures, into sexual situations. Now, in what is likely the largest takedown of explicit deepfake websites to date, officials in New York have seized more than a dozen of the harmful sites.
On Monday, the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office announced the seizure of 12 domains which it says have been used for “unlawfully” sharing, publishing, and selling celebrity deepfake videos. Around 1,200 people—overwhelmingly women—were depicted in nonconsensual sexual images and videos on the websites, the office says. These included social media influencers, actors, activists, athletes, musicians, and politicians.
“These horrific violations of privacy follow victims into their careers and personal lives and take an immense toll on emotional and mental well-being,” district attorney Alvin Bragg said in a statement, urging potential victims to come forward and contact his office’s cybercrime bureau. The office says its investigations into who is responsible for the websites, plus those who uploaded damaging videos of victims, are ongoing.
The seizures, carried out under New York’s criminal procedure laws, mark perhaps one of the most significant and sweeping actions against websites hosting explicit deepfake videos since the technology first emerged at the end of 2017. As artificial intelligence technology has improved, a dark industry of websites, apps, and bots has appeared: They are designed to “undress” photos of women or create graphic sexual videos that include them. The images and videos are increasingly realistic and can be generated in seconds.
While deepfake technology is widely used against non-famous women and girls—often being shared in private social media groups—celebrities have spoken out about the many harms of being depicted in the content and the challenges of getting it removed. While laws against deepfakes have been slow to emerge, the US Take It Down Act increasingly allows images to be removed, with part of the law allowing law enforcement officials to take down and seize websites.
The Manhattan District Attorney’s Office has not publicly named the websites it has seized. However, ahead of Bragg’s announcement, WIRED independently observed several of the sites’ homepages being replaced by takedown notices—“THIS DOMAIN HAS BEEN SEIZED”—late last week, with the sites now saying they have been taken over following a seizure warrant issued by a New York State Supreme Court.
“The takedowns are a significant win in the fight against synthetic nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII),” says Leonie Oehmig, a researcher at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), who has studied the deepfake creation ecosystem. Oehmig says that enforcement of state laws shows that the harmful content can be tackled and that the seized sites don’t appear to be accessible if using VPNs to try and access them from other locations. “This shows that meaningful, coordinated enforcement is achievable even where regulation itself remains fragmented across jurisdictions.”
The websites were likely viewed millions of times. Many used names that included phrases such as “sex celebrity” or promised “real deepfakes.” They hosted false videos of some of the world’s most famous celebrities, with one saying, “various actresses’ faces are used for deepfakes.”
Videos could be several minutes in length and include fully sexually explicit scenes—often swapping the faces of celebrities or public figures into existing pornographic videos. Archived versions of the websites show some videos had been watched tens of thousands of times, with one of the websites claiming to have been online since 2018.
“Most videos took the shape of actual pornographic movies, manipulated to instead show targets’ faces instead of the original actors,” says Benjamin Shultz, the lead researcher at the American Sunlight Project, a nonprofit. Shultz, who has been documenting deepfake abuse against political figures and had come across some of the websites during this research, says that many videos appeared to be reposts of content that had originally be shared on the MrDeepFakes website, a notorious deepfake platform that was taken offline after its creators were unmasked by reporters.
“On at least two of the seized websites, elected officials were given profiles containing their name and position, along with a grid of manipulated videos hosting their likeness,” Shultz says. Through recent research, Shultz says that 56 European politicians had been mentioned or appeared on the websites, including 16 US politicians and two based in the UK.
While Oehmig, the ISD researcher, says the takedowns are encouraging, there are many other parts of the deepfake industry that are causing serious harm. “Effective intervention needs to target the ecosystem at multiple points, including the tools used for the creation of synthetic NCII, the discovery and promotion of these, the hosting and technical infrastructure that keeps them online, and the payment and affiliate systems that enable operators to monetize them,” Oehmig says.

Feature: In eastern DR Congo, Bukavu mourns as fire victims laid to rest
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
00:49:34 CST
01:49:34 KST

People grieve during the funeral for victims of a recent fire, in Bukavu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sept. 14, 2026. (Str/Xinhua)
BUKAVU, DR Congo, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Bukavu, a city in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), was in mourning Monday as thousands of residents gathered to bid farewell to victims of a devastating fire that struck a densely populated neighborhood last week.
Silence, tears and grief marked the arrival of bereaved families at a memorial ceremony in the city, where 28 coffins were laid side by side before the victims were taken to their final resting place.
According to those currently in control of the city, the buried included 26 students and two teachers who died after the fire swept through a densely populated neighbourhood crowded with households and schools.
From early morning, large crowds filled roads leading to Alfajiri College, where families, teachers, students and residents gathered for a final farewell. Shops and markets in parts of Bukavu closed during the morning as residents joined the mourning.
For the families, the ceremony brought an unbearable finality to days of shock.
Mwamini Mubwirana, whose family lost children in the fire, said they had left home that morning as they did every school day. "They went out in the morning to go to school because they loved studying so much. They never missed even a single day of school and would refuse to stay at home," she told Xinhua.
"I am very sad. I lack the words to express my pain. These children were pearls of the family. Until now, I still cannot understand their deaths."
At the cemetery, rows of coffins were placed before the graves as inconsolable relatives looked on. Red Cross teams carried them one by one toward the burial sites. Some family members stood silently. Others broke down in tears as the coffins were lowered into the ground.
Anny Badari came to bury her younger sister Bernadette. "We are very sad to have lost our little sister Bernadette," she said. "She was greatly loved because she was always making people laugh, but today we have lost her."
The fire broke out last Thursday, destroying two schools and hundreds of homes in an area where houses are tightly packed together and many are built with highly flammable materials.
Different casualty figures have since been reported by various authorities. Earlier local reports had put the death toll at 29 students, while the authorities administering Bukavu said 28 victims -- 26 students and two teachers -- were buried during Monday's ceremony.
A day after the disaster, Xinhua reporters saw blackened walls, homes reduced to ashes, sheets of metal twisted by the heat and personal belongings scattered among the debris.
On one wall in the devastated neighborhood, 10 photographs from the same family had been placed side by side. Residents stopped before them, exchanging a few words in low voices or simply staring silently at the faces of those who had died.
For residents, the tragedy has been particularly painful because so many of the victims were children who had gone to school only hours before the blaze.
Fires are not uncommon in Bukavu, where rapid urban growth, densely packed housing, narrow access roads and the widespread use of wooden and other combustible building materials have long increased the risk of major fires. But residents interviewed by Xinhua said they could not remember another blaze that had claimed the lives of so many schoolchildren.
"Bukavu may have long been used to fires. We have seen many of them. But Bukavu had never lost so many innocent children in a fire, especially schoolchildren," Bashengzei Chrispin, whose home was destroyed, told Xinhua after the disaster.
According to accounts collected after the fire, the two schools were full of students when the flames spread through the neighborhood. Panic broke out as children tried to flee and parents and residents rushed toward the schools. One teacher interviewed by Xinhua said around 900 students were at the two schools at the time.
Serge Chirimwami, a teacher at Furaha Primary School, recalled the chaos as the flames approached. "Most of the students died in the panic while they were inside the school and the gate was closed," he said. "By the time the teacher arrived, it was already too late for them."
The March 23 Movement rebel group, which has controlled Bukavu since February 2025, declared three days of mourning across South Kivu Province last Friday following the tragedy.
The M23 has also temporarily prohibited new construction on the disaster site and said an assessment committee would be established, pledging to continue investigations to determine the exact cause and circumstances of the fire. ■

China Focus: China fosters birth-friendly environment with better services
China
Unknown Publisher

00:49:22 CST
01:49:22 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- China will take further steps to support child-rearing, including making childcare more accessible and affordable, to build a birth-friendly society and boost its birth rate, according to health officials on Monday.
Lei Haichao, head of the National Health Commission (NHC), told a press conference that continuous efforts will be made to promote the integrated development of services at kindergartens and nursery centers, and to support communities and employers in setting up childcare facilities.
The aim is to ensure that families can access childcare services close to their homes or workplaces and at relatively affordable prices, Lei explained.
The country will work to raise coverage of childcare services among young children to effectively reduce families' costs of having, raising and educating children, he said.
The country will also work to improve access to pediatric care at grassroots medical institutions, he noted.
By the end of this year, 1,000 more community-level medical and health institutions will be capable of offering pediatric care compared with 2025, Lei said, adding that by that time, over 95 percent of the country's township-level clinics and community health service centers are expected to have the capacity to provide relevant services.
More than 3,000 pediatricians have been sent from higher-level hospitals to grassroots medical institutions to strengthen pediatric services at the community level, Lei said.
China has developed a full-cycle maternity support system covering pre-pregnancy, pregnancy and childbirth, and child-rearing, with measures that include maternity allowances, childcare subsidies, medical insurance reimbursement and affordable childcare services, to ease the financial burden on families with children.
A total of 12,562 early pregnancy care clinics have been established, covering almost all counties, said Lei. Pregnant women can visit these clinics in the early stages of pregnancy for counseling and other services. If there is a risk of miscarriage, the clinics can help women assess the risk and take preventive measures.
In 2025, China's maternal mortality rate and infant mortality rate dropped to 13.4 per 100,000 live births and 3.8 per 1,000 live births, respectively, placing China among the leaders in these indicators among upper-middle- and high-income countries and countries with populations exceeding 100 million.
In terms of incentives, the country introduced a nationwide childcare subsidy program in 2025, offering an annual tax-free subsidy of 3,600 yuan (about 530 U.S. dollars) for each child under the age of three. It also began waiving childcare and education fees for the final year of kindergarten in the 2025 autumn semester.
As of August, more than 25 million infants and toddlers had received childcare subsidies for 2026, and roughly 24 million children enrolled in kindergartens had benefited from the fee-waiving policy.
Also, 260 million people are currently covered by maternity insurance, and many regions are expanding coverage to allow flexible workers to enroll in maternity insurance alongside employee medical insurance.
These policies are among China's broader efforts to build a birth-friendly society amid declining birth rates and an aging population.
Building a "birth-friendly society" has become a key focus of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). The outline sets out measures, including incentives to encourage births and efforts to reduce the costs of childbirth, childcare and education.
It says the goal is to stabilize the number of newborns and support long-term balanced population development.
"China's population currently stands at 1.405 billion, and the fundamentals of China as a populous country remain unchanged," said Lei.
Although the number of newborns has declined in recent years, it has remained at around 8 million, a number very few countries can match, he added.
BETTER HEALTH FOR ALL
Officials at the press conference also expounded on other key aspects of a national health plan for the 2026-2030 period unveiled in July, including making health services more accessible, inclusive, comprehensive and continuous.
China has built the world's largest healthcare service system, with more than 1.1 million medical and health institutions nationwide, while over 90 percent of residents can reach their nearest healthcare facility within 15 minutes, said Guo Yanhong, deputy head of the NHC.
However, the system still falls short of people's needs in some respects, Guo noted, urging a shift of efforts from ensuring access to improving quality, with faster progress in developing a high-quality, efficient and integrated healthcare service system.
For instance, community health centers and health centers in central townships should gradually expand their medical service capabilities, develop specialty departments suited to local needs, and improve their capacity to diagnose and treat common and frequently occurring diseases and provide health management services.
Efforts should also be made to further strengthen the workforce of rehabilitation and nursing professionals and step up the training of rehabilitation nurses and therapists, to have seven rehabilitation physicians and 16 rehabilitation therapists per 100,000 people across the country by the end of 2030, Guo said.
Lei noted that the demographic trend of the growing divergence in population changes across regions, with population development becoming increasingly uneven. With various factors considered, over the next five years, demand for healthcare services, particularly for healthcare professionals, is expected to continue growing in China, he said.
China will therefore expand the training of medical students via increased enrollment in high-quality undergraduate and master's programs, targeted training programs for medical students to serve in rural areas, and a special program for university graduates to work as rural doctors, the official said.
Through closer coordination between medical education and healthcare, China will continue to increase its number of medical professionals while making healthcare positions more attractive via improvements in remuneration and personnel incentive systems, so that medical workers are willing to build long-term, stable careers. Efforts will also be made to foster a social environment that respects medical professionals and values healthcare workers, said Lei. ■

Roundup: Somalia steps up climate risk mitigation ahead of El Nino rains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
00:49:08 CST
01:49:08 KST

MOGADISHU, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Somalia is ramping up emergency preparations ahead of the October-December rainy season to mitigate potential flood impacts, as climate experts warn that a strengthening El Nino could bring unusually heavy rainfall.
Somalia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change and the Somali Disaster Management Agency (SoDMA) convened strategic meetings from Sunday to Monday with local and international partners to strengthen multi-agency flood prevention and emergency preparedness ahead of the anticipated rains.
The forum brought together government institutions, climate experts and international partners to strengthen early warning systems and promote timely action against floods, droughts and other severe weather events, including potential El Nino impacts.
The meeting also evaluated the impacts of previous climate seasons, specifically the 2026 Gu rainy season, and presented the climate outlook for the upcoming Deyr season, spanning October through December.
The emphasis on early action was echoed by SoDMA Disaster Risk Management Director Khadar Sheikh Mohamed, who urged vulnerable communities to take early precautions as the Deyr rains approach at a three-day strategic meeting convened by SoDMA in partnership with the International Rescue Committee (IRC) in Mogadishu and concluded on Sunday.
"The rains are expected during the Deyr season in October, November and December, with communities in vulnerable areas advised to take early precautions," Mohamed said on Sunday.
Mohamed said the disaster agency had already placed 29 districts across 14 regions on high alert for riverine and flash flooding.
Heavy seasonal rains across Somalia and the upper catchments in Ethiopia are expected to push the Jubba and Shabelle rivers toward dangerous levels, while short-duration, high-intensity downpours threaten to trigger severe flash floods in urban and rural areas.
SoDMA has advised residents to monitor official alerts, identify evacuation routes, and assemble emergency kits containing food, water, medical supplies and essential documents.
Communities situated along the Jubba and Shabelle rivers are urged to track water levels continuously.
According to the agency, local authorities must prepare evacuation centers, rescue craft, temporary shelters and emergency response units.
SoDMA further called on community leaders, commercial enterprises and media outlets to actively disseminate public safety notices and flood warnings.
Disaster agency officials have emphasized the critical role of early and anticipatory action in mitigating flood impacts before severe weather strikes.
SoDMA Commissioner Mahamuud Moallim stressed recently that unified, collective action is essential to offset forecasted climate risks, calling for urgent inter-agency coordination to strengthen local preparedness and protect vulnerable communities.
The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction's El Nino climate impact outlook for Somalia highlights a credible risk of severe flooding in the Jubba and Shabelle river corridors if El Nino strengthens alongside a positive Indian Ocean Dipole.
While this scenario is not certain, the report, released on Sept. 7, emphasizes the value of early action given the lead time available and Somalia's limited capacity to absorb additional shocks.
It identifies the Jubba and Shabelle river corridors as high-concern zones and outlines critical preparedness priorities, including finalizing the collective flood anticipatory action framework, establishing trigger protocols, strengthening early warning and evacuation systems, improving WASH and health readiness, and managing compounded displacement.
Additionally, the outlook examines financing and recovery strategies, incorporating lessons from the 2023 floods to support a seamless transition from anticipatory action to long-term recovery.
According to the UN, El Nino could have devastating effects in Somalia, such as heavy rains and flooding along the Juba and Shabelle rivers, flash floods in central Somalia and Puntland, and worsening droughts in parts of Somaliland, putting over 600,000 people at risk.
These impacts could be particularly severe for vulnerable communities already facing dire humanitarian conditions in Somalia. More than 3 million people need humanitarian assistance, 1.1 million of whom are internally displaced.
Previous El Nino events have caused massive flooding in Somalia. Some 900,000 people were affected in 1997-1998, and more than 440,000 people were affected in 2006-2007.
The effects this year could extend several months into 2027, according to the UN. ■

Upfront payments in these deals have exceeded 10 billion dollars, while the average value per deal has continued to rise, according to figures published by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), at the launch ceremony of a nationwide drug safety awareness week.
China's drug regulator has in recent years accelerated reforms to bolster the quality of the pharmaceutical industry and boost innovation, an NMPA official has noted.
In 2025, more than 2,900 clinical trials for new drugs were registered nationwide, a rise of 18 percent year on year and a record high in scale. The number of clinical trials of cell and gene therapies grew by about 30 percent last year, highlighting strong activity in cutting-edge areas of drug development.
Regulatory reforms have also helped to deliver more innovative products to the market. Since the beginning of 2026, a total of 59 innovative drugs and 51 innovative medical devices have been approved for market, including 13 first-in-class drugs featuring new mechanisms or targets.
Eyeing China's innovative ecosystem, multinational pharmaceutical companies have ramped up investment in the country by building and expanding R&D centers and manufacturing bases.
In March, U.S.-based pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly, banking on China's big market demand for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity, announced that it planned to invest 3 billion U.S. dollars in China over the coming decade to expand supply-chain production capacity. This investment marked another significant move by the company to deepen its roots in China.
The NMPA said it will further improve communication mechanisms for early-stage drug development, provide tailored regulatory guidance for key products, and ensure smooth expedited testing channels to support pharmaceutical innovation. ■

Europe's rush to fill gas storage amid LNG shortage drives prices higher — expert

MOSCOW, September 14. /TASS/. Europe's efforts to rapidly fill its underground gas storage facilities ahead of winter are driving up gas prices amid an acute crisis in the LNG market, Research Director at the Institute of Energy and Finance Alexey Belogoryev told TASS.
Earlier, the price of the October futures contract at the TTF hub in the Netherlands exceeded $1,000 per 1,000 cubic meters for the first time since December 2022. Meanwhile, spot gas prices at Europe's main trading hubs had already exceeded $1,000 per 1,000 cubic meters last week. Gazprom noted that the approaching heating season is rapidly reducing opportunities to replenish gas reserves in Europe's underground storage facilities, while gas prices have already reached levels seen during the energy crisis in late 2022. Russian President Vladimir Putin did not rule out that European gas prices could rise as high as $1,500 per 1,000 cubic meters.
"The current sharp rise in European prices is largely due to an increase in the pace of injections into underground gas storage facilities. European companies are trying to accelerate the process as much as they can in order to bring the EU's average storage level to at least 75%. At the previous pace seen in July-August, inventories would have reached only 70% of active gas storage capacity by November 1. This is increasing current demand from Europe and, amid an acute LNG shortage on the market, driving prices higher," Belogoryev said.
According to him, the gas market is currently experiencing an acute crisis due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and seasonally record-low gas inventories in EU underground storage facilities. Between March and August, the LNG market lost 15% of the supply that had been expected, and the situation is not improving.
At the same time, the expert considers a rise in European gas prices to $1,500-$2,000 this winter unlikely. "But prices could remain at $1,000-$1,300 for a short period, provided that the Strait of Hormuz remains blocked and injections into EU underground storage facilities remain just as intensive. Overall, however, for now I would expect prices to return closer to $800. Winter price dynamics are difficult to predict -- they will depend decisively on weather conditions and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, both of which are highly uncertain factors," he concluded.

====================================================================================================

The art of not making an AI safety deal with China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:45:16 UTC
01:45:16 KST

Silicon Valley leaders keep painting artificial intelligence (AI) doomsday scenarios, yet they also cannot stop racing to build and sell it. They often point to China as the reason they have no choice, even as the post-ChatGPT era suggests the fiercest pressure comes from one another.
Yet the prevailing assumption is that cooperation with Beijing on frontier AI risks is impossible. It does not help that China itself is often viewed as the AI safety threat.
It all culminates in a terrible spot for the rest of us, but there is a narrow opening for something better. After a two-year halt in official AI safety engagement, the US and China said they would resume talks. The dialogue could come this month, Reuters reported, perhaps around the anticipated summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
Illustration: Yusha
What would count as success? Not trusting Beijing, and certainly not negotiating some package deal. The aim should be simpler. Each side needs enough visibility into what the other fears about AI’s capabilities, and what it is doing to manage that, to keep suspicion from becoming an excuse for reckless acceleration.
Just as crucial, the talks must be insulated from the rest of the US-China economic contest. Existential risks cannot become bargaining chips.
Beijing has signaled its biggest concern ahead of discussion. Yuyuan Tantian (玉淵譚天), a social media account affiliated with state broadcaster China Central Television, has warned that safety talks could become another attempt to contain China’s technological rise. Having seen Washington invoke “national security” to justify blacklists and export controls, officials clearly fear that AI safety could become a similar tool for restriction.
Xi made this tension explicit in July, saying the world must “ensure that AI is always under human control,” while opposing “overstretching the national security concept” and “placing one country’s security over that of others.” Beijing believes that who gets to write the rules has leverage for geopolitical power, and is already proposing a World AI Cooperation Organization and backing two UN initiatives. The goal cannot be getting China to accept US rules, but finding guardrails that both sides can live with that simultaneously tame internal race dynamics.
Beijing’s approach to AI safety is also changing. Earlier regulation, still often cited as the centerpiece of its model, emphasized political controls. With the rise of agentic applications, the concern has shifted from what systems can say to what they can do, according to research group Concordia AI’s annual report on the state of AI safety in China. The number of papers published in the country on frontier AI safety has grown substantially, with monthly output up about 60 percent from June last year to April.
It means the challenge is not convincing China to take the risks seriously, but persuading officials that AI safety is not another name for holding China back. Trust is unrealistic, but mutual visibility can be achieved.
Without it, leaders on both sides “will understandably assume the worst: that the other side is sacrificing any action on safety in a reckless race for building the most powerful system,” Carnegie Endowment for International Peace senior fellow Matt Sheehan wrote. Safety calculations will be driven by “self-interest,” he said.
Transparency is the obvious place to start establishing this. Hugging Face chief executive officer Clement Delangue wrote on X that he sometimes wonders what would have happened if they had not disclosed the OpenAI agent-related cyberattack. The episode has become the most recent warning shot for AI risks that are likely to grow as systems become more capable, gaining attention on both sides of the Pacific. It reveals that we need “100x more transparency in AI,” Delangue wrote.
Some of this sunlight can be shed not just via diplomacy, but through so-called Track 1.5 and 2 talks, more informal meetings bringing together officials in a private capacity or nongovernmental AI experts. Since 2023, Chinese and Western groups have held a dozen such discussions. Much more of them are needed to establish what each side is fearing and watching.
The official dialogue notably comes as advances in AI systems’ ability to improve on their own is sowing new alarm. On Sept. 6, OpenAI’s chief scientist advocated for “voluntary slowdowns” until “shared safety bars are established.” Anthropic PBC similarly said in June that slowing development “would likely be a good thing,” while acknowledging that any pause would be extraordinarily difficult to enforce.
Silicon Valley could stand to tone down the fearmongering if it has no intention to act on its warnings. Meanwhile, Chinese companies need to improve basic safety practices. Only five of 10 leading foundation model developers in China reported safety evaluation results alongside any release over the past year, according to Concordia. If Beijing wants to help set global rules, it should first demand more from its own industry.
Investors from both sides should push for the same. Avoiding catastrophe is essential to sustain confidence in the technology; a sharp reversal in sentiment would devastate markets at a moment when the global economy remains heavily exposed to the AI boom.
The best outcome from US-China AI safety talks will not be a sweeping accord that can be packaged in a flashy social media victory lap. Tariff truces and chip access should not be bartered for promises on risks that know no borders. The real art of the deal is ensuring enough visibility — and enough self-interest — to keep both sides from racing in the dark toward a cliff.
Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

S Korea aims to save older people lost in digital age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:45:14 UTC
01:45:14 KST

A little cheer rose for 79-year-old Hwang Sun-hee after she managed to place an online order at a training session in South Korea, which has one of the world’s starkest digital divides for older people.
Age gaps in digital literacy are a global concern, yet the gulf has widened massively in the hyper-connected and fast-aging country, prompting national campaigns to bridge it.
“You can’t do anything without smartphone apps or a kiosk machine... It’s too much for old folks,” Hwang said at a senior community center in Suwon, south of Seoul, during government-organized digital survival training.
Photo: AFP
The so-called gray digital divide has provided some striking examples in the nation of about 52 million, home to world-leading smartphone and memory chipmakers.
Last year, several baseball clubs began reserving a small number of tickets for on-site sales after reports that older fans, cash in hand, approached younger people at stadiums and pleaded with them to buy tickets from machines.
About 90 percent of taxi drivers use ride-hailing apps, yet more than 80 percent of South Koreans older than 60 still hail cabs by hand, a survey showed.
A 71-year-old retired public servant at the same training session as Hwang recalled spending more than 30 minutes trying to flag down a taxi on a busy Seoul street.
The cabs kept passing him to pick up younger riders just meters away who were using smartphone apps to hail their rides.
“I felt utterly useless,” said the man, who gave only his surname, Park.
The digital divide can also pose a real threat, leaving older people vulnerable to high-tech crimes such as online scams or limiting their access to medical services, experts say.
A South Korean state survey last year found that 60 percent of South Koreans older than 60 struggle to use public and commercial services due to lack of digital skills — compared with just 6 percent of those younger than 40.
“The intergenerational digital divide [in South Korea] appears wider than elsewhere,” said Kim Jeung-kun, professor of senior business at Kangnam University in Seoul.
The nation’s “intensely compressed” industrialization happened in just a few decades, while it took centuries in many Western countries, he said.
South Korea — which had a GDP per capita below US$100 in the wake of its 1950 to 1953 war — is now the world’s 15th largest economy, according to the IMF.
“Many of our elderly grew up at a time when many had no electricity, landline phones or proper schooling,” Kim added.
The nation’s older cohort is massive — South Korea is what the UN calls a “super-aged society,” in which more than 20 percent of the population is older than 65.
In response, South Korea’s public tech training for older people began in 2020, when businesses and services turned online during the COVID-19 lockdown.
Hwang, echoing others in the two-hour class, said she has made it this far by relying on her children for daily tasks she once managed herself — including enrolling in her favorite dance class at the local community center.
“Before, I could easily do all of these just by calling or showing up in person,” Hwang said.
Officials now provide nationwide training for the “digitally vulnerable” for using mobile devices, apps and artificial intelligence. Vans packed with tech devices and mock kiosks drive to community centers and regional festivals popular among older people.
Last year, more than 65,000 sessions were held for about 650,000 people older than 60.
Hwang last month gathered along with 30 neighbors for a session, practicing how to pay hospital bills at mock kiosks, patting a prancing robot dog or asking their phones: “Gemini, tell me about tomorrow’s weather.”
She has undergone similar training several times — and said the lessons helped her confidence — but added she was “so envious of young people who can do all this so easily.”
“I wish I had been born young in today’s world,” she said.

對話 Dialogue
清清：你在看什麼？看得這麼認真！
Qīngqing: Nǐ zài kàn shénme? Kàn de zhème rènzhēn!
Photo: Pxhere / 照片：Pxhere
華華：我在看一些災害的影片，這兩年颱風好多。
Huáhua: Wǒ zài kàn yìxiē zāihài de yǐngpiàn, zhè liǎng nián táifēng hǎoduō.
清清：對啊！放了不少颱風假呢！每次放颱風假，我朋友就找我去唱歌。
Qīngqing: Duì a! Fàng le bùshǎo táifēngjià ne! Měicì fàng táifēngjià, wǒ péngyou jiù zhǎo wǒ qù chànggē.
華華：這樣是不對的，颱風來就應該好好在家，不要隨便出門，很危險。
Huáhua: Zhèyàng shì búduì de, táifēng lái jiù yīnggāi hǎohǎo zài jiā, búyào suíbiànchūmén, hěn wéixiǎn.
清清：特別是現在這個季節，秋天的颱風最可怕了。
Qīngqing: Tèbié shì xiànzài zhège jìjié, qiūtiān de táifēng zuì kěpà le.
華華：秋颱常常風大雨大，到處都淹水，山區還容易有土石流。
Huáhua: Qiūtái chángcháng fēng dà yǔ dà, dàochù dōu yānshuǐ, shānqū hái róngyì
yǒu tǔshíliú.
清清：所以啊！我們都只去唱歌，不敢跑到山上或海邊玩。
Qīngqing: Suǒyǐ a! Wǒmen dōu zhǐ qù chànggē, bùgǎn pǎodào shānshàng huò hǎibiān wán.
華華：你還說！下次颱風來，你就買好食物和水，在家自己唱就好了，注意安全。
Huáhua: Nǐ hái shuō! Xiàcì táifēng lái, nǐ jiù mǎihǎo shíwù hàn shuǐ, zài jiā zìjǐ chàng jiù hǎole, zhùyì ānquán.
翻譯 Translation
Qingqing: What are you watching? You look so focused.
Huahua: I’m watching some videos about natural disasters. There’ve been so many typhoons in the past two years.
Qingqing: That’s right. We’ve had quite a few typhoon days off. Whenever we get a typhoon day off, my friends ask me to go to karaoke with them.
Huahua: That’s not right. When a typhoon comes, you should stay safely at home. Don’t go out unless it’s necessary. It’s very dangerous.
Qingqing: Especially during this time of the year. Typhoons in autumn are the most frightening.
Huahua: Autumn typhoons often bring strong winds and heavy rain. Many places become flooded, and landslides can easily occur in mountain areas.
Qingqing: That’s why we only go to karaoke. We don’t dare go to the mountains or the beach.
Huahua: I can’t believe you’re saying that. The next time a typhoon comes, buy enough food and water and sing by yourself at home. Stay safe.

EDITORIAL: Aging population policy overlooked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:45:08 UTC
01:45:08 KST

As of the end of last month, Taiwan had a total population of 23,224,721, declining for the 32nd consecutive month, the latest household registration data released on Thursday by the Ministry of the Interior showed. The figure was down 103,622 from a year earlier — or an average decline of 283.9 per day — and 10,281 from the previous month.
Last month, Taiwan recorded 7,492 births — averaging about one baby every 6 minutes — dropping by 972 from the same month last year and 414 from July. From January to last month, the number of newborns was 61,742, decreasing by 11,036 from 72,778 in the same period last year.
Meanwhile, the number of people aged 65 or older at the end of last month was 4,797,100, accounting for 20.62 percent of the total population.
The latest data showed an alarming pace of decline in the number of births. A decade earlier, the total number of births was about 207,600, but that number was almost halved to a record-low 105,676 last year, while the number of people aged 65 or older rose to 3,106,105. The National Development Council last month forecast that the number of births could fall below 100,000 for the first time this year to about 94,000.
Taiwan officially became a “super-aged society” this year, with people aged 65 or older accounting for more than 20 percent of the population. What is concerning is that in just 10 years, the number of newborns plummeted nearly 50 percent while the elderly population jumped by more than 50 percent. The number of senior citizens is 1.8 times that of children aged 14 and younger, which stood at 2,616,236 as of the end of last month, the data showed.
Another set of data released by the ministry in June showed that, as of the first quarter of this year, Taiwan had approximately 923,400 households consisting exclusively of residents aged 65 or older, a record high. Of these, about 713,600 were households where elderly people lived alone, about 190,300 were households comprising an elderly couple and nearly 19,600 households were home to three or more senior residents. That means more than 77 percent of elderly people lived alone, while about 22 percent were elderly people living together and caring for each other.
In May, President William Lai (賴清德) announced an 18-point population strategy to counter the nation’s low birthrate and aging population. The policy, which is expected to require NT$380 billion (US$11.99 billion) in funding, addresses five priority areas: a secure start for families, strengthened childcare, investing more in education, family-friendly workplaces and easing housing pressures. However, it remains focused on incentivizing births.
As the number of elderly people has rapidly increased due to longer lifespans, the demographic shift and changes in family structure necessitate new policies to care for and protect the physical, mental and social well-being of elderly people. That is especially true because retirement communities are still uncommon in Taiwan. Major factors include people’s preference for staying in their own homes, concerns about monthly expenses, worries about a lack of freedom and personal privacy, and a dislike of institutional rules and unfamiliar surroundings.
In Taipei and New Taipei City, programs encouraging younger people to live with older people who are not their relatives and to care for each other have been implemented over the past few years. While these intergenerational living programs offer a solution to housing shortages, loneliness and elderly care challenges, they have had limited success. Unless the government offers more incentives, such as bigger rent discounts and more social resources, and create a friendlier community environment to enhance interactions and reciprocal exchanges among residents, the gap between actual implementation and expected outcomes would remain.
With a rapidly aging population, it is inevitable that the number of households in which elderly people live alone or with other older people and care for each other would continue to increase. Changing this trend through policy alone is difficult, while implementing non-familial intergenerational living programs faces cultural hurdles. Taiwan could learn from the experiences of developed countries, which have shown that it would be more viable for the government to allocate more resources to projects such as grocery shopping, home repairs and tax relief to reduce older people’s living and housing burdens, while arranging regular visits and building support networks to help them stay connected.

As the title suggests, Shuster views a deal between Taiwan and China as an increasingly inevitable alternative to a costly war — one that Taiwan, lacking reliable allies and military capabilities, would eventually be destined to lose. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

Surveillance cameras in schools not the answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:45:08 UTC
01:45:08 KST

To quell public anxiety sparked by allegations of child abuse in preschools, the Keelung City Government last month floated the idea of mandating the installation of surveillance cameras in every classroom. The proposal has drawn collective protest from the National Federation of Teachers’ Union and five major early-childhood education organizations nationwide.
While the idea might appear to offer an easy deterrent, at its core it is a classic case of cutting corners and lazy governance. Believing that a few cameras can eliminate incidents of abuse not only misses the root of the problem, but risks undermining trust between teachers and parents on the front lines, and further driving capable professionals out of early-childhood education.
Of course, there should be zero tolerance for any inappropriate or abusive treatment in schools, and unsuitable personnel should be removed from their positions in accordance with the law. There can be no ambiguity on this point. However, surveillance cameras are merely tools for reviewing evidence after an incident has occurred. They cannot prevent a crisis in the first place, nor can they ease the chronic pressures and heavy workloads that teachers face.
The reality on the ground is this: Non-public preschool educators earn an average monthly salary of only NT$32,000 to NT$45,000, yet each day they are expected to teach, care for children with special needs and handle a host of administrative duties. At the same time, they face the risk of penalties that can easily reach several times their monthly salary.
This combination of low pay, high pressure and heavy responsibility has left the early-childhood education sector with a severe staff shortage. If the Keelung City Government were to add round-the-clock surveillance, it would send the wrong message to frontline early-childhood educators: that they must be continuously watched to be considered trustworthy. This would only accelerate the flight of dedicated professionals.
Early-childhood education is not an assembly line; it is a profession rooted in human interaction and emotional connection. The tense atmosphere created by constant surveillance would only further reduce communication between parents and teachers to a defensive and adversarial exercise of footage-checking. Children’s safety concerns the future of the nation. The Ministry of Education should take a more active role in coordinating policy and providing resources, using systemic reform to establish sound, consistent standards nationwide.
What would truly protect children is not the background presence of cameras, but a stable and respected professional workforce. Central and local education authorities should work together to return to root problems and pursue systemic reform: Teacher-to-child ratios must be improved across the board and practical mechanisms established for substitute and relief staffing; an early-warning system should be created for staffing shortages at preschools, with proactive intervention before overwork reaches a crisis point; and there must be transparent, credible communication guidelines and channels established through which parents may raise concerns and teachers may seek outside assistance when under extreme pressure.
Cameras can record what happens, but they do nothing to improve education, nor can they prevent talented professionals from leaving the field. If we truly want to protect children, resources should be directed toward systemic reforms that improve working conditions. Keeping dedicated, professional teachers in the field is the strongest line of defense for children’s safety.
Yang Chih-chiang is a teacher.

Foreign workers for hotel industry arrive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:45:08 UTC
01:45:08 KST

The first group of foreign skilled workers recruited for Taiwan’s hospitality sector arrived yesterday from Indonesia, as part of a government program aimed at easing labor shortages in the hotel industry.
The 35 Indonesians recruited by Regent Taipei arrived at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport under the Cross-border Workforce Enhancement Program, which Taiwan launched in January to allow hospitality businesses to recruit foreign skilled workers.
At a welcoming ceremony at the airport, Cross-Border Workforce Recruitment Center Deputy Director Huang Wei-cheng (黃偉誠) said that the new category of foreign skilled workers is “different from general migrant workers.”
Photo: CNA
Their jobs “require a certain level of technical skill,” while they must also meet requirements for education, skills and language ability, he said.
The 35 Indonesians — mostly in their 20s — had previously spent at least a year interning in Taiwan and are required to obtain at least A2-level Mandarin speaking or listening proficiency within three years of starting work in Taiwan, he added.
Citing figures from the Tourism Administration, Huang said Taiwan’s hospitality sector faces an annual labor shortage of about 6,000 workers.
Regent Taipei human resources group director Jason Feng (馮昌俊) said the workers had returned to Indonesia after completing their internships, during which they had all “performed well.”
Regent remained in contact with them and approached them individually after the new program became available, he said, adding that the workers would mainly return to the departments where they previously worked as interns, including food and beverage and housekeeping.
“Previously, they were interns. Now they are becoming full-time employees,” Feng said, expressing hope that they could develop their careers at Regent.
Regent had previously been approved to hire 37 Indonesians.
Indonesian Economic and Trade Office to Taipei (IETO) Representative Arif Sulistiyo said that two workers did not pass the required medical examinations and are expected to arrive with a later group.
He called it “remarkable” that Indonesian workers were the first to benefit from Taiwan’s decision to open its hospitality sector to foreign skilled workers, saying Indonesia was ready to supply more experienced workers.
The program is “zero cost” for the Indonesian workers, with recruitment-related expenses borne by employers, Arif said.
The IETO had already received “several job orders” from other hotels in Taiwan and was in the process of verifying them, he added.
Among the workers is 19-year-old Martin Lawrence, who said one of the biggest differences he noticed between working in Taiwan and Bali was workplace discipline, which he found stricter in Taiwan.
He also identified Mandarin as his biggest challenge.
“We have to keep upgrading our language [skills] continuously,” particularly when communicating with hotel guests who use words he does not yet understand, he said.
Another worker, I Nyoman Miyoga, 23, said improving his Mandarin was one reason he chose Taiwan, as the language could make him more competitive in Indonesia and abroad.
“If possible, three years. If I am comfortable, then maybe I will continue,” he said when asked how long he planned to stay.
Under the program, hotels that raise the wages of their lowest-paid full-time Taiwanese rank-and-file workers by at least NT$2,000 can receive a quota for one foreign skilled worker for each eligible Taiwanese employee given the pay raise.
As of the end of last month, more than 60 hospitality businesses had applied to conduct domestic recruitment, with recruitment certificates issued for staffing shortfalls totaling more than 600 workers following the required domestic recruitment process, Huang said.
The figure does not represent the number of foreign skilled workers to be hired, as employers must still obtain eligibility certification, with quotas tied to pay raises for local workers and capped at 10 percent of their workforce, he said.

Photo: CNA
“Taiwan and Ukraine are the structural safety pins of global stability. Pull them and the whole transatlantic system unzips,” Sakaliene wrote on social media yesterday.
“Vilnius and Taipei are not two separate stories. Russia and China are one problem working two fronts, and whichever of us folds first makes taking the other one cheaper,” she added.
Sakaliene served as Lithuania’s minister of national defense from December 2024 to October last year, when she stepped down following disputes over increasing defense spending.
She gave a presentation over the weekend titled: “Resilience Under Pressure: Lessons from Lithuania and NATO’s Eastern Flank,” and participated in the panel “Frontline Democracies — Geopolitical Resilience in an Era of Authoritarian Pressure.”
Taiwan must invest sufficient resources to maintain its self-defense capabilities, as China’s military aircraft and exercises have become the “new normal,” she said.
If you cannot protect your country, then who would be left to benefit from education spending, she asked, adding that if nations do not strengthen their own military, they are only strengthening that of the enemy.
As cooperation grows between China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, Taiwan faces a similar situation to Europe, she said.
There are no shortcuts to democratic resilience; it is built day by day through strengthening social trust, maintaining defense capabilities and ensuring that democratic institutions can continue functioning during a crisis, said Atte Harjanne, member of the Finnish parliament and First Vice Chair of the Taiwan Friendship Group.

====================================================================================================

Summit sheds light on global south
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:45:04 UTC
01:45:04 KST

At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, people will remember less what China achieved and more what the global south attained. China did not lose face: President Xi Jinping (習近平) was an honored guest in India, was endorsed as the chair of BRICS for next year, and China is to host the next summit. Yet the carefully crafted 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration (NDD), the longest BRICS declaration so far, reveals a subtle, but important shift. BRICS is moving from a loose grouping toward a more substantive platform for the global south, giving developing countries greater voice and bargaining space in international governance. This has constrained the gradual effort to make BRICS an instrument of China’s geopolitical strategy.
The central tension is that China is a major power, while most BRICS members are developing countries whose interests do not always coincide with Beijing’s. China wants BRICS to increase the strategic weight of a multipolar order and reduce Western dominance. Much of the global south wants something different: not to replace dependence on the West with dependence on China, but to acquire greater autonomy and bargaining power with both. New Delhi brought this distinction into sharper focus.
Xi’s vision contrasted with the summit’s outcome. In his opening address, Xi spoke of BRICS as an important global platform for cooperation among emerging-market and developing countries. He sought enhanced cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI), supply chains, peace and stability, WTO-focused trade and reform of global governance, and greater representation for the global south. He also proposed cooperation with China on AI-driven new industrialization.
Many of these issues found their way into the NDD; their emphasis was placed within a broader multilateral framework acceptable to all members.
Consider the financial agenda. China and Russia have supported reducing dependence on Western financial systems, enhancing local-currency settlements and developing alternatives to the US dollar. The NDD supports cross-border payments and settlements in local currencies, but does not commit BRICS to a common currency or a formal de-dollarization agenda. Instead, the India-led approach emphasizes interoperability of payment systems, the proposed BRICS Risk Lab in GIFT City, and continuing work on investment and financial infrastructure.
The distinction is important. For China, financial alternatives can contribute to a broader alternative to Western-dominated systems. However, for developing countries, the attraction is diversification rather than replacing one dominant system with another. Many want access to Chinese finance without becoming financially dependent on China, just as they want alternatives to Western financial institutions without abandoning them.
The same tension exists in trade. The declaration opposes unilateral tariffs, non-tariff measures and protectionism, and supports WTO reform. These positions can be read as criticism of Western trade policies, but they also touch a sensitive issue within the global south itself. China is by far the largest trading power in BRICS, yet several developing countries complain of difficulties in accessing the Chinese market, trade imbalances and non-tariff barriers. They want greater market access to China as much as they want relief from Western restrictions. Thus, language against protectionism cannot automatically be interpreted as an anti-US position.
Technology presents another dimension. China has enormous strengths in AI, manufacturing and supply chains and naturally wants BRICS cooperation to reinforce these advantages. However, developing countries want access to technology, investment, skills and value chains,not simply to become markets for Chinese technology or suppliers of raw materials to Chinese industry. The global south wants technological cooperation that builds productive capacity and autonomy, not another form of dependency.
The NDD consequently moves beyond the China-versus-West narrative. The question is no longer whether the US dollar should be replaced or whether the US should be challenged at China’s behest. The objective is to give developing countries better access to finance, technology, markets and decisionmaking, without having to depend exclusively on either Washington or Beijing.
The Chinese positions had their complexities. Xi arrived in India for the first time since 2019 and met Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Peace and stability on the border, trade imbalances, supply chains, people-to-people exchanges and building trust were among the issues discussed. Modi emphasized that peace and stability on the border were critical for improving bilateral relations.
India’s position demonstrated the variation between Chinese and Indian approaches. India is simultaneously a member of BRICS and the Quad, a partner of many Western countries, and a country invited to the G7, while also having an unresolved boundary question with China. It showed that participation in BRICS does not require alignment with Beijing. India’s concept of multipolarity envisions the global south gaining greater heft without abandoning relations with the West.
India’s convening power created space for countries with differing interests to engage. The consensus around the NDD, including on west Asia, was achieved with precision.
The New Delhi Summit represents a transition. China remains BRICS’ dominant economic power and its next chair, but it has not secured a BRICS organized primarily around its geopolitical contest with the West. The tensions between China’s interests and those of other developing countries have instead encouraged a broader definition of BRICS.
The true winner of the summit is therefore the global south. China gained the chair; India helped define the narrative. China seeks to make BRICS a stronger pole in a changing world order. The global south wants BRICS to give it greater space within that order, including greater room to negotiate with China itself. If this distinction is preserved, BRICS can become less an instrument of great-power rivalry and more an instrument of global south agency.
Gurjit Singh is a former Indian ambassador to Germany, Indonesia, ASEAN, Ethiopia and the African Union.

Taiwan trailing Malaysia, Philippines in English education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:45:04 UTC
01:45:04 KST

Taiwan should improve its English-language education by more closely aligning with English proficiency indicators and learning from systems used in Malaysia and the Philippines, the National Academy for Educational Research said in a report published earlier this month.
Much like Taiwan, Malaysia and the Philippines have multilingual, multicultural societies, but in the past few years, they have ranked above Taiwan in the EF English Proficiency Index, Research Center for Translation, Compilation and Language Education associate researcher Li Shih-min (李詩敏) said in the academy’s e-newsletter on Sept. 1.
She cited research on elementary-school curricula, education policy and textbook materials from Malaysia and the Philippines from July 2022 to the end of 2023.
Photo: Taipei Times
Li and an associate researcher found that elementary-school students in Malaysia and the Philippines receive 2.5 to five times more English teaching hours compared with Taiwan, with instruction beginning at age six, emphasizing communication skills and real-world proficiency.
Textbooks also included 2.5 to four times more vocabulary than Taiwanese textbooks, and a large proportion of vocabulary was above the most basic A1 level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), the study found.
Malaysian and Philippine textbooks shared 93 important vocabulary words at the A1 and A2 levels of the CEFR, it said.
The countries also foster a multilingual learning environment, with Malaysia adopting a language policy placing Malay first, followed by English and a third language, while the Philippines’ policy prioritizes native language, then Tagalog, then English, Li said.
Malaysia allows English to be used as a medium of instruction from preschool, while the Philippines places greater emphasis on students’ native language and allows English to be used as a medium of instruction from fourth grade, she added.
The study made three suggestions to improve English education in Taiwan.
First, Taiwan should foster a multilingual learning environment and clearly define the role and function of each language, it said.
Second, Taiwan’s system should more closely follow the CEFR standard, and third, it should strengthen vocabulary instruction through scientific methods, it added.

China sports activity participation restricted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:45:02 UTC
01:45:02 KST

The Ministry of Sports has amended and promulgated the Regulations Governing Cross-Strait Sports Exchanges (兩岸體育交流處理規範), strengthening restrictions on how Taiwanese athletes participate in sporting activities involving China.
The regulations, first established by the former National Council on Physical Fitness and Sports in 1998, serve as a key guideline for cross-strait sports exchanges. They have been amended five times, including this revision.
In addition to changes stemming from government restructuring and updates to references to relevant laws and regulations, the main amendment adds provisions to Article 7 explicitly stating that Taiwanese may not compete in international sporting events as members of China’s national teams.
Photo: CNA
The ministry said that serving as an athlete on China’s national team involves issues of national identity and contravenes Article 33 of the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例), as well as related restrictions on holding positions.
The amendment incorporates the intent of the relevant laws into Article 7, establishing a policy red line for cross-strait sports exchanges, the ministry said.
The ministry reiterated that public and private organizations and individuals in Taiwan conducting cross-strait sports exchanges should uphold the principles of “equality, dignity and mutual respect,” and engage in mutually beneficial interactions within the professional sphere of sports.
The ministry would also continue to follow guidance from the Mainland Affairs Council and use various channels to promote the cross-strait act, the regulations and the latest cross-strait policies among sports organizations and schools, it said.
The ministry urged organizations invited to China for exchanges to maintain a strong awareness of potential risks and carefully examine the backgrounds of organizers, itineraries and promotional materials.
They should not participate in activities with “united front” objectives or nationwide events organized by Chinese authorities, and must not join China’s national teams as athletes, the ministry said, urging them to protect their individual rights and Taiwan’s sovereignty.

Taipei health department probes high-school over suspected food poisoning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:59 UTC
01:44:59 KST

The Taipei Department of Health yesterday said it sent inspectors to a high school in the city to check its cafeteria, after two students reported gastrointestinal symptoms following their school lunch.
It was the third suspected food poisoning incident in the city last week.
A Taipei Municipal Zhongshan Girls’ High School student on Sunday evening wrote on social media that she began feeling ill about two hours after she ate fishcake tempura from the school’s cafeteria on Monday last week.
Photo: Taipei Times
A friend who shared the food with her experienced the same symptoms, even though she only ate two pieces, she added.
They visited the school’s health center in the afternoon and were told to observe their symptoms for a few days, but the student sought emergency treatment at a hospital that evening for abdominal pain and returned home to rest, she said.
Her discomfort worsened the next day, so she sought emergency treatment again and was diagnosed with peritonitis and hospitalized, she said.
Her mother reported the situation to the school’s health center on Thursday, but the cafeteria continued to sell the fishcake, the student wrote.
The school yesterday confirmed that the student had felt discomfort after lunch on Monday last week and was diagnosed with gastroenteritis.
After her homeroom teacher contacted the student’s mother, the school learned that she received a blood test and an X-ray, and recovered after taking antibiotics, while another student who felt ill that day recovered the next day, the school said.
The cafeteria sells about 40 bags of fishcake each day, and only two students reported feeling ill on Monday last week, so whether the illness was caused by food poisoning has yet to be determined, it said.
The cafeteria has been ordered to temporarily stop selling deep-fried food, while the school would continue to follow up on the student’s blood test results and cooperate with inspections, it added.
The department said it did not receive a report of suspected food poisoning from the hospital or the school, but has sent inspectors to check the personnel hygiene of workers in the cafeteria, food handling, pest control and workplace hygiene.
If food safety issues are found, the cafeteria would be required to improve the situation within a specified time, and might face a fine if it fails to meet required standards in a second inspection, it said.
Two high schools in Taipei — Chengyuan High School and Da Li Senior High School — also reported suspected food poisoning cases after students ate school lunch provided by the same contracted vendor last week.

Kuai Kuai workers protest land sale, demand compensation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:59 UTC
01:44:59 KST

Workers at Taiwanese snack maker Kuai Kuai Co yesterday protested outside the Presidential Office in Taipei, demanding compensation after the company sold the site of its factory in Taoyuan’s Zhongli District (中壢) and announced plans to relocate operations to Hsinchu.
The Kuai Kuai Zhongli factory union said the company sold the land for NT$5.672 billion (US$178.6 million) in late July and accused San-Ti Group, which controls the snack maker, of failing to adequately safeguard the interests of long-serving workers.
Among the dozens of people taking part in the Taipei protest was union chairman Liu Neng-hung (劉能宏), who said the Zhongli factory had operated since 1968 and that more than one-third of its employees had worked there for more than 30 years.
Photo: CNA
"Now that the group has made substantial profits from selling the land, it should give priority to compensating long-serving, low-paid workers," Liu said in a statement issued after the protest.
Employees only learned about the land sale through news reports and were not formally informed until Sept. 1 of plans to relocate the factory to Hsinchu, the union said.
The move was not expected for another two years, the Ministry of Labor said.
The distance between Zhongli and Hsinchu is more than 39km, making the proposed relocation impractical for many employees, Taoyuan Confederation of Trade Unions secretary-general Tracy Sun (孫語謙) said.
"That is already too far. Most of our employees would not be able to accommodate such a transfer," Sun said.
Nearly 20 workers had resigned since the sale, the union said in the statement, accusing the company of hoping employees would leave voluntarily so it could avoid paying severance.
Kuai Kuai workers "might not be the only ones" affected by the expansion of Taiwan’s artificial intelligence (AI) industry, Sun said.
Rising industrial land prices could make it more attractive for companies to sell factory sites than continue production as AI and semiconductor companies seek more space to expand, she said.
San-Ti Group is primarily involved in land and commercial development, Sun said, adding that it may have been more interested in the value of Kuai Kuai’s land when it acquired the company than in "operating the food manufacturer and looking after its workers" over the long term.
The union is seeking compensation above statutory severance levels and has said it could hold a strike vote if no satisfactory agreement is reached.
The Ministry of Labor said it had asked the company to engage in "proactive and transparent" dialogue with workers and the union at a labor-management mediation meeting scheduled for tomorrow.
"The rights of grassroots workers who have worked for the company for many years cannot be ignored, nor can workers’ rights be allowed to suffer because of adjustments to business operations," the ministry said.
Any factory relocation or reassignment of workers must comply with the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) and other labor laws, the ministry said.
The relocation could significantly affect workers’ families and daily lives, it said, urging the company to consult workers on issues including longer or more difficult commutes and possible changes to working conditions.
The ministry also called on Kuai Kuai, which it described as a household name, to "demonstrate corporate social responsibility" and properly address the union’s demands for compensation or other concrete protections.
Kuai Kuai has not responded to a request for comment as of press time.
Kuai Kuai is one of Taiwan’s best-known snack brands, particularly for its eponymous puffed corn snacks.
Its green-packaged butter-coconut-flavored Kuai Kuai is also a familiar sight in Taiwan’s tech sector, where packets are often placed beside equipment in the belief they would help the equipment "behave" and operate smoothly — a play on the meaning of "Kuai Kuai" in Mandarin.

Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi’s ally wins election in Okinawa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:44:58 UTC
01:44:58 KST

A candidate backed by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s ruling party on Sunday ousted the incumbent governor of Japan’s southern Okinawa Prefecture in an election, delivering a boost to Takaichi’s push for a stronger military to stave off threats from China.
Genta Koja won more than 50 percent of votes cast in the election, defeating Okinawa Prefecture Governor Denny Tamaki, national broadcaster NHK said, giving Takaichi greater influence over the strategically important cluster of islands in the East China Sea that host the bulk of US military facilities in Japan.
“This election was a referendum on bringing about a fresh start and moving Okinawa forward,” said Koja, who at 42 becomes the youngest governor of Okinawa since it was handed back to Japan in 1972 by the US, which had been the occupying power after World War II.
Photo: Kyodo, via Reuters
Tamaki, 66, has sought to move a major US military base out of Okinawa, but Koja supports a plan for the base to remain in Okinawa in a new location. Koja’s victory might also make it easier for Takaichi to expand Japan’s own military footprint on its southern islands, which stretch toward Taiwan and have assumed greater strategic importance as Chinese military activity in the region intensifies.
“I accept the will of the people,” Tamaki said in conceding to Koja, who is part of a younger generation of Japanese more supportive of building up military power to counter challenges from China and North Korea.
Koja’s win adds to recent electoral gains for Takaichi in Okinawa after her ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) won all four of the prefecture’s seats in the Japanese House of Representatives election earlier this year for the first time.
The former deputy mayor of Naha, Okinawa’s capital city, campaigned on a platform of boosting wages and building a health and wellness industry in Okinawa to help drive growth. His campaign was backed by Takaichi’s LDP and other right-of-center political parties, with heavy hitters from the parties regularly appearing with him on the campaign trail.
Okinawa has traditionally been a center of resistance to US military presence, but the latest election result underscores a shift in the political debate away from that topic as China’s military activities increase near Taiwan and Japan.
“Looking at the global situation, there are problems that can’t easily be solved just by appealing for peace,” Koja said in an interview a few days before the election.
“Our [Japanese] Self-Defense Forces alone are not sufficient to maintain deterrence. I also understand that the Japan-US security framework is necessary,” he said.

An official speaking on condition of anonymity said that this shows that high-level interactions between Taiwan and Europe are deepening, shifting from “highly sensitive” exceptions to a new interactive mode.
Photo from Hsiao’s Facebook page
Frontline diplomatic and security teams were highly discreet about Hsiao’s visit to Italy in terms of itinerary planning, communication with European personnel and emergency response, given that it was a vice president-level visit to a non-allied nation, the official said.
Alert levels were also raised after President William Lai’s (賴清德) visit to Eswatini in April was disrupted by China’s weaponization of flight information regions, they said.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs immediately reported to Lai after it received the invitation from the conference, the official said.
The ministry discussed the invitation with Hsiao and personnel from the offices of the president and vice president, as well as the national security team, they said.
The official cited Lai as saying that Taiwan should seize every opportunity that helps expand its international space and deepen partnerships with like-minded countries, the official said.
Lai ordered the ministry and relevant teams to facilitate and asked Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) to communicate with involved parties, they said.
Lai also hosted the itinerary and contingency meeting before Hsiao’s departure and ordered officials to “follow the host country’s lead,” the official said.
Hsiao’s two visits to Europe brought about a new diplomatic working model, they said.
Lai provides strategic direction and political authorization, while Lin and the diplomatic team continue to expand Taiwan’s political credit and activities in Europe, the official said, adding that Hsiao can transform the diplomatic gains into higher-level political interactions based on her extensive diplomatic experience and strong connections in Western countries.
Another foreign affairs official yesterday said the balance between diplomatic breakthroughs and security is also a key concern.
Hsiao’s schedule was not announced prior to the visit to ensure her safety, they said, adding that it took the delegation 27 hours to travel by plane, vehicle and ferry to Italy.
