Israel's High Court signals it will not order police probe into 2023 death of Yuval Kestelman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:23:44 UTC
00:23:44 KST

The High Court of Justice on Monday signaled that it was unlikely to order a criminal investigation into Jerusalem police officers over their handling of the inquiry into the death of Yuval Kestelman, killed in 2023 when mistaken for a terrorist, dealing a setback to his family’s effort to have the conduct investigated as possible obstruction of justice.
Kestelman, a 38-year-old attorney from Mevaseret Zion, intervened when two Hamas terrorists opened fire at the entrance to Jerusalem on November 30, 2023. He helped stop the attack before he was shot by Sgt. (res.) Aviad Frija, who allegedly mistook him for a terrorist.
Police released Kestelman’s body for burial without an autopsy. He was exhumed a week later after the military investigation determined that an autopsy was needed. The examination found a bullet and two fragments, contradicting the police’s earlier account that no bullets had been found in his body.
Kestelman’s family argues that the decision to release the body, followed by what it describes as false and changing accounts from officers involved, created reasonable grounds to suspect that police had deliberately obstructed the investigation. The state acknowledges serious professional failures but says there is no evidence they were intentional.
Justice panel urged Kestelman's family to withdraw petition
The petition concerns the conduct of the police officers who initially handled the case. It is separate from Frija’s military trial over the shooting itself.
After hearing both sides on Monday, the three-justice panel urged the family to withdraw its petition. The family declined and requested a reasoned judgment, which the court said would be sent to the parties.
Until that ruling is issued, Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara’s decision not to order a criminal investigation remains in force.
“There was negligence and unprofessional conduct, but it does not cross the threshold,” Justice David Mintz said, after the panel consulted. He added that it was “very, very difficult” to conclude that there had been criminal intent and a criminal act.
Justice Yael Willner said it was possible that the affair contained a criminal element but that such a possibility was not enough for the court to intervene.
The judges’ task, she stressed, was not to decide criminal responsibility. They were reviewing whether the attorney-general’s decision fell outside the broad discretion given to law-enforcement authorities – a threshold the panel indicated had not been met.
Kestelman's family's lawyers say evidence sufficient for criminal investigation
The family’s lawyers, Daniel Haklai and Amit Shelef, argued that the evidence went beyond poor judgment and was sufficient to justify opening a criminal investigation. They emphasized that the evidence needed to begin investigating is less than what would be required to file an indictment or secure a conviction.
Their allegations focus in part on Supt. Nadav Kogan, a Jerusalem District investigator involved in the decision to release Kestelman’s body.
The petitioners allege that Kogan had decided to release the body before receiving a CT report referring to metal fragments. They further allege that he later gave inaccurate or false accounts of consultations with doctors and the family, including an account suggesting that Kestelman’s father had opposed an autopsy on religious grounds.
The family also argued that the Justice Ministry’s Police Investigation Department (PID) had conducted an inadequate examination before deciding there was no reasonable suspicion of a crime. Its lawyers said PID did not question several potentially significant witnesses, including Military Police investigators and doctors.
'No evidence' that police deliberately impeded investigation, state says
The state acknowledged in court that releasing the body without an autopsy was a mistake and part of a series of administrative and professional failures “that should never have happened.” It said, however, that there was no evidence that officers acted deliberately to impede the investigation.
State counsel said police misunderstood the initial CT report and believed no bullets remained in Kestelman’s body. According to the state, a trauma doctor also understood police to be asking whether bullets had been removed during treatment, rather than whether any remained in the body.
The error was corrected after the body was exhumed and an autopsy was conducted on December 8, 2023, the state said.
Frija has argued in the military proceedings that the failure to conduct an autopsy before Kestelman’s burial caused evidentiary harm. The military court has not yet decided that claim or the criminal case against him.
Frija faces military trial on charges of reduced-responsibility manslaughter
According to the military indictment, Frija continued firing after another soldier called for the shooting to stop and after Kestelman raised his hands, removed his jacket, and no longer held a weapon. Frija has denied criminal wrongdoing. He is charged with reduced-responsibility manslaughter, and his trial is continuing in the Southern District Military Court.
The state said the PID, the appeals department, and the attorney-general had all reviewed the evidence and reached the same conclusion: The failures did not establish reasonable suspicion that officers intended to obstruct justice.
An internal police review led to tighter procedures, including requirements to document decisions and conversations in real time and to send bodies for forensic examination following deaths caused by trauma or other unusual circumstances, even when police do not initially suspect a crime. Prosecutorial approval is also required before a body is released following an unnatural death.
The family’s current legal challenge followed an earlier High Court ruling in December 2025, directing the attorney-general to reconsider the handling of its appeal. Baharav-Miara reviewed the matter and again declined in March to order a criminal investigation.
Moshe Kestelman, Yuval’s father, told the court that the family was seeking accountability to prevent similar failures in future cases.
“Why not investigate the officer’s motives?” he asked.
Mintz said the family’s pain was shared by the court but maintained that the legal line between grave professional failure and a criminal offense had not been crossed. With the family declining to withdraw its petition, the court will now set out its conclusion in writing.

‘NYT’ coverage framed Israel as ‘sole aggressor,’ Palestinians as ‘passive victims,’ study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:23:24 UTC
00:23:24 KST

The New York Times’ reporting after October 7 consistently portrayed Palestinians as “passive victims” and Israel as the “sole aggressor,” a new peer-reviewed study by Edieal Pinker of Yale School of Management found.
The study, How The New York Times Framed the War Between Israel and Hamas, was published in the academic journal Studies in Conflict & Terrorism last week. It is an expansion of an initial quantitative study published by Pinker in February 2025, as covered by The Jerusalem Post at the time.
Drawing on a body of 1,559 news articles written between October 7, 2023, and 7 June, 2024, Pinker documents a dominant narrative that assigned “near-exclusive agency and responsibility to Israel while diminishing Hamas’s role in sustaining the conflict.”
According to Pinker, in this narrative, from October 8, 2023, onward, Israel “has been the sole aggressor” whereas Palestinians are portrayed as “passive victims whose suffering grows daily as they are relentlessly attacked by the Israeli military.”
Pinker at no point makes the claim that the NYT is “biased” in its reporting. “To determine if bias exists one needs a benchmark of what “unbiased” reporting would look like,” he notes.
Rather, he says, he intends to document several imbalances in the reporting of the war that could “plausibly influence the opinions of a reader in a direction that is at odds with reality.”
Details of the study reveal that most articles conform to 'dominant narrative'
Of the 1,559 articles examined, Pinker concludes that 969, or about 70%, fit what he calls the “dominant narrative.”
Pinker says the NYT frequently did not mention Israelis killed after October 7, Hamas fighters killed during the fighting, or Hamas or other Palestinian attacks carried out after October 7.
In many cases, mention of Israeli hostages was also omitted. In fact, he finds that only 42% of those 969 articles mentioned the Israeli hostages, even though the hostages were central to ceasefire negotiations. Fifty-five percent did not mention the Israeli deaths on October 7 or at all.
Pinker also reports that Israeli violence was almost always mentioned in these articles, while the Hamas attack itself was omitted on many occasions. There were only 38 cases in which Israeli violence was absent, compared with 237 in which the Hamas attack was absent.
“Taken as a whole, this narrative reinforces a distorted view of the conflict, namely that Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, killing many Israelis, and this led to Israeli violence that has been killing only Palestinian civilians since then with no further Israeli deaths,” he writes.
Pinker also opines that the absence of mention of Israeli casualties, including soldiers, in much of the NYT’s reporting “creates the appearance of a hierarchy of human life that is perhaps linked to degree of victimhood.”
This framing is also at odds with how Israelis view the war, he adds.
For example, in his 244-day sample, 128 days had at least one IDF death. Most of these made front page news in Israel. In comparison, in the NYT, there were only 74 days with a mention of Israeli casualties post-October 7 (including both military and civilian mentions). There were also nine stretches of a week or longer with no mention of Israeli military casualties.
What a reader therefore may not understand is how costly the war was in terms of Israeli lives and the impact the war had on the wider society.
“For The New York Times reader, the cost that Israelis are bearing will not be salient,” Pinker writes. “Given their sensitivity to casualties, the Israeli public expects its military and political leadership to conduct the war in a manner that reduces risk to their soldiers. This approach will inevitably lead to greater civilian deaths among the Palestinians. This context is lost to the reader of The New York Times.”
Diminishing Hamas's responsibility for the war
Pinker also explores assignment of responsibility.
One way in which he does this is by counting mentions of “Hamas” vs. mentions of “Israel.”
Of the 1,559 articles in the sample, there are only 105 (7%) in which the number of times the word “Hamas” appears is greater than or equal to the number of times the word “Israel” appears.
In total, the word “Israel” appears 27,205 times vs 8,499 for “Hamas” across all articles in the analysis. Pinker writes that this imbalance in mentions diminishes Hamas's responsibility for the war and the situation. He also says it supports the view that all agency is in the hands of Israel and thus most blame should fall on Israel for negative sentiment about the war.
Regarding the balance of suffering, Pinker says that Palestinian suffering was mentioned in the large majority of articles about the war, whereas less than 4% of articles made any reference to some dimension of Israeli suffering among the population not in reference to direct victims of October 7.
Again, he explains that this reinforces the view that Israelis incurred little cost from the war.
Overall, Pinker concludes, there were imbalances in the NYT’s reporting post-October 7 that created a specific framing of the war.
These imbalances have created sympathy for the Palestinian people while at the same time diminishing Hamas’ responsibility for their situation and the continuation of the war, he writes.
When Pinker published his initial findings last year, The New York Times issued a statement saying that it has “covered this war with more rigor than virtually any other US news organization, reporting on the conflict from all angles.”
It added, “We remain open to good-faith disagreement but will not change our coverage to buttress entrenched perspectives.”

Mountain bikers head north as Winner Epic Israel announces return to Galilee after 3 years of war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:23:05 UTC
00:23:05 KST

Winner Epic Israel 2026 will return to the Western Galilee for the first time since the war forced the closure of the region’s trails nearly three years ago, bringing hundreds of mountain bikers back to the North from October 14-17.
Held in memory of the late Giora Tsachor and in partnership with Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF), the four-day event is sponsored by Winner and Specialized. The race will take place throughout the Mateh Asher Regional Council and Nahariya, passing through forests, singletrack trails and off-road terrain that have recently been rehabilitated and reopened.
The race will cover approximately 300 kilometers and 3,000 meters of cumulative climbing. In addition to the full four-day competition, the event will feature one-day races, a junior race and a relay race.
For Gal Tsachor, founder and producer of Winner Epic Israel and one of the leading figures in Israel’s cycling industry, the return to the North is about far more than a change of scenery.
“For us, Winner Epic Israel’s return to the North is about much more than choosing a new route,” Tsachor said. “After three years in which this region was almost entirely off the cycling map, we want to be among the first to return. When hundreds of riders come here, they bring with them families, friends, overnight stays, restaurants and business for local establishments. We want the race to be part of this movement and to help bring the North back to life.”
Tsachor said the event also carries a personal significance as it continues the legacy of his father, the late Giora Tsachor, in whose memory the race is held each year.
“Winner Epic Israel was born out of a love for this country, cycling and community, and it continues the legacy of my father, the late Giora Tsachor, whom we commemorate every year,” he said. “Returning to the North after three years is a significant moment for us. This is not just about riding trails – it is a statement. We want to be there, to ride there and to show that the North is coming back.”
Race's return coincides with KKL-JNF rehabilitation of northern Israel
The return of the race coincides with extensive rehabilitation work being carried out by Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund throughout northern Israel. KKL-JNF has developed more than 2,500 kilometers of cycling trails across the country and is currently upgrading approximately 100 kilometers of singletrack trails in the North, including those in Hanita, Kabri, Yehiam and Matzuva that were closed during the war.
Winner Epic Israel will pass through some of these rehabilitated trails, once again bringing cyclists to one of Israel’s premier cycling destinations, with its extensive network of forests, woodlands and Galilee landscapes.
KKL-JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrinsky described the race’s return as a symbol of the region’s recovery.
“Winner Epic Israel’s return to the North is a powerful symbol of the North coming back to life,” Ostrinsky said. “For three years, the trails and forests in the region were closed to the public, and throughout this period KKL-JNF has been and continues to carry out extensive work to rehabilitate, upgrade and restore these natural and recreational areas.”
Ostrinsky added that seeing hundreds of cyclists return to the reopened trails demonstrates the tangible impact of that rehabilitation.
“KKL-JNF will continue to invest in the North, in its forests, cycling trails, and tourism and recreational infrastructure, based on the belief that bringing the public back to these spaces is an integral part of the region’s rehabilitation and growth,” he said.
The event will also include wounded IDF veterans from Brothers for Life, an organization that supports soldiers wounded during their military service and assists them throughout their rehabilitation. Their participation will add another dimension to the race’s return, bringing together competitive cycling, community activity and the public’s renewed access to northern Israel’s natural spaces.
Winner Epic Israel collaborated with Toto Winner, KKL-JNF for 2026 race
The Toto Winner, which is partnering with the event alongside KKL-JNF, also views the race as an opportunity to support the North’s recovery.
“The Toto is proud to once again partner with Winner Epic Israel, in partnership with KKL-JNF – a competition held to high professional standards that presents Israel in a positive light,” said Meir Bardugo, CEO of the Toto Winner (The Israel Sports Betting Board). “For us, this is another way to express our commitment to advancing Israeli sports and, this year, also to take part in the effort to strengthen the North, support its rehabilitation and help restore normal life.”
The 2026 race will also mark the first year of a partnership between Winner Epic Israel and Matzman-Specialized.
“This is our first year together with Winner Epic Israel, and we have two reasons to be proud,” said Roy Kapach, Head of Commerce and Strategy at Matzman-Specialized. “On the one hand, we are taking part in the race’s return to the beautiful North after several difficult years, and on the other, we are partnering with one of Israel’s most significant and prestigious sporting events.”
Kapach said the partnership would help reconnect Specialized with cyclists in the region.
“For us, this is an opportunity to reconnect with the cycling community, restore confidence in and the love of cycling in the North, and be part of the movement bringing the region back to activity and normal life,” he said.
Nahariya Mayor Marelli says race promotes sports, tourism
Nahariya will host the event for the first time, with Mayor Ronen Marelli highlighting the city’s efforts to promote both sports and tourism.
“Nahariya is delighted to host the Winner Epic Israel competition for the first time, in partnership with KKL-JNF and the Toto,” Marelli said. “Hosting the international competition is part of the city’s efforts to promote sports and tourism and will introduce participants and visitors to our coastline and unique seafront.”
“Nahariya has been and will continue to be Israel’s cycling city,” he added. “I am confident that this partnership will expand in the years ahead and contribute to strengthening northern Israel and the State of Israel.”
Mateh Asher Regional Council head Moshe Davidovich similarly welcomed the return of the event, saying the region needs to see tourism, activity and visitors return after years of disruption.
“The return of Winner Epic Israel to the North is important news for Mateh Asher and the Western Galilee,” Davidovich said. “After three years in which our residents endured a difficult period and the entire region was forced to put its daily routine on hold, we need to bring activity, tourism and people back here.”
“A sporting event like Winner Epic Israel puts the North back in the spotlight and reminds everyone of the region’s beauty and strength,” he added. “I congratulate the organizers, KKL-JNF and the partners on their decision to return here, and I hope this will mark the beginning of a new period – one of rehabilitation, growth and a return to normal life.”

Can a party be leftist and Zionist?

Can a party be leftist and Zionist?
No, it cannot. But the concept of leftist Zionism is still being pushed to cover up its racist, colonial nature.
Ahead of Israel’s October 27 elections, Israel’s Young Democrats, the youth wing of the newly formed Democrats party, are seeking foreign allies. They recently announced a joint campaign with the Young Greens of Austria to support “progressive voices on the ground and work with them towards a sustainable peace”.
Meanwhile, another youth group described as “leftist”, Hamahanot Haolim (the Ascending Camps), is exploring plans to build a new kibbutz in the occupied West Bank, near Jericho.
When questioned about the impact on the Palestinian population, the group’s director, Ilan Gazit, explained that since Israeli settlements are being built regardless, “the left” should make sure it is Israeli “leftists”, not far-right settlers, who populate them. “We aren’t ashamed of this, and we aren’t hiding it,” he said.
These two youth movements and their foreign sympathisers appear to treat “leftist Zionism” as a coherent political identity. But can a party, a movement, or an individual be both leftist and Zionist?
The short answer, from a Palestinian and anti‑colonial perspective, is no. So why is it touted in Israel and beyond as a legitimate ideological belief? Because it is a political technology designed to shield Zionism from any critique while preserving the structures of oppression.
A question with history
The question about the viability of “leftist Zionism” is not new. Zionism emerged as an organised Jewish nationalist movement in Europe in the 19th century. At its core was the aim of establishing a Jewish national home, an idea shaped by European nationalism, European anti-Semitism, and colonial expansion.
Its early political architects advanced two connected projects: redefining Judaism as a national identity and colonising Palestine. Theodor Herzl, a Hungarian Jewish journalist who is seen as the founder of Zionism, was motivated not by religious zeal, as he espoused secularism, but by the growing anti-Semitism in Europe.
After Herzl’s death in 1904, leftist ideas entered the movement as various socialist factions rose to dominance within the World Zionist Organization and in early settler communities in Palestine itself.
But these leftist elements were not driven by a genuine commitment to class-based struggle and internationalism. Rather, they used a socialist vocabulary to justify a settler-colonial nation-building project, carried out through kibbutzim, labour unions, and diplomacy.
Whatever position early Zionists staked out on the political spectrum, what the movement ultimately produced — the state of Israel — was in direct contradiction with the anti-colonial, anti-racist politics the left was supposed to stand for.
In 1975, the United Nations General Assembly acknowledged this by adopting Resolution 3379, declaring that “Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination”. The resolution was revoked in 1991, after sustained pressure from Israel and its allies and in the wake of the Soviet collapse.
The debate about “leftist Zionism” continues till today. The issue is not whether individual Zionists can hold progressive views on particular social or economic questions. Some might.
The real question is whether a political project organised around building and sustaining a state premised on Jewish supremacy through ethnic cleansing, dispossession, apartheid, and now genocide can be reconciled with the left’s foundational commitments: equity, anti‑racism, decolonisation, and social justice for everyone.
It clearly cannot.
Leftist politics in Israel
When considering the historical record, it is important to note that for decades, Israel was governed by parties that would self-describe as “leftist”.
Mapai was established as a Labour Zionist party in 1930, led by David Ben-Gurion. It became the dominant force within early Zionist politics and the principal architect of the pre‑state and early institutions, including the Haganah, which carried out various terrorist attacks and massacres against the Palestinians.
Mapai governed Israel well into the 1960s, giving way to the Labour Party, which dominated Israeli politics until the 1990s.
Labour Zionism spoke the language of workers’ solidarity while building institutions that excluded Palestinians by design.
The Histadrut, Israel’s dominant trade‑union confederation, was founded in 1920 as an instrument of the Zionist “conquest of labour”: a project designed to build Jewish settlements by systematically displacing Palestinian workers from the economy and reducing dependence on Indigenous labour. After 1948, this exclusion was institutionalised: Palestinian workers were either barred from membership outright or confined to second‑class status for decades, denied voting rights and meaningful representation even as they paid union fees.
Today, even when on paper Palestinians should have the same rights as Jewish Israeli workers, in practice, they do not. Collective bargaining agreements in key sectors, such as construction, are consistently not applied to them because their employment is rendered unstable, informal, and “temporary” by design. In this way, the Histadrut functions less as a defender of workers’ rights and more as a key actor in reproducing a settler‑colonial order that segregates, exploits, and disempowers Palestinian labour.
The school system set up by early Labour governments functioned as an instrument of ideological formation: forging Jewish national consciousness while erasing Palestinian presence, and recasting settlement as national redemption rather than colonisation.
The kibbutz and moshav movements, the flagship institutions of Labour Zionism, were central to the project of land theft and displacement. Many kibbutzim, due to their location, served as staging grounds for Haganah operations in 1948, including the depopulation of nearby Palestinian villages, making the settlement map itself part of the operational infrastructure of the Nakba.
Falling into the left-right Zionist trap
Despite the long historical record of crimes committed by Mapai and Labour governments against the Palestinians, many leftists in the West continue to fall for the “leftist” label within the context of Israeli politics. They appear to believe that what is happening in Palestine could be solely blamed on Israel’s right-wing political forces led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Campaigns like that of the Young Greens of Austria and Israel’s Young Democrats seemingly reinforce this misguided belief. In the end, their ultimate aim is not to amplify “progressive voices” or deliver a “just peace” to the Palestinians, but to impose a political category – “leftist Zionist” – that is, in essence, incoherent and contradictory.
The constant reference to a “far‑right Netanyahu government” does real political work. It implies that a “Zionist left” could be a credible progressive alternative, one that is capable of changing the colonial reality Palestinians live under and one that is not to blame for Israeli crimes.
That framing lets the underlying structure – Israel’s settler colonialism – off the hook, treating it as a policy choice of the Israeli far right specifically rather than the logic of Zionism itself.
Palestinians do not need political theory to see the truth. Generations of them know, in their flesh, that there is no difference between Zionism on the left and Zionism on the right when it comes to their dispossession. The occupation did not start with Netanyahu, and a change in government will not end it.
Any leftist party in Europe or beyond that wants to remain aligned with its own values has one path. It should listen to Palestinians, follow and support forces like the Green Party of England and Wales in naming Zionism for what it is: a racist, settler-colonial ideology. Not a policy to be reformed, but an ideology to be abolished.

Muslim region in Philippines holds landmark parliamentary vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:18:00 UTC
00:18:00 KST

A predominantly Muslim region in the southern Philippines voted Monday in its first parliamentary election, marking a major milestone in a decadeslong push for greater autonomy following years of insurgency and conflict.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was established under a 2014 peace deal in which the largest Muslim rebel group gave up its goal of a separate Muslim state in the south of the largely Roman Catholic country in exchange for broader autonomy. The group’s 40,000 fighters promised to demobilize and join civilian life.
Officials said that the election was largely peaceful despite a person being killed following commotion in a polling station in the main city of Cotabato on Monday. Some supporters of a political party also damaged two vehicles belonging to a rival politician using steel bars.
Three people were killed late Sunday and 15 others were wounded in a shooting in Cotabato, which houses the Bangsamoro regional government offices, including the local parliament.
Meanwhile, the town of Maluso on Basilan Island was put under the control of the Commission on Elections after preshaded ballots were found in 36 out of 68 precincts. Commission Chairman Erwin Garcia said that he immediately ordered the reprinting of ballots and that voting will be delayed there. He said those responsible will be held accountable.
As of early Monday, 98.1% of the region’s polling stations were open to voters, according to the commission.
"Whoever wins, hopefully we will see change,” said Sittie Ashuya L. H. Omar, a 22-year-old voter from the city of Marawi. "Hopefully they can implement their promises.”
Eighty seats are at stake in the election, which will determine regional members of parliament. The region comprises five provinces, three cities and 63 villages with nearly 2.4 million voters. Election officials said they expected an 80% turnout. After polling was postponed for several years.
The region’s chief minister, who heads the executive branch, will be elected by parliament in its first session.
"The elections stand on generations of Bangsamoro struggle for homeland, identity, and self-determination, in the face of dispossession, marginalization, conflict and sacrifice,” Garcia said in an earlier statement
In May 2017, Daesh terrorist group-linked militants laid siege to Marawi, triggering five months of ground assaults and airstrikes that left more than 1,100 people, mostly militants, dead and destroyed the mosque-studded city’s commercial and residential districts.
Since the 1970s, about 150,000 combatants and civilians have died in the southern Philippines, while development was stunted in the country’s poorest region. Western and Asian governments feared the tenacious insurgencies could help foster terrorism in Southeast Asia. With bombing attacks and kidnappings, Mindanao used to be a haven for al-Qaida and Daesh before a U.S.-backed Philippine offensive weakened the militants.
More than 20,000 soldiers and police forces were deployed for the election, while troops patrolled roads.
Monday's vote ended at 7 p.m. local time (1100 GMT), except in areas where voting was delayed, extending the closing time.
Candidates running unopposed are expected to be declared winners late Monday.

French court strikes down burkini ban at Riviera beach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:17:00 UTC
00:17:00 KST

A court in Nice on Friday struck down a ban on burkinis at beaches in the French Riviera resort of Mandelieu-la-Napoule, overturning restrictions on the full-body swimwear worn by some Muslim women.
The Nice Administrative Court ruled that the ban on the full-body swimsuits – which are used by many Muslim women – egregiously and unlawfully infringed upon three fundamental freedoms: freedom of movement, freedom of conscience and personal liberty.
The court stated that the municipality near Cannes justified the measure by claiming that individuals wearing clothing like the burkini, which clearly expresses religious affiliation, pose a threat to public order.
However, the judges said no evidence to support the claim was provided and the municipality merely cited two incidents that occurred 10 and 14 years ago.
The court found that there was no evidence to suggest that such garments posed a risk to the safety of beach-goers and swimmers.
The ruling is the latest flashpoint in the fierce debate that has been raging in France for many years over the headscarf and other Muslim garments for women.
Although the Council of State, France's highest administrative court, overturned a burkini ban on beaches years ago, some coastal towns still upheld a moratorium during the summer.
In 2012, Mandelieu-la-Napoule became the first seaside resort to impose a ban. Despite the Council of State's ruling, the town's conservative mayor has repeatedly renewed the measure.

NEW DELHI: India and China should view each other as partners rather than rivals, Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi said on Monday, citing the consensus reached between president Xi Jinping and Prime Minister Narendra Modi during their meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi.Wang said the two leaders held a “candid and in-depth exchange of views” on strategic and long-term issues concerning bilateral ties, according to news agency PTI. “The most important consensus they reached was that China and India should be partners,” he told Chinese official media.According to Wang, Xi said China and India could draw on each other's strengths, support one another, help each other succeed and pursue common development. The two leaders also agreed to maintain peace and tranquillity in border areas and support each other during their respective BRICS chairmanships.The Chinese foreign ministry said the relationship had moved from a “restart” to a “renewed elevation” under the strategic guidance of the two leaders. Wang said areas of cooperation were expanding, trade had reached record levels and people-to-people exchanges were becoming more active.
Wang also quoted PM Modi as saying India was ready to be “a partner, not an adversary” to China and viewed each other’s development “as an opportunity rather than a challenge”. He said PM had reaffirmed that India’s approach to China was independent of third-party influence.The two leaders, according to Wang, agreed to deepen political trust, appropriately manage differences and strengthen cooperation in areas including cultural exchanges and direct air connectivity. They also agreed to coordinate more closely through the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the G20, while advancing cooperation among Global South countries.The Indian foreign ministry’s account of the meeting highlighted the need for a “strategic and long-term perspective” in managing bilateral ties. Both sides backed a “fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution” of the boundary question.
On trade, the leaders discussed structural imbalances, supply-chain concerns and the need for “meaningful and predictable market access”. They also welcomed progress in people-to-people ties and called for greater cultural, business and travel links.Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing would work with New Delhi to implement the understandings reached by the leaders and “make the cooperation list longer”.She said, "As the two leaders have charted the course for the future development of the bilateral ties, China will work with India to implement the important common understandings reached between the two leaders."With China set to assume the BRICS chairmanship in 2027, both sides are expected to build on the latest engagement.

Iran's proxies using Yemen to compound war's impact on oil prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:12:13 UTC
00:12:13 KST

How Iran's regional allies' attacks in Yemen are compounding the war's impact on oil prices
Escalating fighting between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia, and attacks by other Iranian proxy forces on Saudi infrastructure, are increasing the threat to tanker traffic in the Middle East and driving up global fuel costs more than six months after the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran.
Direct clashes between the U.S. and Iran have severely reduced shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, but the Houthi-Saudi tension, and attacks on Saudi infrastructure blamed on other Iran-backed groups, are also squeezing global fuel supplies in the nearby Red Sea.
Before the war began, about 30% of oil supplies typically reached the global markets by tanker from the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz (about 20%) and the Red Sea via the Bab el-Mandeb Strait (about 10%) combined.
The ongoing threat to ships in the Strait of Hormuz, combined with rising tension around the Bab el-Mandeb and attacks on Saudi infrastructure, helped push the price of Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, up to a near-4-month-high on Monday of about $108 per barrel.
Brent crude was trading at an average of $67 per barrel in the days leading up to the start of the war at the end of February.
Saudi pipeline offline after drone strike
"The spike in price is due to the East-West pipeline in Saudi being damaged and shut," Dimirtis Maniatis, head of the Greece-based Marisks maritime risk agency, told CBS News on Monday, referring to an attack last week on a vital Saudi Arabian crude oil pipeline.
Saudi Arabia has used the East-West pipeline to export oil from its Red Sea ports as an alternative to ports in the Persian Gulf since Iran started attacking ships and infrastructure around the Strait of Hormuz early in the war.
The pipeline, originally built during the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s in response to the same threat from Iran to shipping in the Persian Gulf, was brought back up to full capacity in April after being hit by Iran early in the war.
It enables Saudi Arabia to divert its oil about 745 miles west across the kingdom from the Persian Gulf to its Yanbu Port on the Red Sea. From there, energy products can typically be shipped to markets in Europe and Asia via the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea.
But the Houthis, a powerful Iranian proxy force, declared a blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports in late July and started targeting tankers owned or operated by Saudi Arabian companies, giving the kingdom little room to maneuver.
No group has claimed responsibility for the attacks on the pipeline, although Iraq's government said Saturday they were launched from its territory, where a number of Iran-backed militias operate. Tehran has denied any involvement in the attack.
Saudi Arabia's crude oil output fell under 6 million barrels per day in August, down from around 8 million barrels per day the previous month and well under its target of 10.42 million barrels per day, according to the latest International Energy Agency (IEA) oil market report.
Long-term disruption to the East-West pipeline could take about 4% of the world's oil supply offline, according to Reuters, compounding the losses created by the Strait of Hormuz closure and the threat to Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
The Associated Press quoted two anonymous regional officials Monday as saying the pipeline could take 3-5 weeks to bring fully back online.
The Houthis and Iran's "longer-term aim"
Maniatis noted that the Houthis have not yet threatened global shipping in the Red Sea, focusing their attacks so far entirely on Saudi assets.
The Houthis said last week that the Red Sea remained safe for the majority of tanker operators, but the Lloyd's List maritime intelligence firm said that had done little to reassure shipowners or operators, especially after the rebels seized the port city of Mokha on Yemen's Red Sea coast and captured the strategically important island of Perim in the center of the Bab el-Mandeb.
Previous Houthi disruption of shipping has forced ships to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb by using a much longer, much more expensive route around the Cape of Good Hope in southern Africa, accessed via the Suez Canal, the northern exit from the Red Sea.
Although Saudi ship traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb dropped to close to zero in August, data from the IEA shows the overall number of ships passing through the waterway have remained relatively stable since the U.S.-Iran war began.
That has likely helped keep oil prices from going even higher already, but it also means Iran, through its proxies, may still have levers to try and pull if it wants to squeeze global energy supplies even harder.
"Tehran's longer-term aim is to establish a daunting status quo: Houthi control over the Bab el-Mandeb alongside Iranian control of Hormuz," wrote April Longley Alley, a Senior Fellow at the Washington Institute who previously served as Senior Political Adviser to the United Nations Special Envoy to Yemen, and the Atlantic Council's Allison Minor, who served as Deputy U.S. Special Envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2023, in a Foreign Policy analysis published Friday.
"If it could be sustained, such a strategy would make Iran and its regional partner de facto gatekeepers for trillions of dollars' worth of trade each year."

US man allegedly threatens to kill Muslim men handing out Qurans in Michigan
A man allegedly threatened to kill four Muslim men who were distributing copies of the Quran outside a library in Troy, Michigan, prompting a US Muslim civil rights group to call for hate crime charges.
The four men were answering questions about Islam and handing out copies of the Quran when another man approached them and allegedly said he had a gun and threatened to kill them after learning they were Muslim.
The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) called on police to investigate the incident as a potential hate crime and review all available evidence.
"This cannot be dismissed as offensive speech or a heated disagreement," said Amy V. Doukoure, lead staff attorney at CAIR-Michigan.
The New Arab has contacted the Troy Police Department for comment.
Rising Islamophobia

Last week, families of victims of the 9/11 attacks and Republican politicians demonstrated outside New York City Hall, calling for Mamdani not to participate in a commemoration marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks.
Former New York mayor Rudy Giuliani said Mamdani's presence at the ceremony "offends me".
Mamdani, New York's first Muslim mayor, has previously spoken about the impact of the 9/11 attacks, which were carried out by al-Qaeda.

While no subsequent year has recorded as many anti-Muslim hate crimes as 2001, reported incidents have remained above 2000 levels.

Int'l travel trade show in Dubai focuses on tech, innovation

DUBAI, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- The Arabian Travel Market (ATM) 2026 opened in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates, on Monday, bringing together tourism and industry professionals from around the world to discuss artificial intelligence (AI), emerging technologies and the future of personalized travel.
Held under the theme "Travel 2040: Driving New Frontiers Through Innovation and Technology," the four-day event features the inaugural ATM Travel Tech, with more than 180 companies from 30 countries showcasing applications in AI, virtual and augmented reality, robotics, fintech and green technology.
"The data shows that consumers in the Gulf region are highly tech-savvy and digitally advanced, with diverse age groups and interests," said Siddharth Sudhakar, general manager for MENA at Trip.com.

Sudhakar said the two sides could leverage their respective strengths by bringing the Middle East's unique culture and travel experiences to the Chinese market while introducing Chinese technology and AI innovations to the Middle East.
The annual trade exhibition covers tourism destinations, airlines, hotels and travel technology, among other sectors. According to the organizers, ATM 2026 has attracted more than 2,800 exhibitors and over 55,000 tourism professionals. ■

IAEA General Conference opens amid growing nuclear proliferation concerns
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
23:11:48 CST

Monica Juma, director-general of the United Nations Office at Vienna, speaks at the 70th General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna, Austria, Sept. 14, 2026. The conference opened in Vienna on Monday, with calls to strengthen multilateral cooperation and efforts to uphold the global nuclear non-proliferation regime amid heightened geopolitical tensions. (Xinhua/He Canling)
VIENNA, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- The 70th General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) opened in Vienna on Monday, with calls to strengthen multilateral cooperation and efforts to uphold the global nuclear non-proliferation regime amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
In a message delivered by Monica Juma, director-general of the United Nations Office at Vienna, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said this conference comes at a time of profound global turbulence and uncertainty. Attacks on nuclear facilities are rising. The drivers of nuclear proliferation are accelerating while the guardrails against it are falling.
"The world is on the cusp of a revolution in nuclear power generation, a revolution that requires careful management and monitoring. More than ever, the world needs the IAEA's professionalism, impartiality and technical excellence," Guterres said in the message.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the conference that the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) remains the cornerstone of the global non-proliferation regime.
"At this time of heightened tensions and distrust, we must work to underpin this legal framework by supporting the IAEA and working towards its aims. A world with more nuclear weapons and more countries armed with nuclear weapons is not a safer world," Grossi said.
The 70th Regular Session of the IAEA General Conference, running through Sept. 18, has drawn nearly 4000 senior officials and representatives from IAEA member states, and delegations of international organizations and non-governmental organizations.
Held annually since the IAEA was founded in 1957, the General Conference considers a wide range of issues related to the peaceful uses of nuclear technology, from energy production and cancer care to food security, water management, nuclear safety and security, and safeguards. ■

The incidents in Türkiye in April marked an unprecedented shock for many Turkish families.

The attacks raised widespread concerns over school safety and prompted calls for stronger preventive measures in Türkiye.
Emre Yalcin, a cafe owner and father of a fifth-grade student at a school in Ankara, said his children had been deeply affected.

Yalcin welcomed the additional security personnel around the school, saying their presence appeared reassuring. However, he cautioned that security measures should remain proportionate to the educational environment.

Authorities also plan inspections around schools and school buses throughout the academic year, covering issues including drugs, traffic safety and cybersecurity.
The Education Ministry has instructed schools to implement controlled entry and exit procedures, review potential risks and maintain a safe school environment.
In Kecioren, parents said the visible security presence helped ease anxieties on the first day, although concerns about the psychological impact of the attacks remained.

====================================================================================================

Maldives celebrates 900 Hijri years since conversion to Islam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:07:33 UTC
00:07:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Maldives celebrates 900 Hijri years since conversion to Islam
The Maldives has celebrated 900 Hijri years since its conversion to Islam, marking nearly nine centuries of a faith that has become inseparable from the identity of the Indian Ocean island nation.
President Mohamed Muizzu led official commemorations on Sunday, with sermons, religious lessons and cultural events held across the country to remember the conversion traditionally dated to 548 AH, or 1153 CE.
The anniversary also saw the laying of the foundation stone for the Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah Grand Mosque and Centre for Islamic Civilisation in Hulhumale, named after the ruler credited with beginning the country's Islamic era.
But how did a predominantly Buddhist island kingdom south-west of India become one of the world's most thoroughly Islamic societies?
A Buddhist kingdom on Muslim trade routes
The Maldives was inhabited long before the arrival of Islam, with early settlers arriving principally from the Indian subcontinent and Sri Lanka.
Buddhism became the dominant religion and remained deeply embedded in the islands for centuries, as demonstrated by archaeological remains of monasteries, stupas and other Buddhist structures.
But the Maldives also occupied an important position within the vast maritime trading system of the Indian Ocean.
Arab and Persian Muslim merchants increasingly travelled the routes connecting the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula with East Africa, India and Southeast Asia.
The islands were particularly famous for cowrie shells, which were exported in enormous quantities and used as currency across parts of Asia and Africa. Dried tuna, coconuts and coir made from coconut fibre were also important commodities.
Muslim contact with the Maldives therefore preceded the country's formal conversion.
The king who became Sultan Muhammad
Maldivian tradition dates the decisive change to 1153, when King Dhovemi converted from Buddhism to Islam and adopted the Muslim name and title Sultan Muhammad ibn Abdullah.
His conversion is traditionally attributed to a visiting Muslim scholar and preacher named Abu al-Barakat Yusuf al-Barbari.
Exactly who Abu al-Barakat was remains disputed.
The description "al-Barbari" has traditionally led to claims that he was a Berber from North Africa, likely Morocco, while Somali tradition has also claimed him. Another historical tradition identifies the missionary with Yusuf Shams al-Din al-Tabrizi, suggesting a Persian origin.
Whatever his precise identity, the conversion attributed to him became the foundational story of Maldivian Islam.
Following Dhovemi's conversion, Islam spread throughout the islands and the Buddhist monarchy was transformed into a Muslim sultanate. Muslim dynasties would rule the Maldives, with interruptions and changes of dynasty, for centuries.
The legend of Rannamaari
The conversion also acquired a famous supernatural tradition.
When Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited the Maldives in the 14th century, he recorded a local story that islanders had once lived in fear of a sea demon known as Rannamaari.
According to the story, a young woman was periodically offered to the creature until a visiting Muslim confronted it by spending the night reciting the Qur'an.
The demon failed to return, and the king, impressed by what had happened, embraced Islam.
The story cannot be treated as a literal historical account of the conversion, but Ibn Battuta's recording of it is significant: it shows that a story connecting the country's Islamisation with a foreign Muslim was already established in Maldivian memory around two centuries after the event.
Ibn Battuta himself spent months in the Maldives and served as a qadi, or Islamic judge, providing one of the most important medieval descriptions of Maldivian Muslim society.
Islam and Maldivian identity
Over the following centuries, Islam became deeply interwoven with Maldivian culture, government and architecture.
Among the most distinctive surviving examples are the islands' historic mosques constructed from carved coral stone, an architectural tradition unique to the country's maritime environment.
The modern Maldives remains overwhelmingly Muslim, and Islam occupies a formal place in the country's national and constitutional identity.
This year's commemorations deliberately connect that contemporary identity with the conversion of Dhovemi nine Islamic centuries ago.

PLO moves forward with plans to restructure of the Palestinian National Council ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:06:31 UTC
00:06:31 KST

The Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) is moving forward with plans to restructure its legislative body, the Palestinian National Council (PNC) ahead of Palestinian Legislative Council (PLC) elections scheduled for November 28, according to Palestinian reports.
The plans, ratified in June after being announced by Palestinian Authority (PA) President Mahmoud Abbas last year, will expand the use of elections to select PNC members, partially replacing the previous system of factional quotas, allocations, and special appointments.
The new system will also more than halve the number of PNC members, from 747 to 350, including 132 PLC members representing the Palestinian territories, 150 members from the Palestinian diaspora, and 67 members selected by consensus to represent PLO factions.
Last week, Kuwait’s Palestinian community elected the first two PNC members from abroad, Hisham Ibrahim and Saleh Qannam. Shortly afterward, Tamer Kadash was elected to represent the Palestinian community in Bahrain, while Muhannad Al-Shorbaji Al-Agha and Imad Al-Bal‘awi were elected to represent Palestinians in Qatar.
Efforts are underway to hold similar elections under an electoral college system in Lebanon and Syria, according to Arab reports. Independent Arabia reported that Palestinians in Europe, the United States, and South America have formed preparatory committees to reach consensus on the selection of future PNC members, with one seat allocated for every 35,000 Palestinians.
Palestinians in Jordan are not currently slated to participate in direct PNC elections.
Abbas pushes new system as a win for Palestinian democracy
Though Abbas has pushed the new system as a win for Palestinian democracy, Palestinian officials from other camps have strongly criticized forming a council without including Hamas.
Ramzi Rabah, a member of the PLO Executive Committee representing the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP), told Independent Arabia that the council “can be formed through consensus among everyone following a national dialogue that opens the door to everyone joining, including Hamas, which does not require postponing [the elections] for two years. It can happen within a month.”
Rabah called on Abbas to invite the secretaries-general of the factions “to an expanded meeting to establish mechanisms for forming the National Council and mechanisms for holding elections in an atmosphere of understanding.”
The International Commission to Support Palestinian Rights also released a statement last week, raising concerns that the new process allows the adoption of different electoral arrangements, “including the use of electoral colleges or selection mechanisms that do not necessarily allow all Palestinians within those communities to participate.”
ICSPR also condemned the exclusion of “Palestinian political forces and figures.”
Despite ICSPR’s critique, Hamas has indicated that it is seeking to participate in the PLC and PNC elections as part of a broader national coalition rather than running under its own name.
However, candidates are required to recognize the PLO as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people and commit to its political and national program and relevant international legitimacy resolutions – a term that has also generated criticism of the new system.
According to information published by the Amit Terrorism and Intelligence Research Institute, Hamas’s officials have already been actively screening for potential alliances.
Broadening participation in Palestinian elections
Husam Badran, a member of the Hamas political bureau and head of the national relations office, spoke by telephone with Salem Atallah, secretary-general of the Palestinian Mujahideen Movement, earlier this month, regarding the elections, as well as with Hassan Mahmoud Abu Halima, secretary general of the Palestinian al-Ahrar Movement, about the need to broaden the participation of Palestinian “organizations, forces and figures” in the elections and oppose the appointment of representatives.
Badran also complained to Independent Arabia that continuing with “the same approach of exclusivity and disregarding the right of the Palestinian people to choose their representatives is a national crime and a confiscation of the right of the Palestinian communities present in every country.”
Given the lack of consensus, members of the The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) have reportedly urged Abbas to postpone the PLC elections, an option that some experts and Palestinian officials have suggested he may be inclined to pursue out of concern that the vote could allow Hamas to gain greater control in the West Bank.
The PFLP submitted the “National Rescue Plan” last Monday, which proposed postponing the November 28 elections, launching comprehensive national dialogue, forming a consensus government, rebuilding the PLO, and then holding presidential, legislative, and National Council elections together.

The delegation includes representatives of 50 companies and more than 80 participants, according to Syria’s state-run SANA news agency.
US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Jake McGee said American companies were being encouraged to invest in Syria. “We encourage US businesses to invest in the Syrian market, which offers significant opportunities,” he said, according to SANA. He noted that companies such as Chevron, HKN, Visa and Mastercard had already taken steps to enter the Syrian market or reached agreements with Syrian counterparts..
Syria has undergone major changes since the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime
The visit is the first US Chamber of Commerce mission to Syria. It comes amid improving ties between Washington and Damascus following the removal of broad US sanctions in 2025. Syrian officials said they hope political progress can now lead to investment and longer-term economic partnerships.
Syria has undergone major changes since the fall of the Bashar al-Assad regime in December 2024. Assad fled the country after a rapid offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) captured Aleppo and then Damascus, ending more than five decades of Assad family rule.
HTS, which emerged from groups linked to al-Qaeda but broke with the organization years ago. It had previously controlled Idlib in northwest Syria. Its leader, Ahmed al-Sharaa, subsequently became Syria’s transitional president and has sought to transform the former rebel movement into the nucleus of a new Syrian government.
Syria has also begun a political transition. Parliamentary elections were held in October 2025, the first since Assad’s fall. Two-thirds of the 210-member People’s Assembly were chosen through electoral colleges, while Sharaa was given authority to appoint the remaining third. Voting was postponed in areas outside Damascus’s control, including parts of northeast Syria and Sweida.
A key challenge is unifying Syria after years of war. Damascus has sought to integrate armed groups into new national institutions. This includes the US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces, which signed an agreement with Sharaa in March 2025 to integrate its military and civilian institutions into the Syrian state. The process has continued into 2026, potentially bringing much of eastern Syria back under Damascus’s authority.

China Postponed Its Chang’e 7 Lunar Mission. What Does That Mean for Its Space Program?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

China’s postponement of its Chang’e 7 lunar mission on August 23 came with a curt explanation from the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA): “China’s Chang’e-7 lunar probe does not meet launch conditions, and its launch therefore cannot take place during the planned window this year.” While there is speculation that the Chang’e 7 launch will take place in 2027, the CMSA has not made any official announcement to that effect.
Given that the Chang’e 7 and Long March 5 Y14 were moved to Launch Complex 101 at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in Hainan Province on August 19, the postponement without adequate explanation, just hours before the launch, is a bit of a surprise. Space missions are often postponed and subsequently rescheduled, but given Chang’e 7’s criticality and its strategic importance to China’s long-term lunar goals, the lack of a rescheduled launch date has been perplexing.
To be sure, China’s Chang’e 7 mission is the most consequential of its phased lunar missions, aimed at showcasing novel technologies like digging for lunar ice and addressing key strategic questions: where are the strategically useful resources on the Moon, and what is the operating environment like? The CMSA said that the Chang’e 7 “mission will employ a comprehensive detection approach, which involves orbiting, landing, roving and hopping to conduct environmental and resource surveys of the lunar south pole.”
The Chang’e 7 departs from China’s earlier missions like Chang’e 3 or 4, since its goal is to demonstrate space resource utilization capabilities. The Chang’e 7 mission includes a hopper to support its planned Chang’e 8 mission, which aims to scale the Moon’s surface toward establishing an International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) by 2036. A statement by the China National Space Administration (CNSA) on April 24, 2025 specified that “the Chang’e-8 mission will target the Leibnitz-Beta Plateau near the Lunar South Pole region, working with the earlier Chang’e-7 mission to conduct scientific exploration and in-situ resource utilization experiments. These efforts will lay the groundwork for the future International Lunar Research Station.” Chang’e 8 is planned to launch in 2029.
Clearly, Chang’e 7 is a core part of Phase Four of China’s Lunar missions. Wu Yanhua, the CNSA’s deputy director, stated that “the main goal of the fourth phase is to carry out scientific exploration on the moon’s south pole and set up a fundamental type of lunar scientific research station. The fourth phase will be carried out in three steps, with the Chang’e 6, Chang’e 7, and Chang’e 8 probes being launched before 2030.”
Phase One of China’s lunar program – Chang’e 1 and 2 – focused on the ability to reach and orbit the Moon. Phase Two – Chang’e 3 and 4 – included a soft landing on the lunar surface, including the far side of the Moon and robotic exploration. Phase Three, Chang’e 5, showcased sample return from the Moon’s near side, which consisted of the collection of lunar material and surface ascent, orbital rendezvous and docking, and safe sample return to Earth. Phase Four moves beyond just demonstrations. Chang’e 6 in 2024 successfully collected and returned samples from the Lunar South Pole. Chang’e 7 is supposed to conduct resource assessment and utilization, with Chang’e 8 following to create the basic lunar infrastructure for the ILRS.
Based on the samples brought back by Chang’e 5 and Chang’e 6, the Institute of Geology under the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences (CAGS), in collaboration with the Institute of Geochemistry under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), Jilin University, Shandong University and China University of Geosciences (Beijing), developed a “1:5,000,000-scale Geological Map of the moon [that] marks 13,519 impact craters, 81 impact basins, 14 types of geological structures and 17 rock types, and includes detailed inset maps of the lunar north and south poles.” In 2024, China published a 1:2,500,000-scale high-precision lunar geological atlas. These maps are vital because they help create the knowledge infrastructure for where a base on the Moon should be located.
As this brief overview indicates, China has consistently and successfully built the groundwork to support the lunar resource utilization capability it was about to demonstrate with Chang’e 7. So the mission’s postponement without an in-depth, publicly available assessment and a clear rescheduled date raises three significant factors of concern.
First, the abrupt delay suggests that Phase Four is technologically more difficult than China’s earlier lunar phases. Chang’e 7 requires a complex orbiter-lander-rover-hopping explorer architecture, precise calculations and operations in the Lunar South Pole environment, and investigation of permanently shadowed regions for resources such as water. A paper in National Science Review by Chi Wang, et.al., highlighted that “CE-7 [Chang’e 7] is a new type of probe developed for the fourth phase of the CLEP [Chinese Lunar Exploration Program]. It will explore the environment and resources in the lunar polar region by conducting a series of steps: orbiting, landing, roving and mini-flying.”
These novel capabilities are directly relevant to China’s transition from exploring the Moon to prospecting, resource utilization, and eventually building infrastructure. An unexplained postponement after Chang’e 7 reached an advanced stage of launch preparation underscores how difficult this technological transition really is.
Second, the lack of a substantive explanation since the postponement suggests this is not just a safety issue, as the official CMSA statement claimed, nor is it about missing a launch window due to bad weather. The silence over the delay suggests an engineering problem that is proving difficult to resolve. If it had really been about the weather, a rescheduled launch date would have followed quickly. While delays occur in every major space program (like NASA’s Space Launch System under the Artemis program), Chinese space institutions have provided remarkably little public information about how serious the problem is with Chang’e 7, what corrective action is required, or when the mission can realistically launch. This opacity suggests that Phase Four is proving harder for China to accomplish within the set deadlines.
Third, the delay of Chang’e 7 creates potential schedule pressure on the ILRS roadmap. Chang’e-7 is important because it is meant to characterize the Lunar South Pole’s environment and resources. Chang’e-8 will then advance toward in-situ resource utilization and technology demonstrations, with the two missions contributing to the basic ILRS architecture. A substantial delay in Chang’e 7 could therefore delay Chang’e 8 and ILRS development beyond the stated deadline of 2036. This would also result in a delay of China’s planned human lunar landing by 2030.
Lunar missions are an integral part of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), which directs the CMSA to ensure China is a major space power. Yet the sudden delay of a critical mission, and the absence of any verifiable explanation for the causes, undermine the goals China seeks to accomplish.
The views expressed are those of the author and do not reflect the official guidance or position of the United States Government, the Department of Defense, the United States Air Force, or the United States Space Force.

Why You Should Never Wear Shoes in Your House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:03:10 UTC
00:03:10 KST

Every time you welcome a guest into your home, you may be letting in thousands of other ones as well—if you allow your visitors to wear their shoes when they enter. The world outside your door is a messy place—full of bacteria, viruses, and environmental toxins—and the soles of your shoes can pick up a lot.
According to one 2023 CBS News/YouGov poll, 63% of Americans regularly remove their shoes when they get home, and 24% ask their guests to do the same. This year, the Indiana Department of Health launched a “Shoes Free Protects You and Me” ad campaign about the benefits of a no-shoes policy at home, targeting tracked-in lead in particular.
How serious is the risk that shoes pose, and should your house be a no-shoes zone?
What the research says about wearing shoes inside
The published research on shoe contamination is not extensive, but some stands out. In one 2008 study, Charles Gerba, professor of virology at the University of Arizona, studied 26 pairs of shoes that had been worn for three months in the outside world and came up with some alarming results. The shoes carried between 3,600 and 8 million colony-forming units of bacteria, both on the inside and outside of the shoes. E. coli, or fecal bacteria, was the most common organism being tracked around.
“[About] 80% of the bottoms of the shoes had fecal bacteria on them,” Gerba wrote in an email to TIME, “largely picking them up from the floors of public restrooms, which always have fecal bacteria on them. They may also pick them up outside, in places that dogs and birds are.”
According to Gerba’s numbers, shoes are significantly more germ-ridden than public toilet seats, which have an average of 3,200 colony forming bacterial units.
E. coli is not the only infectious agent that shoes carry around. According to University of Houston researchers, 40% of shoes tested carry C. difficile, an intestinal bacterium that causes diarrhea. Health care settings are particularly germ-filled. One 2016 meta-analysis in the Journal of Applied Microbiology surveyed 13 studies, tracing where shoes have traveled and what they picked up there. A small study in that group found that after physicians did rounds in hospitals, 65% of their shoes tested positive for either antibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) or Enterococcus faecalis, another gastrointestinal bacterium. Another found that 48% of shoes worn in operating rooms tested positive for at least one pathogenic bacterium, most commonly Staphylococcus.
Rural areas, where livestock, birds, and other animals are common, are ready sources of Salmonella and other bacteria. One 2009 study conducted in rural Alaska had people put on sterilized boots, then walk along a randomly selected outdoor path, and finally step onto a piece of sterilized linoleum and remove the boots. From just that walk, 70% of the boots were positive for multiple gut bacteria. People then wore the contaminated boots on short walks across a sterile floor. On half of those walks, bacteria were transferred to the flooring.
Urban settings present their own perils, particularly as a result of dogs being walked on sidewalks and in parks. Even in cities where owners routinely pick up after their dogs, traces of fecal bacteria—and pools of urine—regularly collect on heavily foot-trafficked routes.
The type of flooring bacteria love
In one 2023 study published in Design, Architecture, and Ergonomics, investigators from Northeastern University in New York City sampled sidewalk rain puddles, shoe bottoms, and flooring inside one of the school’s buildings on its urban campus. On average, they found 30,000 gut bacteria per 100 milliliters of water in puddles on the neighborhood sidewalks. Every shoe sole they sampled from student and teacher volunteers carried varying levels of the same bacteria, and the interior of the building was also contaminated—especially in carpeted areas.
“The surface of your flooring makes an enormous difference,” says Alessandra Leri, professor of chemistry and biology at the school and the lead author of the study. “If you have carpets, they function as a reservoir of bacteria.” But no matter the interior floor surface, she says, “shoe soles are a serious vector of transmission of fecal bacteria from the outdoor environment to the indoor environment.”
Shoes track in more than germs
PFAS, the “forever chemicals” so named for how long they linger in the environment and our bodies, are regularly picked up by shoes and used in manufacturing the soles. Lead dust, which can often be stirred up and released into the air during remodeling of older homes and other buildings, can cling to shoes as well. Pesticides, used both on farms and in home gardens, are similarly free-riders on our shoes.
Where shoe-removal matters most
In most homes in which people do not remove their shoes upon entering, the area nearest the front door is generally the most contaminated. “We found that the first four steps at the entrance to the household are the germiest floor area in the home,” says Gerba. “We also did tracer studies putting dye and tracer viruses on the bottom of shoes and could see how they left a trail on the floor.”
Wherever contaminants spread in the home, they present the greatest danger to the household members who have the most contact with the floor—typically babies and small children who crawl and play on surfaces.
Leri follows a no-shoes policy in her home and leaves her shoes by the door when she enters. She does not ask guests to remove their shoes, especially when she hosts parties. “If you are having a cocktail party, you are sensitive to guests feeling like shoes are a part of their ensemble,” she says. But she does roll up the rugs before company arrives, making it easier to clean the floors when the guests are gone.
More people—especially younger people—may be taking a harder line, enforcing a universal ban on shoes for anyone in the home. While only 7% of people over 65 and 13% of people ages 45 to 64 require guests to remove shoes before entering, according to the CBS/YouGov poll, 44% of people in the 18 to 29 demographic do.
“I find that many people have already adopted that custom,” says Leri. “It is a more hygienic way of living.”

Some in Silicon Valley are questioning the calls for an AI slowdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
15:01:01 UTC
00:01:01 KST

Some in Silicon Valley are questioning the calls for an AI slowdown
Kalley Huang and Mike Isaac
- Silicon Valley leaders are divided on calls to slow AI development, with some supporting tighter safety regulations and others fearing it would stifle competition and innovation.
- Critics argue AI safety concerns may be exaggerated or self-serving, questioning motives behind calls for regulation and urging transparency beyond leading AI labs.
- Lawmakers and tech CEOs acknowledge AI risks but hesitate on strict regulation, emphasising the need to balance safety with maintaining global AI leadership and innovation.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – It took just a few hours over the weekend for well-known Silicon Valley figures to push back on calls by leading artificial intelligence companies to slow down the development of AI and regulate the technology more tightly.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in an essay on Sept 12 that AI was advancing too quickly for researchers to continue building it safely.
He proposed that independent auditors monitor AI labs’ safety work and that regulators allow the labs to work together to coordinate safety standards.
Although they appeared to differ on what should be done about it, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis all agreed on the need for a slower pace.
But other technology industry leaders were quick to question Amodei’s motivations and whether he was sensationalising the risks of AI to make it harder for other companies to compete with leading AI companies.
“Stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic,” said David Sacks, a technology adviser for President Donald Trump and the White House’s former AI and cryptocurrency czar, in a social media post.
The criticism of the calls for a slowdown highlighted a deep divide between people who believe the government should police AI and others who believe regulatory intervention would crush competition.
Worries about the safety of AI gained wider attention in recent weeks as details emerged about how AI built by Anthropic’s top competitor, OpenAI, went rogue and hacked another company. And several days ago, one of Amodei’s own employees quit his job and began a public pressure campaign to draw attention to the risks of AI.
But a number of tech industry leaders, including several who have been advising the Trump administration on tech policy, believe those concerns are overblown.
Sacks, a frequent critic of Amodei, questioned why tech companies needed government intervention to slow down their AI development when nothing was stopping them from doing just that – particularly as they pursued a wildly ambitious goal to create so-called superintelligence, or AI that is far more intelligent than humans.
“The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it,” he added. “Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system.”
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said his company supported proposals like independent auditors and “broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk” in a social media post on Sept 13.
“We also need to accelerate and spread the benefits of AI, such that they are diffused broadly across countries, communities and companies,” he said.
“The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation,” he added.
For years, the people most concerned about AI safety have often been the executives and employees of AI labs such as Anthropic. They are developing AI, they often say, because progress is inevitable, and they are the researchers best suited to build it with safety in mind.
That has opened those safety-conscious AI developers to aggressive criticism.
“Should a handful of select, market-dominant AI companies from Silicon Valley get to define the rules and safety standards of a generational technology for the entire world?” said Aidan Gomez, CEO of Canadian AI startup Cohere, in an essay on Sept 13.
“These oligopolies are now requesting to bend competition rules and be permitted to dictate the terms for everyone else,” he added. “A wolf in sheep’s clothing, a cartel by any other name.”
Amodei suggested in his essay that AI companies accept scrutiny of their products by “embedded evaluators” from third-party organisations.
But critics questioned whether Anthropic has too many ties to two organisations mentioned by Amodei, the non-profit groups METR and Redwood Research.
“If we’re going to regulate, it can’t be anyone they know, and they can’t write the rules,” said Bill Gurley, a venture capitalist and vocal critic of the leading AI companies.
Even before Amodei’s essay, some in Silicon Valley argued that AI labs’ safety concerns are self-serving. At a conference in San Francisco last week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI labs were emphasising security issues because they planned to introduce cybersecurity products.
“What better way to create demand than to create a problem?” Huang said. “Who doesn’t want their market to be hysterical about their product and line up around the corner for it?”
On Sept 12, Clement Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, the company hacked by OpenAI’s technology, said in a social media post that AI safety would not “be solved behind the closed doors of a handful of frontier labs”. Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face earlier this month for US$12.9 billion (S$16.4 billion).
A number of lawmakers in Washington appeared sympathetic to Amodei’s concerns. But just like many in Silicon Valley, they seem reluctant to embrace regulation.
“If developers of AI want to slow down development of their product, they are free to do so,” said Senator John Cornyn, a Republican, in a social media post on Sept 13. “One thing is for sure: Their competitors won’t, including our nation’s adversaries.”
During a news conference on Sept 13 in Ireland, Trump said the United States was “leading China in AI” and that he wanted to “keep it that way”.
“We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up,” Trump said. “They’re bringing up things that won’t happen, but whoever wins with AI wins.” NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.
