A specific thinking style explains why dark personality traits are linked to creativity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
14:00:51 UTC
23:00:51 KST

People with darker personality traits tend to achieve more creative success, and a recent study suggests this is linked to their highly analytical, self-directed way of processing information. Published in Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, the research indicates that a thinking style known as field independence acts as a bridge between socially aversive personality traits and real-world creative accomplishments.
To understand this connection, it helps to look at the Dark Triad. The Dark Triad is a group of three socially undesirable personality traits: Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and narcissism. People high in Machiavellianism tend to be manipulative, cynical, and highly strategic.
Psychopathy is characterized by impulsivity, thrill-seeking, and a lack of empathy or remorse. Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, a constant need for admiration, and a sense of entitlement. While these traits are often viewed negatively, they appear in varying degrees among the general population and have been linked to certain positive outcomes, including creativity.
Creative achievement refers to actual, recognized accomplishments in fields like visual arts, scientific discovery, writing, or cooking. Past research established that dark personality traits can predict these creative accomplishments. For instance, a 2021 meta-analysis found a small positive association between creative behaviors and traits like narcissism and Machiavellianism.
Additionally, a study covered by PsyPost in 2021 indicated that Dark Triad traits play a role in how people generate novel, sometimes harmful, ideas. While this link is well-documented, the exact mental mechanisms explaining why these dark traits lead to creative success have remained open to debate.
“Much of the research on creativity has focused on its ‘bright side,’ particularly traits such as openness to experience, along with intelligence and divergent thinking,” study author Marco Giancola, a researcher at the Department of Biotechnological and Applied Clinical Sciences at the University of L’Aquila in Italy, told PsyPost.
“However, these well-established factors explain only part of why people differ in their real-world creative achievements, while considerably less attention has been paid to darker personality characteristics and, especially, to the cognitive mechanisms through which they might relate to creativity,” Giancola explained. “Therefore, I was interested not simply in asking whether Dark Triad traits are associated with creative achievement, but in understanding how this association might emerge through the way people process information.”
Separate studies showed that an autonomous, analytical thinking style called field independence also fuels creativity. Field independence is a cognitive style, meaning it describes how a person naturally perceives and organizes information. A field-independent person can easily separate specific details from a complex, distracting background.
These individuals tend to rely on their own internal judgment rather than being influenced by the people or social cues around them. A 2024 study of children found that a field-independent cognitive style acts as a mental bridge connecting core intelligence to creative thinking. The new study connects these two lines of research to see if field independence is the underlying cognitive bridge linking dark personality traits to creative success.
To explore this potential pathway, Giancola recruited 212 university students with an average age of 21. About half of the participants were female. The participants were drawn from various degree programs, including biology, medicine, and psychology, and none had a history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
During individual laboratory sessions, participants completed several assessments. To measure Dark Triad traits, they filled out a standard 12-item questionnaire. They rated how much they agreed with statements like “I cheat or lie to get what I want” to measure Machiavellianism, or “I expect special attention from others” for narcissism.
To assess cognitive style, the researcher used the Embedded Figures Test. In this task, participants looked at a complex, colorful geometric figure for 15 seconds. Then, they were shown a simple black-and-white shape. Finally, they looked at the complex colorful figure again and were timed on how fast they could find and trace the simple shape hidden within it. Faster times indicated a more field-independent cognitive style.
Creative achievement was measured using a questionnaire that asked participants to check off concrete, real-life creative successes they had achieved across ten different domains. These domains included visual arts, music, dance, architectural design, creative writing, humor, scientific discovery, invention, theater, and culinary arts.
Because creativity is influenced by many factors, the researcher controlled for several other variables. These included age, sex, education level, and openness to experience, which is a personality trait known to predict creativity. The study also controlled for fluid intelligence, which is the ability to solve new problems, and crystallized intelligence, which is accumulated knowledge. Finally, it accounted for divergent thinking, measured by asking participants to list as many alternative uses for a newspaper and a brick as possible in three minutes.
“The indirect effects of the Dark Triad on creative achievement through cognitive styles were statistically reliable even after accounting for several established predictors of creativity,” Giancola noted.
The results showed a consistent pattern connecting dark traits, cognitive style, and creativity. Participants with higher levels of Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and narcissism were faster at finding the hidden shapes in the visual test. This indicates that people with these traits tend to process information in a highly field-independent way.
When looking at the paths connecting all these variables, the direct relationship between the Dark Triad traits and creative achievement was not statistically significant on its own. Instead, the relationship operated indirectly through cognitive style. The presence of dark personality traits predicted a field-independent thinking style, which in turn predicted higher scores in real-life creative achievements.
“The findings suggest that some characteristics associated with Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and narcissism may coincide with a more field-independent way of processing information,” Giancola said. “That is, a greater tendency to rely on one’s own internal frame of reference, separate relevant information from its surrounding context, and be less constrained by external cues. It was through this cognitive style that emerged as an important bridge from the Dark Triad to higher creative achievement.”
The researcher suggests that each dark trait might drive this analytical thinking style for different reasons. For Machiavellianism, field independence might reflect a highly strategic orientation. These individuals tend to filter out distractions and focus strictly on information that helps them achieve their goals, allowing them to break problems down and find novel solutions.
For psychopathy, the connection might stem from a reduced sensitivity to social norms and emotional disinhibition. People high in psychopathy care very little about what others think. This allows them to ignore external constraints and take risks on unconventional ideas.
For narcissism, the link to field independence may come from a deep self-focus. Narcissistic individuals have high confidence in their own judgment and a strong desire to stand out. They tend to prioritize their own internal feelings over external feedback, which supports self-directed problem-solving and the pursuit of creative recognition.
“What I found particularly interesting was how similar the pattern was across Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and narcissism,” the researcher said. “Although these traits are psychologically distinct, the three mediation models showed no meaningful differences in their effect sizes, significance patterns, or explained variance.”
“This suggests that a characteristic they may share—a reduced reliance on socially anchored or contextual constraints—could be particularly relevant when it is expressed through field-independent information processing,” Giancola continued.
By bypassing conventional constraints and social expectations, people with dark personality traits naturally lean into a field-independent cognitive style. This specific way of filtering the world seems to foster the conditions needed to generate novel and useful ideas, resulting in measurable creative achievements.
“A major misinterpretation would be to conclude that dark personality traits are inherently beneficial or that becoming more narcissistic, Machiavellian, or psychopathic would make someone more creative,” Giancola warned. “These traits can have substantial interpersonal and behavioral costs, and our results concern statistical associations with certain modes of information processing, not a general advantage of dark personality.”
As with all research, there are a few other things to keep in mind. The study used a cross-sectional design, meaning all data was collected at a single point in time. Because of this, the results cannot prove a strict cause-and-effect relationship between personality traits, cognitive styles, and creativity.
Additionally, the participants were university students who generally reported low average levels of dark personality traits. This is typical for a non-clinical group of people, but it is something to consider when applying the findings to individuals with more extreme or severe personality traits.
The study also did not measure every possible personality factor. For example, it did not assess everyday sadism, which is sometimes grouped with the Dark Triad. It also did not account for broader personality dimensions like extraversion, which can also influence social status and creative output. Future research could follow people over longer periods to see how these traits and cognitive styles interact over a lifetime of creative work.
“I am interested in moving beyond the Dark Triad toward broader models of dark personality, including the Dark Tetrad and the general Dark Factor of Personality, and in examining whether different dark traits lead to creativity through distinct cognitive, motivational, or self-regulatory pathways,” Giancola said.
“Ultimately, I think the more interesting question is not whether a personality characteristic is simply ‘good’ or ‘bad’ for creativity, but under what conditions and through which psychological mechanisms it can facilitate or inhibit creative behavior,” he added. “I think understanding how personality interacts with the way people process information may be more informative than simply asking if particular personality traits are associated with creativity.”
The study, “Breaking the Mold: How Dark Personality Traits Shape Creative Achievement Through Cognitive Styles,” was authored by Marco Giancola.

====================================================================================================

Google to deploy AI for underage detection in Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:59:51 UTC
22:59:51 KST

Yasin Gungor
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Google will begin rolling out machine learning systems across Canada to detect minor users and implement default youth privacy protections, the company announced Monday.
"While some would like a system that imposes a universal arbiter of age, we believe that liability and responsibility rest with every service owner — the developer, the publisher, the app creator — because they know their users and services best," Jeanette Patell, director of government affairs and public policy at Google Canada, wrote in an official blog post.
Patell explained that developers designed the architecture "with user privacy in mind," emphasizing that the algorithms analyze existing account signals, such as historical Google Search queries and YouTube viewing patterns, to estimate whether an individual is under 18 without collecting new data.
Once identified as a minor, the account receives automatic safeguards, including the deactivation of Google Maps Timeline, the disabling of personalized advertising, restrictions against adult-rated downloads on the Google Play app store, and automated break reminders on YouTube. Misidentified users retain the ability to dispute classifications by submitting a selfie or a government-issued photo identification card.
The system aims to minimize data ingestion and ensure platforms avoid "sharing granular user information with apps and websites unnecessarily," Patell noted.
The rollout follows similar measures by US social media company Meta, which expanded automated systems to transition Canadian teenagers into restricted settings.
The move also comes as Canadian lawmakers review Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, federal legislation that would require online platforms to restrict accounts for individuals under 16 years old unless sufficient safety protections are established.

Erdogan praises Türkiye's gains in PISA education rankings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:56:26 UTC
22:56:26 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has praised Türkiye’s improved performance in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), saying the country’s ranking in reading, writing and science has increased by 50 percent.
Speaking at Gazi Anatolian High School during a ceremony marking the start of the 2026–2027 academic year in Ankara on Monday, Erdogan said Türkiye was the only country to significantly improve its performance across all three fields.
He criticised attempts to downplay the results, saying the achievement should be a source of pride for the Turkish nation.
According to results released by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Türkiye recorded the largest score increases among OECD countries in science, reading and mathematics in PISA 2025.
Türkiye’s scores rose in all three subjects compared with 2022, with the country climbing 15 places in science, 18 in reading and 11 in mathematics among participating countries.
The assessment covered 91 countries and economies and evaluated the skills of 15-year-old students. Türkiye has participated in the programme since 2003.

Overhead wire damage limits trains between Ringsted and Slagelse until Tuesday morning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:56:15 UTC
22:56:15 KST

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.

Police see more cases of crime-for-hire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:55:59 UTC
22:55:59 KST

Danish police brought 79 new charges linked to possible crime-for-hire cases from January through the end of July, the Ministry of Justice said Monday.
In total, police brought 316 charges from April 2024 through the end of July this year that may involve crime-for-hire, a practice also known as “Violence as a Service.”
The figures come from NSK, a Danish police unit that handles serious and organized crime. In January, authorities had recorded 237 charges, according to figures released by the ministry in February.
The government disclosed the latest figures as it sent a bill proposing stricter penalties and other measures against gangs and crime-for-hire for consultation. That process allows judges, lawyers, police and other groups to submit concerns or objections before the proposal moves forward.
The bill would increase penalties for crime-for-hire and treat criminal families in the same way as gangs.
“We will not tolerate children and young people being recruited into a life of crime, and residential areas being marked by fear, control, and parallel power structures,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said in a statement.
The proposal would also add a provision to the penal code intended to make it easier to convict people who provide minor services to gang leaders.
Other measures include allowing background checks for dockworkers and increasing the penalty for violating a stay ban. Police have recorded a large increase in such violations.
A stay ban can be imposed on a person who has committed a crime connected to a gang. It prevents that person from entering a specific area, such as part of a town or municipality, for a set period.
Violating a stay ban currently carries a fine of 10,000 DKK. Under the proposed law, a violation would result in 30 days in prison.
Russian frigate fires flares near Danish military helicopter in international waters
A Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Gedser on Monday, Denmark’s Armed Forces said.
The Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the ship when the flares were fired. One passed close to the aircraft, according to a military statement.
Flares are pyrotechnic devices normally used as attention signals at sea. No personnel were injured, and the helicopter was not damaged.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats called the incident serious and described Russia’s actions as “very unprofessional seamanship.”
“It is serious. It is an expression of the boundaries having been moved regarding the willingness to take risks from the Russian side,” Bruus said.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen will summon the Russian ambassador to discuss the incident, though the date of the meeting has not been announced. Bruus said he did not expect further action beyond that meeting.
The defense minister said the incident would not change Denmark’s monitoring operations.
“We view it seriously, but it is not the case that we will change our behavior, understood in the sense that we have a completely legitimate task in monitoring what is going on,” Bruus said.
Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party, said the incident showed that Russian provocations had reached Denmark.
She called for NATO unity and continued support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
“It is therefore crucial that NATO stands united, and that we continue to support Ukraine,” Støjberg said. She added that she expected a briefing from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Danish electricity prices head for most expensive month in years as gas costs rise
September could become the most expensive month for Danish electricity customers in several years, energy company Norlys said.
Halfway through the month, the average electricity price was 1.11 DKK per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 1.12 DKK in eastern Denmark.
It is the first time since December 2022 that the monthly average has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour, according to Norlys.
“We are halfway through September, so a lot can still change, but with the rising gas prices, we unfortunately have to expect that it will be an expensive month,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
Electricity prices were set to rise above 7 DKK per kilowatt-hour Monday evening, their highest level in almost two years.
Norlys said the increase was caused by higher gas prices and limited electricity production from wind and solar power. Natural gas plants often supply electricity when the weather does not provide enough wind and sunlight, making power prices more sensitive to gas costs.
Kristian Rune Poulsen, an analyst at Danish energy organization Green Power Denmark, also pointed to gas prices.
“The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which doesn’t really want to come to an end, means that a great deal of the liquefied natural gas that we have become so dependent on cannot get out onto the world market,” he said.
Poulsen said prices would continue to fluctuate but were unlikely to fall soon while the conflict continued.
“We expect that the elevated price level will persist throughout the winter, as it looks right now,” he said.
Nearly 12 percent of Danish ninth graders fail to pass Danish or mathematics exams
More than one in 10 Danish ninth-grade students failed to earn a passing grade in Danish or mathematics in this summer’s final exams, new government figures show.
The Ministry of Education said 11.8 percent of students did not receive at least 2, the minimum passing grade, in one or both subjects during the 2025-2026 school year.
“It is too high a proportion. Because it means that they initially will not have the opportunity to move on to youth education programs,” Andreas Rasch-Christensen, a school researcher at VIA University College, a Danish higher education institution, told DR, Denmark’s public broadcaster.
DR reported a failure rate of 10.5 percent, while the ministry listed 11.8 percent. The difference is that the ministry included students whose schools did not register that they sat the exam. DR excluded those students.
The result marks a small decline from the previous school year, when 9.9 percent failed to pass Danish or mathematics. The rate was 10.1 percent in 2023-2024 and 6.9 percent in 2018-2019.
The average final exam grade was 7.3, in line with the previous four years, DR reported.
The figures follow the release of a PISA study showing that Danish students’ performance had declined in reading, mathematics and science.
The government said similar declines were occurring across much of Western Europe. Danish politicians have pointed to mobile phones as a possible cause, saying quick stimulation from phones may make it harder for students to concentrate.
The government wants to introduce a complete ban on mobile phones in schools.
Lower food VAT would cost Danish businesses about 725 million DKK a year to administer
Lowering Denmark’s value-added tax on food would cost businesses about 725 million DKK annually in added administration, according to a parliamentary response.
Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates said Monday that the government wants to lower the general VAT rate on food and remove it from fruit and vegetables as soon as possible. The changes will not take effect this year.
“It is of great importance to the government to make it cheaper for Danes to fill their shopping baskets,” Engel-Schmidt said at a consultation.
The estimate is uncertain because the government has not decided how the new VAT system would work. Shops and other businesses would have to cover the administrative costs.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main business and employers’ association, said the actual cost would be higher.
“When the VAT rules for food become more complicated, it affects the VAT accounting in virtually all active businesses,” tax policy chief Jacob Bræstrup said.
Bræstrup said the change would affect more than wholesalers, supermarkets and restaurants. He said total administrative costs would be “significantly higher” than the estimated 725 million DKK.
The broader proposal would cost the state 17.4 billion DKK a year, according to the Ministry of Taxation and Growth.
Leading economists have criticized the plan as an expensive and inefficient way to help people. They warn that businesses might not pass the full tax reduction on through lower prices. Some savings could instead pay for administration or increase company earnings.
The government plans to present several possible models in the second half of 2026.

CPH Half will expand to 45,000 runners for its race on September 19, 2027, because of high demand, organizer Sparta Atletik og Løb, a Danish athletics and running organization, said in a news release.
Around 35,000 people are taking part in this year’s half marathon, up from about 32,000 in 2025.
Tickets for the 2027 race will be sold through a lottery instead of on a first-come, first-served basis.
Registration for the lottery opens September 16 and remains open for two weeks. People can register alone or in groups of up to three. Each group will either be selected together or not selected at all.
Selected runners will have 48 hours to buy a ticket. The price is DKK 795 plus a small administration fee.
“When demand is so high, access to the bib numbers must also function in a way where everyone has a fair and equal chance of getting a bib number,” Dorte Vibjerg, CEO of Sparta Atletik og Løb, said in the release.
The organizers also used a lottery to sell tickets for this year’s CPH Half, which is part of the World Athletics Road Running Championships. Similar systems are used for major marathons in Berlin and London.
This year’s race starts Sunday. Elite international runners will begin first, followed by the other participants.

Power and diesel prices heading for nearly two-year high
The electricity price on Monday evening is the highest level in almost two years, when the price exceeds seven kroner per kilowatt-hour. The energy company OK writes this in a press release Monday morning.
According to Troels Skipper, commercial director at OK, the high electricity price is due to a combination of rising gas prices and a lack of wind and solar energy.
“Right now, we are in the unfortunate situation where the high gas price pushes the electricity price up along with it. And unfortunately, we do not get enough electricity production from wind turbines and solar cells to push the price the other way,” he said.
The last time the hourly price was at around seven DKK per kilowatt-hour was in December 2024.
Also, Diesel prices in Denmark rose to a record high on Monday, reaching 19.19 kroner per litre after an increase of 20 øre, according to FDM, the Danish motorists’ association. Denmark is set for a week of changing autumn weather, with periods of rain, sunshine and mild temperatures, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI.
Monday began cool, particularly in central Jutland, where temperatures fell to between 6 and 8 degrees.
“The temperature is down to 6-8 degrees, so if you are going out cycling, you can clearly feel that autumn has arrived,” DMI duty meteorologist Jesper Eriksen told Ritzau.
The rest of Monday is expected to remain dry, with a mix of sunshine and clouds. Temperatures will reach between 15 and 18 degrees, with light to moderate winds from the west.
### Tuesday to be warmest day
Tuesday is expected to be the warmest day of the week.
Winds will turn to the south, bringing slightly warmer air over Denmark and pushing temperatures to between 17 and 21 degrees.
There will be periods of sunshine, although some rain is possible, particularly in Jutland.
More rain is expected to reach Jutland later Tuesday afternoon before moving east during the evening and overnight.
Wednesday will bring some sunshine but also showers.
Temperatures are expected to fall back to between 15 and 18 degrees, while winds will turn west again.
Thursday and Friday are expected to bring periods of rain and showers, with temperatures remaining between 15 and 18 degrees.
Winds from the west and southwest are also expected to strengthen gradually toward the end of the week.
Eriksen said the week would not be particularly cold despite the unsettled weather.
“In the week as a whole, you will not need the really warm clothes, but in periods you will need rainwear and rubber boots,” he said.
It remains unclear whether September will bring another spell of warmer weather later in the month.
“We will have to see what happens, whether the last spasms with some warmth arrive. It is not decided yet,” Eriksen said.
More than half of the Danish schools that were selected for the latest Pisa survey declined to participate. In total, 398 schools were drawn for the survey. Of those, 215 chose not to participate, writes Kristeligt Dagblad.
When a selected school chooses to decline, a reserve school could step in. In advance, two reserve schools had been designated for each of the drawn schools.
Therefore, a total of 283 schools ended up participating in the survey. However, this is significantly fewer than in 2022, when 347 schools participated.
According to Kristeligt Dagblad, the number also remains below the OECD’s “technical minimum requirement”.
According to Monika Klingsbjerg-Besrechel, chief consultant at Statistics Denmark, which was responsible for the practical part of the survey, the many declines have not affected the quality of the survey.
“Fortunately, we reached a higher response rate, but despite that, we were unfortunately still below the minimum requirement from the OECD. If we had not had the reserve schools, we really would have been in serious trouble,” she says to Kristeligt Dagblad.
She points out that it was subsequently investigated whether the many declines had affected the result.
Silkeborg debuts as first host city for Royal Run 2027
Danmarks Idrætsforbund (DIF) has announced Silkeborg as the first of five host cities for the 2027 edition of the Royal Run, making it the first time the Central Jutland city is on the bill for the event.

The Royal Run offers three distances to run, including 1.6 kilometers (also known as one mile), five kilometers, and ten kilometers.
The event first took place in 2018, when the then Crown Prince turned 50 years old. Since then, it has been held every year on Whit Monday.

What Ukraine’s Strike on Molniya Drone Plant Reveals About Russian Defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:55:54 UTC
22:55:54 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
What Ukraine’s Strike on Molniya Drone Plant Reveals About Russian Defenses
Ukrainian drones destroyed three production and storage buildings at Russia's Atlant-Aero drone plant in Taganrog overnight on September 12, marking the manufacturer's second major loss since April.
Satellite imagery published to the "Absolutely Reliable Source" Telegram channel documented the damage in Taganrog, in Russia's Rostov region. The channel's analysis identified the main strike site as Atlant-Aero's primary production facility, which builds the Molniya line of strike-reconnaissance drones.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to that imagery, further production and storage buildings were destroyed at a second location in the city, reportedly used by the same company. Satellite fire monitoring and local reports indicated blazes across multiple industrial sites. The confirmed and suspected results included:
- Three production and storage buildings were destroyed at Atlant-Aero's main site;
- additional production and storage buildings destroyed at a second Atlant-Aero location;
- prolonged fires at fuel tanks on the grounds of the Taganrog-Central military airfield;
- fires at no fewer than four industrial facilities, including the Taganrog Automobile Plant.
The Taganrog-Central airfield, home to Russia's 708th Military Transport Aviation Regiment, was a separate target. Fuel tanks there burned for hours after the strike.
Satellite imagery also showed scorched vegetation beside a Russian S-400 air-defense position. The traces may indicate an attempt to hit the system, though its destruction remains unconfirmed.
Atlant-Aero runs the full development, production, and testing cycle for the Molniya family of drones. The line includes the Molniya-1 and Molniya-2 strike variants, as well as the Molniya-2R reconnaissance model.
The company also produces components for other Russian unmanned systems, making it a node in Moscow's drone-manufacturing network.
Taganrog's military-industrial sites have drawn repeated Ukrainian strikes in recent weeks. Earlier, drones hit a Russian military airfield in the city overnight on September 6-7, with satellite monitoring recording a fire in the aircraft parking area at around 2:44 am.
That facility, roughly 40 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, hosts the 325th Aircraft Repair Plant and sits beside the Beriev complex that maintains Russia's scarce A-50U early-warning aircraft.

Antidepressants for dogs during wartime: when an animal needs medication
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
16:54:57 EEST
22:54:57 KST

Antidepressants for dogs during wartime: when an animal needs medication
Kyiv • UNN
Explosions can cause anxiety, aggression, and behavioral disorders in animals. Medication is prescribed only by a veterinarian, and the effect takes 2–4 weeks.
Explosions, sirens, and constant stress affect not only people but also pets. A veterinarian, veterinary dermatologist and dietitian, and PhD in veterinary medicine, Eduard Kotliarov, told UNN journalist in more detail about when an animal needs help from antidepressants, how the medications work, and what owners can do during shelling.
Details
According to the doctor, animals can develop behavioral disorders similar to those experienced by humans, although they manifest somewhat differently. Against the backdrop of the war, the reaction of dogs and cats to explosions has become a particularly noticeable problem.
Animals have many mental disorders similar to those in humans, but they may manifest somewhat differently. In veterinary medicine, we more often talk about behavioral disorders, although the essence is similar. These may include acute stress disorder, anxiety and depressive disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, hyperactivity, and so on. Animals can also experience separation anxiety, when they are afraid to be left alone
According to the veterinarian, animals’ reactions to explosions can indeed be very strong, but they are not always easy to notice immediately. A dog may even change its attitude toward people or other animals because of such stress.
A great many animals react severely to explosions. They may hide, tremble, refuse to go outside, stay close to their owner, refuse to eat, or constantly sit under the bed or a blanket. If an animal is hiding and a person tries to pull it out, it may show aggression not because it has become aggressive, but because it is frightened and does not want to leave its makeshift safe zone
Eduard Kotliarov separately draws attention to the fact that animals may absorb their owner’s emotional state during explosions. This particularly applies to dogs, which are good at reading human behavior, but the point is that even an owner’s calmness does not always guarantee that the animal will also cope normally with shelling.
Animals are very good at reading their owners’ reactions. If the owner is highly anxious, the animal may also begin to feel nervous. But the opposite can happen as well: the owner is calm, while the animal still reacts severely to explosions. This is often more noticeable in dogs, whereas cats may simply hide more and not show their condition
Therefore, the doctor says, it is not always worth waiting after another attack ends for everything to pass on its own. If changes in the animal’s behavior have already become постоянними or are already affecting the lives of the animal and its owners, the specialist advises seeking help. There are specific specialists who deal precisely with behavioral problems.
It is impossible simply to dismiss everything as the animal being old, fearful, or having merely experienced an explosion. An animal cannot say how frightened it is or how severely it is stressed, while prolonged stress can negatively affect both physical and mental health. If it seems that something is wrong, it is better to consult an animal behavior specialist and determine the cause
At the same time, the veterinarian advises against viewing medications for behavior modification solely as "antidepressants." According to him, this is a broader concept, since such medications can be used for various behavioral problems.
We more often talk about medications for behavior modification rather than simply antidepressants. They are used not only for depression but also for various behavioral disorders, anxiety, sleep problems, separation anxiety, and other conditions. Very often, a comprehensive approach works best, when the animal is treated simultaneously by a veterinarian and a behavior specialist
The veterinarian also emphasizes that the need for medication is determined not by the mere fact that the animal is afraid of explosions. It is important to assess how much the animal’s condition changes its usual life and whether it is becoming постоянним.
When such behavior leads to destructive or dysfunctional consequences for the animal itself or its owners, then it is worth considering treatment. For example, if an animal stops eating, urinates in the house, becomes aggressive, or lunges at people, this already worsens its quality of life. If the dog simply hides during an explosion, sits beside its owner, and calms down after a few minutes, that is a completely different situation
He says that in Ukraine, only human medications are used to correct animals’ behavior, but one must categorically not give a dog medication intended for humans without professional guidance.
We do not have separate veterinary antidepressants of this type, so human medications are used. But doing this without a doctor’s prescription is extremely dangerous. The medication and dosage must be selected correctly, and other medications the animal is taking must be taken into account, because some drugs cannot be combined with one another or used for certain illnesses
Moreover, one should not expect the first effect of such medications immediately, because, according to Eduard Kotlyarov, the clinical, that is, lasting, effect takes a long time to develop.
Antidepressants have an interesting mechanism of action that has not been fully studied. The biochemical effect may appear after just a few hours, but the actual clinical effect usually manifests after two to four weeks. The body needs time to readjust the functioning of its neurotransmitters and the entire system, rather than simply receive more of a certain substance
Instead, side effects may even occur at the beginning of treatment, although, according to the veterinarian’s observations, they are not particularly common in animals. That is why the dog’s condition at the start of therapy must be monitored very closely.
At the beginning, side effects may include diarrhea, constipation, drowsiness or, conversely, less sleep. Agitation, meaning increased irritability, or sluggishness may appear. Sometimes the animal becomes more sensitive to sounds to which it previously did not react. This usually happens during the early stages of therapy
The course of treatment must also not be stopped independently after the first improvements.
The course must be long enough to recalibrate the system, so the medications are taken for months, not a few days. They must be discontinued gradually, under a doctor’s supervision, because abrupt withdrawal can cause negative side effects. Sometimes an animal genuinely needs such therapy for a long time, although this is uncommon
Kotlyarov also advises not waiting for the explosions to begin if it is known that the dog experiences them very badly. Instead, it is better to take the dog to a veterinarian so that the doctor can prescribe the animal a medication used specifically when anxiety intensifies.
If we understand that the anxiety will last for several hours and that explosions will recur, the doctor may prescribe a fast-acting medication that will help calm the animal at that particular moment. If it is known in advance that there will be heavy shelling, it may sometimes be better to give such medication beforehand, because after taking it, it also needs time to take effect. But it must be a medication prescribed by a doctor
However, medication is not the only way to help an animal during an attack. First and foremost, it is important for the owner to remain as calm as possible.
The animal should not be left alone at this moment. One should speak to it in a calm voice and stay nearby. If the owner is very nervous, it is better for someone who is calmer to look after the dog, because the animal senses intonation, rapid breathing, and a trembling voice, and understands that something is wrong
The animal should also be allowed to stay wherever it feels safer. If the dog chooses a hiding place on its own, it should not be forcibly pulled out.
If an animal wants to hide in the bathroom, under the bed, or somewhere else, it should be allowed to do so. You can make a bed there, put out water and food, and simply stay nearby. There is no need to scold it, shout, or forcibly pick it up. If the animal wants to be held, you can pick it up; if it wants to hide, let it hide
Ultimately, the main thing is not to ignore changes in the animal’s behavior that have arisen after the stress it experienced, the doctor emphasizes. Even if a dog outwardly returns to its normal life quickly, repeated explosions can still trigger an anxious reaction again. That is why, in the case of persistent problems, it is better not to experiment with medications on your own, but to consult a veterinarian.
If it seems that something has changed with the animal, it is better to consult a specialist and determine together whether medication support is needed. Medications are not inherently something frightening—it is only important to use them correctly and under a doctor’s supervision
How to help a dog during shelling: advice from a police dog handler19.01.26, 23:59 • 4562 views

Denmark 'optimistic' on Greenland talks with US: PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:54:29 UTC
22:54:29 KST

Denmark's prime minister has said she was "optimistic" that discussions launched between Denmark, the United States and Greenland after the US threatened to take over the territory could resolve the dispute.
US President Donald Trump insisted earlier this year that Washington needed to control Greenland - an autonomous Danish territory - for national security reasons, though he ultimately ruled out annexing it by force.
A "high-level working group", gathering representatives from Denmark, the United States and Greenland was created in January to address US concerns, but since its creation little information about the negotiations has emerged.
"This working group is still working and therefore it's too early to draw any conclusions but I'm quite optimistic that we can find a way," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said on Monday at a summit on Arctic security in northern Finland.
"As long as the working group is still working, there are no conclusions, but my hope is, of course, that we will find a way forward peacefully," Frederiksen told reporters in Rovaniemi.
The United States wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, according to several media outlets, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory.
A 1951 defence pact, updated in 2004, already allows Washington to ramp up troop deployments and military installations on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance.
At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO.
Since then, tensions have cooled somewhat, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.
"When I became prime minister in Denmark, the Arctic region was not really on the agenda in the European Union, neither in NATO," Frederiksen said.
"Now, as we speak, we have 10 allies exercising together in Greenland."

Asia’s Democracy Is Being Rewired: An Early Warning for Global Democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:54:00 UTC
22:54:00 KST

Asia’s democratic trajectory is no longer defined by the binary struggle between democracy and authoritarianism. Instead, the real contest is being waged over the frameworks of participation: who controls the technology, the narrative, and the information ecosystem itself.
As we mark International Democracy Day 2026 on September 15, the global conversation on the state of democracy often focuses on the defense of established institutions. Yet, for Asia, this year’s commemoration should serve more as a moment of reckoning. The challenges facing the region are no longer solely about upholding democracy: they are about fundamentally adapting to a new, digitally-manipulated architecture of political control.
The emerging contest in the region is between open political systems and “managed” political systems – rather than explicitly closed ones. In a managed system, the boundaries of institutions and processes – such as parliaments, elections, courts, civil society, media, and free expression – are set by a manipulated information ecosystem that constrains the parameters of its operations. These “managed” systems – once thought to be unique to Asia – are increasingly being adopted by actors in the West, making the regional struggle an early warning for global democracy.
In the old system, the game plan for undemocratic control was to stop people from speaking. In the new model it is to flood the information environment until citizens internalize the boundaries of permissible political articulation and action. The problem isn’t censorship anymore. It is epistemic disinformation – making citizens believe and act based on falsehoods.
AI is accelerating this transition from the explicit repression of citizens to their systemic manipulation. Deepfakes, synthetic political content, microtargeting, automated influence operations, and algorithmic amplification now manipulate political perceptions and actions at scale. Exploited not only by authoritarian governments but also by political parties, commercial actors, foreign networks, and domestic entrepreneurs, this manipulation operates unevenly across borders – fueling distinct regional trajectories.
Rather than a uniform regional slide, Asia’s democratic map is fragmenting into divergent trajectories, characterized by specific, localized struggles over information manipulation. Asia Centre has recorded such trajectories in its reports “State-Sponsored Online Disinformation: Impact On Electoral Integrity In Thailand” and “Youth And Disinformation In Malaysia: Strengthening Electoral Integrity.”
This fragmentation confirms that Asia is not moving uniformly toward authoritarianism. Instead, the region is splitting into distinct manipulated trajectories – a distinction that is critical for anyone trying to navigate the current political landscape. Democracy is being transformed through information manipulation, and how Asian civil society responds to this transformation is critical.
Asia Centre’s 2023 empirical research published in Routledge’s “Fake News and Elections in Southeast Asia: Impact on Democracy and Human Rights” confirms that the manipulation of information, political parties, state actors, social media, and electoral institutions poses a fundamental threat. In Asia Centre’s further evaluations in 2025 assessing whether elections serve as mechanisms for authoritarian consolidation rather than democratic change, the findings were clear: an election does not automatically produce democracy. We published these findings in the Kyoto Review of Southeast Asia, “Eroding Electoral Integrity: Reasons for Democratic Backsliding in Southeast Asia.”
When examining governance, civic participation, inclusivity, legal protection, and resistance, Asia Centre recognizes civil society as essential democratic foundations rather than a mere NGO sector. The evidence demonstrates that democracy exists between elections, not just during them. As we note in our report, “Online Content Regulations in the Asia-Pacific: Limiting Civil Society’s Capacity to Hold Governments Accountable,” a combination of restrictive regulations and funding constraints continues to shrink civic space and hamper civil society operations.
Amid youth-led political movements in the region, in 2025 Asia Centre convened a conference, “Youths, Democracy & Electoral Legitimacy in Asia.” The meeting explored the role of youth participation as a vital buffer against democratic erosion. A key concern that emerged was the urgent need to remove barriers to youth political involvement and transition young people from a passive electoral demographic to active political leaders. In 2026 we see that youth-led reform movements in India, Thailand, and Sri Lanka have struggled to achieve democratic consolidation. The question remains: can Asian democracy renew itself through a new generation?
The emergence of artificial intelligence complicates this challenge further, fundamentally altering the frameworks of political participation and presenting new hurdles for these movements. With the rise of digitalization, AI is intensifying divisions across various fault lines – from ethnicity and religion to economic inequality and political ideology – effectively driving deep societal polarization.
But as AI presents hurdles, it also represents a significant opportunity to expand the democracy agenda by changing the systems through which democracy operates – the relationship between citizens, information, governments, elections and civil society.
Democracy – through pluralism, accountability, and non-violent political engagement – can serve as an antidote to polarization. The question for the region is whether Asia has a democracy movement capable of responding to these changes.
The good news is that there continues to be a proliferation of democracy organizations in Asia. In 2026, when the Centre convened the Global Democracy Coalition (GDC) Asia Regional Forum, members noted that what is needed is greater coordination and better use of resources, including the use of AI for democracy work.
To this end, the Asia Centre has established an AI Hub to support digital transformation of CSOs. In a previous commentary, we outlined our mission to ensure CSOs are not passive observers of the AI revolution but active shapers of it.
Asia doesn’t need another democracy rescue package designed elsewhere. It needs Asian democratic foundations: locally rooted research, civic education, information integrity, AI literacy, youth participation, cross-border civil society cooperation, and stronger connections between political parties and citizens.
In short, Asian democracy is undergoing a profound transformation. The future will not depend solely on whether authoritarian regimes intensify repression or democratic governments defend liberal norms. The question is no longer whether we can defend liberal norms, but whether we can build a new digital-era architecture before the old political ecosystem is fully rewired by those who oppose those norms.
Asia Centre is a member of the Global Democracy Coalition. For more information about Asia Centre and the AI HUB, visit asiacentre.org.

As Houthis advance, some Yemenis are fleeing to Djibouti
As Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis swept through the battered country's Red Sea coastline, thousands of panicked people fled to makeshift camps, adding to an already vast population of internally displaced people, with some even crossing the Gulf of Aden to Djibouti.
Aisha Muhammad, like others who escaped from coastal areas and arrived in the southwest province of Taiz, left behind her two daughters and three sons, trapped in their homes as fighting turned a once-vital corridor for trade into a route of displacement.
"They are being blocked and shot at. Right now, they cannot reach us, and we cannot return to them. This is a trial from God," said Muhammad, boiling water in an old black teapot placed on rocks over a flame.
More than 82,000 people have been displaced by the fighting since the start of the month, the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) said on Sunday, including over 2,000 who have crossed the Gulf of Aden to Djibouti in the Horn of Africa.
The advance by the Houthis, who already control most of the north and Yemen's most populous areas, is strengthening Tehran's hand in its conflict with the US.
Hardship is not new in Yemen, where a long civil war between forces of the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed administration and the Houthis created one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major fighting, despite expiring six months later, but efforts to turn it into a lasting political settlement have stalled as regional tensions have intensified.
The Houthis—mountain fighters in sandals who have transformed into a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones—have opened a second theatre of war with their lightning western offensive.
Their advance has put them in a strong position to tighten their grip over the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait—a vital chokepoint for global oil and commodities shipping—more than six months after the US and Israel attacked Iran.
"Behind every number is a family who's lost everything," said Amy Pope, IOM director general. "Many have been displaced multiple times. People are crossing the sea with nothing because they have no other choice left. Yemen is a country torn by poverty and conflict, and it cannot carry this crisis alone."
Video shared by IOM showed Yemenis who arrived in boats on Djibouti's northern coast receiving food and water at a nearby refugee settlement.
Djibouti's finance minister, Ilyas Dawaleh, said on Sunday that the situation was "becoming increasingly difficult for our country, despite our unwavering commitment to humanitarian resources".
Back in Taiz, many, including Abdullah Qaiyd, an elderly man walking with a stick, are once again longing for stability. "We are tormented and shaken to our core. We long for a basic livelihood, and we long for safety," he said.

Israelis want peace – realistic, lasting peace - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:48:03 UTC
22:48:03 KST

As Israel prepares for its first election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led massacres in Israel, it is critical to understand the mindset of many Israelis.
Most will never again vote for a two-state solution, not because they hate peace, but because they now understand that creating a Palestinian state was never a realistic path to it.
Two reasons guide this view. The first is historic: Jews have been indigenous to this land for over 3,000 years. The evidence: our language, our Bible, our kingdoms, our ruins, our prayers, and our continuous presence are here.
The people called “Palestinians,” marketed to the world as a separate ancient nation, have no indigenous claim to the land. They are Muslims from surrounding Arab countries and local Arab clans, many of whom arrived hundreds of years ago, while most came at the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century.
As the Soviet dissident Lt.-Gen. Ion Mihai Pacepa, acting chief of Romania’s foreign intelligence service, exposed years ago that the “Palestinian” national identity was invented by the Soviet Union in the 1960s as a political weapon to deny Jewish sovereignty, legitimize terror against Israel and the Jews, and weaken the United States.
Our names say it all. Jews are from Judea; Arabs are from Arabia.
The second reason is both theological and strategic. Peace, in the Western sense – a final and sincere end of claims and acceptance of a legitimate Jewish state that is here to stay – is impossible under the Islamic doctrine that formed this conflict.
In Islam, Muhammad permitted temporary treaties when Muslims were weak, as in the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah.
Those agreements were instruments of delay, not reconciliation: a way to regroup, deceive an enemy, and return to war when stronger.
Anyone who studies the Quran and the life of Muhammad knows that a central theme of Islam is jihad: the drive to conquer in the name of Allah and bring other peoples into submission.
Not every Muslim follows this; many want quiet, spiritual lives based on Islamic teachings. But that does not change Islam’s jihadi doctrine.
There isn’t a separate, peaceful “Islam” waiting to be discovered by diplomats. There is one Quran, one Islam, and its political doctrine does not allow for peace with any non-Muslims.
October 7 was not a breakdown of that worldview. It was its true expression. The massacres, rapes, abductions, and public celebrations in Gaza and the region were not the result of “despair over settlements.” They were the result of an Islamist jihad that cannot accept Jews as sovereign anywhere, including Jerusalem, Judea, or Samaria.
Every Israeli withdrawal was followed not by moderation but by more rockets, tunnels, and monuments to terrorists. The concept of “land for peace” and 30 years of adhering to the Oslo “peace” process have only resulted in land for jihad, and pushed peace further out of reach.
Israelis who had hopes for Oslo have since experienced the Second Intifada, decades of suicide bombings, bus explosions, and daily terror attacks. They watched Israel’s disengagement from Gaza and saw the world demand yet another experiment after our children were burned alive.
They will not vote to recreate the conditions of October 6, 2023. A two-state formula that requires Israel to shrink, reward a neighboring jihadi entity with the prestige of statehood, and call that “peace” is not diplomacy.
It is suicide with better stationery.
Acting like a Jewish nation
And yet the future of the Jewish people in our God-given, indigenous, ancestral homeland is bright. Each day, more Israeli Jews are discarding the Western fantasy that if only we speak softly enough and appease more, the other side will turn into a neutral, Sweden-like entity.
They are returning to a simpler, older truth: we are the Jews, this is our land, and weakness, as seen in the Muslim Arab Middle East, only invites war. Even the Quran, in verses our enemies prefer not to quote, records that this land was assigned to the children of Israel.
When a Jewish nation acts like a Jewish nation, rooted, unapologetic, unwilling to outsource its survival to foreign capitals, the Muslim world understands the language. It will not love us.
But it will respect our strength, both spiritual and physical. Strong, identity-based deterrence is not a slogan. It is the only way for our jihadi enemy to conclude that attacking us is not worth the price.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has begun the turnaround. After decades of Oslo’s appeasement, after years of denying we are in a war against jihad and treating an invented “Palestinian people” as the key to history, he has started to lead from Jewish strength rather than fear of international scolding.
But that process is incomplete. Too many of our political, organizational, and rabbinic leaders are still thinking like it’s October 6. Too many still treat the Palestinians as a permanent diplomatic sacrament.
The direction has changed, with the Israeli public leading ahead of the old elite. Perhaps this is why almost none of Israel’s left-wing parties are campaigning as proud leftists.
Instead, they are trying to outflank Netanyahu from the right, even though their actions and statements during the war remained stuck in October 6 thinking: end the fighting with negotiated deals, without destroying the military threats of Hamas or Hezbollah.
As one political strategist, Ronen Manelis, asked US pollster Arthur Miller in a recorded meeting with Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot: “How do we convince the public we are Right, not Left?” They understand that the generation that fought this war is not going back to the way things were.
True peace will never come from giving away land or creating a Palestinian state; it will come only through strength, by reinforcing Israel as the Jewish homeland.
As Prof. Mordechai Kedar of Bar-Ilan University often states: “If Israel wants short-term peace, [it has to] be invincible in the short term. If Israel wants long-term peace, [it must] be invincible for the long term.”
That is the peace worth seeking, not the Western idea of peace based on slogans. October 7 buried all of that.
The upcoming election will test how many Israelis see through slick campaigns, Left and Right, that ignore these truths while trying to outflank Netanyahu.

Iran tried to intimidate Saudi Arabia - it may have made Riyadh more powerful instead - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:47:58 UTC
22:47:58 KST

Tehran can drive up oil prices. What it cannot control is the rising price of Saudi cooperation.
Iran wants Saudi Arabia to remember a simple geography fact: it may be rich, heavily armed, and close to Washington, but it still sits on the Gulf and is dependent on energy routes Tehran can threaten.
The current war is exposing the flaw in that strategy.
Iran can make the Strait of Hormuz more dangerous, push oil prices higher, and pressure US President Donald Trump through American gas prices.
But Tehran’s own ability to profit from those higher prices has been crippled, while Saudi Arabia enters the crisis with infrastructure that allows it to bypass Hormuz and a regional position that is becoming more valuable by the day.
In other words, the more Iran raises the cost of confrontation, the more it may also raise the price of Riyadh.
And that is where the story gets bigger than oil.
Washington needs Saudi Arabia to help build a regional order capable of containing Iran. Israel wants Saudi normalization. Trump could use Riyadh to turn an expensive confrontation with Tehran into a strategic realignment of the Middle East.
Mohammed bin Salman, meanwhile, can afford to wait and see what everyone is prepared to offer.
Iran can raise oil prices. Saudi Arabia can still sell
Iran’s strategy depends partly on making the war economically painful far beyond the battlefield.
That makes the US an obvious target. Over Labor Day weekend, US gasoline prices were expected to average about $4.03 a gallon as renewed fighting pushed crude prices higher. With the midterm elections only weeks away, Tehran does not need to defeat Trump militarily. It needs Americans to feel the war every time they fill their tanks.
But there is a problem.
Iran can help make oil more expensive while increasingly struggling to sell its own. The US blockade has sharply reduced Iranian crude exports, with loadings falling from around two million barrels a day in March to roughly 220,000 to 255,000 barrels a day in August.
Saudi Arabia prepared for a different scenario.
For years, Riyadh invested in infrastructure designed to reduce its exposure to Hormuz. Its East-West Pipeline carries crude from the kingdom’s eastern fields to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing part of Saudi exports to bypass the strait.
That investment is paying off. The IMF found in July that rerouting crude through the pipeline helped limit the decline in Saudi oil deliveries, while higher prices more than compensated for lower volumes and produced an oil-revenue windfall.
The irony is hard to miss.
Tehran can make every barrel more valuable while losing the ability to sell enough barrels to fully benefit. Riyadh can still reach the market.
Iran’s energy weapon may be enriching the rival it was supposed to intimidate.
MBS built options before he needed them
Saudi Arabia’s advantage is not limited to pipelines.
For years, Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) has been building relationships designed to give Riyadh room to maneuver between competing powers.
Saudi Arabia deepened its economic relationship with China without abandoning its strategic partnership with Washington. More recently, Riyadh joined Turkey and Pakistan in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, adding another layer to a security strategy no longer built exclusively around the United States.
None of these relationships can replace Washington. The United States still offers military reach, intelligence, advanced weapons, and financial access that no other Saudi partner can match at the same scale.
But replacing America was never the point.
MBS does not need another America. He needs enough credible alternatives to make America compete for Saudi cooperation.
Iran is making that strategy more valuable.
The more dangerous the Gulf becomes, the more Washington needs partners capable of shaping what comes next. And few countries now occupy a more consequential position than Saudi Arabia.
Washington is no longer the only side setting the price
For years, the Saudi-Israel normalization debate revolved around what Riyadh wanted from Washington.
That is no longer enough to understand the negotiation.
The more important question is increasingly what Washington wants from Riyadh.
The United States wants Saudi weight behind a regional order that limits Iran. Israel wants normalization with the most important Arab state still outside the Abraham Accords. Trump wants an outcome he can present as something larger than another costly confrontation with Tehran.
All three roads run through Riyadh.
That changes MBS’s hand.
The proposed 30-year US-Saudi civilian nuclear cooperation agreement illustrates what is at stake. Washington has linked the deal to normalization with Israel, while Riyadh continues to demand meaningful movement on the Palestinian issue.
Iran’s pressure does not make those differences disappear.
It makes Saudi cooperation more valuable despite them.
The more indispensable Riyadh becomes to the regional architecture Washington wants, the harder it becomes to expect MBS to accept that architecture cheaply.
Iran may be creating Trump’s opening
Tehran’s strategy is supposed to trap Trump between two bad choices. Show restraint, and Washington risks looking unable to protect Gulf shipping and its regional partners. Escalate, and oil prices rise, Americans pay more at the pump, and the political cost grows at home.
But there is a third possibility: Trump could try to turn the Iranian threat into the argument for a much larger bargain with Saudi Arabia.
Washington and Jerusalem would get Saudi participation in a stronger regional framework and, potentially, normalization. Riyadh would seek the security commitments and strategic benefits it has wanted for years.
The Palestinian issue remains a major obstacle. So do the competing interests of all three governments. Nothing about such a bargain is inevitable.
But MBS has something increasingly valuable on his side: time.
He does not have to rush toward Washington, distance himself from China, or accept the first normalization package put in front of him. He can watch the pressure on the Gulf rise and ask a simple question: How much is Saudi cooperation worth now?
For years, Iran’s argument to its Arab neighbors rested on geography. America might eventually leave the Middle East. Iran would not. The Gulf states would therefore have to learn to accommodate Tehran.
Threatening Hormuz was supposed to reinforce that reality. It may be doing the opposite.
Every threat to Gulf shipping makes secure Saudi export routes more valuable. Every escalation makes Saudi cooperation more important to Washington. Every attempt to destabilize the regional order increases the country’s value, and everyone may need to rebuild it.
Iran wanted Riyadh to feel vulnerable enough to compromise. It may instead be making Riyadh indispensable enough to name its price.

Amit Shabi is a former analyst in Intelligence Unit 8200, an investment and capital markets professional, author of several finance books, and a competitive chess player.

World Food Programme funding for Sudan plummets as more go hungry, head says

World Food Programme funding for Sudan plummets as more go hungry, head says
Sept 14 - The World Food Programme's funding for Sudan — the world's largest hunger crisis — has fallen by about half this year, its acting head told Reuters, as war drives more people into hunger while the regional crisis raises prices and aid budgets plummet.
Speaking from the Darfur region after a trip across the country, acting Executive Director Carl Skau said that while access had represented humanitarians' largest obstacle in the past, now "we have (a) presence that we are not fully utilising because of the lack of funding."
The gap to sustain current operations was just short of $300 million, he said.
"This year, we're about half what we were in terms of funding last year," Skau said. Last year, WFP received $645 million, but almost three-quarters into this year funding is only at $206 million.
The war between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has devastated wide swathes of the country, displacing up to 14 million people, ruining harvests and decimating the economy.
Almost 20 million people face hunger in Sudan, but budget cuts have forced the WFP to focus efforts on the 5 million most in need, of whom it has recently scaled up to reach 4 million people.
Even then, the organisation, the UN's largest by budget, is forced to make difficult decisions.
In Tawila, North Darfur, the makeshift home to about 1 million people, the WFP is able to reach everyone monthly but with only a half ration that covers two weeks' food, Skau said.
"It's not clear how they really are surviving the other two weeks," he said.
In El Obeid, the central Sudanese city where about 1 million and counting have sought refuge since the start of the war in April 2023, WFP is only able to provide help to those who arrived in the past several months.
"We are providing, but less and less. A year ago it was better because of resources," Skau said.
WFP recently began providing aid in the city of al-Fashir, once home to 1 million people, where an RSF attack last year, "bore the hallmarks of genocide," according to investigators. Skau said, "there is little sign of life having returned."
His organisation is not the only one struggling as major donors reduce aid. The International Organization for Migration said on Monday that emergency relief supplies for hundreds of thousands of people displaced by the war could run out within weeks unless donors step in with urgent funding.
The UN agency said supplies of shelter materials, sanitation items and emergency household goods are expected to run out by the end of September. The aid system itself can only keep functioning until December without more money.
Aid groups like IOM are struggling with funding shortfalls after the Trump administration — the United States was previously the world's biggest aid donor — cut billions of dollars in foreign assistance to UN agencies and charities over the past year. Other major donor countries have also cut aid budgets, citing tight finances and higher defence spending.
"We simply can't turn our back on the people of Sudan," IOM Director General Amy Pope said in a statement, adding: "The entire humanitarian system could collapse within weeks if we don't act now."
IOM says 8.6 million people remain displaced within Sudan, while another 4.9 million have returned to their homes. The agency says it needs $15 million to keep the aid pipeline running for the rest of the year, supporting about 305,000 people. Without it, more than 100 humanitarian organisations would struggle to quickly deliver lifesaving aid. REUTERS

Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:46:25 UTC
22:46:25 KST

Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles may adapt to the wild far better than expected, opening a promising new path for restoring endangered populations.
- Date:
- September 14, 2026
- Source:
- Murdoch University
- Summary:
- Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.
- Share:
A new study suggests that saltwater crocodiles born or raised in captivity may not try to return to their breeding centers once they are released into the wild. The finding could help conservationists improve efforts to restore declining crocodile populations.
Finding the way back home is an important behavior across the animal kingdom. For many species, it can play a major role in survival and reproduction. Some animals make short daily trips back to nests or burrows after searching for food, while others navigate across vast distances over weeks or months.
Crocodiles Have a Powerful Homing Instinct
"Crocodilians, the largest predators in most tropical, subtropical freshwater and brackish environments, are a unique case when it comes to homing behavior," said behavioral ecologist and Adjunct Associate Professor Ru Somaweera, from Murdoch University.
"Crocodiles are remarkably good at finding their way home, often returning to their original capture sites and limiting the success of relocation programs. What we still don't fully understand, though, is how this behavior plays out in individuals that have been bred or kept in captivity for long periods before being released back into the wild."
Researchers carried out the study in the Sundarbans mangrove forest in Bangladesh, one of the country's last major refuges for saltwater crocodiles. Heavy commercial hunting for crocodile skins severely reduced the species in Bangladesh until the 1970s. Although saltwater crocodiles have been legally protected there since 1973, their numbers have shown no measurable recovery.
Most of the country's remaining known crocodiles are now found in the Sundarbans. Even there, the population is small, with the most recent survey estimating just 140 mature individuals.
Could Older Captive Crocodiles Help?
"If crocodiles who are bred and raised in captivity subsequently return to their enclosures or breeding facilities after being released, attempts to reintroduce them into the wild as part of conservation efforts will ultimately fail," Associate Professor Somaweera said.
"The traditional approach has been to use hatchlings in reintroduction programs, but their survival rates are extremely low and they take a long time to reach reproductive maturity. Understanding whether larger, captive-bred crocodiles can be used instead represents an important knowledge gap."
To investigate, the researchers fitted five mature saltwater crocodiles with satellite tracking devices. The group included three captive-reared females that had spent 8-22 years in captivity, one local wild crocodile that was captured and then released at the same site, and another wild crocodile that was moved (translocated) a long distance from where it had been caught.
The scientists then tracked the animals for several months after release.
Captive Crocodiles Did Not Try To Go Back
According to Associate Professor Somaweera, the most encouraging result involved the three captive-reared crocodiles. None showed signs of attempting to return to the breeding facility where they had lived.
"Instead, they settled into small, well-defined areas and moved in much the same way as the local wild crocodile we tracked, which tells us they are possibly able to adapt to their new environment seamlessly," he said.
The outcome was very different for the translocated wild crocodile, named Jongra.
"Unfortunately, the results weren't as good for the wild crocodile Jongra, who was translocated about 132km from his home before being released.
"Although Jongra didn't make it back to his original capture site during the study, his movements were very clearly going in that direction. He traveled far more each day than any other crocodile we tracked, covered an exceptionally large area, and even recorded single-day movements of more than 30 kilometers: all typical signs of homing behavior."
A Potential Tool for Crocodile Conservation
The contrast between the captive-reared and translocated wild crocodiles could have practical value for conservation programs.
"These findings suggest that releasing subadult and adult captive-reared crocodiles can be a viable strategy to strengthen wild populations," Associate Professor Somaweera said.
"For translocated crocodiles, it's important there is careful release planning to manage their tendencies to return home."
The study, What is home? Post-release movements of captive-reared and translocated mature saltwater crocodiles in Bangladesh, was published in the journal Wildlife Research. It was funded by the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit and led by IUCN Bangladesh and the Bangladesh Forest Department.
