====================================================================================================

South Korea and Arctic Shipping: A Game Changer on Thin Ice?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

On September 16, 2025, South Korea’s Lee Jae-myung administration formally adopted Arctic shipping development as a national policy. The Ministry of Ocean and Fisheries has subsequently moved to Busan, aiming to establish the city as South Korea’s maritime hub for Arctic shipping.
South Korea sent its first trial container, the PanStar Acro (under the flag of Panama), via the Northern Sea Route (NSR) to Europe in August 2026, following a few weeks behind the Chinese container ship Dubai Tower (under the flag of Liberia).
On September 11, 2026, Hanwha Ocean, one of Korea’s big three shipbuilders, began constructing the country’s second ice-breaker, which is expected to be more than twice the size and 50 percent better than the existing RV Araon.
South Korea, an Asian middle power, is clearly ambitious about seizing potential economic and strategic opportunities of the development of Arctic shipping. The challenges and prospects for South Korea’s Arctic ambitions hold insights for other interested countries as well.
The Arctic is warming at an alarming rate due to human-induced climate change. According to NASA, in September, when the Arctic sea ice reaches its minimum extent, the ice-covered area is now “shrinking at a rate of 12.2 percent per decade, compared to its average extent during the period from 1981 to 2010.” A decrease in the extent of sea ice and the loss of older, thick ice makes longer navigation seasons possible and generates new access to previously difficult to reach regions of the Arctic.
According to the Arctic Council, the number of ships operating in the Arctic reached a record high in 2025, with 1,812 unique ships entered the Arctic Polar Code area. This is a 40 percent increase compared to 2013. The shipping activities in the Arctic are likely to further increase in years to come, since the Arctic Ocean could possibly have its first ice-free day in summer 2027.
The Arctic shipping routes, especially the NSR along the Russian Arctic coastline, could cut shipping times by 10-20 days between East Asia and Europe, compared to traditional routes via the Strait Suez Canal or the Cape of Good Hope. Moreover, the freedom of navigation in “strategic chokepoints,” such as the Strait of Hormuz, is being shaken by geopolitics. This makes Arctic shipping routes strategically attractive for East Asian economies as an alternative for their foreign trade and energy security. China is so far the most active user of the NSR. And here comes South Korea.
In my view, the development of the NSR must be considered in the context of the China-Russia-U.S. strategic triangle. Both Russia and the United States are Arctic states, but they hold divergent views about the legal status of the NSR. Article 234 (“Ice-Covered Areas”) of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea provides a legal basis for Russia to exert jurisdiction over the NSR. However, Russia actually treats the NSR as its domestic waters. The United States, on the contrary, views the NSR as straits used for international navigation. Under this view, ships should have free transit rather than needing to apply for a permit from Russia’s Northern Sea Route General Administration.
China is in a tense geopolitical rivalry with the U.S., while Russia is now China’s most important partner in international affairs. Nevertheless, Russia and China have profound differences about how the Arctic should be governed. China is not openly challenging Russian regulation of the NSR, but that does not mean China is satisfied with Russia’s position. China wants to be seen as an equal partner with Arctic states and have a bigger say in Arctic governance.
Therefore, when South Korea enters into the scene as an active user of the NSR, there are potential risks and challenges from three aspects.
First, there is geopolitical risk. Russia is interested in increasing the use of the NSR and welcomes foreign investment and technology to develop the Russian Arctic. However, since the Ukraine War, national security concerns now supersede economic development and environmental protection in many parts of the Arctic. The region has sadly become confrontational again. Any future geopolitical incident, such as a Freedom of Navigation Operation (FONOP) by the U.S. against Russia’s “excessive claims” of the NSR, could spark fierce Russian retaliation. South Korea, as a U.S. ally, might be caught in the crossfire.
Second, and related, is the sanctions risk. The U.S. has introduced massive sanctions against Russian entities, both primary sanctions and secondary sanctions. Those sanctions paid special attention to Russia’s oil and gas industry as well as the banking system, to cut the Russian economy off from the West and reduce Russia’s revenue to fund its war. Secondary sanctions are particularly powerful. They are used to maintain or put additional pressure on the sanctions target by penalizing third parties that engage with the primary sanctions target in activities that could undermine or evade the purpose of the primary sanctions.
Therefore, Chinese and Japanese enterprises have become very cautious about doing business with Russia. For example, according to the website of Northern Sea Route General Administration, in 2025,only one Chinese-flagged ship submitted an application for a navigation permit on the NSR. The R/V Tan Suo San Hao is a scientific vessel owned by the Institute of Deep-sea Science and Engineering, Chinese Academy of Sciences, which was delivered in 2024 with capacity to conduct scientific expedition in the Russian Arctic. China’s state-owned global shipping giant, COSCO, has tempered its enthusiasm about using the NSR. Rather, unknown shipping companies, such as New New Shipping and Sea Legend (which runs Dubai Tower), were established to provide regular container service only between Russian and Chinese ports, using the NSR. The U.S. secondary sanctions are applied universally. South Korea’s status as a U.S. ally does not necessarily shield its companies from future U.S. sanctions.
Third is the competition South Korea will face in Arctic shipping. China is the most active user state of the NSR so far. The Polar Silk Road was officially announced by China’s 2018 Arctic Policy White Paper. Originally, the PSR aimed to cover the whole Arctic as China’s overall strategy in the region. However, due to what I call a “push and pull effect” between the U.S., Russia, and China, the PSR has evolved to focus on collaboration with Russia.
Building upon China’s “unlimited” bilateral cooperation with Russia, the PSR has two dimensions. It reflects China’s strong interest in developing and using Arctic shipping routes, not only connecting the Chinese and Western European markets, but also China and the resource-rich Russian Arctic for China’s energy security. Therefore, South Korean companies will be facing economic and technological competition from Chinese companies in the Russian Arctic.
That being said, I think South Korea’s ambitions for Arctic shipping should be lauded. The NSR has potential to serve South Korea’s national interest as an alternative, strategic shipping route. Moreover, because Russia wants to diversify sources of foreign investment and increase the usage of NSR, South Korea’s interest in the Arctic shipping is likely to be welcomed by Russia. Therefore, South Korea could become a game changer in the Arctic amid geopolitical headwinds.
As a middle power that has been thriving in the epicenter of East Asian geopolitics for decades, South Korea has a proven record for managing great powers relations for national security and prosperity. Now it will try to make use of that experience in the Arctic.

What’s Behind One Nation’s Attacks on Andrew Hastie?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

What populist nationalists find most offensive about liberal democracy is the rule of law. The idea that there should be an equal and impartial exercise of laws is an affront to both their belief in social hierarchies, and also their desire to exercise power in an arbitrary manner. To them, the law should be used to advance their concept of the nation, and privilege or discriminate based on who represents or challenges their beliefs. This hostility toward the rule of law intensifies when they find a prominent symbolic vehicle for their political ambitions.
This attempt to bend the country to their will is now being demonstrated in Australia through the One Nation party and its relentless attacks on Liberal Party MP Andrew Hastie. The party has commissioned cartoons that refer to Hastie as a “traitor” and a “gutless maggot.” The social media swamp that One Nation swims in and facilitates has become so aggressive and threatening that Hastie has had to employ security at both his electorate office and his home – something incredibly rare in Australia.
Hastie’s crime, in One Nation’s eyes, is that he testified in the defamation case that Ben Roberts-Smith, a former corporal in the Special Air Service (SAS) Regiment, launched against the publishers of The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age, and The Canberra Times, after they reported on allegations that he had committed war crimes in Afghanistan.
Hastie, a former SAS captain himself, and 20 other SAS veterans were subpoenaed to provide evidence in the case. A Federal Court judge found that on the balance of probabilities, Roberts-Smith was responsible for, or complicit in, unlawful killings in Afghanistan. The full bench of the Federal Court subsequently unanimously dismissed Roberts-Smith’s appeal. A criminal trial for Roberts-Smith remains pending.
For One Nation, the question of Roberts-Smith’s guilt is irrelevant because they believe the law itself to be fraudulent. The idea that there should be rules of engagement that the Australian Defense Force (ADF) is held to is something One Nation rejects. The military is considered an institution that sits above both domestic and international law.
For the ADF to investigate itself – as it did over allegations of war crimes committed in Afghanistan – is evidence to One Nation that it has been captured by a weak and “woke” series of ideas that have no place on a battlefield. Roberts-Smith has therefore become a symbol of the unrestrained manhood that the military should be a demonstration of. Those SAS soldiers – and especially Hastie – who testified in the defamation case therefore are guilty of betrayal.
It is here that “patriotism” in One Nation’s view has shifted from loyalty to the country’s institutions and principles toward loyalty to an individual who is deemed to embody what they see as a national virtue. This has also become bound to an immense sense of victimhood that One Nation cultivates. The rule of law is victimizing not just Roberts-Smith, but the nation itself. And if this is the case, then the rule of law must go. What is being challenged is whether Australian institutions have the authority to determine what conduct in war actually means.
Hastie has also become a perfect target for One Nation because he is a Liberal Party MP. One Nation may be mired in dystopian fantasies about global left-wing conspiracies, but the electoral threat they pose is actually to the Liberal Party. This is the party they want to replace, and it is the Liberal Party’s traditional voters from which One Nation are drawing most support. Bringing down Hastie therefore also has an electorally symbolic value. One Nation just won a by-election in a Western Australian state seat that overlaps with Hastie’s federal seat. It was another shot over Hastie’s bow.
One Nation’s attempt to replace the Liberal Party has further symbolic value because as the party that claims to be the holder of the classical liberal tradition in Australian politics, belief in the rule of law should be central to the Liberals political project. Theoretically, it should make the Liberals the party most resolutely opposed to One Nation and its radical objectives. Bizarrely, however, the Liberal Party seems to be a willing participant in its own decline. The party’s psychology is bound to its opposition to the Labor Party; it can’t comprehend threats from anywhere else.
Yet the threat here is not just against the electoral fortunes of the Liberal Party, or the reputation and physical personhood of Andrew Hastie. There is a wider battle taking place over what “patriotism” actually means. One Nation’s political strategy is to wrap itself in the flag and present its politics as an expression of national loyalty, while directing its hostility toward the institutions and principles that actually constitute the nation’s liberal democracy.

Russia Recruits More Than 28,000 Foreign Nationals for War in Ukraine

Russia Disguises Warship as Building in Bid to Evade Ukrainian Drones

Russia Disguises Warship as Building in Bid to Evade Ukrainian Drones
A Russian Navy corvette stationed at Kronstadt has been painted to resemble a waterfront building and fitted with protective netting, as Moscow continues adapting its Baltic Fleet vessels against Ukrainian drone attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on September 14, photographs published by military observer Massimo Frantarelli show a Project 1331M corvette, known by NATO as the Parchim II class, with painted outlines resembling windows and doors across its hull. Netting has also been installed above parts of the deck as a physical barrier against incoming drones.
The vessel was photographed at the Leningrad Naval Base in Kronstadt on August 22. Frantarelli said the ship could be either the Zelenodolsk or Kazanets, although its exact identity has not been confirmed. Russia operates roughly six of the East German-built anti-submarine corvettes, each displacing about 800 tons.
The modified vessel is part of a broader effort to alter the appearance of Russian warships based at Kronstadt. Naval analyst H I Sutton has documented several Baltic Fleet ships using black-painted bows and sterns, checkerboard patterns, and other disruptive designs since mid-2026.
Two Project 22800 Karakurt-class missile corvettes, Mytishchi and Burya, were also seen in July with unusual paint schemes and anti-drone netting.
The measures followed successful Ukrainian strikes against Russian naval assets in the Baltic region. On June 3, Ukrainian forces struck the corvette Boikiy while it was undergoing work in dry dock at Kronstadt, causing significant fire damage. Ukrainian officials said the vessel may have been damaged beyond repair.
In March, Ukrainian drones also sank the Russian patrol ship Purga near Vyborg, northwest of St. Petersburg. According to Defence Blog, neither vessel had protective anti-drone netting installed when it was targeted.
Similar techniques have historical precedent. During World War Two, warships were sometimes painted to distort their outline or blend into nearby infrastructure. Germany’s battleship Tirpitz reportedly carried a scheme during fitting-out at Wilhelmshaven that included painted features intended to make the hull resemble buildings along the waterfront.

14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk weighed in on the debate over artificial intelligence Monday, saying his concerns about the technology's potential risks date back more than a decade.
“I was thinking about AI safety long before 2014,” he said on US social media platform X, which is part of his artificial intelligence venture SpaceXAI.
Musk pointed to his involvement with philosopher Nick Bostrom's 2014 book Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies, saying he contributed to the work and was thanked by name in its foreword.
The book examines the potential consequences of AI surpassing human intelligence, warning that humanity's survival could hinge on engineering precise control mechanisms before superintelligent systems emerge.
Musk also pointed to a post from August 2014 in which he recommended the book and warned that advanced AI was “potentially more dangerous than nukes.”
His comments come as senior technology executives call for slowing the development of cutting-edge AI systems over safety concerns.
Over the weekend, Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei proposed giving independent safety evaluators access to AI companies to verify their safety practices, an approach backed by OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman and Musk.
Amodei told CBS Sunday that “there are real dangers," about the development of AI.
"If we build in the right way, I think the probability of something bad happening is very low," he said. “If we build in the wrong way, the probability of something bad happening is very high.”

Red Sea blitz: What Houthi gains mean for Yemen and the Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:05:04 UTC
22:05:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Red Sea blitz: What Houthi gains mean for Yemen and the Iran war
In a highly consequential development for Yemen and the region, the Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mocha from the internationally recognised Yemeni government, along with a strategic Red Sea island.
The lightning advance over the past week puts them in a prime position to close the Bab al-Mandab Strait more easily than ever before.
The loss of Mocha on 10 September cuts the government’s direct access to the Red Sea, while the capture of the strategic island of Mayun, also known as Perim, a day later enables them to effectively close the Bab al-Mandab in tandem with Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The offensive, which displaced almost 50,000 people, represents one of the biggest strategic setbacks for the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in several years.
The Houthis captured Yemen’s capital Sanaa and the major port city of Hodeidah in 2014. The Zaydi Shia group fought the government, which relocated to the southern port city of Aden, and its Saudi backers in a devastating war that from 2015 until 2022.
Approximately 150,000 Yemenis have perished, and the country endured a severe humanitarian crisis that pushed it to the brink of famine.
A 2022 Saudi-Houthi ceasefire largely held until July, when fighting resumed after Riyadh attempted to block a direct Mahan Air flight from Tehran to Sanaa, the first since 2015.
The official purpose of that Iranian flight was to pick up and return a Houthi delegation attending the funeral of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Riyadh and the Yemeni government feared an unopposed air bridge would enable Tehran to conveniently fly military equipment directly to its Houthi allies.
The emboldened Houthis have since resumed striking Saudi infrastructure and energy sites with drones and missiles. The kingdom now faces Iran-backed militia attacks from Yemen to its south and Iraq to its north. The latest advance inside Yemen marks the most significant escalation with Aden and its Saudi backer in years.
Serious territorial gains
“The Houthi advance into Mocha is a strong indicator that Iran is seeking to undermine the US-led coalition in its strategic rear, which is the Bab al-Mandab,” Nicholas Heras, Interim Executive Director at the Middle East Policy Council and Senior Director at the New Lines Institute, told The New Arab.
According to reports, Iran told the Houthis to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia, promising them more funding and weapons, and Tehran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) paramilitary directly guided the group’s coastal offensive.
“Saudi Arabia is a wavering member of the American coalition against Iran and the resumption of the war in Yemen with rapid Houthi gains is an embarrassing predicament for Saudi Arabia,” Heras said.
Ryan Bohl, a senior Middle East and North Africa analyst at the risk intelligence company RANE, pointed out that Mocha “certainly matters” to the Houthis since it expands the “buffer zone” for Hodeidah.
Additionally, it opens up a route for any subsequent attempts to encircle the southwestern city of Taiz, entrenches their influence over the Red Sea, and provides “new launch positions” for striking shipping passing through that vital but narrow Bab al-Mandab.
“I think the Houthis will continue to advance so long as there is military opportunism,” Bohl told The New Arab. “They can always trade away territory for a final settlement since there is the suggestion that they may only be interested in controlling those Zaydi portions of Yemen,” he noted.
“The most likely block on further advances will be the almost certain furious counterattacks by the IRG (Yemen’s Internationally Recognised Government) and the Saudis who will do whatever they can to prevent the fall of a major city like Marib or Taiz or an advance on Aden,” Bohl added.
More broadly, the RANE analyst noted, these advances certainly help the Houthis with their broader Red Sea strategy and potentially give them additional territory which they can trade for a future settlement with Riyadh and the Yemeni government.
Heras echoed this assessment. “The Houthis understand the limits of their power in Yemen beyond the core areas of Zaydi population concentration and are instead seeking to improve their ability to pressure the Saudis to pressure the Americans to support Iran,” he said.
“This Houthi campaign along Yemen’s coast is a declaration that the Houthis are key actors in global geopolitics who are able to undermine the US geostrategy in the Middle East.”
Sherwan Hindreen Ali, a Yemen analyst at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), assesses that these Houthi advances mark the “most serious territorial gain” the group has made in years, putting the entire Hodeidah governorate under its effective control.
“This is a major defeat for the IRG - which just a few days ago was boasting of military advances in the very same governorate - and a sign of the extreme unpredictability of the current escalation," he told The New Arab.
Saudi support
RANE’s Bohl expects Saudi air support will prove critical for blunting any further Houthi advance and supporting IRG counterattacks.
“At the same time, so will unity amongst the IRG's ground forces,” he said. “This latter element is the most critical because without a sense of unity these counteroffensives will be stuck being localised and unable to comprehensively roll the Houthis back.”
According to an Axios report, Saudi Arabia’s powerful Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman twice called US President Donald Trump during the Houthi advance, requesting renewed US strikes against them.
Trump declined. Nevertheless, US military advisors in Saudi Arabia are providing expanded intelligence and targeting support for the kingdom’s operations against the Iran-backed group, according to a CNN report.
Bohl noted that Saudi Arabia is already responding to Houthi attacks and advances and is “likely to be drawn into further involvement” in the civil war raging over its southern border. That further involvement could potentially lead to a deployment of Saudi forces into Yemen alongside “enhanced airstrikes” against the group.
The escalation, and ongoing Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, come a little over a month after the kingdom signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan on 7 August.
Pakistan has already clarified that it hasn’t planned any military response against the Houthis for their attacks.
“There is no such thing under discussion right now … When the time comes (we) will act under the agreement,” Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said on 10 September, the same day Mocha fell.
“As for other members of the Mecca pact, they will remain wary of conducting military operations inside of Yemen given the distant geographies from Turkey and Pakistan, as well as the prospect of trapping their forces in an intractable conflict,” Bohl said.
“But most notably, the change in the Trump administration from the first to the second term may prove to be important.”
He recalled that in its first term at the end of the 2010s, the Trump administration focused on “containment and mitigating the humanitarian impacts” of the Yemen conflict.
Now, in its second term, it perceives Yemen as “part of the struggle” against Iran. Consequently, it may be more likely to support broader Saudi military operations against the Iran-backed group while making “fewer demands” to change tactics that could have a significant humanitarian impact.
Potential scenarios
ACLED’s Yemen analyst Ali sees several potential scenarios for Yemen after these latest Houthi advances.
“The Houthis may press their advantage and launch more attacks to seize the coast of Taiz governorate just south of Hodeideh, bringing the entirety of the Yemeni Red Sea coast under their control,” he said.
“Alternatively, IRG forces may regroup to carry out a counterattack and attempt to reclaim lost territories.”
Both scenarios would mean a “heightened level of violence” and “increased risk for civilians” in Yemen in the coming weeks in addition to “hundreds of military casualties” from “deadlier clashes” along other internal frontlines. Ali anticipates fighting focused in al-Jawf in the east, which borders Saudi Arabia.
Both sides are engaged in heavy clashes there, with strategic sites “changing hands” at a rapid rate.
“Alternatively, the Houthi blitzing may force Saudi Arabia - which is the IRG’s main backer - back to negotiating with the group to avoid further potential losses for their Yemeni allies in the IRG, which could mean an abrupt end to the current round of escalation,” he said.
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs

These neutrinos from the sun have the lowest energies ever seen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

These neutrinos from the sun have the lowest energies ever seen
The ethereal subatomic particles were born in the sun’s main type of fusion reaction
Barely-there particles called neutrinos just got caught acting even more ethereal.
With tiny masses and no electric charge, the subatomic particles rarely interact with anything, making them difficult to detect. Scientists have now spotted neutrinos with lower energies than any they’ve seen before. And they did it using a detector meant for another purpose entirely.
XENONnT, at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso in Italy, is designed to search for dark matter, the mysterious substance that is needed to explain the behavior of galaxies across the universe. It has yet to find any — although a similar detector has seen a tantalizing hint. What it has found, instead, are neutrinos — hundreds of them, researchers report in a paper submitted August 29 to arXiv.org.
Neutrinos are born in vast numbers in the sun — about 100 billion of them pass through your thumbnail every second. Some of those solar neutrinos are expected to interact in XENONnT. So the researchers went neutrino hunting.
The team found evidence of neutrinos smacking into electrons within the detector, producing light that revealed their presence. It’s the first time a dark matter detector has spotted neutrinos based on their electron-jostling antics. The detection met a statistical benchmark of 5 sigma, which physicists typically consider the threshold for a definitive detection.
Other dark matter detectors have seen hints of this process. In July, PandaX-4T, at the China Jinping Underground Laboratory in Liangshan, saw evidence of low-energy neutrinos, but at a statistical significance of about 2.2 sigma — not enough to make the detection a sure thing.
The neutrinos have energies as low as 17 kiloelectron volts. That’s about a tenth the energy of the wimpiest neutrinos previously detected. The newfound low-energy neutrinos are produced in the main fusion reaction that powers the sun, in which two protons merge to form a larger atomic nucleus.
The particles could carry the sun’s secrets. With a proposed, more advanced detector, “we expect to be able to extract valuable knowledge about the sun’s composition,” says XENONnT physicist Florian Jörg of the University of Zurich.
In 2024, XENONnT saw higher energy neutrinos from the sun, as did PandaX-4T. Those neutrinos are by-products of a different, less predominant type of fusion reaction, making them less numerous, but easier to spot. Detectors can catch these higher-energy neutrinos interacting with an entire nucleus instead of just a single electron.
The signature of a low-energy neutrino bouncing off an electron is easily confused with hordes of other interactions that can mimic it, called background. “The difficulty is picking the neutrino needles out of the background haystack,” says neutrino physicist Kate Scholberg of Duke University, who was not involved with the study. The researchers “look to have done a pretty heroic job on this.”

"The Culmination of a Lifetime" — Media Star Oprah Winfrey Announces a Series of Live Performances in Las Vegas
Kyiv • UNN
Oprah Winfrey will perform at Sphere in Las Vegas on April 2–4, 2027. Her show will combine music, poetry, storytelling, and visual art.
In 2027, American media star Oprah Winfrey will hold a series of live performances at the Sphere arena in Las Vegas. According to her, these events will be the culmination of decades of work dedicated to encouraging self-discovery and personal growth through television, publishing, and public events, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The three performances, scheduled for April 2–4, are part of a project titled "Oprah Winfrey's AHA." The name refers to moments of sudden insight, which Winfrey has long called "AHA" moments and which have become a recurring theme throughout her work.
Producers said the two-hour show will combine music, poetry, storytelling, and visual art. The program will feature Grammy Award-winning musician Jacob Collier, poet and writer Ocean Vuong, musician Ajita, and gospel performer Wintley Phipps.
Winfrey said the idea for the project emerged after she attended a concert by the rock band U2 at the Sphere.
"This is the culmination of everything I have wanted to say to people throughout my entire life," the television host told Reuters.
She recalled standing in the audience during the concert, listening to the crowd's cheers, and realizing that this immersive space could serve as something more than just a venue for entertainment. For her, it became a powerful platform for fostering human connections.
"I was standing there alone, looking up, and thinking: 'What was that just now?'" she said, describing the moment when her idea began to take concrete shape.
"'Wow, this could be used for something more significant than a concert. It could be used to change the way people perceive themselves,'" Winfrey recalled thinking.
Inspired by this experience, she decided to create her own event for the venue. The project draws on themes that have played an important role in Winfrey's career, including self-discovery, personal development, and human relationships.
In addition
The 72-year-old Winfrey rose from working in local television news in Nashville and Baltimore to becoming one of the most prominent figures in American media through "The Oprah Winfrey Show," which aired for 25 years. She later built a business empire spanning television, film, publishing, and digital media, and also became a prominent philanthropist and interviewer who spoke with world leaders, celebrities, and writers. Live Nation is organizing the event, while Winfrey is one of its executive producers. According to the producers, registration for the ticket presale will begin on Tuesday.

- list 1 of 3Israeli checkpoints in the West Bank are choking the Palestinian economy
- list 2 of 3Israel arrests 100 Palestinians in a week as West Bank pogroms continue
- list 3 of 3How significant are new European sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements?
The report argues that while Israeli policies have been rooted in a long-term settler colonial framework, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has entered an accelerated phase of this objective since late 2022, particularly after the Hamas-led October 2023 attack on southern Israel.
“What Palestinians are living through in the West Bank is not a series of separate incidents. It is a single political project that reaches into every part of life,” said B’Tselem executive director Yuli Novak.
The report outlines five interconnected mechanisms Israel uses to advance its West Bank project, drawing from roughly 2,000 testimonies given by Palestinians.
Firstly, Israel is “using military forces and armed settler militias to impose violence, fear and coercion”, according to the report.
Between October 2023 and September 2026, Israel killed at least 1,107 Palestinians in attacks across the occupied West Bank, the NGO said.
The Israeli army uses military operations and demolitions and assists armed settlers in driving Palestinians from their land to expand its presence in the territory, the report said.
To date, at least 75 Palestinian communities have been forcibly displaced, it said. Israel has, via armed settlers, taken control of more than 1,070,000 dunams of land, equivalent to 18 percent of the West Bank as of July, 2026, it said. A dunam is a unit of land area commonly used in the region, equal to 1,000 square meters (about 0.247 acres or 0.1 hectare). Furthermore, about 33,000 Palestinians have been displaced from refugee camps in the northern West Bank.
Israel also actively restricts Palestinians’ movement, with the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs documenting 925 movement obstacles, including roadblocks and unmanned checkpoints, throughout the territory by the end of last year.
The Israeli government has purposefully stifled the West Bank’s economy, with unemployment rising from 13.1 percent in 2022 to more than 31 percent in 2024.
Lastly, Israel actively criminalises political organising, suppressing protests and arresting activists, students and journalists.
Since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, it has arrested at least 60 Palestinian journalists working in the occupied West Bank.
B’Tselem urged the international community to stop viewing Israel’s violations as isolated incidents and to end complicity in its actions.
It also called for immediate global action to protect Palestinians and dismantle Israel’s military rule and apartheid system.
“Palestinians are being left exposed to escalating violence while Israel advances its project of elimination in the West Bank. Governments cannot condemn these crimes while granting Israel the impunity to continue,” said Novak.
“Together with international institutions, they must use every means available under international law to stop Israel’s crimes and halt the machinery of violence and destruction that is tearing Palestinian life apart.”

Iran learn volleyball fixtures for 2026 Asian Games
TEHRAN - The schedule for Iran’s men’s national volleyball team at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, has been announced, with Roberto Piazza’s side set to open their campaign against Kyrgyzstan.
The men’s volleyball tournament at the 2026 Asian Games will be held from Sept. 26 to October 2, with 16 teams competing for the gold medal.
Iran have been drawn in Group B alongside Indonesia, Thailand and Kyrgyzstan and will begin their campaign against Kyrgyzstan on Sept. 27.
Piazza’s squad will then face Thailand before completing the preliminary round against Indonesia in the following days.
 
  
Group Stage Draw
Group A: Japan, Pakistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan
Group B: Iran, Indonesia, Thailand, Kyrgyzstan
Group C: Qatar, India, Vietnam, Hong Kong
Group D: South Korea, China, Chinese Taipei, Philippines
The top two teams from each group will advance to the knockout stage and compete for places from first to eighth. The remaining eight teams will enter the classification phase, where they will battle for positions ninth through 16th.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tuvalu Foreign Minister Paulson Panapa arrived in Taiwan on Sunday for a five-day visit at the invitation of the Taiwanese government.
Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) hosted a luncheon for Panapa and his delegation on Monday, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In his remarks, Lin said he was happy to see Taiwan and Tuvalu continue to deepen cooperation across various fields.
He also highlighted several recent agreements between the two countries, including those on labor cooperation, double tax avoidance, and unmanned systems. This demonstrates a shared commitment to strengthening institutional cooperation and expanding mutually beneficial partnerships, he said.
Both countries are exploring new cooperation mechanisms under the principles of comprehensive diplomacy and the Diplomatic Allies Prosperity Project to enhance Tuvalu’s resilience and promote sustainable development, Lin said.
Lin added that in agriculture and fisheries, the two countries are advancing projects such as milkfish farming to improve Tuvalu’s food security and enhance knowledge sharing.
Panapa thanked Taiwan’s long-standing support for Tuvalu. He noted that many cooperation projects have been centered on improving livelihoods and promoting development. Facing increasingly severe challenges such as rising sea levels and intensifying extreme weather, Panapa said Tuvalu urgently needs to enhance its capacity for climate adaptation and sustainable development.
He expressed hope that the two countries will further deepen cooperation in these areas to achieve lasting shared prosperity.
The foreign ministry said it will continue to deepen bilateral ties and expand areas of cooperation through the Diplomatic Allies Prosperity Project.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The DPP and Japan’s Liberal Democratic Party held talks Monday on security and China’s gray-zone tactics.

DPP Legislator Wu Szu-yao (吳思瑤) said the expanded format also brought expertise in education and culture into discussions that had traditionally focused on security and economic issues.
DPP Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) said China’s pressure was no longer limited to military activities and also included cyberattacks and cognitive warfare, per Liberty Times. He said Taiwan and Japan should develop stronger ways to resist such threats.

Tainan opens drone training center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:55:09 UTC
21:55:09 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tainan Fire Department said Monday that it had opened a drone training center at CTBC University of Technology.
The department said the center would improve emergency response efficiency. It has trained 64 drone operators with advanced professional qualifications.
Mayor Huang Wei-che (黃偉哲) presided over the opening ceremony. He said drone operators could now train locally instead of traveling elsewhere, according to a city government press release.
Huang said technology requires skilled operators to achieve maximum efficiency. He cited the deployment of 12-lead electrocardiogram equipment, which helped paramedics increase the success rate for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest cases from 27% to 39%.
Huang said drones were becoming increasingly important for surveying rough terrain and monitoring rescue efforts. He added that firefighters had previously needed to travel to Kaohsiung for drone training.
The partnership with CTBC University of Technology saves time and manpower while developing local expertise.
The department said professional training requires certified facilities. The university has classrooms and testing sites approved by the Civil Aviation Administration, allowing the department’s drone operators to train regularly.
The department said the partnership would extend beyond access to facilities to include professional training, technical exchanges, and new technology.

Taiwan’s China Airlines cuts emissions with sustainable fuel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:54:38 UTC
21:54:38 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China Airlines said Monday that it used a 40% blend of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) on a long-haul flight to Amsterdam for the first time, cutting an estimated 93.2 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.
The Sunday flight from Taoyuan to Amsterdam marked China Airlines’ fifth participation in SkyTeam’s Aviation Challenge and its first use of a 40% SAF blend on a long-haul route, per CNA. The airline said the emissions reduction was equivalent to one-quarter of Daan Forest Park’s annual carbon absorption or the emissions produced by 40 passenger cars.
China Airlines President Chen Han-ming (陳漢銘) said the airline had used SAF eight times since 2022, with the latest flight using about 36.3 tonnes, per Liberty Times. He said Amsterdam was chosen because the Netherlands had extensive experience with sustainability initiatives.
The demonstration flight also used meal trays and cutlery that were 30% lighter than previous versions, as well as lower-carbon meals and soy-based ink for printed materials. Michelin Green Star restaurant Little Tree Food provided vegetarian meals, while passengers were encouraged to use digital boarding passes.
Chen said SAF had historically cost about 2.5 to three times as much as conventional jet fuel, although the difference varied with oil prices. He said China Airlines hoped to reach a more advanced level of sustainability before considering whether the higher cost of SAF could be passed on to passengers.
This year’s Aviation Challenge focuses on bringing airlines and supply-chain companies together to support the transition to net-zero emissions, CNA reported. China Airlines has also cooperated with Formosa Plastics and Foxconn on sustainability projects.

Experts expect Brent crude at $95-115 per barrel in near term
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:51:39 UTC
21:51:39 KST

MOSCOW, September 14. /TASS/. The price of Brent crude will hover around $95-115 per barrel in the near term, while a surge to $150 is not currently seen as a base-case scenario, experts surveyed by TASS believe.
Alexey Belogoryev, Research Director at the Institute for Energy and Finance, noted that many oil futures traders were "badly burned" in the spring and summer of 2026 after betting on a much stronger and more sustained price rally, leaving them skeptical about prospects for further growth.
"Therefore, I would expect prices to hold within the $95-115 per barrel range for Brent for now. If the situation does not improve fundamentally by the end of the year, a move toward $150 is indeed possible, though it is far from the base-case scenario at this stage," he said.
Nikolay Dudchenko, an analyst at Finam Financial Group, also downplayed the likelihood of prices hitting $150, though he admitted a potential rise to $120. "It appears that national oil reserves may still be sufficient to curb further price growth. Moreover, high oil prices could eventually impact demand itself, leading to its gradual destruction," he explained.
The average oil price for 2026 is projected at $93-95 per barrel by Belogoryev, and $80-90 under Finam's base-case scenario, according to Dudchenko.
Analysts explained that the Middle East conflict and the lack of progress toward its resolution remain the key factors driving prices, alongside declining crude and petroleum product inventories and upward pressure from rising refined product costs. Brent crude futures for November delivery on the ICE currently trade at $107.9, up 3.15% from the previous close.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has said that a drone attack near a train carrying European officials in Ukraine was intended to intimidate Western countries and discourage them from supporting Kiev.
"I think about that it is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support," Kallas told reporters on Monday on the doorstep of the European Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi, Finland.
"The question for us is: What do we take from that message? I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine, and we are not scared off," she said.
Kallas argued that backing down would serve Russia's objective of forcing Ukraine into "submission."
"And like I've said several times, this is not their end goal. Their end goal is much more. So we have to stand firm on this," she added.
Her remarks came after German newspaper Der Spiegel reported that a privately chartered train traveling from Kiev toward Poland on Sunday, carrying European officials and former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson, was evacuated following a nearby drone attack.
Kallas also highlighted growing security concerns in the Arctic, pointing to Russia's reopening of former Soviet military bases, missile exercises in the High North and China's increasing interest in the region.
She said the EU is preparing a new Arctic strategy with security at its core, which is expected to be presented in October.
Kallas said the EU must maintain a unified position on Arctic security and other issues affecting the region, adding that Greenland would probably not be discussed specifically.
US President Donald Trump repeatedly called for US control of Greenland during his presidency, calling it a historical and strategic necessity. However, both Danish and Greenlandic leaders firmly rejected the proposal, maintaining that Greenland "is not for sale."

Sixty-six-million-year-old fossil unearthed in Türkiye's capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:48:25 UTC
21:48:25 KST

A fossil belonging to a gastropod that lived along the shores of the Tethys Sea 66 million years ago has been discovered at an archaeological site in Ankara, Türkiye’s Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said.
The fossil was unearthed during excavations at Kulhoyuk in the Oyaca neighbourhood of Ankara’s Golbasi district.
Ersoy said on social media on Monday that the specimen was believed to date from the final phases of the Tethys Sea, a prehistoric body of water that once covered parts of what is now central Anatolia.
Researchers are examining whether residents of Kulhoyuk found the fossil elsewhere and deliberately brought it to the settlement thousands of years ago.
The possibility could offer new insights into how the object reached the site and what significance it may have held for its inhabitants.
Gastropods are a class of molluscs that includes snails and slugs.
Ancient settlement
Kulhoyuk is a roughly 5,000-year-old settlement associated with the Hattian and Hittite civilisations. The fossilised creature therefore did not live alongside the settlement’s inhabitants.
The discovery follows the identification of what archaeologists described as the earliest-known seed remains of Ankara’s distinctive “Sevgi Cicegi”, or Love Flower, inside a 4,000-year-old Hittite vessel at the same site.
Excavations at Kulhoyuk have been ongoing since 2021 under a long-term archaeological programme backed by the Turkish presidency.
The work is led by Associate Professor Derya Yilmaz Tekin on behalf of Ankara University and the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
Ersoy said excavations would continue to shed light on Kulhoyuk’s history through further discoveries.

Kremlin comments on Trump's call, Finland's decision, situation on oil markets

MOSCOW, September 14. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump's call on Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian civilian infrastructure, Finland's decision on "nuclear deterrence" and the situation on oil markets became the main topics of briefing by Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the Kremlin representative.
On the president's schedule
- Russian President Vladimir Putin returned from his trip to India late on Sunday evening.
- The head of state held a meeting today with Novgorod Region Governor Alexander Dronov.
On Trump's call to Kiev
- Russia can only welcome calls on Kiev to stop attacking Russian civilian infrastructure: "We can only welcome any call on the Kiev regime to end strikes on civilian economic infrastructure."
On the situation on oil markets
- The situation in global oil markets is worsening rapidly due to instability and a new round of escalation in the Persian Gulf: "We see the general situation in oil markets deteriorating rapidly, which is largely due to instability and new rounds of escalation in the Persian Gulf region."
- The loss of Russian petroleum products from international exports is affecting global markets: "Is the volume of Russian petroleum products no longer available for international export due to the export ban large enough to affect global markets? Yes, indeed, it is."
- The deteriorating situation on oil markets cannot but cause concern for global economies: "We are seeing huge volumes of oil being taken off the market. The disruption of the oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia alone has removed more than 4% of global supplies from world markets. This cannot but have the most serious consequences, and it cannot but cause concern for global economies."
On the ban on petroleum product exports
- The ban on exports of Russian petroleum products remains in effect and is aimed at ensuring conditions for saturation of the country's domestic market: "As for our supplies, Russia has indeed imposed a ban on the export of petroleum products. The ban is currently in effect and is aimed primarily at ensuring sufficient supply for the domestic market."
- The issue of lifting the ban on the export of Russian petroleum products will appear on the agenda once the country's domestic market is saturated: "As our domestic market becomes reliably saturated, the issue of lifting such a ban will appear on the agenda, and an additional volume [of petroleum products] will then be directed to global markets."
On the fulfillment of tasks by the Russian army
- The Russian Armed Forces continue to carry out their missions across Ukraine: "Our forces carry out their missions throughout Ukraine, and they will continue to do that."
- "It was a major misconception even before to claim that Ukraine supposedly had the potential to withstand Russian pressure. Those were deeply flawed notions."
- Some continue to hold the mistaken view that Ukraine has the potential to withstand Russian pressure: "Some people stick to this mistaken view."
- It is becoming increasingly evident to Western analysts and professionals that Russia -- judging by the dynamics on the frontlines -- is consistently moving toward achieving its goals: "It is becoming increasingly clear to professionals and truly serious analysts -- based on the dynamics observed on the frontlines -- that Russia is indeed improving its positions day by day and is consistently moving to its goals."
- The momentum of the advance on special military operation fronts will be maintained, "no one should have any doubts about this."
On third countries' contribution to the settlement in Ukraine
- Any country can use its influence over the Kiev regime to encourage it to be more flexible and to bring the conflict to a resolution: "On the whole, any country can use its influence over the Kiev regime to encourage it to be more flexible, which would be a significant contribution to the settlement process."
- Russian President Vladimir Putin welcomed the readiness of the Chinese and Indian leaders to contribute to efforts to settle the Ukraine conflict: "Indeed, both [Chinese] President Xi [Jinping] and [Indian] Prime Minister [Narendra] Modi took an active interest in Ukraine-related issues during meetings in New Delhi and spoke about their countries’ readiness, if necessary, to play a role in settlement efforts and make their own contribution. President Putin took it quite positively."
- The Russian president had provided other leaders with "additional clarification of what the settlement situation is really like and where things stand on the front."
On Finland's decision
- The Kremlin declined to comment on Finland's decision to join the France-promoted project of so-called advanced nuclear deterrence: "I don't quite understand what this concept is, to be honest. I still need to learn some details. Therefore, I would refrain from any comments."
On the possibility of BRICS expansion
- The expansion of BRICS and specific candidates for membership were not discussed at the summit held in New Delhi: "In concrete terms, specific candidate countries for expansion were not discussed."
- Russia supports Cuba's desire to join BRICS: "Of course, Russia supports Cuba's desire to join the work within BRICS."

PISA student assessments: President Erdogan says Türkiye sees improved ranking in reading, math, and science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:44:26 UTC
21:44:26 KST

Fatma Zehra Solmaz and Seyit Kurt
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
The ranking of Turkish students in science, mathematics and reading -- the three core subjects assessed under the 2025 Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) -- rose 50%, said the nation’s president on Monday.
 
Speaking at a ceremony in the capital Ankara marking the start of the 2026-2027 school year and the opening of newly completed education investments, Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the latest PISA results confirmed the country’s progress in education.
 
According to the PISA 2025 report, which included 91 countries, Türkiye saw the largest increase in scores among OECD countries in science, mathematics, and reading, he said.
 
“Türkiye’s ranking in all three areas rose 50%. We became the only country to significantly improve its performance in all three,” Erdogan said.
 
He added that Türkiye was also the only OECD country to improve performance among both advantaged and disadvantaged groups of students in terms of equal opportunities.
 
Erdogan congratulated teachers, students, and parents who contributed to the results.
 
He also criticized attempts to downplay the assessment results, saying the achievement should be a source of pride for the Turkish nation.
 
Erdogan said Türkiye’s young people are increasingly achieving success not only in education but also in sports, arts, science, and other fields.
 
“Despite some constant pessimistic scenarios, a truly successful generation is emerging -- one that follows the world, uses technology well, and strives to improve itself,” he said.
Education investments
 
Erdogan also highlighted Türkiye’s education investments, saying education has received the largest share of the central government budget for the past 24 years, since the Justice and Development (AK) Party came to power.
 
He said the share allocated to education more than doubled from 7.6% of the central government budget in 2002 to 15.33% in 2026.
 
The number of classrooms across Türkiye climbed from 343,000 in 2002 to 626,000 today, he added.
 
In Ankara alone, 30 new schools with a total investment value of 1.989 billion Turkish liras have opened over the past two years, adding 544 new classrooms, Erdogan said.
 
He said the investments seek to ensure equal and fair access to education for all children, regardless of their income level, while providing better conditions for teachers to do their work.

Japan’s Failed Centrist Experiment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:43:00 UTC
21:43:00 KST

The Centrist Reform Alliance (CRA), once thought to pose a significant threat to Takaichi Sanae’s hold on power, came to an unremarkable end. After nearly seven months of negotiations among the CRA and its sister parties, the Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP) and Komeito – both of which had dissolved in the lower house but continued to exist in the upper chamber – the three parties concluded that a complete merger would not proceed. As a result, the CRA is set to split into two groups, with former Komeito members returning to their former party and former CDP-affiliated members launching a new party. One member of the latter group will remain in the CRA to oversee its dissolution.
While the process of ending the CRA is already complicated enough, what makes it even more difficult for voters to grasp is that former CRA members will form a parliamentary group in the lower house. In other words, while the two parties have decided that they cannot be part of the same party, they still believe that they need to act as one, at least within the lower house.
The main cause of the breakdown in negotiations has been said to be the CDP’s reluctance. While Komeito was willing to join the CDP, which essentially shared its policy positions, the CDP ultimately could not reconcile its policies with those of Komeito. Komeito is more right-wing than the CDP’s positions on national security and nuclear energy.
Moreover, with local elections approaching next spring and the CRA having performed poorly at the February 2026 polls, local branches of the CDP have grown concerned that joining the party could put them at a disadvantage electorally. With the CDP having the largest number of local legislators among the opposition parties, second only to the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), it had much to lose by alienating its local candidates and organizations.
However, confidence may also have factored into the CDP’s calculations. While the CRA had consistently struggled in the polls, the CDP has significantly outperformed the alliance in some polls. According to an August poll by TV Asahi, the CDP recorded 4.7 percent support, compared with just 1.8 percent for the CRA. Similarly, an NHK poll put support for the CDP at 2.8 percent, compared with 1.7 percent for the CRA. These figures may have reinforced the CDP’s belief that it could perform better on its own than as part of a broader alliance.
Nevertheless, the CDP’s record in national elections tells a different story. Since its reorganization in 2020, the CDP has either lost seats or significantly underperformed other opposition parties in terms of changes in its parliamentary strength. In both the 2021 lower house election and the 2022 upper house election, the CDP ended up with fewer seats than it had before the election.
Although the party surged from 98 to 148 seats in the 2024 lower house election, the increase came overwhelmingly from single-member districts, where the CDP benefited from a favorable electoral environment, including the political-funds scandal involving LDP candidates. By contrast, its performance in the proportional ballot barely improved from the previous election: its proportional vote total increased only marginally, despite higher voter turnout.
In the 2025 upper house election, the CDP’s parliamentary representation remained essentially flat, while it fell to third place among the opposition parties in the proportional vote, behind the Democratic Party for the People and Sanseito.
Before the 2026 lower house election, the CDP’s alignment with, and eventual incorporation into, the CRA alongside Komeito was intended to reverse the party’s declining appeal among younger voters. Younger Japanese were thought to favor tangible policy outcomes – from lower costs of living to robust national security measures – over simply opposing the governing party. However, the electoral strategy failed.
This does not mean that so-called “resistance opposition,” a label that some pundits have come to associate with the CDP brand, lacks sufficient appeal to give the party staying power. Especially among older generations, opposing the LDP on normative issues such as the interpretation of Article 9 of the constitution and a zero-tolerance stance on nuclear energy – both core issues on which the CDP has refused to compromise – remains essential to their political orientation. However, as past election results make manifestly clear, those who could be described as “resistance liberals” do not constitute a majority, while parties that have performed well electorally in recent elections are gaining ground among younger voters.
With a weakening yen driving up prices across the board and a deteriorating security environment not only across the region but around the globe leading to abandonment of strict application of pacifism, resistance-oriented politics is increasingly seen as an unrealistic approach to governing a country. The CDP may be playing it safe by relying on tactics that succeeded in a different era, but by going it alone, it risks doing a disservice to its constituents and diminishing the political standing it might otherwise have strengthened through its alignment with the CRA.

European states warn of 'long-term Russian threat' in Arctic, urge EU to take proactive role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:40:30 UTC
21:40:30 KST

Melike Pala
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
European countries warned on Monday that Russia poses a "significant and long-term threat" to Euro-Atlantic security, calling on the European Union to strengthen its presence and preparedness in the Arctic.
In a joint declaration adopted at the European Arctic Summit, leaders from Finland, Denmark, Estonia, France, Greece, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Romania and Sweden said growing geopolitical competition and the ongoing war in Ukraine are reshaping the Arctic's strategic environment.
"We note with serious concern the significant and long-term threat Russia poses to Euro-Atlantic security," the leaders said, pointing to what they described as Moscow's efforts to increase its influence in the Arctic and growing hostile and hybrid activities against Europe.
The leaders called for a stronger and more strategic EU role in the European Arctic, stressing the need for enhanced preparedness amid changing security conditions.
"We call for the European Union to take on a more strategic and proactive role in the European Arctic and commit to strengthening the Union’s Arctic engagement in a coherent and forward-looking manner with adequate resources and in line with evolving geopolitical realities," the declaration said.
They called for increased maritime domain awareness and greater use of space-based capabilities to improve information-sharing and develop a more integrated picture of developments in the region.
The statement also highlighted the need for greater investment in military mobility, cross-border connectivity and infrastructure in the EU's northernmost regions.
They stressed the importance of developing dual-use infrastructure and protecting critical infrastructure on land and at sea as the Arctic becomes increasingly accessible and strategically contested.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his desire to take control of Greenland for strategic and historical reasons, pointing to China and Russia's interest in and growing presence in the region.

Joyce dismisses threats of 'tanked economy' from negative migration rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:40:21 UTC
21:40:21 KST

Barnaby Joyce says One Nation will follow 'will of the people' over economist warnings on migration
In short:
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce says voters are "tired" of economists, dismissing warnings about the impacts his party's migration policy could have on the economy.
The party has proposed sending migration to net negative rates for three years by heavily restricting student visas and blocking visas for family members of skilled workers.
What's next?
Labor and the Coalition are also proposing to slash migration, but have not detailed their policies.
One Nation is "not afraid" to drive migration to negative levels, with its Treasury spokesman saying he will follow the will of the people, not warnings from economists, in deciding how deeply to cut migration rates.
Business and the university sector have warned One Nation's proposal to cut migration by about 750,000 places over three years would devastate the economy.
Speaking on ABC National Forum, Mr Joyce said voter concerns on migration had to be respected.
"The will of the Australian people is so pronounced, this has to be dealt with, we will deal with it," Mr Joyce said.
Political commentator George Megalogenis said no government had ever purposefully caused a net outflow of migrants.
He said migration had been negative only four times in Australia's history: twice during the depressions of the 1890s and 1930s, and twice during the deployment of soldiers during the first and second world wars.
"If you're going to take … 766,000 people out of the Australian economy and society for three years, you have tanked the economy in a way that is on the scale of the depression of the 1890s and 1930s," Mr Megalogenis said.
Net overseas migration has been falling from its peak in mid-2023, when international borders reopened after the COVID-19 pandemic.
While the surge of migrant arrivals has slowed to pre-COVID rates, the number of migrants departing has also remained flat, leading to migration rates still above the government's long-term forecasts and above the pace of housing construction.
Joyce: People 'tired' of economists
The National Forum heard views on migration amid a raging debate on the issue — while Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all taken a position to cut migration rates, the details of which visa categories should be cut often prompts fierce reactions from sectors where there are sometimes already workforce shortages.
One Nation yesterday announced its plan to heavily restrict the number of international students allowed to study in Australia and block skilled workers from bringing family to Australia.
Net migration would be net negative for three years — meaning more people leaving the country than arriving — until an ongoing cap of 130,000 places a year took effect.
Mr Joyce defended One Nation's proposal, but dismissed questions about the economic impact it could have.
"The issue of what it is going to cost I think is contentious, but I have no concern about following the will of the Australian people," Mr Joyce said.
"I think the Australian people are sort of tired of the fact that you have to go to an economist to come up with public policy, to go to the Parliamentary Budget Office, and, to be quite frank, I have been around this game for a while and I have never seen a forward estimates in any budgetary paper be even close to the mark."
Mr Joyce said he was not worried about what the Parliamentary Budget Office or another office might conclude about One Nation's migration policy "because they're not elected, I am".
He noted that the party's policy did not touch demand-driven visa programs, like the Pacific worker program which many farmers relied on, or visas for skilled workers themselves — just those that would allow them to bring family.
Earlier, the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) warned that pursuing a pre-determined migration target was a mistake.
"If you are basing the outcome on a set of arbitrary numbers and an arbitrary target, which is not achievable without across-the-board cuts in a whole range of categories, then you are going to do long-term damage to the Australian economy," ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar said.
Speaking on National Forum, former deputy prime minister and Nationals MP John Anderson said Australia had only avoided recession because of high migration rates.
But he said that voters were being drawn away from the major parties by a concern about migration.
"A balanced, reasonable immigration rate is good economically," Mr Anderson told National Forum.
"It's good socially, whilst we agree 'the law of the land' really does apply, but we need to realise how badly broken [the migration system] is."
"We are here because One Nation has captured the initiative, because vast numbers of Australians think the system is now not working for them."
Labor and Coalition yet to settle migration policy
Both Labor and the Coalition have announced their own intentions to cut migration as One Nation's popularity has surged.
The federal government has a target to reach a net migration rate of 225,000 a year by 2028, but is yet to detail new policy intended to bring down migration from the current rate of about 300,000 a year.
Labor's planned changes to migration were postponed several weeks ago, and continue to be debated by cabinet.
The Coalition, meanwhile, has signalled its intention to tie Australia's migration program to housing construction rates to ensure that migration does not outpace housing supply — though it has not yet detailed that proposal.
Frontbencher Andrew Hastie said cutting migration would require "trade-offs", which was why his party was still working through its position.
"We are committed to this, to getting it right, though — that is the difference between us and One Nation," Mr Hastie said.
Mr Hastie said he agreed with One Nation's proposal to reduce temporary graduate visas, as was "stopping the visa hopping", but he said it was unclear how One Nation intended to do that.
Loading...
Nyadol Nyuon: Migration debate a proxy for race
While much of the debate has focused on what level to cut migration by, and population pressures on housing and infrastructure, there has also been a question around who should be allowed to migrate to Australia.
One Nation has proposed banning some migrants by preventing travel from countries where the Department of Foreign Affairs has issued a "do not travel" advisory due to terrorism or other security risks.
The Coalition has proposed tightening the test for prospective migrants to make compliance with a statement of Australian values a binding visa condition, and delaying access to social security supports for non-citizens.
Human rights advocate and lawyer Nyadol Nyuon said trying to pin criminality on certain communities was the kind of thing dividing Australians.
Ms Nyuon said the migration debate was often used as a placeholder for conversations around race.
"I don't have to look a particular way to love this country, but whenever we attempt to speak about how our belonging can look like, you meet such resistance, and the majority of the time that resistance comes from how you look," Ms Nyuon said.
Loading...
Multicultural Affairs Minister Anne Aly said she feared losing the Australia she grew up in.
"I grew up playing cricket in a street with kids from Greece and Yugoslavia at the time, Italian, Chinese, and nobody cared. Nobody cared what language your mum spoke," Ms Aly said.
"Nobody cared that my skin got darker as the sun was over us. Nobody cared about any of that. And that's the Australia that I know. And I fear that that is the Australia that we're losing."

‘Small-Yurt Diplomacy’ Prevails at Kyrgyzstan’s World Nomad Games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:38:00 UTC
21:38:00 KST

You are walking through an ethno-village in rural Kyrgyzstan. On the right is a string of cultural zones organized by each of the country’s seven regions and two major cities, Bishkek and Osh. In each, traditional music is played, food is cooked, and dances are performed.
You keep walking, beyond a mound where spectators are watching age-old martial arts, past a bazaar where local wares are being bought and sold, before you finally reach the end of the road. You see another cluster of yurts.
As you approach, you get the feeling that you’re truly in a place where custom and culture still reign supreme. And then you almost get hit in the head with a lacrosse ball, flung in your direction from a tent conspicuously featuring an American flag.
Such was the setting in eastern Kyrgyzstan’s Kyrchyn Gorge at the start of September, as the country again hosted the World Nomad Games. The alpine valley was one of seven major locations during the games, featuring an extensive cultural program that included traditional games, music and dance, and sports such as eagle hunting, horseback archery, and tug-of-war.
For foreign governments and international organizations — including the United States, Qatar, South Korea, Turkiye, the European Union, and UNICEF — the occasion offered an enormous opportunity to engage with Kyrgyz visitors and practice a little cultural diplomacy of their own.
At some level, the strategy of directly appealing to people from across Kyrgyzstan made perfect sense.
Kyrchyn drew more than 150,000 people a day during the weeklong festivities, organizers say, more than four times the average attendance at previous editions of the games. The ethno-village offered foreign governments and organizations something formal diplomacy in Kyrgyzstan rarely provides: thousands of casual, face-to-face interactions with ordinary people.
The U.S. yurt, for example, let visitors try a number of American sports, like lacrosse, corn hole, and American football. It also featured a cardboard version of George Washington, mini tutorials on U.S. history, and a cutout of an American prairie wagon.
The European Union, meanwhile, brought eight European countries together under one canopied roof, allowing visitors to sample German pastries, Norwegian brown goat cheese, Swiss fondue, and Spanish olives while learning about the countries behind them.
The goal, according to yurt organizer Zarina Toichubekova, who works for a Kyrgyz-German organization aimed at helping the needs of the Kyrgyz diaspora in Europe, was to “demonstrate the friendship and cultural connections between Europe and Kyrgyzstan” while building new “people-to-people connections.”
“Many people were genuinely curious to learn about the traditions behind the products,” Toichubekova told me. “So while it was certainly an opportunity to present European culture and traditions, it was [also about] having a genuine two-way cultural exchange.”
That two-way exchange was perhaps most readily apparent at the UNICEF Yurt, where the focus was less on promoting a particular country than on connecting with the next generation. The organization opened its space for children and families to play traditional Kyrgyz games while learning about child rights, nutrition, and other issues.
“That intergenerational interaction was especially valuable. It showed that promoting a healthy lifestyle and preserving cultural heritage can reinforce each other,” UNICEF Kyrgyzstan’s Cholpon Zhanadylova told The Diplomat.
But beyond what was being put on show for local attendees, the fact that foreign countries used the World Nomad Games to appeal to Kyrgyzstan’s domestic audience is another reminder of how the event’s original logic has been turned on its head.
As Dr. Arzuu Sheranova, an independent researcher based in Germany, recently told The Diplomat, the games were initially intended to be “a kind of instrument” to “improve Kyrgyzstan’s national image” to the outside world.
“Especially after the coups in 2005 and 2010, and the looting [that took place] during those periods of time, the trust of foreign businesses and investors had been shattered,” Sheranova said. “So the games were introduced in order to attract foreign investments again, to develop tourism, and to rebrand the country as a stable, safe place.”
But this outward-facing focus seems to have largely dissipated. During this year’s games, despite the authorities’ repeated claims that the games will spur a “significant increase” in international tourism moving forward, attending almost any of the week’s events left you with the impression that the organizers were not measuring their success by the number of foreigners they had attracted.
That apparent shift in priorities is part of a broader change in how the government views the World Nomad Games, Kyrgyz political scientist Emil Juraev told The Diplomat.
“The primary target these days is actually a domestic audience,” Emil Juraev said, noting that the Kyrgyz government seemed to have intentionally arranged for host privileges of the World Nomad Games to cycle back to the country ahead of its elections in 2027.
Several major infrastructure projects completed before the games got underway, he also pointed out, had to be worked on around the clock to finish in time.
“Hosting the [Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit], the World Nomad Games on a whole different level… this is all supposed to be very legitimacy- and approval rating-confirming for the Kyrgyz government,” Juraev said.
