====================================================================================================

Xinhua Headlines: Southern Europe shows renewed economic resilience amid eurozone slowdown
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:51:23 CST
19:51:23 KST

* Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece, all deeply affected by Europe's sovereign debt crisis over a decade ago, have shown renewed vitality and resilience in recent years.
* Southern Europe's service-heavy economies and growing use of renewable energy had made them less vulnerable to some of the energy and trade shocks weighing on Europe's industrial core.
* The IMF's 2025 Regional Economic Outlook urged Europe to accelerate structural reforms while keeping trade open. Southern European countries have sought to combine the two, building on post-crisis reforms and existing industrial strengths while pursuing trade and investment ties with emerging economies.
* China has played a constructive role in this process through trade, investment and industrial partnerships.
MADRID, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- As the eurozone faces a subdued growth outlook, a different economic picture has emerged along its southern flank: Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece, all deeply affected by Europe's sovereign debt crisis over a decade ago, have shown renewed vitality and resilience in recent years.
In the second quarter of 2026, seasonally adjusted GDP in the euro area increased by 1.0 percent year-on-year. In contrast, Spain, Portugal and Greece recorded growth of 2.7 percent, 2.5 percent and 1.9 percent, respectively, while Italy matched the eurozone rate.
A report published in June by Allianz, an insurance company, described Southern Europe's post-2021 performance as "a clear shift in the geography of Eurozone growth, with Southern economies moving from chronic underperformance to cyclical leadership."
Analysts and market observers attribute this resilience to three overlapping shifts: a broader mix of growth drivers, financial and institutional repair reinforced by EU investment, and a pragmatic openness to external markets, capital and technology, including expanding industrial partnerships with China.
Together, these factors have helped Southern Europe withstand some of the pressures weighing on the eurozone's traditional industrial core.
SHOCKS SHIFTED SIDES
Recent shocks -- from supply-chain disruptions to energy-price spikes and trade tensions -- have not fallen evenly across the eurozone.
"In the current cycle, the asymmetry of external shocks has, so to speak, shifted sides," Pablo Sanz, a professor at Spain's National University of Distance Education, said in an interview with Xinhua.
Sanz said Southern Europe's service-heavy economies and growing use of renewable energy had made them less vulnerable to some of the energy and trade shocks weighing on Europe's industrial core.
The difference is also visible in the drivers of growth. In the second quarter of 2026, Spain's economy ministry said growth was supported by domestic demand, investment and industry, while Portugal's rebound was driven mainly by net external demand.
Investment, construction and services have supported Italy in recent years, while investment, consumption and net exports all contributed to Greece's growth in 2025. Tourism also remains an important source of activity, employment and services exports, particularly in Spain, Portugal and Greece.
A changing energy mix has provided another buffer. Eurostat data showed that over 60 percent of gross electricity consumption in Portugal, Greece and Spain came from renewable sources in 2025. The European Commission said growing renewable generation had lowered wholesale electricity prices, with gas influencing prices in only a minority of market hours in the Iberian Peninsula.
Labor supply has provided further support, particularly in Spain. According to Sanz, labor-market reforms that reduced excessive reliance on temporary contracts helped stabilize household incomes, while immigration expanded the workforce and supported employment and domestic demand.
Public investment has added another leg to the recovery. Allianz estimates that Italy, Spain, Portugal and Greece together account for almost 60 percent of funding under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), the centerpiece of NextGenerationEU.
"Public capital injected through NextGenerationEU funds has therefore served as a countercyclical firewall, financing green-transition infrastructure, digitalization and key industrial projects without placing excessive strain on national finances," Sanz said.
REFORM DIVIDENDS
The recent divergence also reflects differences in the timing of adjustment. The sovereign debt crisis forced Southern Europe to confront long-standing financial and structural imbalances.
The process varied across countries. Greece and Portugal entered broad assistance programs covering fiscal consolidation, bank repair, pension reform, and changes to labor and product markets. Spain received assistance focused on its banking sector, while Italy remained outside a bailout program and followed a more gradual course.
The adjustment carried a high economic and social cost, as domestic demand contracted and unemployment surged. Over time, however, banks reduced non-performing loans, households and businesses cut debt, and labor- and product-market rules were revised.
Spain and Portugal also broke with a pattern of running external deficits during periods of expansion and began regularly recording current-account surpluses.
A 2026 study by the National Bank of Belgium found that Spain, Portugal and Greece grew at an average annual rate of 1.7 percent between 2019 and 2025, compared with 0.6 percent for Germany, France, the Netherlands and Belgium. It linked their stronger performance partly to post-crisis reforms and fiscal consolidation.
Greece shows how the repair extended to the functioning of public institutions. According to the IMF, measures targeting tax evasion and informality helped narrow its value-added tax compliance gap from 24 percent in 2019 to about 9 percent in 2024.
Reforms have also covered the judiciary, business regulation and tax administration, although weak productivity and judicial delays remain constraints.
After the pandemic, EU conditionality took a different form. Rather than focusing primarily on correcting imbalances, RRF funding was tied to national recovery and resilience plans combining investment projects with reform commitments, with at least 37 percent of the budget allocated to climate and biodiversity and a further minimum of 20 percent to digital measures.
The plans have directed funding toward renewable energy, power grids, sustainable transport, industrial decarbonization and digitalization.
According to Sanz, Spain and Portugal have used EU funding for electric-vehicle value chains, industrial decarbonization and the digitalization of public administrations and small businesses, while Italy has coupled investment with reforms of public administration, the justice system and public procurement.
However, these gains should not be overstated. Sanz cautioned that, except in some technological and renewable-energy niches, Southern Europe's productivity gap with Northern Europe remained substantial.
An analysis published by the Jacques Delors Institute noted that the four countries entered the pandemic on different growth trajectories and have deployed RRF funds at different speeds. Although the facility has supported demand and investment, the analysis said, its lasting impact will depend on whether the projects and reforms raise productivity and potential growth.
The IMF's 2025 Regional Economic Outlook urged Europe to accelerate structural reforms while keeping trade open. Southern European countries have sought to combine the two, building on post-crisis reforms and existing industrial strengths while pursuing trade and investment ties with emerging economies.
COOPERATION WITH CHINA
China has played a constructive role in this process through trade, investment and industrial partnerships.
In Spain, cooperation with Chinese companies is increasingly moving beyond trade toward local manufacturing in the electric-mobility supply chain. Chery's partnership with Spanish automaker Ebro has revived production at the former Nissan plant in Barcelona, while CATL and Stellantis are jointly investing in a lithium iron phosphate battery plant in Zaragoza.
"Spain has become a gateway not only for distribution but also for manufacturing, taking advantage of the auto manufacturing ecosystem that our country has," said Raul Morales, communications director at Faconauto, Spain's federation of automotive dealers' associations, in an interview with Xinhua.
Portugal is following a similar pattern. Chinese battery manufacturer CALB is developing its first European factory in the Sines Industrial and Logistics Zone. The 2 billion-euro project is expected to create 1,800 direct jobs and help Portugal develop a battery value chain around its lithium resources.
In Greece, China COSCO Shipping Corporation (COSCO) acquired a majority stake in Piraeus Port Authority in 2016, becoming the operator of the entire port. The port has since strengthened its position as a major Mediterranean container hub.
Stefanos Gkikas, Greek deputy minister of maritime affairs and insular policy, described the cooperation between COSCO and the port authority as "productive," saying it had enhanced the port's competitiveness and strengthened Greece's position in global shipping.
In Italy, the Ministry of Enterprises and Made in Italy, Italian renewable-energy developer Renexia and China's MingYang Smart Energy have agreed to work toward establishing wind-turbine manufacturing capacity. The proposed investment, worth around 500 million euros (579.2 million U.S. dollars), is linked to the planned 2.8-GW Med Wind floating offshore wind project off Sicily.
Sanz described the four countries' approach to China as "a form of reasonable industrial pragmatism aligned with their growth needs."
"Greater openness to emerging economies is an undeniable advantage for Southern Europe's economic dynamism, provided that it takes the form of co-investment, technology transfer and local job creation," he said.
"The success of Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece will therefore depend on their ability to manage the complex balance between attracting highly competitive global capital and complying with EU regulations," he added. ■

Snail shells could help reconstruct prehistoric cyclones: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
18:51:11 CST
19:51:11 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Snails carry weather records on their backs that could be used to map extreme weather events and reconstruct the paths of past cyclones even in prehistoric times, a new study has found.
Researchers examined the rings on the shell of a Biggenden Banded Snail collected from Coalstoun Lakes National Park in Australia's southeast Queensland, linking its bands to weather records, according to a statement released Monday by Australia's University of Queensland (UQ).
Tiny samples taken from the shell at millimeter intervals were analyzed using high-resolution radiocarbon dating, revealing the age of the snail, when it lived and the weather during its lifetime, said Nicholas Patton, lead author of the study published in The Holocene.
"It contained elevated levels of radiocarbon from the nuclear tests in Australia in the 1960s, meaning we could date the growth bands and reveal the snail had lived for about 4.5 years," Patton said, adding that analyzing the oxygen and carbon stable isotopes of the different bands revealed insights into the rainfall the snail experienced.
Researchers found that the shell did not grow continuously during the snail's life, with periods of rapid growth separated by periods of little or no growth. They initially expected rapid growth to correspond to years of heavier rainfall, making more food available for the snail, but found the snail was responding to extreme rainfall events rather than annual wetness.
The study showed the growth spurts were linked to periods immediately following cyclones in 2015 and 2017.
"It shows that snail shells could be used to map extreme weather events for periods before modern meteorological records," said Honorary Professor Jamie Shulmeister in UQ's School of the Environment.
"It was surprising and quite exciting that the humble snail could be a tool to reconstruct the paths of past cyclones even in prehistoric times," he said.
The researchers' next step is to test the method using shells preserved in different sediment layers and combine the individual shell records to extend this information further back in time. ■

====================================================================================================

Parasitic worms aren’t just a gut problem—they can infest the brain, too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:50:52 UTC
19:50:52 KST

Tapeworms are typically thought of as a gut problem: Eat undercooked meat and you could be left with an intestinal parasite. But there’s another, more unsettling way these creatures can enter your body: you can swallow their microscopic eggs in food or water contaminated by an infected person’s feces.
That’s exactly what happened to a 52-year-old woman in the Philippines. She had no idea. For four months, she suffered headaches and visual hallucinations—and she eventually went to the emergency room at her local hospital.
The woman spoke fluently, but her words often did not make sense, resembling a “word salad.” She struggled to understand speech, name objects, repeat words and follow simple commands, says Bonifacio C. Pedregosa II, a neurologist at Jose R. Reyes Memorial Medical Center in the Philippines.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine, Pedregosa and a co-author lay out how the woman’s symptoms presented a medical mystery—one with a gory solution.
The woman’s visual hallucinations came and went, Pedregosa says. “She described seeing animals and people who were not actually present during these episodes,” he explains. Doctors initially wondered whether she had a psychiatric disorder, but her pronounced language comprehension problems prompted them to image her brain to get a closer look.
The scans revealed the source of the mystery: cysts scattered throughout her brain. Many contained a tiny bright dot—the scolex, the headlike part of a developing tapeworm larva, armed with suckers and hooks.
That telltale sign led the doctors to diagnose neurocysticercosis, an infection in which larval cysts of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium lodge in the brain.
Brain-wave testing also showed abnormal electrical activity, leading doctors to suspect her hallucinations were related to seizures.
Once swallowed, the tapeworm’s eggs hatch in the intestine, releasing larvae that can enter the bloodstream and travel to other tissues throughout the body—including the brain.
A common route of infection is fecal-oral spread: a person carrying an intestinal tapeworm sheds microscopic eggs in their feces, and poor hand hygiene while preparing food or even touching surfaces can allow those eggs to be swallowed by someone else.
Doctors couldn’t pinpoint where or how the woman became infected. In the previous year, however, she had spent time in evacuation centers where sanitation and food-handling hygiene were poor, Pedregosa says. In this case, the doctors treated the woman for the parasitic infection and suspected seizures. A month later, her symptoms had resolved, and repeat brain scans showed that the cysts had shrunk and the distinctive dots had disappeared.
But neurocysticercosis can be fatal. Dying parasites can trigger swelling in the brain, while cysts in certain locations can block the normal flow of fluid around the brain or cause seizures.
Hallucinations have appeared in other cases. In one case, a 15-year-old in Peru had brain scans resembling Swiss cheese and developed visual and auditory hallucinations, while another patient presented with hallucinations, as well as paranoid delusions.

Ukraine secures guaranteed capacity in future Klaipėda LNG terminal – PM

13:50:32 EEST

Ukraine has secured guaranteed LNG regasification capacity in the new Klaipėda terminal, which is currently under construction, Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky has announced.
"Ukraine has already made commitments and, in return, received guaranteed capacity in the new LNG terminal in Klaipėda, which is currently under construction. As soon as it is put into operation, we will be able to ensure guaranteed gas supplies for Ukraine's energy resilience and security, for which I sincerely thank our partners," Koretsky said at a press conference with Prime Minister of Lithuania Mindaugas Sinkevičius in Lutsk, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent reports from the scene.
He did not specify the volume of such capacity.
According to open sources, the construction of the new modern LNG terminal in Klaipėda, valued at over EUR 50 million, is scheduled to be fully completed by the end of 2027.
As reported, in June 2026, Naftogaz Group booked long-term LNG regasification capacity in Europe for the first time, specifically at the LNG terminal in Klaipėda (Lithuania) for the period from 2033 to 2044. The corresponding allocation procedure was successfully completed by the terminal operator KN Energies.
During Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's visit to Canada in September 2026, Naftogaz signed a memorandum with Kino Aski LNG regarding potential long-term supplies of Canadian liquefied natural gas. According to Acting CEO of Naftogaz Serhiy Fedorenko, within the framework of cooperation, the group, together with Kino Aski LNG, will assess potential demand for Canadian LNG in Europe and supply opportunities, in particular through the use of Naftogaz's long-term capacities at the Klaipėda LNG terminal, as well as other European terminals.
Kino Aski LNG is a Canadian LNG terminal project with a declared potential capacity of up to 15 million tons per year. It is being developed under the leadership of Canada's Indigenous peoples and aims to create economic opportunities for their communities in Quebec and Ontario.

Warm, but rainy: what the weather will be like in Ukraine on September 15
Kyiv • UNN
On September 15, it will be warm in Ukraine, with rain in some places and temperatures reaching +23°C. Colder weather and more precipitation are expected starting September 21.
On Tuesday, September 15, it will be warm and mostly dry in Ukraine, although some rain is expected. Precipitation is most likely in the eastern regions, as well as in Sumy, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk regions. This was reported by meteorologist Natalka Didenko, writes UNN.
Tomorrow, September 15, the weather in Ukraine will truly be like being in the mountains — windy, rainy, with clear spells and beautiful clouds. Rain is most likely in the eastern regions, in Sumy, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk regions — due to the activity of an eastern cyclone
Light rain is also possible in the western regions and in some areas of Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Kyiv and Chernihiv regions. According to the meteorologist, dry and sunny weather is expected across the rest of Ukraine.
According to her, daytime temperatures will range from +18 to +23 degrees in most regions. It will be cooler in Sumy, Kharkiv, Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions, where temperatures of +14 to +18 degrees are expected.
Weather in Kyiv
Comfortable weather is expected in Kyiv on September 15. During the day, temperatures will rise to approximately +20 degrees. Significant precipitation is unlikely, although light rain may occur in some places.
Weather next week
Didenko noted that, overall, the current week in Ukraine will be warm and comfortable, with little rain expected. At the same time, according to preliminary forecasts, which will still require clarification, next week, starting September 21, will be considerably colder and bring more rain.

New 9/11 records, a controversial AI math breakthrough and the hidden costs of the AI boom

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners. For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly news roundup.
Last Friday marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. Even a quarter century after that one devastating day, people are still dying as a result of the terrorist incursion—and, at least in some cases, as a result of government inaction. The World Trade Center Health Program, which is authorized to provide no-cost medical monitoring and treatment for certain health conditions determined to be connected to the 9/11 attacks, has around 140,000 members. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that some 400,000 people were exposed to toxic contaminants, risk of physical injury, and physically and emotionally stressful conditions following the attacks. According to previously undisclosed records released last week, New York City officials told the public that the air around Ground Zero was safe to breathe even when testing showed otherwise.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the release of more than 170,000 pages of documentation at a news conference last Tuesday. In addition to air quality reports, the packet includes internal memos discussing elevated levels of asbestos and other toxins found in environmental testing.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
[CLIP: Zohran Mamdani speaks: “ People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air. And then when they began to contend with the symptoms of the illnesses that followed, the government that had not hesitated to send them into harm’s way was nowhere to be found.”]
Feltman: The documents are available to the public via a searchable Web portal at sept11documents.cityofnewyork.us. Survivor advocates at the press conference on Tuesday said that this documentation could help jumpstart health research and support the legal claims of those in need of medical support. Mamdani also noted that many people who are eligible for assistance from the WTC Health Program are not registered for it.
[CLIP: Mamdani speaks: “ For so many New Yorkers who lived or worked or studied near Ground Zero, and for the thousands of others who worked on the pile, recovering those we lost and clearing the rubble, that was only the beginning of years of hardship and illness that would follow. Thousands of ironworkers and firefighters and office workers and so many more remember September 11th, not just each time we mark the passage of another year, but as Congressman Nadler once said, ‘Each time they take a struggling breath, each time they have to swallow a pill, each time another chemo dose is administered.’”]
Feltman: If you were below Canal Street in Manhattan or in the Dumbo or Brooklyn Heights neighborhoods of Brooklyn on 9/11 or in the immediate aftermath of the attacks, you can still sign up for medical assistance. You’re also eligible if you worked as a first responder for the attacks outside of NYC. Go to cdc.gov/wtc/apply.html for more information.
Now let’s move on to some AI news. You may have seen headlines last week about artificial intelligence solving one of math’s so-called million-dollar problems. But it turns out this story is actually pretty contentious. Luckily we’ve got just the guy to unpack it for you: Joseph Howlett. Joe is a senior reporter at Scientific American who covers physics, math, astronomy and more. He also happens to have a Ph.D. in particle physics from Columbia, so we’re in great hands. Take it away, Joe!
Joseph Howlett: Hey, Rachel! Last Tuesday was the craziest day in mathematics history, maybe. For the first time in 20 years, someone solved one of the seven Millennium Prize problems, which are, like, the biggest problems in math. If you solve one, you're supposed to get a million dollars. But this time the person that solved it was an AI or a group of AIs.
It’s called the Navier-Stokes problem. The Navier-Stokes equations govern how fluids move. So, like, any fluid, like air or water, how it swirls around in space, there’s these simple equations that tell you how that’s supposed to work. But those simple equations are really hard to work with. Mathematicians like after 150 years had no idea whether the equations work all the time or whether they sometimes completely fall apart. They call this blowup, and they’ve been looking for a blowup for decades. That’s the millennium problem, to find one or prove that it can’t happen
So about a year ago, two mathematicians got together and started using AI to try to solve this problem. About a month ago, they made really significant progress, but then rumors started to spread. One of these two mathematicians worked for Anthropic. So they were mainly using Anthropic’s Fable AI, but they were also checking its work all the time with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Codex. So they were going back and forth. About a month ago, they had this breakthrough.
There was also an effort underway to try to solve Navier-Stokes with an internal model at OpenAI. And at some point they heard news of this, and then they redoubled their efforts. The OpenAI model figured out the full problem, Navier-Stokes, in just a couple of days. And it did it with a method that was really similar to what those two mathematicians had been doing for a year. So to them, it seems like maybe the AI, kind of, was referencing their proof that they had been giving it in prompts, right? OpenAI insists that this isn’t what happened, that user data was not accessed, but it’s caused a big stir in the math community. Nobody’s really sure who to give credit to, and everybody’s really angry.
This is a huge deal for math for a couple of reasons. Like, any millennium problem being solved, like, it’s something people have been waiting for for decades, it’s what mathematicians, like, build their whole career trying to accomplish.
If Navier-Stokes were solved by a human, I would be on Science Quickly trying to tell you why math matters, right? That, like, fluids are in our everyday life, they determine how airplanes fly, and we don't understand them, and understanding them could have all kinds of ramifications for climate modeling and all kinds of stuff like that, right? That’s far more remote. You should care about this because mathematicians are now having a conversation that we all are soon gonna have to have, which is, like: Why do we do what we do? What is the value we get from it? And is the purpose to get as much done as quickly as possible by whatever means? Like, is AI a boon to the human experience, or is it taking something away? And like this is a question mathematicians are being forced to confront today, like, more than any other day and maybe more acutely than we’ve seen any field. But it’s a question that's coming for all of us.
Feltman: Thanks for that, Joe. Listeners, you can keep up with the latest on this story at scientificamerican.com.
Next up, we’ll check in with another one of our favorite correspondents from the SciAm newsroom: Chief Newsletter Editor Andrea Gawrylewski. She’s here to tell us about the backlash against SpaceXAI’s huge data center, which sits right at the border between Tennessee and Mississippi. Aptly dubbed Colossus 2, it’s an incredibly dense computing center that’s largely being powered by gas-fueled turbines. Thanks for coming on to talk about this, Andrea.
Andrea Gawrylewski: Thanks for having me, Rachel.
The data centers where SpaceXAI trains its chatbot Grok are in Memphis, Tennessee.
SpaceXAI decided to build its Colossus data centers in Memphis.
But the local power grid couldn’t deliver enough electricity on SpaceXAI’s timeline, so the company brought power generation onsite with portable gas turbines rather than waiting for a conventional power plant to spring up.
The temporary power plant for Colossus 2, the second of the data centers, backs up to a residential area in Southaven, Mississippi, which is just across the state line from the data center. So the power is generated in Mississippi and transmitted over the border into Tennessee.
As of a survey in July, the temporary power fleet was up to 69 turbines. And those temporary turbines are now being phased out as the permanent facility comes online.
But as for the people living next door? They say they’re plagued by the exhaust from the turbines and the relentless noise. The sound is like a jet plane revving up on the tarmac but it never takes off.
This is a story popping up around the country.
As AI companies build huge data centers, power becomes a constraint. Data centers now use around 4 to 5 percent of U.S. electricity, and the Electric Power Research Institute projects that that share could reach 9 to 17 percent by 2030.
As for the residents of Southaven, they filed a class action lawsuit alleging lost sleep from the noise and falling property values—the turbines are in their backyards and directly across from their houses.
Meanwhile, a preliminary analysis of air quality that was taken over four months around one Southaven home found that the fine particulate matter concentrations exceeded the EPA’s daily health-protection standard about a third of the time.
Plus, dozens of gas turbines in one place can produce very high levels of nitrogen oxides. Those pollutants can irritate the lungs, worsen asthma, and form ground-level ozone, the main ingredient in smog.
At least 10 schools, three daycares, two libraries, 11 parks and 27 churches sit within two miles of the plant, according to a local advocacy group.
In April the NAACP sued, calling the operation an unpermitted power plant.
But the Department of Justice moved to intervene on SpaceXAI’s behalf and asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit. They said that shutting down the power source for Colossus 2 would threaten AI innovation and national security.
One of the area residents told Scientific American, “It’s so easy for me to see just how our federal government is being leveraged against us”.
Feltman: Thanks, Andrea. Listeners, you can read SciAm’s feature article on Colossus online right now as well as in our October print issue. And don’t forget to subscribe to Today in Science to get stories like this one sent straight to your inbox.

‘Spirit of country is pluralism’: Owaisi hits back at Amit Shah’s UCC pledge, questions BJP allies’ independence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:46:10 UTC
19:46:10 KST

AIMIM chief Owaisi opposes Shah’s 2029 UCC deadline, says BJP allies must speak up
NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi on Monday hit back at Union home minister Amit Shah’s announcement that BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states would implement the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) before 2029, questioning whether the BJP’s allies had an independent political voice.Owaisi said the allies should demonstrate that they were not merely “choti BJP”, while arguing that the UCC was not about equality but about targeting Muslims.
In a post on X, Owaisi said the Law Commission appointed by the NDA government had concluded that a UCC was “neither necessary nor desirable” for India.Speaking to news agency ANI, Owaisi said the BJP was pursuing the UCC not for equality but to target Muslims. He alleged that the move was contrary to constitutional provisions including Articles 14, 25, 26 and 29.
“The very soul and spirit of this country is pluralism,” Owaisi said, adding that he believed the BJP and RSS were attempting to impose Hindu law on non-Hindus.
Owaisi challenges BJP to implement UCC in Goa
Owaisi also challenged Shah, the BJP and RSS to implement in Goa the same UCC framework introduced in Uttarakhand, Gujarat and Assam.“Go ahead and implement it in Goa,” Owaisi said, referring to the BJP’s stated plans for the state.
He questioned whether the party would actually introduce the same UCC there.Owaisi also cited provisions he said exist under Goa’s current legal framework, including provisions concerning second marriages in certain circumstances and exemptions relating to Catholic marriages and divorce proceedings.He said these provisions raised questions about the BJP’s argument for a uniform legal framework across religions.
Owaisi also questioned the BJP’s support for the UCC while BJP-ruled states have laws such as the Disturbed Areas Act, which he said prevents Hindus and Muslims from freely transferring property between each other.“It’s ironic that the BJP wants a UCC while its own states pass laws like the Disturbed Areas Act, which prohibit the sale of property between Muslims and Hindus,” he said.Owaisi also referred to laws concerning “love jihad”, alleging that such provisions had been applied against Muslims and Christians.“A UCC isn’t about equality; it’s about targeting Muslims,” he said.
Shah says UCC will be implemented before 2029
Shah had on Sunday said BJP-led NDA governments in all 21 states under their rule would introduce the UCC before 2029.“We have introduced the Uniform Civil Code in several states, and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA-ruled states, we will introduce the UCC before 2029,” Shah said in Mumbai.The UCC proposes a common set of personal laws covering matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption, irrespective of religion.Owaisi also drew a parallel with the controversy surrounding the National Register of Citizens (NRC) and the anti-CAA/NRC protests of 2019.He alleged that Shah’s “misplaced arrogance” and “chronology” had contributed to the protests and recalled that Prime Minister Narendra Modi had clarified at the time that no NRC was going to be implemented.
Owaisi said a similar situation was now unfolding around the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, which he alleged had caused hardship, particularly to minorities, SC/STs and migrants.He warned that an NRC would be “100 times worse” and referred to the experience in Assam.“The National Register of Citizens will force everyone to stand in line and prove their citizenship. In a country where 80 crore people depend on ration for food, you want them to find documents and prove their citizenship?” he said.

After 18 years flying Eagles, Barnes pilots get the F-35A
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:45:31 UTC
19:45:31 KST

- The 104th Fighter Wing at Barnes Air National Guard Base officially received the F-35A Lightning II in a September 13, 2026 ceremony.
- The jet replaces the wing's F-15C/D Eagles, which were retired in October 2025 after 18 years of service at Barnes.
The Massachusetts Air National Guard’s 104th Fighter Wing formally welcomed the F-35A Lightning II to Barnes Air National Guard Base on September 13, 2026, marking the aircraft’s arrival after a transition process that began more than three years ago. The ceremony drew Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, military officials and representatives from Kenya and Paraguay, whose militaries partner with the Massachusetts Guard through the state partnership program.
The Air Force picked Barnes in April 2023 as the preferred site for a new F-35A squadron, a decision that became final in December 2024 after an environmental review. The F-35A replaces the wing’s F-15C/D Eagles, which the 104th flew for 18 years after the aircraft arrived at Barnes in 2007. The wing retired its last three F-15Cs on October 23, 2025, sending them to the Air Force’s aircraft storage facility at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona.
“For generations, men and women at the 104th Fighter Wing have answered the call, protected the skies, served our state, and defended our country,” Healey said. “The arrival of the F-35A represents a new chapter for this great military installation here.”
The Air Force plans to base 18 F-35As at Barnes. The wing has not said how many aircraft have arrived so far or when it expects to reach full operational capability with the new jets. U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. David Halasi-Kun, who led the wing through the early stages of the conversion before Col. Michael Glass took command in December 2025, said the shift to a fifth-generation aircraft would take considerable work from the unit.
“The F-35A brings with it incredible capabilities that will be able to support combatant commanders around the world, as well as continued defense of the United States from our 24-hour alert site,” Halasi-Kun said.
The F-35A is a single-engine, radar-evading fighter built by Lockheed Martin. Its sensor suite is designed to combine data from multiple onboard systems into a single picture for the pilot, a capability the Air Force calls sensor fusion, and it can carry precision-guided weapons for strikes against ground and air targets. The jet’s stealth shaping and coatings are intended to reduce its radar signature compared with older fighters like the F-15.
The 104th’s mission includes providing armed fighters on 24-hour alert to respond to airborne threats over the northeastern United States, a role known as Aerospace Control Alert that the wing has carried out with the F-15 for nearly two decades. Air Force Maj. Gen. Gary Keefe, the adjutant general of the Massachusetts National Guard, said the F-35A purchase secures that mission for the base well into the future.
“We are securing our role as a cornerstone of national security for the next fifty years and beyond,” Keefe said.
Some 104th pilots who flew the wing’s final F-15 sorties last October have since trained to fly the F-35A and returned to Barnes among the unit’s first F-35A pilots. U.S. Air Force Capt. Kyle Eckert, one of those pilots, said the shift from flying the last Eagles out of Barnes to flying the base’s first F-35As felt like a “full circle moment.”

all images by Alix Urien, unless stated otherwise
a studio for conversation
The temporary space was busy from the beginning of the week. Alongside the social gatherings, it became a working studio for a series of podcast recordings with INDX|Global, bringing architects, designers, and other voices together for conversations around ideas shaping contemporary design.
Our conversations focused on utopia, with some of India’s leading architects and designers joining the discussion. The subject connected directly to designboom’s 2026 editorial direction, which has been exploring Utopian Optimism and the idea of utopia as something that can be used to imagine and work toward different ways of living.
the paris.designboom studio at 72 rue des Archives in the Marais
an apéro in the marais
On Thursday evening, the studio changed character again. The paris.designboom apéro welcomed the wider designboom community for an informal evening of drinks, food, and conversation. Friends, designers, architects, partners, and creatives came through the doors; familiar faces caught up, new introductions were made, and the studio gradually filled up as the evening went on. It was also a chance for people who usually know designboom through its editorial output to meet some of the people behind it. There was plenty of design-week talk, of course, but it was not really the focus. Conversations moved from projects and exhibitions to Paris, travel, work, upcoming plans, and whatever else came up.
hosting a week of conversations, gatherings, and workshops
clarks originals and topologie bring making into the mix
On Saturday, the studio became a workshop space. To close Paris Design Week, Clarks Originals and Topologie created an experience around customization, Japanese craft, the Clarks Wallabee, and Topologie’s Konbini bag. The workshop took its cue from katagami, the traditional Japanese technique of cutting paper stencils to create intricate patterns. Guests selected from a series of pre-cut designs and used them to customize the two pieces, starting with the Wallabee. They chose a stencil and color before applying the pattern to the vamp of the shoe, gradually building up a design of their own. The same idea continued with the Konbini bag, where selected motifs were applied through screen printing. From there, guests could add their own finishing touches, choosing laces and fobs for the Wallabee and straps for the Topologie bag.
Across the week, 72 Rue des Archives became a place where different parts of designboom could happen at once. But paris.designboom was also the first stop in a new travelling series of talks, exhibitions, and gatherings, moving from one design city to the next. Paris Design Week was the starting point, a few days of bringing the designboom community together.

USS St. Louis returns to patrol the southern border again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:42:08 UTC
19:42:08 KST

- USS St. Louis (LCS 19) departed Mayport on September 13, 2026, relieving USS Cooperstown to patrol near the U.S. southern border for U.S. Northern Command.
- The mission has rotated among Mayport-based littoral combat ships since 2025, with St. Louis, Wichita and Cooperstown each taking turns.
The littoral combat ship USS St. Louis (LCS 19) left Naval Station Mayport on September 13 to take over U.S. Northern Command’s mission patrolling waters near the U.S. southern border, the U.S. Navy said. The ship relieves USS Cooperstown (LCS 23), which returned to Mayport on August 31 after a four-month deployment to the region.
St. Louis previously served in the same role, completing a surge deployment that ended in November 2025. Since then, the mission has rotated among Freedom-variant littoral combat ships based at Mayport: USS Wichita (LCS 13) relieved St. Louis in November, and Cooperstown relieved Wichita in May 2026.
“Our crew has trained relentlessly for this deployment, and they stand ready for whatever challenges lie ahead,” said Cmdr. Lester Shewmake, commanding officer of USS St. Louis. “I could not be more proud to lead these Sailors.”
U.S. Northern Command is working with the Department of Homeland Security to add military support to U.S. Customs and Border Protection operations along the southern border. Navy ships assigned to the mission operate under the command’s maritime homeland defense authorities, working to interdict drug trafficking and other illegal activity at sea. Ships taking part typically carry an embarked U.S. Coast Guard Law Enforcement Detachment, which handles the actual boardings and arrests during interdictions, since Navy personnel do not have law enforcement authority on their own.
Cooperstown’s deployment, part of an effort the Navy has named Operation Ardent Vanguard, included stops at Corpus Christi, Texas, and patrols in the Gulf of America, the name the Trump administration adopted for the Gulf of Mexico in 2025. The Navy has not said whether St. Louis’s deployment will follow a similar track or how long it is expected to last.
Littoral combat ships are shallow-draft vessels built to operate close to shore, a design suited to patrolling coastal waters rather than open-ocean combat. St. Louis is the 22nd LCS delivered to the Navy and the tenth Freedom-variant ship in the class, which is built around a steel monohull, distinct from the aluminum trimaran design used on the competing Independence variant. The ship is assigned to Littoral Combat Ship Squadron 2 and homeported at Mayport, Florida.
St. Louis is the seventh Navy ship to carry the name. The first, a sloop of war launched in 1828, spent much of its service patrolling the coasts of the Americas and served as flagship of the West Indies Squadron, which worked to suppress piracy in the Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico during the 19th century.

Istanbul Airport expands as international traffic grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:39:35 UTC
19:39:35 KST

(AA Photo)
Istanbul Airport is expanding its runway and cargo facilities as international passenger traffic rises, while operator İGA plans to increase annual terminal capacity to 120 million passengers.
The airport handled 56.65 million passengers in January-August, up about 2 percent from a year earlier, according to provisional data from the General Directorate of State Airports Authority (DHMİ).
International passenger numbers rose about 3 percent to 44.71 million, accounting for nearly four-fifths of the total. Domestic traffic was broadly unchanged at 11.93 million. The airport serves more than 340 destinations through over 110 airlines, according to the Transport and Infrastructure Ministry.
Its summer traffic also put it ahead of London Heathrow.
Istanbul handled about 8.15 million passengers in July, compared with 7.9 million at the British hub, making it Europe’s busiest airport by passenger numbers that month.
On Aug. 16, Istanbul recorded its busiest day, with 290,287 passengers and 1,739 flights.
The latest addition to its infrastructure is a fourth main runway, due to open on Sept. 18 at a ceremony attended by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu said.
The 2,820-meter runway will be the airport’s first running east-west. It will bring the total to six, alongside three main and two reserve runways aligned north-south.
“We will shorten taxiing and flight times, especially for domestic flights and eastbound routes,” Uraloğlu said, adding that this would save fuel and time.
Uraloğlu said the east-west alignment would give controllers more options in crosswinds and other adverse weather conditions, helping improve on-time departures. Its proximity to hangars would also allow faster, more independent general aviation operations, he said.
The airport has already increased the number of aircraft it can handle through changes to runway operations. In April 2025, it became the first in Europe to introduce simultaneous operations on three independent parallel runways. The change raised hourly capacity from 120 to 148 aircraft movements, according to the European air traffic management organization Eurocontrol.
The terminal expansion is part of the airport’s second phase of development. İGA chief executive Selahattin Bilgen outlined the plan in December, saying adjustments within the existing terminal would be needed to accommodate 120 million passengers annually. He also set a target of close to 90 million passengers for 2026.
Cargo investment is expanding alongside the passenger business. The airport handled more than 2 million tons of cargo last year, according to Bilgen. Turkish Cargo, the freight division of Turkish Airlines, is enlarging its SmartIST terminal at the airport to handle 4.5 million tons annually.
The expanded cargo facility will have 370,000 square meters of enclosed space, with automated storage and handling systems designed to speed up processing. German equipment supplier Lödige Industries, which supplied systems for the terminal’s first phase, was selected again for the expansion.

Accoding to European Pravda, a European official expressed appreciation for Canada’s support for Ukraine, adding that the EU was ready to deepen cooperation with Ottawa as it seeks to forge closer ties with the country.
The talks follow a further expansion of relations between Kyiv and Ottawa. On September 10, Ukraine and Canada signed several bilateral agreements, including a declaration outlining plans to establish a 100-year partnership.
During their meeting in Calgary, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also discussed financial and defense support for Ukraine, including Canada’s potential participation in the FREYJA anti-ballistic program and cooperation on drone production.

Russia’s $100,000 Jet-Powered Weapons Are Outpacing Ukraine and the US, WSJ Reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:38:34 UTC
19:38:34 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s $100,000 Jet-Powered Weapons Are Outpacing Ukraine and the US, WSJ Reports
Russia has accelerated the development and mass production of a new generation of relatively inexpensive precision weapons, including the jet-powered Geran-5 drone and Banderol cruise missile, moving from testing to large-scale manufacturing faster than Ukraine and the United States.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Wall Street Journal on September 14, Russia has managed to develop, combat-test, modify, and begin serial production of the new systems within several years, highlighting Moscow’s ability to rapidly convert battlefield experience into weapons produced at scale.
The Geran-5 and Banderol represent an attempt to combine some of the capabilities of more expensive cruise missiles with the lower production costs traditionally associated with one-way attack drones. Both weapons are estimated to cost around $100,000 each, while US-made Tomahawk cruise missiles and comparable high-end systems cost more than $2 million.
WSJ reported that the weapons rely heavily on commercially available and dual-use Chinese components, including jet engines, navigation equipment, and communications electronics. Ukraine and other countries have identified Chinese-made parts in debris recovered from Russian weapons.
China has maintained that it regulates the export of technologies that could have military applications.
The Geran-5 marks a significant change from earlier Russian versions of Iran’s Shahed-series drones. While the original designs used propeller engines and traveled at relatively low speeds, newer Russian variants have incorporated faster propulsion, improved navigation, and communications systems intended to make interception more difficult.
Mike Monnik, chief executive of drone-threat intelligence company DroneSec, described the Geran-5 to WSJ as “essentially a poor-man’s cruise missile.”
The shift presents a new problem for Ukrainian air defenses, which have spent years developing methods to intercept slower Shahed-type drones. Faster jet-powered weapons can require different detection and interception systems and further complicate efforts to maintain a favorable cost ratio between incoming weapons and the interceptors used against them.
According to WSJ, Russian manufacturers have also benefited from an ability to move quickly from experimental designs to large-scale production once a system proves effective in combat.
Kateryna Bondar, a senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies’ Wadhwani AI Center, told the newspaper that Russian industry can move “very fast from idea and experimentation to production.”
Ukraine has also demonstrated an ability to rapidly develop new weapons, including jet-powered drones and long-range strike systems. However, WSJ reported that Ukraine faces greater constraints in production capacity and long-term industrial planning than Russia.
The challenge is also affecting the United States and other NATO members. Western governments are attempting to expand production of air defense interceptors, including missiles for Patriot systems, while shortening the time required to move new military technologies from development into mass production.
For Western militaries, that creates an economic challenge. High-end air defense missiles and fighter aircraft can successfully intercept drones, but repeatedly using expensive interceptors against weapons costing around $100,000 is difficult to sustain during large-scale attacks.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the US and NATO are consequently investing in cheaper counter-drone systems, including new jet-powered interceptors capable of engaging faster targets.
The technological developments have implications beyond Ukraine. Russia, Iran, and North Korea have expanded military cooperation and exchanged weapons and technical expertise, while lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine are increasingly shaping drone and air defense development in other theaters.
The production surge is already visible on the battlefield. Russia launched around 2,800 jet-powered drones against Ukraine in August, up from roughly 350 in June.

Russia Increases Jet-Powered Drone Attacks on Ukraine Eightfold, Launching 2,800 in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:38:28 UTC
19:38:28 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Increases Jet-Powered Drone Attacks on Ukraine Eightfold, Launching 2,800 in August
Russia sharply increased its use of jet-powered drones against Ukraine over the summer, putting growing pressure on Ukrainian air defenses with faster, harder-to-intercept systems.
Russia increased the intensity of its jet-powered drone attacks on Ukraine more than eightfold over the summer, launching around 2,800 such drones in August compared with roughly 350 in June, The Moscow Times reported on September 13, citing The Times.
Jet-powered drones travel significantly faster than older propeller-driven models, reducing the time available for Ukrainian air defenses to detect and intercept incoming targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said Russia launched around 800 jet-powered drones over just four days in late August, with most of them targeting Kyiv. According to Ihnat, the drones are being deployed in combat almost immediately after leaving production lines, according to The Moscow Times.
Russia currently uses two main types of jet-powered strike drones. One is the Geran, based on Iran’s Shahed design. Its latest fifth-generation version can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour, carry a warhead weighing up to 90 kilograms, and travel approximately 1,000 kilometers.
The second system, the Banderol jet-powered drone, has been used since the summer. It can reach speeds of up to 595 kilometers per hour, has a range of up to 480 kilometers, and can carry a 114-kilogram payload.
Anatolii Khrapchynskyi, a Ukrainian Air Force reserve officer and head of an air defense company, said the systems effectively provide Russia with a lower-cost alternative to cruise missiles. Their increased speed has sharply reduced the reaction window available to Ukrainian mobile fire teams, the outlet reported.
According to Khrapchynskyi, crews previously had around one minute to detect and engage older Shahed drones. Against jet-powered models, that window has fallen to approximately six seconds.
The higher speeds have also affected interception rates. Ihnat estimated that Ukraine can intercept up to 95% of older Shahed models, while the interception rate for jet-powered drones stands at around 60%.
The pressure intensified further in late August and into September, when Russia subjected Kyiv to an almost continuous two-week drone barrage, striking warehouses, civilian infrastructure, educational facilities, and other sites across the capital and surrounding region.
As a result, Ukraine is increasingly forced to use more expensive air defense assets against the faster drones, including scarce Patriot interceptor missiles as well as F-16, Mirage, and MiG-29 fighter aircraft.
A Ukrainian fighter pilot previously said even an older MiG can shoot down roughly a dozen jet-powered Shahed-type drones in a single mission, underscoring the importance of crewed aircraft in Ukraine’s multi-layered air defense system.
“Financially it’s painful, but that’s our purpose,” the pilot said. “In a single sortie even an old MiG can take out a dozen or so. You have to understand that since there aren’t many other options, you end up relying on skill and experience.”
Despite the higher cost of operating fighter aircraft, the pilot said their use against such drones remains justified, as intercepting aerial threats is a core function of combat aviation within Ukraine’s broader air defense network.
At the same time, Ukraine aims to have its first FREYJA anti-ballistic defense system completed by the end of 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 10, as the country pushes ahead with developing a domestically produced defense against ballistic missile threats with support from an expanding group of international partners.

Unwanted in the U.S., old oil equipment finds a new home in Venezuela
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:36:42 UTC
19:36:42 KST

Unwanted in the U.S., old oil equipment finds a new home in Venezuela
HUMBLE, Texas, Sept 14 - In the sweltering heat in Humble, Texas, just outside Houston, two workers were flattening out a yard with heavy compaction rollers, making room for pre-owned and auctioned U.S. oilfield equipment destined for a hoped-for oil revival in Venezuela.
At the edge of the yard sits a weathered, rusting heavy-duty commercial truck covered in dirt. The recently auctioned vehicle is one of a flood of trucks, rigs and other equipment bought up to facilitate an anticipated oil rebound in Venezuela, as U.S. businesses try to get in on Washington's about-face from seven years of sanctions on the OPEC nation to promoting a $100 billion reconstruction plan for the nation's industry.
Venezuela's needs include rigs, pumps, valve stations, welding equipment, and other instruments, according to state-run PDVSA. That equipment is finding its way to U.S. ports from Texas, Oklahoma, Colorado and other states, in various stages of wear and tear.
"Sometimes you get gems. Sometimes you get absolute trash," said Jesse Cole, CEO of Sky Drop Capital, an investment firm involved in acquiring equipment for Venezuela's operations.
Guanta Express, a shipping intermediary named for a key oil port in Venezuela, operates the yard in Humble. The company is shipping goods from around the U.S. in cargo vessels to the ports of Guanta and Maracaibo, Venezuela's largest points of entry for the oil industry.
"To the end of the year, we are going to be at full capacity. We already have orders lined up for the next two vessels," Greg Diaz, president of Guanta Express, said in an interview in Humble.
Containers shipped by Guanta Express carrying workover rigs arrived and unloaded in Maracaibo last week, according to photos seen by Reuters. The company expects to move two 1,500-horsepower rigs in its next two shipments, the largest it has ever sent to Venezuela, Diaz said.
Executives from companies including Chevron, SLB and Formentera Partners expect output capacity will need to expand in challenging basins, including Lake Maracaibo and the vast Orinoco Belt. That will require the procurement of more powerful equipment -- like those large rigs shipped by Guanta Express -- in coming months.
Other energy shipments are expected at the western coast port of Guaranao, according to a terminal source.
Interest from wildcatters looking to revive wells at mature fields is also expected to keep demand high for smaller workover rigs, analysts have said.
Venezuelan oil production peaked above 3 million barrels per day in the late 1990s but is now around 1.25 million bpd following decades of underinvestment, corruption and foreign sanctions.
PDVSA and Venezuela's oil ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
EQUIPMENT CONDITION A CONCERN
One concern in the industry is the reliability of pre-owned and auctioned equipment, the latter of which often comes with thousands of hours of use and no warranty.
In March, a three-year-old truck tractor used to move heavy equipment arrived in Maracaibo with a bright orange sticker distinctive of U.S.-based auctioneer Ritchie Bros., according to photographs seen by Reuters. The truck sold in December for $24,000 from the auctioneer's Newnan, Georgia, site, having already logged 5,551 engine hours and more than 140,000 miles.
While the U.S. Treasury Department has eased a large portion of sanctions on Venezuela, helping pave the way for U.S. insurance firms to underwrite equipment, many providers are reluctant to get into the business, sources said.
"The key issue for insurers is typically the lack of verifiable maintenance and inspection records," said David Peña, who leads the energy and power practice in Latin America for global insurance broker Marsh. Insurers may be less willing to offer coverage without independent inspections, or make coverage terms more restrictive, he said.
Ritchie Bros.' policies state that there are no warranties, and the tractor truck listing also said no guarantees could be made. A company spokesperson said it operates "global, public unreserved auctions" where equipment is sold to the highest bidder.
The equipment rush started not long after the January 3 U.S. raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
"The week after January 3rd, I started getting calls asking to move equipment from Houston," said Jorge Aponte, CEO of Houston-based PetroFarm.
His company buys oil equipment directly from owners and operators across the U.S., allowing the company to verify maintenance records, operating condition and technical integrity. One such purchase was a 2014 workover rig from North Carolina, set to be shipped out of Houston this month.
PetroFarm has also shipped two smaller workover rigs to Venezuela, with plans to send three more in the coming weeks. A small workover rig can cost around $350,000, Aponte said. REUTERS

Turkey accuses Israel of destabilizing Syria, Israel warns of growing Ankara influence - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:34:31 UTC
19:34:31 KST

Jerusalem wants to see a stable federalized Syria in which minorities are protected, rather than a destabilized Damascus that is unable to control its own borders, Prof. Efraim Inbar, founder of the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security (JISS), told The Jerusalem Post on Monday, a day after Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan alleged that Israel was seeking to weaken Syria.
Fidan made the comments during a visit to Damascus, where he met with his Syrian counterpart, Asaad al-Shaibani, and said that Turkey remained committed to diplomacy, despite Israel’s strike on Syria’s disused Abu al-Duhur Air Base.
Israel bombed the airbase last month to prevent Turkish troops from deploying there, according to Israeli officials. Ankara denied that it had planned to deploy troops to the site.
“Just as Syria offers so much hope to the region and the world, there is suddenly an actor striving to destabilize the country,” Fidan said at a joint news conference. “You know the name of that actor: Israel… the policies Israel pursues constitute the most serious obstacle to this positive trajectory. The attack carried out against the Abu al-Duhur military airbase is one of the latest examples.”
Shaibani also claimed the attack “conveyed a destructive message aimed at undermining the path of building the Syrian state,” and insisted that it “had no legitimate or legal justification” and would not impact relations with Turkey.
Israel would benefit from a stable Syrian government
Though Fidan has portrayed Israel as an obstacle to regional stability, Inbar told the Post that Israel would benefit from a stable Syrian government capable of controlling its borders and potentially becoming a “partner for peace.”
He offered Lebanon as an example, arguing that Israel wants to see a government in Beirut strong enough to confront Iranian influence and curb the forces destabilizing the region.
He also admitted that a state weakened by infighting, militias, and instability would pose less of a threat to Israel because it would be unable to direct all of its attention and resources toward the Jewish state.
“Israel has a dilemma with its bordering states,” Inbar acknowledged.
Still, he argued that Fidan was overstating the extent to which Jerusalem could determine “how the neighboring states are being built or derailed.”
“We have limited power,” he reasoned.
Turkish support for Syria's Ahmed al-Sharaa grows
Though Jerusalem may have limited control over Damascus, Ankara’s support for President Ahmed al-Sharaa has continued to expand. Shaibani said that Ankara and Damascus had reached around 40 agreements and memoranda of understanding (MoU), connecting 22 Syrian ministries and government agencies with their Turkish counterparts, and he announced that Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan is expected to visit Syria soon.
Ankara’s growing influence in Syria, along with the presence of Turkish forces there, poses a significant risk to Israel, Inbar said. Given what he described as the “hate spewed by Erdogan,” as well as statements by Turkish officials about aspirations to one day govern Jerusalem, Inbar argued that Ankara’s “neo-Islamic and neo-Ottoman motivation” meant that Israel could not ignore the threat.
“We learned the lesson that we do not try to destabilize regimes or build regimes. Regime change is not an easy thing,” he continued. “We are looking at the capabilities developing there and what they [government officials] say, and trying to minimize the risks that are being posed to Israel.”

Rabbi warns ring proposals could accidentally create a Jewish marriage, need divorce if called off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:34:30 UTC
19:34:30 KST

The Chief Rabbi of Beersheba, Rabbi Avraham Deri, warned that a public marriage proposal in which the groom gives a ring to the bride in front of witnesses could cause a major halachic problem during a statement at a Religious Services Ministry conference on Monday.
Deri, the nephew of Shas party leader Arye Deri, commented that the presentation of a ring in front of witnesses could meet the halachic conditions of kiddusin, the legal requirements for becoming a married couple according to the Talmud, which includes the groom presenting the bride with a ring in front of two valid witnesses, and a declaration of his "consecration" of her with a ring, "in accordance with the laws of Moses and Israel."
Deri warned that the "recent custom" of a marriage proposal including the exchange of a ring could, in certain cases, meet the halachic requirements for a full wedding rather than "merely a romantic gesture."
"[After a] marriage proposal conducted in a format in which the intended groom proposes marriage with a ring to the bride in the presence of friends and relatives, in the event where the groom afterward decides to retract the proposal, it could lead to a situation in which the couple would be required to obtain a get [become divorced in a religious court]," Deri said.
The level of concern over the issue depends on the precise circumstances of each case, including what words were said and how, the manner in which the engagement ring was exchanged, the presence and status of witnesses, and other details, the Religious Services Ministry clarified.
If there is any doubt, those involved should consult with a rabbi or certified marriage registrar, the ministry advised.
Deri was speaking at a study day for rabbis, marriage registrars, and religious council members throughout southern Israel, hosted by the Beersheba Religious Council. The study day conference "dealt not only with complex halachic questions facing the marriage system, but also with its technological failure," the organizers said.
Religious Services Ministry presents national digital infrastructure for managing marriage procedures
The ministry presented its "Shirat Hayam" system - a new national digital infrastructure for managing marriage procedures - during the conference.
As part of the conference, marriage registrars used the new system, including testing the online opening and management of marriage files, verification of documents against national databases, synchronizing systems with those belonging to the Chief Rabbinate's Office, computerizing documentation of procedures for verifying Jewish status and relationship status, and issuing secure digital certificates.
The Religious Services Ministry says it is aiming to use this initiative to make the system more accessible, efficient, and technologically advanced, while reducing bureaucracy and improving service to citizens.
"The series of innovative study days reflects our commitment to the continuous improvement of the service provided to citizens," Rabbi Hizkiyahu Samin, director of the Religious Services Ministry's Marriage and Rabbinate Division, said.
'Connection between deep halachic knowledge, advanced technological tools is inseparable part of process,' rabbi says
"The connection between deep halachic knowledge and advanced technological tools is an inseparable part of the process we are leading. The work in roundtables enables open dialogue and the adaptation of solutions to changing needs in the field, alongside the implementation of the most advanced tools in the marriage system," Samin added.
The ministry also clarified that additional study day conferences will be held in other parts of the country as part of the "comprehensive renewal process."

Man charged with aggravated murder in fatal Beit Shemesh pool stabbing of 7-year-old
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:34:10 UTC
19:34:10 KST

State prosecutors charged Liel Ifergan, 26, on Monday with the aggravated murder of seven-year-old Hillel Mordechai Dadon and the attempted murder of Dadon’s four-year-old cousin in Beit Shemesh last month.
The indictment, filed in the Jerusalem District Court, alleges that Ifergan intentionally stabbed the two children as they played in an inflatable pool in the yard of a family home on August 17. Prosecutors also asked the court to keep him in custody until the criminal proceedings are completed.
According to the indictment, Dadon had been invited to his cousin’s home that afternoon, and the children were playing together in the pool. At about 4:38 p.m., Ifergan allegedly ran from the neighboring housing unit where he lived carrying a knife, entered the yard, and approached the pool.
Prosecutors allege that he stabbed Dadon once in the chest and his cousin once in the neck, intending to kill them both. He then fled to his housing unit and cleaned the blood from the knife, the indictment says.
The chest wound damaged Dadon’s left lung and the sac surrounding his heart, causing injuries that led to his death, according to the indictment. His cousin suffered a neck wound and active bleeding, underwent surgery, was sedated and ventilated, and remained hospitalized for three days.
Aggravated murder, intentional killing of a child
Ifergan was charged with aggravated murder under a provision of Israeli law covering the intentional killing of a child under 14. He was also charged with attempted murder and aggravated grievous bodily harm.
The indictment alleges that Ifergan intended to kill the children but does not identify a motive, which matches earlier police advancements in the investigation.
Dadon’s father, Amos, told reporters after the indictment was filed that the family hoped justice would be done quickly and that they would not be put through further turmoil.
“We are trying to be strong because we have other children,” he said.
The prosecution said it was difficult to comprehend “the gap between two children innocently playing in a pool and the defendant’s decision to arm himself with a knife.” It said the indictment reflected the exceptional severity of the alleged acts and their irreversible outcome.

Himalayas nearing tipping point: Glacier loss puts India at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:33:04 UTC
19:33:04 KST

People collect water from a glacier at Everest base camp, Nepal (Reuters)
The Himalayas are approaching a critical tipping point as accelerating glacier loss threatens to reshape water availability, increase the risk of floods and landslides, and put millions of livelihoods and vital economic infrastructure across south asia at risk, a new study has warned.The warning comes from a study led by Systemiq in partnership with the Integrated Mountain Initiative, the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) and the G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment. It finds that Himalayan glaciers are losing mass 65 percent faster than they were a decade ago, raising the prospect of major changes in the region's water cycle in the decades ahead.The warning comes after the glacier collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 triggered a massive flash flood, killing more than 1,300 people and damaging roads, bridges and hydropower projects. The disaster highlighted the cascading risks linked to accelerating Himalayan glacier retreat.The study's warning goes beyond the familiar concern over melting glaciers. It points to a chain of interconnected risks.
Rapid ice loss can initially increase downstream water flows, while the formation and expansion of unstable glacial lakes can raise the threat of sudden floods and landslides.But as glaciers continue to shrink, the region could eventually pass "peak water", the point after which glacier-fed river flows begin to decline.Major risks for the regionThe study identifies water security as one of the biggest long-term risks for the Himalayan region. It warns that glaciers are losing mass 65 percent faster than a decade ago and the region is moving towards “peak water”, after which declining glacier reserves could reduce river flows. This could put downstream agriculture, cities and communities under increasing water stress.According to the study, the risks extend to hydropower, agriculture and livelihoods. Changes in the timing and availability of water could affect irrigation and electricity generation, while extreme weather and mountain hazards could increase losses for communities dependent on farming, tourism and other local economic activities.India faces a particularly significant exposure, with close to 200 glacial lakes identified as high risk, including 56 classified as very high risk, leaving millions of people downstream vulnerable. The Himalayan region also accounts for roughly 35 percent of India's natural disasters despite covering around 18 percent of the country's land area, according to the report.
The study estimates that the Himalayan system underpins more than 20 percent of India's GDP, meaning disruptions to the region's water and natural systems could have consequences well beyond the Himalayan states.The study also points to a serious early-warning and monitoring gap. Of an estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Hindu Kush-Himalaya, only 21 are monitored on the ground. This limited monitoring capacity could make it harder to detect rapidly developing glacier and glacial-lake hazards and provide timely warnings.
Aryan Singh is a journalist with The Times of India, covering breaking news, defence and global conflicts. An alumnus of the IIMC, he tracks the people, weapons and geopolitics behind the headlines, with a focus on India’s national security, military affairs and conflicts shaping the world.

Roborock Qrevo 2 Review (2026): A New Budget Vacuum King?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Roborock's been a favorite of the robot vacuum game for a while. Here at WIRED, our reviewers are longtime fans of the affordable Qrevo line, but it was left without updates for for years. The company has been more focused on more unique designs, such as the Saros Z70, which has an entire arm attached to it to grab your socks. These have a way to go before they're actually useful.
But this year, the Qrevo line is finally getting some love again. The Qrevo Curv line got a new model that we reviewed back in January, and there's now the Qrevo 2 Pro that just launched at the end of August. After a living with it for the better part of two weeks, it's easily one of my favorite sub-$1,000 robot vacuums, especially for its corner cleaning, and has the power to rival my current budget pick, the Eufy Omni C28. My only complaint is little things. I mean that literally: this robot is great at spotting furniture and navigating large obstacles, but it won't spot your cords or cat toys laying on the floor.
Power Range
The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro has a nice range of specs. It comes with a 20,000 Pa digital motor, 200 RPM rotation speed for the mop pads, LiDar navigation to map your home, a FlexiArm mop that promises to get in hard-to-reach spots (and it delivered in my tests!), and an easy-to-use app. It also has Matter support if you wanted to voice command it with your smart home speaker and an AI-powered “SmartPlan” to better clean your home. I haven't noticed a difference in using SmartPlan compared to just running a regular cycle, but I've only been using this robot for about two weeks. Hopefully, the robot will learn more over time and improve—at least, in theory. It's not the kind of AI that's going to spot spills and stains, though, so keep that in mind when you run this robot vacuum.
Most of all, I was impressed by the edge cleaning with the FlexiArm mop, and the reversible side brush. Both work together to dislodge debris and make sure furniture and wall edges are clean. The vacuum was able to knock out one of my trickier Cheerio tests—specifically a Cheerio I stash in a corner next to my fridge—with the help of the side brush and mop. It didn't achieve a perfect corner score, missing one of the three Cheerios, but I've yet to meet a robot vacuum that can achieve all three. The slim 3.8-inch high design lets this vacuum squeeze underneath many kitchen counter toe kicks to suck up all the debris hiding under your counter, and clean right up into the edge.
The suction level also worked well on carpets and rugs alike, though it worked better on pet hair than my long hair. My low-pile rug downstairs had a nice fluff to it after a run of this robot vacuum, but more importantly the tufts of cat hair were nowhere to be seen in my carpeted bedrooms after this vacuum ran through the top floor of my home. My hair was vacuumed up, but I found it rolled into a massive ball near a corner of the bed. I'll caveat that it had been a handful of weeks since my last good vacuuming upstairs, and I doubt you'd see this with regular cleanings. My husband didn't notice the hairball at all, and immediately complimented how nice the upstairs looked.
