Can Lebanon swap Hezbollah's arms for reconstruction cash?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:47:09 UTC
18:47:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Can Lebanon swap Hezbollah's arms for reconstruction cash?
There's a phrase attributed to Rafic Hariri that captures Lebanon's postwar bargain, because that's what it is, with almost frightening clarity: "we bought peace with debt." After the 1989 Taif Agreement, the men who had waged war entered the state and began administering peace, because it became more profitable than continuing the war.
Reconstruction contracts, borrowed money, bank deposits, Gulf capital and donor support turned the end of fighting into a financial settlement, giving every major bloc a stake in keeping it alive. The end of the civil war in 1990 safeguarded the political class by handing it a new economic arrangement.
Nearly four decades later, Lebanon is being offered another version of the same bargain: disarm Hezbollah, place the south under state control, and the money returns: an IMF programme, World Bank lending, Gulf investment in a southern economic zone. The first bargain was priced in debt and expired in October 2019, when the banks shut their doors. This one is priced in weapons.
Reconstruction is the word being used. Resuscitation is closer.
The arrangement offered to Lebanon is asymmetrical. Hezbollah is asked to disarm, accept verification, and place the south under Lebanese Army control, while Israeli withdrawal remains gradual and conditional. The Lebanese Armed Forces, Lebanon's principal cross-sectarian institution, must enforce state authority against a movement rooted in the same communities from which many of its soldiers are recruited.
Joseph Aoun, president since January 2025, knows what that asks of the army he once led. Ordering it into direct confrontation with Hezbollah – Lebanon's fear – could lead to the same fracture as in the early years of the civil war. And the country supplying the bombs dropped on the south is also the power that decides how the south gets rebuilt. A government that cannot safely fulfil one demand or compel the other keeps both in motion, and both unresolved.
For nearly thirty years, Lebanon spent more dollars than it earned. Diaspora deposits and Gulf capital entered the banks that financed the state, and Banque du Liban defended an artificial currency peg. Governments borrowed to pay salaries, service debt, and rebuild Beirut, while the fixed lira made imports cheap and incomes look stronger than the economy beneath them.
In 2019 the dollars stopped arriving at the rate the system required. The peg became a fiction, the banks locked depositors out, salaries collapsed, and the life built around the 1,500 lira disappeared.
How the money becomes loyalty
The pattern didn't start in 2019. It started at the 1989 Taif Agreement.
The standard complaint at the time was precise: Taif reconciled the warlords, not the people. Reconstruction began only once the political class had survived the war, and the ministries handed out under the new sectarian formula converted that survival into permanence.
Solidere, the Lebanese Company for the Development and Reconstruction of Beirut Central District, founded in 1994, compelled landowners to trade their property for shares rather than compensation, and was financed through the same treasury bills that paid interest to the same banks partly owned by the political class.
Contracts for roads, power and reconstruction were distributed through ministries now held by the men who had fought each other for those buildings a few years earlier, and each ministry became a channel: deposits into debt, debt into contracts, contracts into the jobs, favours, and protection that bind a constituency to its leader. The war had ended. The economy built to finance its end had relocated the same men into the offices that controlled it.
Hezbollah is no outsider to the post-Taif order; it is one of its armed shareholders. Yet disarmament asks one faction to surrender the instrument of its power while the governing order is asked to surrender none of the institutions through which it reproduces itself. The banks, ministries and confessional formula are absent from every agreement on the table. A binding allocation of banking losses, bank recapitalisation or serious tax reform would force every faction to pay. Disarmament concentrates the bill on Hezbollah.
What returns once that condition is met is the same machine that has been running for four decades. An IMF programme supplies the external seal of approval. The World Bank's existing reconstruction framework can expand; bilateral aid and Gulf capital become easier to mobilise; the money returns through the same state machinery. Hezbollah is weakened. The post-Taif order is refinanced.
Disarmament is the maximum reform the system can absorb without dissolving. Everything the system cannot survive – a law dividing the banking losses, a tax base, the confessional formula itself – stays exactly where it has been since 1989. Past that point, real reform starts touching their own accounts, and none of them will vote for that.
What that refinancing looks like in practice is not abstract. A house in the south does not become a reconstruction project on its own. Someone has to recognise the damage, decide who is eligible for compensation, choose which villages are prioritised over others, design the tender and pick the contractor, approve the payment, and rule on whatever delay or appeal follows. Every one of those decisions is political, and Lebanon has followed this exact sequence twice before.
After Taif, reconstruction aid flowed through the Council for Development and Reconstruction, an agency established in 1977 to sit above politics, but captured by it within two decades. Rafik Hariri and, later, Nabih Berri took command of its board, and it became a byword for sweetheart deals.
Its board went essentially unchanged from 2006 until 2025, extended by a 2009 decree that kept the same members in place indefinitely. Split after Taif between Hariri and Jumblatt, the Central Fund for the Displaced was meant to resettle the displaced from the civil war within three years for $500 million. It took ten years and cost over a billion, while investigators found that residents were compensated for properties that never existed and officials at the Ministry of Displaced had accumulated real estate no salary could explain.
The current round runs the same route. The World Bank's Lebanon Emergency Assistance Project, with $250 million in funding against a $1 billion framework, is implemented through the CDR according to international benchmarks. The ministries distributing that money, and appointing those consultants, are the same ones allocated under the sectarian formula in 1990.
Ask, then, what disarmament actually buys, if the framework is implemented, verified and completed. It buys a state with one gun instead of two. It does not, on its own, buy a different state.
A promise with no deadline
The sovereignty case is real. Lebanon cannot remain a country where Hezbollah decides when war begins. But Lebanon's constitutional order has been promising its own abolition for thirty-six years. The 1990 amendments name the end of political confessionalism as a national goal and assign parliament a staged plan for carrying it out. No deadline was imposed on the people who benefit from delay.
At what point do we stop treating each crisis as a separate malfunction? The banking collapse, the port explosion and the stalled IMF negotiations were different events, yet each ran into the same structure: divided authority, protected officeholders, concealed responsibility, and no institution strong enough to impose a settlement on the others.
Today, new loans diagnose a shortage of money. Reconstruction diagnoses destroyed buildings. Neither diagnosis reaches the political machinery that makes accountability impossible. The post-Taif order receives new money, new legitimacy, and another lease on life.
In Beirut's southern suburbs, a resident named Mohammad has been waiting since the ceasefire for someone to open a file on his damaged home and business. Not the state's reconstruction project, which hasn't reached his street. Not Jihad al-Bina, Hezbollah's own compensation arm, which paid out roughly four hundred million dollars after the 2024 war but has gone largely quiet on this one, with its funding from Tehran disrupted by sanctions and the fall of Assad.
Two authorities spent twenty years competing for the right to be the name a family calls when the roof comes down. For the moment, in Mohammad's street, neither one has come.
Karim Salam is a Lebanese writer and researcher focused on Lebanon, political economy and the wider Levant. He is the founder of @lebaneseacademic, a research and media platform exploring the region’s politics, history and society.

Yemen's displaced long for loved ones, stability as Houthis advance

Unknown Publisher

Yemen's displaced long for loved ones, stability as Houthis advance
TAIZ, Yemen, Sept 14 - As Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants swept through the battered country's Red Sea coastline, thousands of panicked people fled to makeshift camps, adding to an already vast population of internally displaced people.
Aisha Muhammad, like others who escaped from coastal areas and arrived in the southwest province of Taiz, left behind her two daughters and three sons, trapped in their homes as fighting turned a once-vital corridor for trade into a route of displacement.
"They are being blocked and shot at. Right now, they cannot reach us, and we cannot return to them. This is a trial from God," said Muhammad, boiling water in an old black teapot placed on rocks over a flame.
More than 82,000 people have been displaced by the fighting since the start of the month, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Sunday, including over 2,000 who have crossed the Gulf of Aden to Djibouti in the Horn of Africa.
The advance by the Houthis, who already control most of the north and Yemen's most populous areas, is strengthening Tehran's hand in its conflict with the U.S.
ANOTHER YEMEN CRISIS
Hardship is not new in Yemen, where a long civil war between forces of the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed administration and the Houthis created one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year. A U.N.-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major fighting, despite expiring six months later, but efforts to turn it into a lasting political settlement have stalled as regional tensions have intensified.
The Houthis – mountain fighters in sandals who have transformed into a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones – have opened a second theatre of war with their lightning western offensive.
Their advance has put them in a strong position to tighten their grip over the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a vital chokepoint for global oil and commodities shipping – more than six months after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.
"Behind every number is a family who's lost everything," said Amy Pope, IOM director general. "Many have been displaced multiple times. People are crossing the sea with nothing because they have no other choice left. Yemen is a country torn by poverty and conflict, and it cannot carry this crisis alone."
Video shared by IOM showed Yemenis who arrived in boats on Djibouti's northern coast receiving food and water at a nearby refugee settlement.
Djibouti's finance minister, Ilyas Dawaleh, said on Sunday that the situation was "becoming increasingly difficult for our country, despite our unwavering commitment to humanitarian resources".
Back in Taiz, many, including Abdullah Qaiyd, an elderly man walking with a stick, are once again longing for stability.
"Now, look at us. We are tormented and shaken to our core. We long for a basic livelihood, and we long for safety," he said. REUTERS

Iran unveils homegrown catalysts for oil, gas industries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:45:16 UTC
18:45:16 KST

The “chromium-free high-temperature shift catalyst” and “medium-temperature shift catalyst” were unveiled at Iran’s knowledge-based Sarv Oil and Gas Industries Development Company on Sunday.
The two products have been developed for use in key industrial processes, including hydrogen and syngas production, where catalysts play a critical role in converting carbon monoxide and adjusting gas composition for subsequent stages.
In the water-gas shift process, carbon monoxide reacts with steam to produce hydrogen and carbon dioxide.
High- and medium-temperature shift catalysts are used, depending on process design and operating conditions, in hydrogen, ammonia, methanol and syngas production units, as well as in parts of the refining and petrochemical industries.
The domestic production of the catalysts is particularly significant for Iran as sanctions and restrictions on access to foreign technologies and equipment have complicated the country’s supply chains.
One of the newly unveiled products is a chromium-free high-temperature shift catalyst.
 
 Conventional high-temperature shift catalysts may contain chromium compounds as promoters.
Eliminating chromium from the formulation can reduce concerns associated with the handling and management of chromium-containing materials and represents a technological step toward safer catalyst formulations.
The second product is a medium-temperature shift catalyst designed to improve carbon monoxide conversion under intermediate-temperature operating conditions.
The developers say domestic production of such catalysts can go beyond replacing imported products by shortening supply chains, reducing foreign-exchange costs and limiting the impact of sanctions and import restrictions.
It can also facilitate access to technical support and replacement catalyst supplies for industrial operators.
Catalysts are considered strategic components of the oil, gas and petrochemical sectors, and disruptions in their supply can affect the operating capacity and costs of industrial plants.

Butenko: Education Ministry recommends 3 learning models for schools amid prolonged air raids
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
12:42:54 EEST
18:42:54 KST

The Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine recommends that schools use three basic models for organizing the educational process—face-to-face, combined, and remote—amid prolonged and repeated air raid alerts, Minister of Education and Science Andriy Butenko has reported.
"The main principle remains unchanged: the safety of children and teachers comes above all. At the same time, we must do everything possible to ensure that children have as many learning opportunities as possible despite the alerts, because every lost hour ultimately affects the quality of education," Butenko wrote on Facebook.
According to him, last week, together with teachers, parent organizations, school principals, and education administration heads, recommendations were developed for organizing the educational process in general secondary education institutions during prolonged and repeated air raid alerts. The recommendations were officially sent to the regions to help schools determine their operational procedures in advance under various security conditions.
According to the guidelines, schools can use face-to-face, combined, or remote learning models and switch between them dynamically depending on the security situation and the capacity of a specific institution.
The framework also defines the procedure for organizing the school day if an air raid alert is active at its start, as well as actions in the event of power or communication outages.
In particular, if a shelter is equipped for conducting classes, the educational process can continue there. If an air raid alert catches children and teachers during remote learning, the lesson can continue online after everyone moves to a safe location.
For regions with prolonged air raid alerts, it is recommended to adapt remote classes so that participants are immediately in safe locations. Asynchronous learning should be available for students who cannot join the classes.
Butenko noted that educational administrators have already reviewed the recommendations, and starting September 15, the educational process must be maximally adapted to the developed approaches.
"It is important to provide schools not with a single rigid instruction for all cases, but with clear tools so they can find the best solution for their conditions, maintaining the main balance: safety always comes first, but we do everything to preserve the quality of education," he emphasized.
According to the minister, the recommendations were developed at the request of educators and take into account the experience and proposals of people who organize education under wartime conditions every day.

Growth of 'Flock cameras' in US key issue for 2026 midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:39:04 UTC
18:39:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Growth of 'Flock cameras' in US becomes key topic for upcoming 2026 midterms
Flock cameras are increasingly coming up in the news as a bogeyman of the 2026 midterm elections in the United States—along with AIPAC, ICE, data centres, and AI.
Like other issues that started with young protesters, Flock cameras have now entered the mainstream campaign lexicon for the upcoming US midterms, wherein candidates' positions on the surveillance technology are seen as something of a litmus test.
What is 'Flock Safety'?
The privately held surveillance company, which uses image recognition technology to identify people through their license plates, known as automatic license plate readers (ALPR) was established in 2017 and is based in Atlanta. It holds contracts with property owners and law enforcement. Their approximately 120,000 cameras are used in more than 6,000 communities in nearly all 50 states, where they do billions of scans every month.
The company is best known for its automatic license plate readers and CCTV cameras, which are becoming increasingly ubiquitous. It is also working on developing broader surveillance systems.
How are they different than regular license plate readers?
Conventional license plate readers are generally used to detect drivers who are speeding and to identify people with criminal backgrounds. Flock cameras scan passing cars for their make, model, colour, location and other details—essentially creating a vehicle fingerprint—to then use the data at a later date.
Why are Flock cameras under scrutiny?
Their widespread deployment without the use of warrants has raised concerns over privacy violations. There are also questions over the constitutionality of the devices that surveille (without warrants) civilians who don’t necessarily have a criminal record.
The leaders of Flock have argued that their technology, through use by law enforcement, has helped catch criminals and find missing people.
Earlier this month, the American Civil Liberties Union released a statement on Flock cameras, saying, “Automatic license plate reader (ALPR) companies like Flock Safety are quietly trying to build a nationwide mass surveillance system. If there are Flock cameras in your city, they are tracking, logging, and sharing your movements without a warrant.”
They go on to describe the system of Flock cameras (the largest of a growing number of such companies) as terrifying.
In a recent campaign ad, Connie Chan, who is running for Congress in San Francisco to replace Nancy Pelosi, accused her opponent, Scott Wiener, of being in support of Flock.
“Right now, our federal government is tracking our personal data and selling it without our knowledge and permission,” Chan says in her campaign ad.
“Across the country, Flock system is using AI in mass surveillance, using that technology to assist ICE, stalk women, monitor protesters, and follow people follow people who have never been suspected of a crime,” she continues. Flock have said they don't work with ICE.
She goes on to say that all federal funding for Flock should be stopped and AI and mass surveillance in general should be prohibited. She also says that Flock is influencing the Democratic Party by helping block bills that would require more transparency in the use of surveillance. She notes that Wiener and a Flock employee (a Democratic Party official) have cross-endorsed one another.
How are states responding?
In response to public outrage over Flock cameras, some states have enacted regulations. Florida has banned the cameras from state highways; Washington state has the first statewide regulations on ALPRs; California killed a bill that would regulate Flock cameras.
How are people protesting Flock cameras?
Protests against Flock cameras have largely been led by young people. On social media platforms, such as TikTok, some Flock opponents have given guidance on how to destroy Flock cameras without being detected. The destruction of Flock cameras has led some cities to cancel their contracts with the company.

Taichung doctor links some hair loss cases to zinc deficiency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:37:09 UTC
18:37:09 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A Taichung dermatologist says zinc deficiency may be an overlooked cause of hair loss after a 37-year-old male patient with a family history of baldness was found to have low zinc levels.
Dr. Ko Wei-li (柯偉立), director of the Department of Dermatology at Taichung Cheng Ching Hospital, said approximately 30% of the hair-loss patients he treats have zinc deficiency, per CNA.
The patient sought treatment because of his father's history of baldness. Blood tests showed he had insufficient zinc levels, which Ko identified as the primary cause of his hair loss.
Zinc is an essential mineral involved in protein synthesis and cell growth. Ko said zinc deficiency can interfere with keratin synthesis, slowing hair growth and leaving hair thinner and more prone to breakage. Hair loss caused by zinc deficiency can also resemble other forms of hair loss, making blood testing and medical evaluation important.
After the patient increased his intake of zinc-rich foods and took zinc supplements, a follow-up examination six weeks later showed increased hair volume and zinc levels within the normal range.
Ko recommends that patients diagnosed with zinc deficiency consume zinc-rich foods such as oysters, beef, and pumpkin seeds. For severe deficiency, he said supplements can also be used following medical evaluation.
The National Institutes of Health notes a tolerable upper intake level of 40 milligrams of zinc per day for adults from food, beverages, and supplements. Excessive zinc intake can interfere with copper absorption and cause other health problems.
Ko advises people experiencing unexplained or persistent hair loss to seek medical evaluation rather than assuming it is solely hereditary or taking supplements without first determining whether they have a deficiency.

More than 1,000 lights along major roads were replaced in the first phase, followed by more than 700 older sodium lights along neighborhood streets in the second phase, per a city office press release.
Cheng said some of the sodium lamps had been in place for more than 20 years. The new LED fixtures can be adjusted according to road width and traffic conditions while reducing electricity costs.
With the high-speed rail district upgrades completed, Cheng said the city plans to extend its streetlight replacement program to other parts of downtown Zhubei and surrounding areas.

DPP defends NT$8.1 billion Cianjhen Fishing Port renovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:36:39 UTC
18:36:39 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) defended the government's NT$8.1 billion (US$255 million) renovation project at Cianjhen Fishing Port on Monday, saying the investment is justified by the hundreds of billions of Taiwan dollars generated by the country's distant-water fishing industry.
Chuang said Taiwan's distant-water fishing industry had previously received a warning under the European Union's illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing rules, adding that extensive legislative work was required to avert potential EU sanctions, per FTNN. He also said the newly built facilities were intended to improve living conditions for foreign fishing crews, adding that suggestions for further improvements to the port are welcome.
A series of reports by UDN identified major problems with the renovation, including issues involving the new crew quarters and fish market. A common theme in the reports was a disconnect between the facilities' designs and the needs of their intended users.
The crew quarters were designed to improve conditions for foreign workers by providing free amenities, including prayer rooms, showers, and Wi-Fi, as well as hotel rooms available for a fee, per UDN. However, an insufficient number of showers and washing machines has prompted some crews to avoid the facility, instead using container-based shower facilities and washing their clothes by hand.
Philippine crew members pointed out that, with an average monthly wage of NT$19,045, the NT$1,000 nightly rate for hotel rooms is unaffordable. Official data puts the number of daily hotel users at about six, though the Kaohsiung Fishermen's Association said it is working to improve occupancy.
Distant-water fishing industry groups have urged the public to take a reasonable view of efforts to improve the human rights and working conditions of foreign fishing crews, per Liberty Times.
The new fish market has also faced criticism.
Fishmongers said traffic flow within the market is inconvenient, requiring more loading and unloading than at the old market, per UDN. They also cited cumbersome regulations and the lack of an announced rental rate as reasons for delaying their move to the new facility.
Access to the new market may also be an issue for buyers. Kaohsiung scrapped plans to extend its metro and light rail systems to the site, leaving bus services as the only form of public transportation, per UDN. Kaohsiung City Councilor Chen Li-na (陳麗娜) said visitors may need to make multiple transfers to reach the market and noted that a lack of sufficient parking space is another problem for people traveling from outside the city.
In addition to the newly built facilities, UDN reported that many mooring posts at the port's east-facing dock have suffered severe corrosion and appeared to have been excluded from the renovation project. The Fisheries Agency said Monday that those facilities were not covered by the renovation project and are instead handled through routine maintenance.
The agency also responded to concerns about the crew quarters, saying foreign crews who use the free amenities have spoken highly of them. It said descriptions such as "luxury bathhouse" do not benefit the workers.
Regarding the fish market, the agency said complaints about inconvenient operating rules stem from a misunderstanding of modern fish-market standards, per a FA statement. It emphasized that traditional retail practices no longer meet modern sanitation requirements or the demands of international markets.
The reports have also become part of the political debate ahead of the November local elections.
KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chair Chen I-hsin (陳以信) said KMT Kaohsiung City Councilor Hsu Tsai-chen (許采蓁) had warned in 2025 that charging for hotel rooms could result in low occupancy, per Tai Sounds. He called on the Kaohsiung city government and Kaohsiung mayoral candidate and lawmaker Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆), who represents the area, to explain their oversight and execution of the renovation project.
Chen also called on the National Audit Office to review the project.
KMT Legislator Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) said that during a December 2025 visit to the new fish market with the Fisheries Agency, she had already raised concerns about traffic flow and other problems at the facility, per China Times. She urged the administration to address the problems rather than tout the NT$8.1 billion in funding for the project.

Source: a European Pravda correspondent in Brussels, citing three EU diplomats

- On 12 September, European Pravda sources in French diplomatic circles explained why Paris wants sanctions lifted on Usmanov.
- It was also reported earlier that EU ambassadors once again were unable to agree on extending personal sanctions over Russian aggression on 11 September, due to demands from Slovakia and France as to changes to the lists of individuals under personal sanctions.

China sets up DNA, hotline mechanism for foreigners missing in Nepal-Tibet disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:30:22 UTC
18:30:22 KST

Faisal Mahmud
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
China has informed foreign embassies about procedures for collecting DNA samples from relatives of foreign nationals missing after last month’s deadly floods and mudslides along the Nepal-Tibet border, Beijing said Monday.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Chinese authorities were continuing search and identification operations in the Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.
“China has informed the relevant foreign embassies in China of the procedures for collecting DNA samples from the families of the missing individuals,” Guo told reporters in Beijing.
If remains of foreign victims are recovered and their identities confirmed, the relevant embassies will be promptly notified about arrangements for handling the deceased, he added.
Authorities in Xizang have also set up a hotline to assist the families of missing foreign nationals.
On the Nepalese side, 1,385 people have been confirmed dead and 5,130 remain missing, according to the latest figures published by Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) on a government flood-update portal.
The authority said 13,676 people had been rescued, while 21,022 security personnel were mobilized for search, rescue and relief operations.
Among those missing in Nepal were 587 foreign tourists. Authorities said the missing-person count remains subject to verification and may include unidentified bodies and people who have already been rescued.
On the Chinese side, the death toll remains at 43, with 519 people missing, including 261 foreigners, in Xizang.
The disaster struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters (17,060 feet).
The fracture triggered an ice-rock avalanche that turned into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley.
The disaster also buried the Gyirong border crossing in Xizang.

Piazzа praises Iran volleyball fighting spirit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-14
09:28:55 UTC
18:28:55 KST

Piazzа praises Iran volleyball fighting spirit
TEHRAN - Iran’s men’s national volleyball team finished runners-up at the 23rd AVC Men’s Volleyball Championship but Italian head coach Roberto Piazza praised his players for continuing to fight until the final point.
Iran lost to hosts Japan 3-0 (25–21, 26–24, 25–23) in the final match on Sunday and failed to book their place at the 2028 Olympic Games.
“I think the most important thing is that we never gave up,” Piazza said. “From the beginning, we were in the game. We lost the first set because of our own mistakes, not because Japan played an incredible volleyball. We also had an important role in the first set and contributed to the result ourselves.”
Piazza stressed that the defeat should be viewed as a team result rather than the responsibility of individual players.
“It doesn’t matter who made the mistake. I don’t want to blame anyone because we play as a team,” he added. “In the end, we were able to fight until the finish.”
“We were ahead in the second set, and in the third set we were leading 6-2,” Piazza explained. “But once again, at the crucial moment, when you need to find a special ball, Japan found it and we couldn’t.”
The Italian coach highlighted Japan’s ability to deliver in decisive moments, particularly when star player Yuki Ishikawa was serving.
“For me, this is the important conclusion,” Piazza said. “In the second set, when Yuki Ishikawa was in the service zone, they found a special ball. But the real question is whether only Ishikawa was special, or whether we could have done something better.”
The silver medal nevertheless marked a strong campaign for Iran, and Piazza said he was proud of the squad’s overall performance throughout the tournament.
“I am proud of my boys. I am really proud of all of them,” he said.
“In volleyball, you have to show your ability every day and on every ball,” he said. “That is why I am very proud of my players.”
The tournament also provided valuable lessons for Iran as the team continue to develop under Piazza. The coach believes his players are beginning to understand what is required tactically, even if they are not yet able to execute those plans consistently.
“This is part of the special conditions of volleyball, and it is something we have to learn,” Piazza said. “First of all, we have to focus on ourselves, not on the opponent.”
“Overall, we became more consistent, and my feeling is that the boys have started to understand what they need to do, even though they cannot always execute it. But the first step is knowing exactly what you have to do. Sooner or later, you will reach the goal. We came very close.”
Piazza nevertheless ended his message by thanking Iranian supporters for their backing throughout the competition.
“I want to thank the people of Iran for their support,” he said.

Women seeking to break barriers in trail running took center stage at the second Kaçkar by UTMB in northeastern Türkiye, where athletes from around the world tackled demanding mountain trails across 4K, 20K, 50K and 100K races in a test of endurance against the rugged terrain of the Kaçkar Mountains.
The event, Türkiye’s first and only UTMB World Series race, brought nearly 2,000 athletes from 60 countries across six continents to Ayder Plateau and the Kaçkar Mountains. Alongside the competition, a panel highlighted women’s empowerment through the Run Like Her initiative, a female trail-running training camp held in the Kaçkar Mountains in July.
First of its kind at UTMB, the initiative was created as a movement to motivate and inspire women of different countries, cultures and backgrounds to take up trail running, whether as amateurs or elite athletes and regardless of distance. Organizers said the long-term goal is to achieve a 50-50 balance between women and men in trail races.
“This is a movement, an initiative to inspire women, to push them, to motivate them to come to trail running,” Carole Muller, a lead visionary behind the initiative, said. “It’s open to everyone, so come, run, no matter the distance.”
The panel also brought together Kaçkar by UTMB ambassador Beyza Güzel, Afghan-born, British-based ultra-runner Fatima Painda, elite runner Elena Polyakova and Turkish athlete Başak Ağdaş who spoke about their experiences.
Güzel, who had competed in the UTMB World Series finals in Chamonix shortly before the event, described her connection to the region as having grown since the project began. “Kaçkar by UTMB, for me, is not just a race,” she said. “The Kaçkars are special because even when you are struggling the most, when you lift your head, you see the view. It reminds you again why you are there.”
For Polyakova, the race carried an added significance as a new mother. “I’m a new mother, so during the difficult moments I’ll think about my baby waiting for me at the finish line, and I hope this will be a good example for our son.”
Painda, who grew up in the mountains of Afghanistan, trail running has also become a way to draw attention to women deprived of access to sport and public life under Taliban rule. “Every woman and girl in Afghanistan deserves to be out there at the start line of any race,” she said. “Mountain is medicine. Nature is medicine.”
Güzel went on to finish second in the women’s 100K, completing the race in 15 hours, 18 minutes, behind Germany’s Joanna Tallmann, who won in 15 hours, 13 minutes.
Türkiye’s Tuğçe Karakaya won the women’s 50K after returning to sport following a traffic accident that had threatened her athletic career. Spain’s Ainara Urrutia Yurreras was second and Türkiye’s Fatma Taş third.
Spain’s Sara Alonso won the women’s 20K, ahead of Ukraine’s Daria Boichuk and Türkiye’s Tuğba Akın. Nergis Durmuş, İrina Petrakova and Asya Esen took the top three places in the women’s 4K Ayder Run
Among the men, Russia’s Dmitry Mityaev won the inaugural 100K in 10 hours, 31 minutes, followed by Australia’s Michael Dimuantes and Ukraine’s Yevhenii Yermolenko.
Spain’s Antonio Martinez Perez won the 50K, while Iran’s Morteza Jafarzadeh topped the 20K. In the 4K, Ömer Asaf Durmuş won the men’s race. The 4K race also carried an environmental message, with participants wearing shirts reading “Running for Climate” to highlight climate change and nature conservation.

Unknown

2026-09-14
09:24:49 UTC
18:24:49 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
14 September 2026•Update: 14 September 2026
Rail freight transport performance in the EU fell by 1.8% in 2025 to 368.2 billion ton-kilometers, marking the fourth consecutive year of decline, the bloc's statistical office announced on Monday.
The volume dropped from 375.1 billion ton-kilometers in 2024 to 368.2 billion ton-kilometers last year.
Germany remained the largest contributor to the union's rail freight transport performance with a 33.5% share, equal to 123.5 billion ton-kilometers.
Poland followed as the second-largest contributor with 54.3 billion ton-kilometers, while France ranked third with 34.4 billion ton-kilometers.
Eurostat data showed that rail freight transport performance decreased in 16 member states and increased in eight countries compared to 2024.
Ireland recorded the largest decrease at 35.2%, followed by Latvia at 18.8% and Estonia at 17.3%.
Greece posted the highest increase at 9.3%, while Portugal and France saw their figures rise by 8.4% and 6.6%, respectively.
Luxembourg registered the highest volume of rail freight transported per capita at 10.7 tons, followed by Austria at 10.5 tons and Lithuania at 8.5 tons.
Ireland recorded the lowest rate at 0.03 tons per capita, while Greece saw 0.06 tons and Spain posted 0.5 tons.

China's consumption market expands steadily amid structural upgrades
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:14:19 CST
17:14:19 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's consumer market continued to expand in the first eight months of the year, while structural upgrading and new growth drivers gathered momentum, official data showed Tuesday.
China's total retail sales of goods and services, a major indicator of the country's consumption strength, increased by 2.5 percent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Despite volatility in international energy markets, domestic market adjustments, and extreme weather in some regions in August, China's consumer market showed strong resilience, with pro-consumption policies continuing to take effect, NBS spokesperson Fu Linghui said at a press conference.
Tuesday's data showed that the consumer market continued to undergo structural transformation, with services and higher-quality consumption accounting for a larger share. Retail sales of services rose 4.9 percent year on year during the January-August period, outpacing the 1-percent growth in goods sales.
Among service categories, retail sales of communication and information services, tourism consulting and rental services, and cultural, sports and leisure services posted relatively rapid growth.
In the first eight months, retail sales of consumer goods, including sales of goods and catering revenue, totaled 32.76 trillion yuan (about 4.84 trillion U.S. dollars), up 1.1 percent year on year, the data showed.
New consumption models also developed rapidly. Online retail sales of goods and services reached 13.48 trillion yuan, up 4.6 percent. Of the total, online goods sales rose 4.3 percent to 8.42 trillion yuan, while online service sales increased 5.1 percent to 5.06 trillion yuan.
Consumption in rural areas also gained momentum as commercial and logistics infrastructure improved. Rural retail sales of consumer goods rose 2.3 percent year on year in the first eight months, 1.3 percentage points faster than in urban areas.
Meanwhile, China's expanded visa-free policies and other measures facilitating cross-border travel helped boost inbound tourism, with overseas visitors showing stronger demand for shopping, cultural tourism and experience-based consumption.
Looking ahead, China has considerable room for further consumption growth, supported by rising demand for services and higher-quality products, as well as increasingly diverse consumption scenarios, Fu noted, adding that household purchasing power and willingness to spend still need strengthening, while the supply of high-quality goods and services requires further improvement.
China will continue efforts to raise incomes, improve supply and stabilize expectations, advance consumer goods trade-in programs, tap the potential of services consumption, and improve production and supply to promote the healthy and sustained development of the consumer market, Fu stressed.
According to an implementation guideline made public last month, China aims to bring total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan by 2030. ■

====================================================================================================

Australia's social isolation nearly doubles over two decades: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:13:42 CST
17:13:42 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Australians are becoming increasingly lonely and socially isolated, according to new research, which found rates of social isolation nearly doubled over the past 23 years.
Loneliness rates also increased over time, though more gradually than social isolation, with the sharpest impacts observed among vulnerable populations, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's University of Sydney (USYD).
The study examined 23 years of nationally representative data from the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey, which provides some of the country's first long-term national evidence on trends in loneliness and social isolation.
It found the rate of episodic social isolation, defined as experiencing social isolation in at least one survey wave, rose from 16.9 percent in 2001 to 29.9 percent in 2023. Chronic social isolation, recorded across at least two consecutive survey waves, approximately doubled from 10.3 percent in 2002 to 20.5 percent in 2023.
Loneliness followed a different pattern, generally declining during the 2000s before increasing again from the 2010s onward, with chronic loneliness rising from 6.3 percent in 2002 to 8.4 percent in 2023, the study showed.
Younger adults experienced some of the largest increases in loneliness, while older adults consistently had the highest levels of social isolation and showed the greatest increases over time, it noted.
The study found loneliness and social isolation were consistently more common among people who were unemployed, lived in more socioeconomically disadvantaged areas, widowed, living alone, or had lower levels of education.
The findings highlight social connection as a public health issue requiring "sustained policy and public health action across the life course," said USYD Prof. Melody Ding, senior author of the study published in the International Journal of Epidemiology. ■

Major Chinese cities report narrowed home price declines in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-15
16:13:38 CST
17:13:38 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- Major Chinese cities continued to report narrowed year-on-year declines in overall home prices in August, official data showed Tuesday.
In the first-tier cities of Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen, new home prices fell 0.9 percent year on year, 0.2 percentage points narrower than the previous month, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Second-hand home prices in the four cities dropped 2.7 percent year on year overall, with the decline narrowing from 3.7 percent in July.
As to second- and third-tier cities, price declines in both new and second-hand homes moderated compared with July.
On a monthly basis, home prices in first-tier cities rose in August, while second- and third-tier cities generally registered narrowed declines.
Among 70 large and medium-sized cities tracked, 21 recorded flat or rising new home prices month on month in August, two fewer than the previous month. Eight cities saw flat or rising second-hand home prices, unchanged from July.
The NBS releases a monthly home price report tracking market changes in 70 major cities, including four first-tier cities, 31 second-tier cities and 35 third-tier cities.
Tuesday's data pointed to further signs that China's property market is bottoming out, as the government maintains its city-specific policy approach, adjusting and optimizing real estate policies, working down inventory and pushing ahead with urban renewal.
NBS spokesperson Fu Linghui said at a media conference Tuesday that overall property transaction volumes have improved, with the area of second-hand home transactions rising 10.6 percent year on year in the first eight months of the year. New home inventory also continued to fall, with the total floor area of unsold new commercial housing down 1.1 percent year on year at the end of August, marking the sixth consecutive month of decline.
As China's property market undergoes a fundamental shift in supply and demand dynamics, more diverse demand for smart, green and elderly-friendly homes is on the rise.
In response, China is accelerating a transition in its property development model. Authorities have this year deepened reforms to the housing provident fund system and refined regulations on commercial housing sales, as part of broader efforts to chart a new path for real estate development.
These policy measures will help advance the transformation of China's property market and better meet people's aspirations for a better life, Fu said. ■

KINSHASA, Sept. 15 (Xinhua) -- More than 7,200 confirmed Ebola cases have been recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as sustained transmission continues in several provinces despite an overall downward trend of the epidemic, according to governmental data released Tuesday.
A government report covering the epidemiological situation as of Sunday said 7,258 confirmed cases had been recorded in seven provinces, including 3,510 deaths and 1,726 recoveries. A total of 905 patients were in isolation or hospitalized, while the overall fatality rate stood at 48.4 percent.
The outbreak has affected 62 health zones across seven provinces -- Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and Sud-Ubangi. Sustained transmission continued in Ituri, North Kivu and Haut-Uele, while sporadic cases were reported in Tshopo and Bas-Uele.

However, he cautioned that the decline was uneven across the country, with some provinces, particularly North Kivu, still reporting increases in cases.
Declared in May, the current outbreak has become the largest and deadliest Ebola epidemic in the DRC's history and the second-largest globally, behind the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa. ■

Yemen forces advance in Taiz; Houthis take key islands, attack Saudi Arabia
Yemeni government forces have advanced in western Taiz after successfully repelling a Houthi offensive.
Armed forces affiliated with Yemen’s internationally recognised government have retaken positions from the Houthis and are advancing in the southwestern Taiz province as clashes intensify.
Reporting from Taiz on Monday, Al Jazeera Arabic’s Yasser Hassan said forces loyal to the Saudi Arabia-backed Yemeni government advanced in western Taiz on Sunday after successfully repelling a Houthi offensive.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3More than 2,000 Yemenis flee to Djibouti as fighting intensifies
- list 2 of 3The Houthis’ escalation in Yemen could flop
- list 3 of 3Fighting continues between Yemen gov’t forces, Houthis: What is the latest?
“This comes with the support of air strikes targeting Houthi gatherings. The air force continues to bomb the Houthis on the west coast in Mocha, Dhubab, and their surroundings,” Hassan said, citing a source in government forces.
In a statement on Monday, the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), said they launched attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia using dozens of ballistic missiles and drones.
The group said the attacks targeted “military facilities and infrastructure, including aircraft hangars, radar installations, runways, ammunition depots and other targets at King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait”, Saudi Arabia.
It said the attacks were a response to a Saudi offensive, which involved more than 300 air strikes across Yemen over five days.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia on the Houthi claims.
On Sunday, the Saudi civil defence agency sent alerts for the city of Abha and the region around Khamis Mushait, but they were quickly lifted shortly afterwards.
Fighting in Yemen’s more than 10-year civil war reignited in July, threatening a United Nations-brokered truce that halted large-scale violence in 2022, after the Houthis declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
The fighting soon spilled over beyond the country’s borders, with the Houthis carrying out air attacks on southern Saudi Arabia, including oil facilities. Dozens of people were wounded in those attacks.
Clashes in Yemen intensified last week after the Houthis captured parts of the country’s Red Sea coast, fortifying their hold on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a key waterway that normally handles about 12 percent of global trade, including 11 percent of maritime oil and 8 percent of liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The waterway has been an economic lifeline for Saudi Arabia and its oil exports, as the Strait of Hormuz has been effectively blocked by Iranian forces since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.
The Houthis captured more strategic islands in the southern Red Sea, The Associated Press news agency reported on Monday, citing Yemeni government and Houthi officials.
Houthi officials reported that the group’s troops had deployed on the islands of Greater Hanish and Lesser Hanish, which sit about 86 nautical miles (160km) north of the Bab al-Mandeb.
Separately, repairs to a crucial Saudi oil pipeline, struck in an attack last week, could last three to five weeks, regional officials told AP, putting the route all but out of service.
Global oil prices gained more than 2 percent as the news increased concerns over the ability of the world’s biggest exporter to get its crude to market, potentially offering Iran additional leverage in its war with the US.
Meanwhile, the International Organization for Migration said on Sunday that the fighting in Yemen in recent weeks had displaced nearly 86,000 people.
It added that some of those displaced by the conflict were fleeing Yemen altogether, with more than 2,000 people reaching neighbouring country Djibouti.

Türkiye is increasing the number of aircraft in its civil aviation sector to meet demand at its major hubs, such as the airports in Istanbul, Ankara and Antalya, which make up some of Europe’s largest and busiest air hubs.

The data showed that airlines have the highest number of aircraft in Türkiye.

The number of aircraft registered to air taxi operators rose from 235 to 259 over the same period.
Air taxi operators include firms providing commercial air transport using registered aircraft with a maximum capacity of 19 seats.
Meanwhile, the number of aircraft registered to general aviation operators, which operate passenger and cargo transport outside commercial air transport, rose from 595 in the first half of last year to 632 as of the end of this year’s first half.
The number of ultralight aircraft in general aviation operations fell from 36 to 35 as of the end of June.
Additionally, the number of hot air balloons rose from 499 at the end of the first half of last year to 528 as of the end of June 2026, the data showed.
The directorate categorizes hot air balloons as aircraft under its rules.

It has also expanded jet fuel shipments to Europe and other African markets as Middle East supply disruptions reshaped global trade flows.
Proceeds from the IPO are expected to support capacity expansion and further strengthen Nigeria’s role as a regional refining and fuel-export hub.

Source: a video on Kravchenko's social media accounts
Quote from the video: "According to judicial proceedings, in April 2008, the defendant, Semen Kryvonos, entered into a criminal conspiracy with other individuals to conduct illegal election campaigning by bribing students at Kyiv National Linguistic University and Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv. According to the court materials, UAH 90,000 (about US$2,000) was provided to Semen Kryvonos and his accomplice to execute this criminal scheme, which was subsequently allocated towards bribing students."
Details: The video features an excerpt from Kryvonos's interview during the candidate selection process for the position of NABU director, in which a commission member mentions that between 2008 and 2009, Kryvonos was wanted in connection with the transfer of UAH 15,000 (US$330) for distribution to students in exchange for votes for the Yuliia Tymoshenko Bloc. However, the case was closed in 2010.
Kryvonos explained the incident as a trumped-up case stemming from an action he took in 2007, together with a group of like-minded students, against the administration of a university, allegedly over its attempts to pressure students into voting for specific candidates. He denied the allegation of voter bribery itself and said he was unaware he had been placed on a wanted list and had not been in hiding.
Kravchenko's video goes on to say: "However, according to investigators, Semen Kryvonos, the future head of NABU, intentionally misled the members of the selection commission, as he was not only well aware of the charges against him and the potential penalties, but also devised a criminal plan whose execution subsequently allowed him to be exempted from criminal liability."
The plan allegedly involved creating a contrived basis to qualify for amnesty. At that time, one such legal ground was having a minor child. Therefore, Kravchenko claims, Kryvonos and an accomplice persuaded a single mother (who appears in the materials under the pseudonym "Rhea", while Kryvonos himself is referred to as "Janus") to submit applications to registry offices to have Kryvonos recognised as the father of the child and a false birth certificate issued.
"Rhea" can be heard on the recording stating that Kryvonos wrote a letter of consent to adopt her child, after which amendments were allegedly made to the birth certificate.
However, according to the investigation, Kryvonos had no intention whatsoever of fulfilling parental duties.
The video states: "After obtaining the forged birth certificate in which he was named as the child's father from the registry office, Semen Kryvonos submitted an application, with the intention of misleading the court, to Kyiv's Holosiivskyi District Court requesting that an amnesty be applied to him, attaching the forged certificate... claiming that he had a minor child to support."
Kravchenko says this application led the judge to exempt Kryvonos from criminal liability without grounds in 2009, applying the amnesty law. The case concerning the bribery of students was also closed.
On the morning of 14 September, Kravchenko stated that he had signed a notice of suspicion against Kryvonos, who is accused of forging documents to obtain an unlawful benefit on an especially large scale, as well as fictitious adoption. The prosecutor general also noted that he is prepared to publish all the materials related to the proceedings.
In a statement this morning, Kravchenko said: "As of today, the Office of the Prosecutor General is providing procedural oversight in dozens of criminal proceedings investigating grave and especially grave crimes committed by employees of NABU and SAPO [the Specialised Anti-Сorruption Prosecutor's Office]."

Celeste Barber returns to theatre for first time in 20 years in The Book of Liz
Comedian Celeste Barber is set to return to theatre for the first time in 20 years in "kooky" comedy play The Book of Liz.
While her last stage role was in 2006, the comedian and actor, known for Wellmania and Colin from Accounts, told ABC Arts in 2023 working at Sydney Theatre Company (STC) was "on the bucket list".
As the company launches its 2027 season, she says starring in The Book of Liz is "a dream come true".
It's a full-circle moment for Barber, who worked at the theatre's restaurant back in 2003, the year after she finished drama school.
She recalls her then-roommate landing a role alongside Hugo Weaving in Tom Stoppard's The Real Thing that year.
"I was cleaning cutlery at the end of the shift and looking down the corridor at them in the green room together running lines," she says.
"I remember thinking, as I scrubbed crusty pasta off a fork, 'One day that will be me'. And now it's happening."
Premiering Off-Broadway in 2001, The Book of Liz is a play by American siblings Amy and David Sedaris — Amy best known for Bojack Horseman and surreal sketch show At Home with Amy Sedaris, and David for his comic essays.
Barber will play the relentlessly positive Sister Elizabeth Donderstock, who decides to leave her cloistered community after she's forced to give up her treasured cheese ball recipe.
She soon finds a job as a waitress at a family-run restaurant, with help from a bizarrely Cockney-accented Ukrainian couple. They're just two of the eccentrics Liz encounters as she adjusts to life away from her community.
It was the opportunity to work on a play by the Sedaris siblings, who write together as "The Talent Family", that lured Barber back to the stage.
"I loved [The Book of Liz] as soon as I read it," Barber says. "It made me laugh.
"I feel like a Sedaris play about an Amish cheese ball maker who is on a quest to find herself is exactly what the world needs: something funny, with heart."
Stepping away from theatre for 20 years wasn't deliberate, the comedian adds, but a "pivot" because she "couldn't book a job or even get an audition".
To play Liz, Barber plans to draw on the skills in character comedy she's finessed over more than a decade as a stand-up, but is most excited by the chance to work collaboratively.
"My favourite part of performing is diving in and picking apart a character and finding out what makes them tick, what makes them laugh, cry, fart, scream," she says.
"That's where the juice is.
"I plan on approaching this play in the way I approach most things: panicked. Then as soon I step into the rehearsal room I'll take on the form of a human sponge.
"I love rehearsal rooms; I love working and performing with other people. I love actors and I love notes!"
The Book of Liz is one of 13 plays in STC's 2027 season, which also includes a Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries play, and an adaptation of Jenny Hocking's The Palace Letters, starring Georgie Parker (Dalliance), about efforts to unseal papers about Gough Whitlam's dismissal in 1975.
The season is artistic director Mitchell Butel's second, with his leadership steering the company to its first surplus — of $765,759 — since 2022.
That success is expected to continue, with ticket sales for 2026 already surpassing last year, thanks to new John Farnham musical Whispering Jack and An Iliad, starring David Wenham.
"There's always work to do and we have massive targets to keep the door open," Butel says.
"But hard as it is to produce theatre that's commercially successful, it's a great privilege and honour to do it, and we should celebrate it."
Companies working together
An Iliad will tour Melbourne in 2027, with more cities expected to be announced. It's just one example of STC collaborating with theatre companies, festivals and venues across Australia in 2027 to extend the life spans of local productions.
In another modern adaptation of an ancient Greek text, Oedipus becomes a political thriller set on election night. It will star Richard Roxburgh and Heather Mitchell and will head to Adelaide Festival.
Keeping with the theme of reinterpreting classic plays, STC also co-produces John Proctor Is the Villain, with Melbourne Theatre Company (MTC), which interrogates Arthur Miller's The Crucible through the eyes of high school students.
In one of the season's literary adaptations, STC and State Theatre Company South Australia (STCSA) will collaborate on The Bookbinder of Jericho, about twin sisters working in a bindery during WWI, from the same team behind the sell-out success of The Dictionary of Lost Words.
Logan St, about an unlikely friendship between an Aboriginal woman and an Afghan cameleer in Adelaide in the 1940s, transfers from STCSA.
Co-produced by STC, Queensland Theatre Company (QTC) and Jones Theatrical Group, Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair is set on a boat and takes as its starting point one of the late Kerry Greenwood's novels not previously adapted for TV.
English writer Jack Thorne's reinterpretation of A Christmas Carol, which has played at Melbourne's Comedy Theatre every year since 2022, will come to Sydney for the first time, starring Tim Minchin in his first play since 2013.
Butel says collaborations across Australian theatre like these are "really important".
"Because you're sharing costs, there's suddenly an ability to up cast sizes," he says.
"Bookbinder's a cast of eight, John Proctor is a cast of nine. Oedipus is a cast of 11, A Christmas Carol is a cast of 18. They're pretty large-scale shows for us."
A theatre for actors
Cast size isn't the only thing determining the scale of a production: The now-international "cine-theatre" hit The Picture of Dorian Gray will return to Australia, with Nikki Shiels (Colin from Accounts) playing all 26 characters.
It's not Shiels's first time in the role, having been the alternate performer, or understudy, for the Australian tour since 2022. Next year she'll be taking over full-time from Eryn Jean Norvill, who originated the production.
Norvill will star in a one-woman show of her own as part of STC's 2027 season: Vanya, a new adaptation of Russian playwright Anton Chekhov's play, first brought to the stage by Andrew Scott (Fleabag).
Vanya is another example, along with The Book of Liz, of how Butel likes to program a season.
"I'm finding actors I love and want to be on our stage and asking 'What's going to float your boat?" Butel says.
That approach also led to Andrea Dimitriades (ABC TV's Return to Paradise) starring in the Australian premiere of Gina Gionfriddo's Becky Shaw, loosely based on William Thackeray's Victorian satire Vanity Fair.
Co-starring in Becky Shaw is Lincoln Younes (Last King of the Cross), in his first theatre role in a decade. He's just one screen star coming to STC, alongside Erik Thomson (Packed to the Rafters) in West End hit The Fifth Step and Gold Logie winner Lynne McGranger (Home and Away) and Annette Shun Wah in Disapol Savetsila's road trip comedy Amah and Nanna.
Developed by Bathurst's Arbour Theatre Company, co-founded by Savetsila in 2020, Amah and Nanna was the winner of this year's Patrick White Award. Earlier play readings were hosted at Bathurst Memorial Entertainment Centre.
"It actually shows the benefit of funding regional arts centres to do this kind of work, because they have the ability to workshop stories that are of the regions," Butel says.
STC's 2027 season feels notable for its sheer breadth, which might account for the company's success since Butel took the reins.
"We're often accused of being elitist … but it's not all high art," he says.
"For every Uncle Vanya, there's also this kooky, Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt-like fall into the rabbit hole [like The Book of Liz].
"Some people like KFC; some people like caviar. We'll provide it all for you."

Kravchenko alleged that NABU Director Kryvonos had a sham paternity arrangement for the sake of an amnesty

2026-09-14

Kravchenko alleged that NABU Director Kryvonos had a sham paternity arrangement for the sake of an amnesty
Kyiv • UNN
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko stated that Semen Kryvonos established paternity over someone else’s child in order to obtain an amnesty in a 2009 case.
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko has made public the first episode of the case underpinning the suspicion against NABU Director Semen Kryvonos. It concerns obtaining an amnesty in a 2009 criminal case by registering paternity of someone else’s child. He reported this on his Telegram channel, UNN reports.
The court established the fact of a crime in Semen Kryvonos’s actions. But no punishment followed: he fictitiously adopted a child and unlawfully obtained grounds for exemption from liability—amnesty. Later, with this past, he successfully passed a competition involving international experts and headed NABU. Integrity as it is
In particular, according to Kravchenko, in 2009 Semen Kryvonos was accused of a crime against citizens’ electoral rights.
In June 2009, the Holosiivskyi District Court of Kyiv was hearing criminal case No. 1-519/09 against Semen Yuriiovych Kryvonos, charged with committing a crime under Part 3 of Article 157 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. Semen Kryvonos was accused of intentionally committing a crime against citizens’ electoral rights while acting in prior collusion with a group of persons
In order to obtain grounds for amnesty, he allegedly organized a criminal scheme involving the registration of paternity of another woman’s child.
This concerned creating an artificial ground that would give him the right to qualify for amnesty. At that time, one such statutory ground was having a minor child. For this purpose, Semen Kryvonos involved an accomplice, who found him an unmarried woman with a child whose birth registration book listed the father’s details at the mother’s direction
According to the investigation, the suspect and his accomplice persuaded the woman to submit an application together with Kryvonos acknowledging him as the child’s father. After that, he received a certificate naming him as the father.
For this purpose, the perpetrators devised a cover story that Semen Kryvonos had allegedly worked abroad and that his immediate employer had asked him to provide documents confirming that he had a dependent child. The essence of the unlawful request was to submit to the civil registry offices a joint application by the woman (the child’s mother) and Semen Kryvonos recognizing Semen Kryvonos’s paternity of the child, followed by the issuance of a forged birth certificate naming Semen Kryvonos as the child’s father. The criminal plan was subsequently carried out
At the same time, the investigation established that after legally acquiring paternity of someone else’s child, Kryvonos had no intention whatsoever of performing parental duties.
Thus, according to the available data, after receiving the document, Kryvonos filed a motion with the court seeking amnesty, citing the fact that he had a minor child dependent on him.
Subsequently, on June 25, 2009, the presiding judge of the Holosiivskyi District Court of Kyiv, having been misled, based on the motion filed by Semen Kryvonos and following the court’s examination of the forged birth certificate attached to it, issued a ruling whereby Semen Kryvonos was groundlessly exempted from criminal liability due to the application of the Law of Ukraine "On Amnesty". The criminal case against Semen Kryvonos for bribing students was also closed
In addition, according to the available data, after carrying out the aforementioned criminal intent and avoiding criminal liability, in May 2018 Semen Kryvonos again applied to the Holosiivskyi District Court, this time with a claim to remove the information identifying him as the father.
The suspect in the criminal act attached to the statement of claim a DNA test report stating that the probability of Semen Kryvonos’s paternity was 0.00%
We remind you
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko stated that he had signed a notice of suspicion for NABU Director Semen Kryvonos, whom he suspects of forging official documents and other offenses. He also reported another notice of suspicion concerning a person close to the head of the SAPO.

Finland has decided to join France’s nuclear deterrence initiative which is significant for security in Europe, the Nordic country's defense ministry said Monday.
"The initiative is a form of bilateral cooperation between Finland and France," the ministry said in a statement, mentioning that both countries have been discussing the initiative both at the highest political level and at the level of officials.
In March 2026, French President Emmanuel Macron launched an initiative on the European dimension of France’s nuclear deterrence. Eight countries were then announced having joined the initiative, followed by Norway at a later stage.
"The French initiative will strengthen Europe’s increasingly active approach to defence. Its objective is to reinforce security and deterrence across Europe," said Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen.
Stressing that the French initiative does not replace or overlap with NATO’s nuclear deterrence, the statement recalled that NATO’s nuclear deterrence is based on nuclear-sharing arrangements and relies on the US' extended deterrent.
"It is ultimately the supreme guarantee of the security of the Alliance," it added.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb also confirmed that the initiative does not replace NATO's deterrence, adding that Finland's primary starting point is to act as part of NATO and the EU.
"Finland does not intend to station nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime," he said.
